Upon the Administrator's finding, without a hearing, of probable cause to believe that the labeling of a vitamin product distributed by the appellee in interstate commerce was "misleading to the injury or damage of the purchaser or consumer," eleven seizures of the product were made and as many libel suits instituted over a four-month period. There was no claim that the product was harmful or dangerous to health. Appellee brought suit in the Federal District Court to have the multiple seizure provision of _ 304 (a) declared unconstitutional and to dismiss all except the first libel suit.

A man who took part in a street fight was accused of attempted murder and was tried in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois. Well in advance of trial, the prosecutor filed a discovery motion requesting a list of defense witnesses. On the first day of trial, defense counsel was allowed to amend his "answer to discovery" by adding the names of two eyewitnesses, neither of whom was called to testify. On the second day of trial, after the prosecution's principal witnesses had completed their testimony, defense counsel made an oral motion to amend his answer to discovery to include two additional witnesses. In support of the motion, counsel represented that he had just been informed about these witnesses and that they had probably seen the entire incident in question. In response to the court's inquiry, counsel acknowledged that the accused had previously told him about the two additional witnesses, but said that the accused had not been able to locate the second one. On the next day, the second witness appeared in court with defense counsel, who was permitted to make an offer of proof in the form of the second witness' testimony outside the presence of the jury. It developed that this witness (1) had not seen the incident itself, (2) had first met the accused more than 2 years after the incident, and (3) had been visited by defense counsel at his home during the week before the trial began. The trial judge, finding that the discovery rules had been violated and that the witness' veracity was doubtful, precluded the witness' testimony as a sanction for the discovery violation. The accused was convicted, and the Illinois Appellate Court, First District, affirmed, holding that the trial court had been within its discretion in refusing to allow the witness to testify (141 Ill App 3d 839, 96 Ill Dec 189, 491 NE2d 3). Upon filing a petition for rehearing in the Appellate Court, the accused for the first time specifically articulated his claim as based on the right of a criminal defendant, under the Federal Constitution's Sixth Amendment, to have compulsory process for obtaining witnesses in his or her favor. The Illinois Supreme Court denied leave to appeal.

A marriage was annulled by the Supreme Court of Vermont on the ground that the woman, at the time of the marriage, was the lawful wife of a third person, although she had, prior to the marriage, obtained a Florida divorce decree against the third person. This decree was held invalid by the Vermont Court on the ground that the findings did not show either of the criteria which under Williams v. North Carolina, 325 US 226, 89 L ed 1577, 65 S Ct 1092, 157 ALR 1366, preclude an attack upon the divorce decree of a sister state, namely, appearance by the defendant or service of process upon him in the state granting the divorce. However, the record did not contain the Florida decree nor any stipulation or evidence showing the material circumstances under which it had been rendered.

A Mississippi jury convicted petitioner Brett Jones of murder for killing his grandfather. Jones was 15 years old when he committed the crime. Under Mississippi law at the time, murder carried a mandatory sentence of life without parole. The trial judge duly imposed that sentence, which was affirmed on direct appeal. This Court subsequently decided Miller v. Alabama, 567 U. S. 460, which held that the Eighth Amendment permits a life-without-parole sentence for a defendant who committed a homicide when he or she was under 18, but only if the sentence is not mandatory and the sentencer therefore has discretion to impose a lesser punishment. In the wake of that decision, the Mississippi Supreme Court ordered that Jones be resentenced in accordance with Miller. At the resentencing, the sentencing judge acknowledged that he had discretion under Miller to impose a sentence less than life without parole. The judge determined, however, that life without parole remained the appropriate sentence for Jones. Jones again appealed his sentence, citing both Miller and the then-recently decided case of Montgomery v. Louisiana, 577 U. S. 190, which held that Miller applied retroactively on collateral review. Jones contended that, under Miller and Montgomery, a sentencer must make a separate factual finding that a murderer under 18 is permanently incorrigible before sentencing the offender to life without parole. The Mississippi Court of Appeals rejected Jones‚Äôs argument.

The administrator of the estate of Howard Hughes filed a statutory interpleader action under 28 USCS 1335 in the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas, asserting that the officials of two states (California and Texas) were seeking to tax the estate on the basis of inconsistent claims that each state was Hughes' domicile at death. The District Court entered a temporary restraining order prohibiting the California and Texas officials from pursuing domicile-based inheritance tax claims in any other forum, including their own state courts. The District Court then dismissed the action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction for failure to satisfy the requirement of 28 USCS 1335 that there be diversity of citizenship between at least two adverse claimants. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed the order of dismissal, holding that the requisite diversity was present, and rejecting the states' claim that although the suit was nominally against state officials, it was in effect a suit against two states barred by the Eleventh Amendment (629 F2d 397).

By the Commodity Exchange Act, the United States has not so occupied and preempted the field of regulation of boards of trade designated "contract markets" as to deprive the states of authority to regulate trading in futures, except to the extent that the state regulations may conflict with the federal regulations.

In the present action brought in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas under the Jones Act, the principal issue was whether, in view of the nature of the work performed at the time of injury, the plaintiff was a seaman or an offshore drilling employee. At trial before a jury, the District Court admitted evidence, over plaintiff's objection, that he had accepted compensation benefits under the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act, as applied through the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed a judgment adverse to the plaintiff, holding that it was error to have admitted the evidence of these compensation benefits, but finding--with one judge dissenting--the error harmless, in view of the fact that the jury, having decided the question of status adversely to plaintiff, never reached the issue of damages. (315 F2d 660.)

In a suit brought by a licensor of a patent in a state court for royalties under a licensing agreement, the licensee challenged the validity of the patent, a price-fixing covenant in the agreement, and the licensor's exercise of its monopoly, and counterclaimed for refund of royalties already paid and for damages resulting from the restraint imposed on him by the licensing agreement. The trial court gave judgment for the licensor.

Section 242(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 USCS 1252(a)) authorizes the Attorney General of the United States to arrest excludible aliens and, pending a determination of their deportability, either to hold them in custody or to release them on a bond containing conditions prescribed by the Attorney General. Several individuals and organizations filed suit against the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) alleging that 8 CFR 103.6(a)(2)(ii)--an INS regulation which is entitled Condition against unauthorized employment and requires that a condition barring employment be included in an excludible alien's release bond issued pending a deportability determination, unless the District Director for the INS determines that employment is appropriate--was facially invalid. After the United States District Court for the Central District of California entered a nationwide preliminary injunction against enforcement of the regulation, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed in part (743 F2d 1365), the District Court, on remand, (1) granted summary judgment for the individuals and organizations on the ground that the regulation was beyond the Attorney General's authority, and (2) certified a class consisting of everyone who had been or might be denied the right to work pursuant to the regulation. After the Court of Appeals again affirmed (791 F2d 1351), and the Supreme Court of the United States vacated the Court of Appeals' judgment and remanded for further consideration (481 US 1009, 95 L Ed 2d 489, 107 S Ct 1881), the District Court held that the regulation was invalid as exceeding the Attorney General's authority under 1252(a). The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that under the statute, (1) a bond had to relate either to securing an alien's appearance at a hearing or to protecting the nation against danger from active subversives, and (2) bond conditions could be imposed on only an individualized basis (913 F2d 1350).

A majority of the stock of a textile manufacturing company was owned by a textile selling house, which was controlled by the manufacturing company's president and his family and which operated 17 textile manufacturers and marketed the products manufactured in 27 different mills. During a union organizational campaign, the manufacturing company threatened to close its one mill if the union won a representation election. Shortly after the union won the election, the mill ceased operations, all its employees were discharged, and all of its machinery and equipment was sold piecemeal at auction. The union filed unfair labor practice charges with the National Labor Relations Board, which found that the company had been closed because of the antiunion animus of its president and that the closing constituted a violation of 8(a)(3) of the National Labor Relations Act, prohibiting discrimination by an employer to discourage union membership. (139 NLRB 241.) The Board also found that the company was part of a single integrated employer group controlled by its president's family through the selling house, and that the selling house could be held liable for the company's unfair labor practice. Alternatively, the Board found that since the company was a part of the selling house's enterprise, the selling house had violated the Act by closing part of its business for a discriminatory purpose. The Board ordered backpay for all of the company's employees until they obtained substantially equivalent work or were put on preferential hiring lists at the selling house's other mills, and the selling house was ordered to bargain with the union in regard to details of compliance with the order. On review, the Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit set aside the Board's order, holding that even if the selling house had the status of a single employer, an employer has the absolute right to close out a part or all of its business regardless of antiunion motives. (325 F2d 682.)

Upon remand by the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, the Federal Maritime Commission concluded that a carrier should pay reparations to the petitioner, a banana shipper, because the carrier, in violation of the Shipping Act, had performed an exclusive carrying contract with another banana shipper and had refused to contract with the petitioner for any carrying space. (7 FMC 635.) On consolidated appeals to the Court of Appeals, the shipper requested that the amount of reparations awarded be increased, and the carrier requested that the award be set aside. The Court of Appeals set aside the award, holding that in view of the substantial evidence showing that it would be inequitable to assess damages against the carrier in favor of the petitioner, the Commission had abused its discretion in granting any award. (119 App DC 345, 342 F2d 924.)
Petition for writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit denied.

The petitioners, a group of college students, organized what they called a "local chapter" of Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), and filed a request for official recognition as a campus organization. Following a hearing at which representatives of the group stated that they would not affiliate with the national SDS and that the group would remain "completely independent," the Student Affairs Committee of the college approved the application and recommended to the college president that the organization be accorded official recognition, the effect of which would have permitted the group to place announcements regarding meetings, rallies, or other activities in the student newspaper, to use various college bulletin boards, and to use campus facilities for holding meetings. However, the college president rejected the application, saying that the organization's philosophy was antithetical to the school's policies, and that the group's independence from the national SDS was doubtful. Thereafter, the petitioners filed suit in the United States District Court for the District of Connecticut, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief against the college's president, other administrators, and trustees, on the ground that their First Amendment rights of expression and association had been denied. Concluding that the college president had impermissibly based his decision on conclusions drawn from materials outside the record, the District Court ordered the college administration to hold another hearing to clarify several ambiguities surrounding the president's decision. The hearing was held, during which the petitioners, though reaffirming that they would have no connection whatsoever with the national SDS, equivocated when asked whether they might respond to "issues of violence" in the same manner as other SDS chapters had responded, and whether they could envision situations where they might advocate interrupting classes. Upon reviewing the hearing transcript and exhibits, the president reaffirmed his prior decision to reject the application, stating that the group would be a disruptive influence at the college and that recognition would be contrary to the orderly process of change on the campus. The case was subsequently returned to the District Court, where it was ordered dismissed (319 F Supp 113). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed on the theory that the petitioners had failed to avail themselves of the due process accorded them by the hearings and the court proceedings, and had failed to meet their burden of complying with the prevailing standards at the college for recognition of "campus organizations" (445 F2d 1122).

A husband and wife who were members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints had two sons who were called to service as full-time, unpaid missionaries for the Church. After the Church informed each son of the estimated amount of money that would be needed to support his service, the parents transferred funds to the personal checking account of each son. Each son was the sole authorized signatory of his account. Operating under Church guidelines, which required such funds to be spent for only missionary work and forbade various leisure or personal activities, the sons used the transferred funds primarily to pay for rent, food, transportation, and personal needs while on their missions. Although the guidelines did not require the sons to obtain advance approval of each expenditure they made from their checking accounts, the sons submitted weekly reports of their total expenses for the week and month to date. In 1984, the parents filed an amended federal income tax return for the years 1980 and 1981, in which return they claimed as deductible charitable contributions the amounts paid to the sons during the missionary service. The Internal Revenue Service disallowed the claims in 1985, and the parents filed suit against the United States in the United States District Court for the District of Idaho for refund of the claimed amounts pursuant to 170 of the Internal Revenue Code (26 USCS 170), which allows a deduction for a charitable contribution or gift "to or for the use of" a qualified organization. In a second set of amended tax returns, filed in 1986, the parents limited their claimed charitable deductions to the amounts that had been indicated by the Church. The District Court, granting summary judgment to the United States, held that (1) the payments were not made "for the use of" the Church within the meaning of 26 USCS 170, and (2) the payments did not qualify as "reasonable expenditures" incurred while providing services to the Church, so as to be deductible under Treas Reg 1.170A-1(g) ( 26 CFR 1.170A-1(g)), which provides that unreimbursed expenditures made incident to the rendition of services to an organization, contributions to which are deductible, may constitute a deductible contribution under 26 USCS 170 (664 F Supp 468). The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, affirming on appeal, held that (1) the funds in question were not deductible under 26 USCS 170, as the Church lacked actual control over the disposition of the funds, and (2) 26 CFR 1.170A-1(g) did not apply to the parents, as the regulation permits a deduction for unreimbursed expenses by only the taxpayer who performed the charitable service (861 F2d 558).

Witnesses appearing before the Ohio Un-American Activities Commission refused to answer certain questions asked them, claiming their privilege against self-incrimination. In prosecutions in the Ohio Courts of Common Pleas of Franklin and Hamilton counties, the witnesses were convicted of violating Ohio statutes providing that a failure to answer as a witness, when lawfully required, may be punished as for a contempt, and providing for the punishment of those, summoned before a legislative committee, who refuse to answer a question pertinent to the matter under inquiry. The convictions were affirmed by the Ohio Courts of Appeals for Franklin and Hamilton Counties, and by the Supreme Court of Ohio, which held that the witnesses were presumed to know that an Ohio immunity statute deprived them of the protection of the privilege and that therefore they committed an offense by not answering the questions as to which they had asserted the privilege, notwithstanding that the legislative commission had indicated clearly its opinion that the privilege was available to them. (164 Ohio St 529, 58 Ohio Ops 411, 133 NE2d 104). On appeal to the Supreme Court, the state court's judgments were vacated and the causes remanded for reconsideration (see 354 US 929, 1 L ed 2d 1535, 77 S Ct 1403), and the remand resulted in a reaffirmance of the prior judgments without discussion. (167 Ohio St 295, 4 Ohio Ops 2d 411, 147 NE2d 847.)

At a statutory rape trial in a Texas state criminal court, the accused's four prior convictions were used to impeach his credibility as a witness. He was convicted and sentenced to a 50-year prison term. Thereafter, he brought a habeas corpus proceeding in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas, alleging that the prior convictions were constitutionally invalid because he was denied the assistance of counsel. His sworn testimony at the habeas corpus hearing was that at the time of the prior convictions, he was unrepresented by counsel, could not afford to hire counsel, and was not advised of his right to counsel. The District Court denied relief, declaring that it placed little or no credence in his testimony and that the question did not rise to constitutional stature. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed on the ground that no issue of constitutional proportions required reversal (440 F2d 934).

Registration and barratry statutes enacted by the Virginia legislature as part of its general plan of massive resistance to the integration of schools of the state were challenged by the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia as invalid under the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court, finding the statutes free from ambiguity, declared them unconstitutional and enjoined their enforcement. (159 F Supp 503.)

The False Claims Act (FCA) imposes civil liability on any person who presents false or fraudulent claims for payment to the Federal Government. See 31 U. S. C. ¬ß¬ß3729‚Äì3733. The statute is unusual in authorizing private parties (known as relators) to sue on the Government‚Äôs behalf. Those suits‚Äîqui tam actions‚Äîare ‚Äúbrought in the name of the Government.‚Äù ¬ß3730(b)(1). And the injury they assert is to the Government alone. But in one sense, a qui tam suit is ‚Äúfor‚Äù the relator as well as the Government: If the action leads to a recovery, the relator may receive up to 30% of the total. ¬ß¬ß3730(b)(1), (d)(1)‚Äì(2). Because a relator is no ordinary plaintiff, he is subject to special restrictions. He must file his complaint under seal and serve a copy and supporting evidence on the Government. See ¬ß3730(b)(2). The Government then has 60 days (often extended for ‚Äúgood cause‚Äù) to decide whether to ‚Äúintervene and proceed with the action.‚Äù ¬ß¬ß3730(b)(2)‚Äì(3). If the Government elects to intervene during that so-called seal period, the action ‚Äúshall be conducted by the Government‚Äù; otherwise, the relator gets ‚Äúthe right to conduct the action.‚Äù ¬ß¬ß3730(b)(4)(A)‚Äì(B). But even if the Government passes on intervention, it remains a ‚Äúreal party in interest,‚Äù United States ex rel. Eisenstein v. City of New York, 556 U. S. 928, 930, and it retains continuing rights. Most relevant here, the Government can intervene after the seal period ends, so long as it shows good cause to do so. See ¬ß3730(c)(3). In this case, the relator‚Äîpetitioner Jesse Polansky‚Äîfiled a qui tam action alleging that respondent Executive Health Resources helped hospitals overbill Medicare. The Government declined to intervene during the seal period, and the case spent years in discovery. Eventu-ally, the Government decided that the varied burdens of the suit outweighed its potential value, so it filed a motion under ¬ß3730(c)(2)(A) (Subparagraph (2)(A) for short), which provides that ‚Äú[t]he Government may dismiss the action notwithstanding the objections of the [relator],‚Äù so long as the relator received notice and an opportunity for a hearing. The District Court granted the request, finding that the Government had thoroughly investigated the costs and benefits and come to a valid conclusion. The Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed after considering two legal questions. First, does the Government have authority to dismiss an action under Subparagraph (2)(A) if it declined to intervene during the seal period? The Court of Appeals held that the Government has that power so long as it intervened sometime later. And the court found that the Government had satisfied that condition here. Second, what standard should a district court use in ruling on a Subparagraph (2)(A) motion? The Court of Appeals held that the proper standard comes from Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)‚Äîthe rule governing voluntary dismissals in ordinary civil litigation. And here, the Third Circuit ruled, the District Court had not abused its discretion in granting the Government‚Äôs motion.

Damages resulting from the picketing of a foreign ship, operated entirely by foreign seamen under foreign articles, while the vessel was temporarily in an American port in Oregon, were awarded against American unions participating in the picketing by the United States District Court for the District of Oregon; the District Court rejected the defendants' contention that it lacked jurisdiction because the Labor Management Relations Act of 1947 had pre-empted the field, holding that the act does not cover a dispute between a foreign ship and its foreign crew.

In 1975, inmates at a state correctional facility brought a class action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, which eventually (1) held that living conditions at the facility violated the Federal Constitution's Eighth Amendment prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment clause, and (2) ordered ongoing injunctive relief that remained in effect, with modifications, over the next 20 years. In 1996, Congress enacted the Prison Litigation Reform Act (including 18 USCS 3626), which (1) in 3626(a)(1), barred the issuance of new prospective relief that was not found to be narrowly drawn and the least intrusive means possible to correct the violations of federal rights; (2) in 3626(b)(2), allowed defendants or intervenors to seek modification or termination of pre-existing prospective relief, where such findings had not been made; (3) in 3626(b)(3), barred termination of relief if a court subsequently made such findings; and (4) in 3626(e)(2), provided that any motion for modification or termination "shall" operate as a stay from the 30th day after the filing of the motion until the date the court enters a final order ruling on the motion, with entry of the stay postponable up to 60 days for good cause shown. The state subsequently filed a motion to terminate the prospective relief ordered in the 1975 action, but the District Court granted a motion by prisoners to enjoin the operation of 3626(e)(2)'s automatic stay. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, in affirming that injunction, expressed the view that (1) 3626(e)(2) was to be construed to bar courts from exercising their equitable powers to enjoin operation of the automatic stay; but (2) the statute, as so construed, violated constitutional principles of separation of powers, by directly suspending a court order (178 F3d 437).

The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey operated airport terminals that were generally accessible to the public and that contained various commercial establishments such as restaurants, snack stands, bars, newsstands, and stores of various types. The Port Authority adopted a regulation forbidding, among other things, the repetitive sale or distribution of flyers, brochures, pamphlets, books, or any other printed or written material within such terminals. However, such activities were permitted by the Port Authority in the sidewalk areas outside the terminals. A religious corporation, whose members wished to perform within the terminals a ritual involving the public distribution of religious literature, brought suit against the Port Authority's police superintendent in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and sought declaratory and injunctive relief under 42 USCS 1983 on the ground that the regulation allegedly deprived the corporation of rights guaranteed under the Federal Constitution's First Amendment. The District Court, granting the corporation summary judgment, held that (1) under the "traditional public forum" doctrine, the terminals were akin to public streets, (2) thus, the Port Authority's regulation could be sustained only if the regulation was narrowly tailored to support a compelling state interest, and (3) the blanket prohibition on distribution of literature had not been shown to constitute such narrow tailoring (721 F Supp 572). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, affirming in pertinent part on appeal, (1) declined to hold that the terminals were public forums for purposes of the First Amendment's free speech guarantee, but (2) held that the Port Authority was required to provide reasonable access to the terminals for the distribution of literature (925 F2d 576).

In a companion case to Holland v. United States, supra, p 150, the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Clark, J., unanimously affirmed a taxpayer's conviction of evasion of federal income taxes, in a case in which the prosecution relied upon the net worth theory. The evidence, indicating that the taxpayer was in relatively poor financial condition over a period of twenty-two years prior to the date as of which the net worth theory was applied, and that five years before that date he had stated that his assets amounted to $ 9,200, was held to support a jury finding that the taxpayer had no substantial cash on hand at the time his opening net worth was determined.

The State of Oregon instituted an action in the Circuit Court of Benton County, Oregon, against an Oregon corporation to settle the ownership of certain lands underlying the Willamette River, which is a navigable river not forming an interstate boundary. One portion of the disputed lands had been within the riverbed since Oregon's admission into the Union, whereas another portion of the lands was not a part of the riverbed at such time, but subsequently became part of the riverbed as the result of a major flood. As to the latter portion of the disputed lands, the trial court found that avulsion, rather than accretion, had caused the change in the river's channel, and that therefore title to the lands remained in the defendant corporation as the original owner of the lands before they became riverbed. As to the other portion of the disputed lands, the trial court found that the state had acquired sovereign title to the lands upon admission into the Union, and had not conveyed such title. The Oregon Court of Appeals affirmed, concluding that it was required to apply federal common law in view of the United States Supreme Court's intervening decision in Bonelli Cattle Co. v Arizona (1973) 414 US 313, 38 L Ed 2d 526, 94 S Ct 517, which held that under the equal footing doctrine--whereby new states, upon their admission to the Union, acquired title to the lands underlying navigable waters within their boundaries--the effect of a movement of a river upon title to the riverbed was to be resolved under federal common law, rather than under state law. The Supreme Court of Oregon affirmed, with modifications as to a factual question concerning the length of a certain channel of the river (272 Or 545, 536 P2d 517; 272 Or 550, 538 P2d 70).

In 2015, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) promulgated the Clean Power Plan rule, which addressed carbon dioxide emissions from existing coal- and natural-gas-fired power plants. For authority, the Agency cited Section 111 of the Clean Air Act, which, although known as the New Source Performance Standards program, also authorizes regulation of certain pollutants from existing sources under Section 111(d). 42 U. S. C. ¬ß7411(d). Prior to the Clean Power Plan, EPA had used Section 111(d) only a handful of times since its enactment in 1970. Under that provision, although the States set the actual enforceable rules governing existing sources (such as power plants), EPA determines the emissions limit with which they will have to comply. The Agency derives that limit by determining the ‚Äúbest system of emission reduction . . . that has been adequately demonstrated,‚Äù or the BSER, for the kind of existing source at issue. ¬ß7411(a)(1). The limit then reflects the amount of pollution reduction ‚Äúachievable through the application of‚Äù that system. Ibid. In the Clean Power Plan, EPA determined that the BSER for existing coal and natural gas plants included three types of measures, which the Agency called ‚Äúbuilding blocks.‚Äù 80 Fed. Reg. 64667. The first building block was ‚Äúheat rate improvements‚Äù at coal-fired plants‚Äîessentially practices such plants could undertake to burn coal more cleanly. Id., at 64727. This sort of source-specific, efficiencyimproving measure was similar in kind to those that EPA had previously identified as the BSER in other Section 111 rules. Building blocks two and three were quite different, as both involved what EPA called ‚Äúgeneration shifting‚Äù at the grid level‚Äîi.e., a shift in electricity production from higher-emitting to lower-emitting producers. Building block two was a shift in generation from existing coalfired power plants, which would make less power, to natural-gas-fired plants, which would make more. Ibid. This would reduce carbon dioxide emissions because natural gas plants produce less carbon dioxide per unit of electricity generated than coal plants. Building block three worked like building block two, except that the shift was from both coal and gas plants to renewables, mostly wind and solar. Id., at 64729, 64748. The Agency explained that, to implement the needed shift in generation to cleaner sources, an operator could reduce the regulated plant‚Äôs own production of electricity, build or invest in a new or existing natural gas plant, wind farm, or solar installation, or purchase emission allowances or credits as part of a cap-and-trade regime. Id., at 64731‚Äì64732. Taking any of these steps would implement a sectorwide shift in electricity production from coal to natural gas and renewables. Id., at 64731. Having decided that the BSER was one that would reduce carbon pollution mostly by moving production to cleaner sources, EPA then set about determining ‚Äúthe degree of emission limitation achievable through the application‚Äù of that system. ¬ß7411(a)(1). The Agency recognized that, in translating the BSER into an operational emissions limit, it could choose whether to require anything from a little generation shifting to a great deal. It settled on what it regarded as a ‚Äúreasonable‚Äù amount of shift, which it based on modeling how much more electricity both natural gas and renewable sources could supply without causing undue cost increases or reducing the overall power supply. Id., at 64797‚Äì64811. The Agency ultimately projected, for instance, that it would be feasible to have coal provide 27% of national electricity generation by 2030, down from 38% in 2014. From these projected changes, EPA determined the applicable emissions performance rates, which were so strict that no existing coal plant would have been able to achieve them without engaging in one of the three means of generation shifting. The Government projected that the rule would impose billions in compliance costs, raise retail electricity prices, require the retirement of dozens of coal plants, and eliminate tens of thousands of jobs. This Court stayed the Clean Power Plan in 2016, preventing the rule from taking effect. It was later repealed after a change in Presidential administrations. Specifically, in 2019, EPA found that the Clean Power Plan had exceeded the Agency‚Äôs statutory authority under Section 111(d), which it interpreted to ‚Äúlimit[ ] the BSER to those systems that can be put into operation at a building, structure, facility, or installation.‚Äù 84 Fed. Reg. 32524. EPA explained that the Clean Power Plan, rather than setting the standard ‚Äúbased on the application of equipment and practices at the level of an individual facility,‚Äù had instead based it on ‚Äúa shift in the energy generation mix at the grid level,‚Äù id., at 32523. The Agency determined that the interpretive question raised by the Clean Power Plan fell under the major questions doctrine. Under that doctrine, it determined, a clear statement is necessary for a court to conclude that Congress intended to delegate authority ‚Äúof this breadth to regulate a fundamental sector of the economy.‚Äù Id., at 32529. It found none. The Agency replaced the Clean Power Plan by promulgating a different Section 111(d) regulation, known as the Affordable Clean Energy (ACE) rule. Id., at 32532. In that rule, EPA determined that the BSER would be akin to building block one of the Clean Power Plan: a combination of equipment upgrades and operating practices that would improve facilities‚Äô heat rates. Id., at 32522, 32537. A number of States and private parties filed petitions for review in the D. C. Circuit, challenging EPA‚Äôs repeal of the Clean Power Plan and its enactment of the replacement ACE rule. The Court of Appeals consolidated the cases and held that EPA‚Äôs ‚Äúrepeal of the Clean Power Plan rested critically on a mistaken reading of the Clean Air Act‚Äù‚Äî namely, that generation shifting cannot be a ‚Äúsystem of emission reduction‚Äù under Section 111. 985 F. 3d 914, 995. The court vacated the Agency‚Äôs repeal of the Clean Power Plan and remanded to the Agency for further consideration. It also vacated and remanded the ACE rule for the same reason. The court‚Äôs decision was followed by another change in Presidential administrations, and EPA moved the court to partially stay its mandate as to the Clean Power Plan while the Agency considered whether to promulgate a new Section 111(d) rule. No party opposed the motion, and the Court of Appeals agreed to stay its vacatur of the Agency‚Äôs repeal of the Clean Power Plan.

Subject to certain exemptions, the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (5 USCS 552) generally requires the disclosure of federal agency records upon request. At the same time, under Rule 32(c) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which outlines the requirements for the preparation and disclosure of a presentence investigation report on a criminal defendant who has been adjudged guilty, (1) Rule 32(c)(3)(A) generally permits the disclosure of the report to the defendant, but prohibits disclosure of those portions of the report that contain three protected categories of information: (a) information that relates to confidential sources, (b) diagnostic opinions, and (c) other information that may cause harm to the defendant or to third parties; and (2) Rule 32(c)(3)(E) requires that all copies of such a report that have been furnished pursuant to Rule 32(c) be returned to the court, unless the court directs otherwise. After a defendant is sentenced, copies of such presentence reports are generally transmitted to the Bureau of Prisons and the United States Parole Commission. Although a provision of the Parole Commission and Reorganization Act of 1976 (Parole Act) (18 USCS 4208(b)) requires that, at least 30 days before a scheduled parole hearing, a prisoner be provided with reasonable access to a presentence report which has been used by the Parole Commission in making a parole determination, the Parole Act also, in 18 USCS 4208(c), exempts from this disclosure requirement the same three categories of information that are protected from disclosure by Rule 32(c)(3)(E). Two federal prisoners sought copies of their presentence reports. In the first case, after the Parole Commission denied the request of an inmate in an Arizona federal prison for a copy of his presentence report, the prisoner, pursuant to the FOIA, brought suit against the United States Department of Justice in the United States District Court for the District of Arizona, which (1) granted the prisoner's motion for summary judgment, and (2) ordered the Federal Government to comply with the prisoner's request for the report. In the second case, after the Parole Commission refused the FOIA request of an inmate in a California federal prison for a copy of the prisoner's presentence report, the prisoner filed an action against the Parole Commission and the prisoner's warden in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, which (1) treated the action as a FOIA suit, and (2) ordered that the presentence report be released. The two cases were consolidated on appeal before the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which (1) affirmed the judgment in each, and (2) expressed the view that, although Rule 32(c)(3) and the Parole Act authorized the withholding of the three protected categories of information, the FOIA did not provide a blanket exemption for withholding an entire presentence report when such a report is requested by the subject of the report, under (a) Exemption 3 of FOIA (5 USCS 552(b)(3)), which exempts from disclosure certain records that are specifically exempted from disclosure by other statutes, or (b) Exemption 5 of FOIA (5 USCS 552(b)(5)), which exempts from disclosure federal "inter-agency or intra-agency memorandums or letters which would not be available by law to a party other than an agency in litigation with the agency" (806 F2d 1411).

Section 32(a) of the Trading with the Enemy Act, as amended (50 USC Appx 32(a)), permits the return of property vested by the United States during World War II to a citizen of a former enemy nation who, as a consequence of any law, decree, or regulation of that nation, "discriminating against political, racial, or religious groups," had, in a specified period, not enjoyed full rights of citizenship under the law of that nation. Relying upon this statute, the plaintiff, a national and resident of Germany at all material times, filed with the Attorney General a claim for the return of the proceeds of certain property, alleging that throughout the relevant period he, as an "anti-Nazi," claimed to have been a discriminated-against group, had been deprived of full rights of German citizenship. His claim was rejected. Plaintiff then sued in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia to review the administrative determination, claiming it to have been arbitrary and illegal. The District Court denied the government's motion to dismiss the complaint for want of jurisdiction. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed, holding that judicial review of the administrative disposition was precluded by 7(c) of the Trading with the Enemy Act. (106 App DC 8, 268 F2d 584.)

Congress passed a statute which conditioned the continuation of military aid to El Salvador upon the President's semiannual certification of El Salvador's progress in protecting human rights; but the President neither signed the bill nor returned it to Congress, and subsequently claimed that it had been "pocket vetoed" during an intersession adjournment of Congress. Members of the House of Representatives, contending that intersession pocket vetoes are invalid and that the statute had thus become law without the President's signature, sought a declaratory judgment to that effect in an action filed in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia against the officials responsible for the publication of new laws. The District Court granted summary judgment in favor of the officials, holding that the pocket veto was valid (582 F Supp 169). The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed and remanded with instructions to enter summary judgment for the Representatives, holding that, given current Congressional practices, pocket vetoes cannot properly be used during intersession adjournments (245 App DC 1, 759 F2d 21). The statute expired by its own terms a few weeks after the Court of Appeals entered its judgment.

The defendant, a semi-illiterate Negro of low mentality, was arrested on a charge of rape of a white woman and held in the county jail until his indictment, three days later, by a grand jury which was impaneled eight days before his arrest, adjourned the day before his arrest, and was reconvened two days later by an order which did not list him as one against whom a case would be presented. The day after his indictment two local attorneys were appointed by the Georgia trial court to defend him. Before his arraignment he moved to quash the indictment on the ground that Negroes had been systematically excluded from service on the grand jury. This motion was overruled and the defendant was convicted and sentenced to death. On his appeal, the Supreme Court of Georgia held that his motion to quash was properly denied because, by Georgia practice, objections to a grand jury must be made before the indictment is returned, but reversed on another ground and remanded the case for a new trial. Before his second trial the defendant filed a special plea in abatement again alleging systematic exclusion of Negroes from the grand jury which indicted him and the petit jury about to be impaneled in his trial. This plea was again overruled and he was again convicted and sentenced to death.

A female dockworker, who had applied for work at a company, filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) after the company, which had assured the dockworker that she would be the first person hired when a vacancy occurred, instead hired a number of men. The EEOC issued a notice of right to sue, which did not identify the forum in which the dockworker could sue but stated that she had 90 days to do so. Within the 90-day period, the dockworker filed a sex discrimination suit under an Illinois human rights statute in an Illinois state court. After the company moved to dismiss the suit for failure to exhaust state administrative remedies, the dockworker--after the expiration of the 90-day period--moved to amend her complaint to allege that the company had also violated Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e et seq.). In response, the company (1) removed the case to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois; and (2) moved to dismiss the amended complaint, on the ground that the dockworker's original filing in state court could not toll the 90-day period because the state court had no jurisdiction over a Title VII claim. The District Court rejected the company's jurisdictional argument, and entered judgment for the dockworker after a trial on the merits (682 F Supp 374). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, affirming, ruled that jurisdiction over Title VII claims is vested in both state and federal courts (874 F2d 402).

New York Judiciary Law _ 749-aa, 29 McKinney's L. N. Y., pp. 511-515, providing for the administrative selection of a special or "blue ribbon" jury panel from the general jury panel in counties of one million or more inhabitants and the use in certain classes of cases of juries drawn from this special panel, does not on its face deny defendants in criminal cases due process of law or equal protection of the laws contrary to the Fourteenth Amendment.
Union Issue. The petition for writ of certiorari is granted and the judgment below is reversed. Meat Cutters v. Jewel Tea, ante, p. 676.

As a party to numerous government contracts, and in order to comply with Executive Order 11246 (42 USCS 2000e note), a corporation, as required by regulations of the Department of Labor's Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP), submitted to the Defense Logistic Agency (DLA) of the Department of Defense (the designated agency for monitoring the corporation's employment practices) written affirmative action programs and annual employer information reports. OFCCP disclosure regulations (41 CFR Part 60-40) provide that notwithstanding exemption from mandatory disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (5 USCS 552), records obtained under Executive Order 11246 can be made available if it is determined that disclosure would further the public interest and not impede the functions of the compliance agency. After the corporation had been notified by the DLA that the DLA had received an FOIA request from third parties for the disclosure of materials furnished to the DLA by the corporation, the corporation objected to the release of the information, but the DLA determined that the material was subject to disclosure under the FOIA and the OFCCP disclosure regulations. The corporation then brought an action in the United States District Court for the District of Delaware seeking to enjoin release of the documents. The District Court held that certain of the requested information fell within Exemption 4 of the FOIA relating to trade secrets (5 USCS 552(b)(4)), and that a Labor Department regulation stating that no officer or employee of the Department was to violate the Trade Secrets Act (18 USCS 1905)--which imposes criminal sanctions on government employees who disclose in any manner "not authorized by law" certain classes of information submitted to a federal agency, including trade secrets and confidential statistical data--required that the information be withheld (412 F Supp 171). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit vacated the District Court's judgment, holding that disclosures made pursuant to the OFCCP disclosure regulations were "authorized by law" by virtue of those regulations (565 F2d 1172).

The plaintiff contractor submitted a bid, which was accepted, for a construction project for the Department of the Air Force. Upon the contractor's refusal to close the contract because of a dispute as to a wage schedule adjustment, the contracting officer canceled the bid and its acceptance and retained the bid security as provided in a letter of acceptability of the bid, and the contractor, pursuant to the disputes clause of such letter, appealed to the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals, which dismissed the appeal as untimely without considering the merits of the case. In the contractor's subsequent suit to recover its deposit and damages for the alleged wrongful cancellation, the Court of Claims concluded that the appeal to the Board of Contract Appeals had been timely, and remanded the case to its own trial commissioner, rather than to the board, to make a record and consider the case on its merits. (170 Ct Cl 688, 345 F2d 808.)

The motion to dismiss is granted and the appeal is dismissed for want of jurisdiction. Treating the papers whereon the appeal was taken as a petition for a writ of certiorari, certiorari is granted and ‚àö¬∂[**2275]‚àö¬∂ the judgment is reversed. Redrup v. New York, 386 U.S. 767.

Two subsidiaries of an American corporation formed joint ventures with a Saudi corporation. When a dispute arose over royalties that the Saudi corporation had charged the joint ventures, the Saudi corporation pre-emptively sued the subsidiaries in the Delaware Superior Court, seeking a declaratory judgment that the royalties were proper. About 2 weeks later, the American corporation and the subsidiaries countersued in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey, alleging that the Saudi corporation had overcharged the joint ventures for sublicenses. [***455]  Before the trial in the Superior Court, the Saudi corporation moved to dismiss the federal suit. After the District Court denied the motion ( 194 F. Supp. 2d 378), the Saudi corporation took an interlocutory appeal. The Superior Court entered a judgment on a jury verdict of over $400 million in favor of the subsidiaries ( 866 A.2d 1). The Saudi corporation appealed this judgment to the Delaware Supreme Court.

A grand jury issued subpoenas to two parties‚Äî‚ÄúCompany‚Äù and ‚ÄúLaw Firm‚Äù‚Äîrequesting documents and communications related to a criminal investigation into the owner of Company and client of Law Firm. In response to the subpoenas, Company and Law Firm refused to disclose certain documents, citing attorney-client privilege and the work-product doctrine because the primary purpose of the documents at issue was to seek legal advice, not to obtain tax advice. The government moved to compel production, and the district court granted the government‚Äôs motion in part. Company and Law Firm disagreed with the district court‚Äôs ruling and continued to withhold the documents. The district court then held Company and Law Firm in contempt. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed, finding the primary purpose of the communications was to obtain legal advice.

Defendant was convicted in a Wisconsin trial court on charges of two burglaries and one attempted burglary, after the trial court found that his oral admissions and a written confession, given while in police custody, were voluntary and the statements were admitted in evidence. The Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed. (35 Wis 2d 146, 150 NW2d 507.)

A New York corporation engaged in the business of selling bottled wines and liquors for export from the United States and delivery to international airline passengers at their overseas destinations brought suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York for declaratory and injunctive relief against the New York State Liquor Authority, alleging that state statutes under which its business was declared to be illegal were repugnant to the commerce clause, the export-import clause, and the supremacy clause of the Federal Constitution. The District Court denied the corporation's motion for impaneling of a three-judge Federal District Court, with leave to renew the motion after state courts had ruled on the constitutional issues presented. (188 F Supp 434.) The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit dismissed an appeal from the District Court's order on the ground that it had no jurisdiction to entertain an appeal, because the District Court lacked jurisdiction to proceed without convening a three- judge court. (289 F2d 426.)

A Virginia prison inmate, while serving a sentence for a first-degree murder conviction, allegedly committed another murder while he was out of prison on work detail. The case engendered substantial publicity in the local news media and, approximately 3 months before trial, the accused submitted to the Virginia trial court 47 newspaper articles relating to the murder. One or more of the articles discussed details of the murder and investigation and included information about the accused's prior criminal record, the fact that he had been rejected for parole six times, accounts of his alleged prison infractions, details about the prior murder for which he had been convicted, a comment that the death penalty had not been available at the time of that conviction, and indications that he had confessed to the second murder. The trial court denied the accused's motion for individual voir dire and refused to ask any of the accused's proposed questions relating to the content of news items that potential jurors might have read or seen. Initially, the trial judge questioned prospective jurors as a group, and, with respect to the prospective jurors who stated that they had acquired information about the alleged offense or the accused from the news media or from any other source, the judge asked four questions--none of which concerned the source or content of the information--about the effect of this information on their ability to be impartial. One prospective juror who admitted to having prior knowledge of the case responded that he could not be impartial and was dismissed for cause. The trial court then conducted further voir dire of the prospective jurors in panels of four. One panel member, who equivocated as to whether she could enter the jury box with an open mind, was removed sua sponte by the trial judge, and other members were dismissed for various reasons. Eight of the 12 venirepersons who were sworn as jurors had answered on voir dire that they had read or heard something about the case, but none of the eight had indicated that he or she had formed an opinion about the case or would be biased in any way. The jury found the accused guilty of capital murder and recommended the death sentence, which sentence was imposed by the trial judge. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed the conviction and sentence, holding that, while a criminal defendant could properly ask on voir dire whether a juror had previously acquired any information about the case, the defendant did not have a constitutional right to explore the content of the acquired information (239 Va 433, 389 SE2d 886).

Upon trial in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California, the defendant was convicted of federal drug offenses, based on evidence seized by Border Patrol agents when they stopped his camper pickup at a traffic checkpoint about 36 miles from the Mexican border and discovered drugs while searching the vehicle for concealed aliens. The United States Court of Appeals for Ninth Circuit affirmed the conviction (462 F2d 347), and while a petition for certiorari was pending, the United States Supreme Court announced its decision in Almeida-Sanchez v United States, 413 US 266, 37 L Ed 2d 596, 93 S Ct 2535, holding that the Fourth Amendment prohibited the Border Patrol's use of roving patrols to search vehicles, with neither a warrant nor probable cause, at points removed from the border and its functional equivalents. The judgment in the case at bar was then vacated by the Supreme Court, and the case was remanded for reconsideration in light of the Almeida-Sanchez decision (413 US 915, 37 L Ed 2d 1038, 93 S Ct 3069). On remand, the Court of Appeals again affirmed the defendant's conviction, holding that although the principles of the Almeida-Sanchez decision were applicable to searches conducted at traffic checkpoints as well as searches conducted by roving patrols, nevertheless the Almeida-Sanchez decision was not applicable to searches which occurred prior to the date of that decision, June 21, 1973 (500 F2d 960).

A federal obscenity prosecution under 18 USCS 1461, which proscribes use of the mails for sending "obscene, lewd, lascivious, indecent, filthy or vile" materials, or advertisements thereof, was tried before a jury in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California. The prosecution was based on the defendants' use of the mails to carry their illustrated version of a government report on obscenity and pornography, and an illustrated brochure advertising the defendants' report--such brochure containing a collage of photographs from the illustrated report portraying heterosexual and homosexual intercourse, sodomy, and a variety of deviate sexual acts. Applying the constitutional tests of obscenity obtaining at the time of trial, the District Court refused to permit the defendants to introduce a survey as to obscenity standards in the immediate area, and instructed the jury that nationwide standards of obscenity were to be applied and that the government was required to show that the materials were utterly without redeeming social value. Although unable to reach a verdict on the charges relating to the report itself, the jury returned a guilty verdict as to the advertising brochure, and the defendants' convictions were affirmed by the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (481 F2d 307). Thereafter, the United States Supreme Court decided Miller v California, 413 US 15, 37 L Ed 2d 419, 93 S Ct 2607, and companion cases, which reformulated the constitutional tests of obscenity, holding, inter alia, that (1) in determining "contemporary community standards" of obscenity, there was no requirement that nationwide standards be applied, (2) obscenity statutes, as written or construed, could proscribe only material depicting or describing patently offensive "hard core" sexual conduct, and (3) the proper "social value" test was whether the work, taken as a whole, lacked serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value, not whether the material was utterly without redeeming social value. After considering the decisions in the Miller cases, the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit denied a petition for rehearing in the case at bar.

A 17-year-old, who was accused of brutally beating and stabbing to death his physically impaired cousin and foster mother while robbing her of $ 15, was tried as an adult and convicted in a Missouri court on a charge of capital murder. At a conference preceding the penalty phase of the trial, one of the accused's attorneys (1) moved for an order prohibiting the prosecution from cross-examining defense witnesses with regard to the accused's juvenile record; and (2) requested that the jury be instructed on the statutory mitigating circumstance that the accused had no significant history of prior criminal activity, even though the attorney also stated that she would not try to show that the accused lacked a criminal past. The trial judge never expressly ruled on the first motion, but did rule that the accused would not be entitled to the requested instruction without supporting evidence, and refused to give the instruction when no such evidence was submitted by either side. The accused was sentenced to death. In affirming the accused's conviction and sentence on direct review, the Supreme Court of Missouri held that, in the absence of evidence to support the statutory mitigating circumstance, the trial court had correctly refused the requested instruction (667 SW2d 712). Subsequently, the accused filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri and alleged in part that the trial judge's failure to give the requested instruction violated due process. The District Court ruled that the accused's conviction and sentence were not invalid under the Federal Constitution. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed with respect to the accused's sentence and remanded with instructions to grant the writ unless the state timely commenced resentencing proceedings, as the Court of Appeals ruled that the trial judge had violated the Constitution's Eighth Amendment by refusing to give the requested instruction (957 F2d 1495).

The plaintiff, a Negro resident of Memphis, Tennessee, when boarding a Memphis bus, was required by the driver, and afterward by police officers, to seat himself in the back of the bus, under a Tennessee statute providing for segregation on transportation facilities. He brought the present action seeking a declaration that the statute was invalid. The United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee, without reaching the merits, dismissed the complaint on the ground that no "actual controversy" within the intendment of the Declaratory Judgment Act (28 USC 2201) had been shown, in that plaintiff had ridden a bus in Memphis on only one occasion and had boarded it for the purpose of instituting the present litigation.

Beneficiaries of New York decedents' estates living in Romania, whose shares of the estates had not been paid to them, filed a complaint in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York. The beneficiaries sought to enjoin enforcement of 2218 of the New York Surrogate's Court Procedure Act, which authorizes the surrogate to order an alien's share of a New York estate paid into court when it appears that the alien "would not have the benefit or use or control of the money or property" constituting the share. The District Court, sitting as a three-judge court, denied the beneficiaries' motion for summary judgment, but did not dismiss the action (299 F Supp 1389). From the order denying summary judgment, the beneficiaries appealed to the United States Supreme Court under 28 USC 1253, which gives the United States Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction over any three-judge Federal District Court order "granting or denying ... an interlocutory or permanent injunction."

Submerged lands located in the seaward portion of Cook Inlet--an elongated body of water extending from the sea some 150 miles into Alaska and having an opening at the sea of some 47 miles across--were offered for competitive oil and gas lease sale by the state of Alaska, prompting the United States to bring an action against the state in the United States District Court for the District of Alaska to obtain injunctive relief and to quiet title between the state and the United States as to the submerged lands. Under the Submerged Lands Act (43 USCS 1301-1315), the states of the United States are declared the owners of submerged lands within 3 miles of their coastlines, with "coastline" being defined in terms not only of land, but also of "the seaward limit of inland waters." The Act does not define "inland waters," but under the Convention on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone, the definitions of which are applicable to the Submerged Lands Act, it is provided that a bay with natural entrance points separated by more than 24 miles of water is considered inland water only if it is an "historic bay" (a term which the Convention does not define). Due to the location of the submerged lands in question, Alaska's ownership of the lands depended upon whether Cook Inlet was an historic bay. Examining evidence relating to the periods of Russian sovereignty in Alaska, of United States sovereignty when Alaska was a territory, and of state sovereignty in Alaska, the District Court found that Cook Inlet was an historic bay and dismissed the United States' complaint. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, ruling that the law applied by the District Court was correct and that its findings were not clearly erroneous, affirmed (497 F2d 1155).

Constitutional law -- defilement of flag -- proprietor of art gallery who displayed construction, comparable to sculptures, made out of American flag for purpose of protesting Vietnam war was properly found guilty of defiling American flag in violation of former Penal Law ( _ 1425, subd. 16, par. d); statute does not impinge on defendant's right of free speech under First Amendment -- statute is not unconstitutionally vague -- intent not essential to conviction for violation of malum prohibitum statute.

A company filed an action in a Tennessee state court to enjoin the union from striking, basing its complaint on a no-strike clause in the collective bargaining agreement by which grievances were to be settled amicably or by arbitration. After the state court issued an ex parte injunction, the union moved in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee for removal of the case, and the District Court held that the action was within its original jurisdiction and dissolved the state court injunction (263 F Supp 177). The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (376 F2d 337).

In a companion case to Bisso v. Inland Waterways Corp., supra, p. 911, six members of the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Black, J., held that the owners of a tugboat damaged as a consequence of the negligent pilotage of the towed vessel by a pilot in the employ of, and supplied by, the tugboat, could not recover damages from the owner of the towed vessel, notwithstanding a provision in the contract between the tugboat and the towed vessel to the effect that a pilot going aboard the latter vessel would become the servant of the owners of that vessel, and that the tugboat would not be liable for any damage resulting from the towage. The majority, although not holding the contract provisions invalid in so far as they made the towed vessel liable for negligence of the pilot, held that they were not to be construed as an agreement that the tugboat was entitled to collect damages for negligence of the pilot supplied by the tugboat.

Two corporations owned by the Republic of France designed, manufactured, and marketed aircraft. After an airplane sold by the two corporations crashed in Iowa, three individuals filed separate suits against the two corporations in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, and alleged that the French corporations (1) had manufactured and sold a defective plane, and (2) were guilty of negligence and breach of warranty. The two corporations answered the complaints, the cases were consolidated and referred to a United States Magistrate, and discovery began. Eventually, the two corporations were served with (1) a request for the production of documents pursuant to Rule 34 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, (2) a set of interrogatories pursuant to Rule 33, and (3) requests for admissions pursuant to Rule 36. The corporations then filed a motion for a protective order, and argued that (1) because they were French corporations and the materials sought through discovery could be found only in France, the exclusive procedures for such discovery were dictated by the Hague Convention on the Taking of Evidence Abroad in Civil or Commercial Matters (23 UST 2555, TIAS No. 7444), to which the United States, France, and other nations had acceded; and (2) under a French penal law (the "blocking statute"), the corporations could not respond to discovery requests that did not comply with the Convention. The Magistrate denied the motion insofar as it related to answering interrogatories, producing documents, or making admissions, and ordered the corporations to comply with the individuals' discovery requests. The corporations then sought a writ of mandamus against the Magistrate from the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, but the Court of Appeals denied their petition, expressing the view that (1) when a District Court has jurisdiction over a foreign litigant, the Hague Convention does not apply to the production of the evidence in that litigant's possession, even though the documents and information sought may be physically located within the territory of a foreign signatory to the Convention; (2) the principle of international comity did not require that the three individuals first attempt discovery through the Hague Convention procedures, and rely on the Federal Rules only if their Convention discovery attempts proved futile; (3) the Magistrate, after balancing competing national interests, properly ordered the French corporations to comply with the discovery requests, despite the French blocking statute; and (4) it was premature to inquire what sanctions the Magistrate ought to impose if the corporations failed to comply with the discovery order (782 F2d 120).

A city and county in Michigan each assessed a tax against a subcontractor under a government contract. The tax was based, in part, on the value of materials and work in process in the subcontractors's possession to which the United States held legal title under the terms of the subcontract. The subcontractor paid this part of each tax under protest and then sued in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan for a refund. It contended that full title to the property was in the United States and that the taxes infringed the federal government's immunity from state taxation to the extent they were based on such property. The government intervened on the subcontractor's behalf. On motion for summary judgment the District Court entered judgment for the subcontractor (132 F Supp 899) and the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (235 F2d 380).

Both the father and the mother were unrepresented by counsel in the contempt proceeding, and the father was found in willful contempt for failure to pay the child support with no finding concerning the father's ability to pay. The U.S. Supreme Court first held that the case not moot, even though the father served the period of incarceration, since the relatively brief incarceration did not permit full litigation of the father's claim and the likelihood of recurrence of the same action was indicated by the father's contempt proceedings both before and after the current proceeding. The Court further held that the father was denied due process, although due process did not automatically require the State to provide counsel in civil contempt proceedings to an indigent parent subject to a support order who faces incarceration. The right to counsel was limited based upon the parent's ability to pay, the equality of representation between the parties, and State procedural safeguards. In the father's case, counsel was warranted since the State did not provide clear notice that the father's ability to pay was the critical question and made no findings concerning his ability to pay.

The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and other organizations petitioned the Federal Power Commission to issue a rule which would (1) require equal employment opportunity and nondiscrimination in the employment practices of companies regulated by the Commission, (2) require regulatees to adopt affirmative action programs to combat discrimination in employment, and (3) give the right to file a complaint with the Commission to any person who believed that he had been subjected to employment discrimination by a regulatee. The Commission refused to adopt the proposed rule (48 FPC 40), but the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, on petition for review, vacated the Commission's order and remanded the case, holding that although the Commission lacked power to prescribe personnel practices of regulatees and to punish infractions, nevertheless in the performance of its regulatory functions under the Federal Power Act (16 USCS 791a et seq.) and the Natural Gas Act (15 USCS 717 et seq.), such as rate review, the Commission had power to take into account evidence that the regulatee was a demonstrated discriminator in its employment relations (520 F2d 432).

A church eldership brought suit in the Circuit Court of Washington County, Maryland, seeking (1) to prevent two local churches from withdrawing from the eldership, and (2) to obtain property claimed by the local churches. The complaint was dismissed, and the Maryland Court of Appeals affirmed (249 Md 650, 241 A2d 691). After the United States Supreme Court remanded the case for further consideration (393 US 528, 21 L Ed 2d 750, 89 S Ct 850), the Court of Appeals adhered to the result reached in its earlier decision, basing its determination upon (1) Maryland statutory provisions governing the holding of property by religious corporations, (2) language in the deeds conveying the properties in question to the local churches, (3) the terms of the charters of the local churches, and (4) provisions in the eldership's constitution pertaining to the ownership and control of church property (254 Md 162, 254 A2d 162).

Upon trial in the Criminal Court of Record for Orange County, Florida, the defendants were convicted for violating the state lottery laws. During the trial, the prosecution was allowed to introduce in evidence recordings of the defendants' telephone conversations, which had been obtained by state police officers by having a telephone connected to the party line of one of the defendants without his knowledge, in such a way as to permit continuous surreptitious surveillance and recording of all conversations on the line. The convictions were affirmed by the District Court of Appeal of Florida for the Fourth District. (191 So 2d 84.)

A group of high school students formed a club with the purpose of promoting "spiritual growth and positive attitudes in the lives of its members." After school officials denied the students' request that their club be permitted to conduct prayers and scripture reading on school premises, the students filed suit in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania against their school district, nine members of the school board, the superintendent of the district, and the principal of the high school. The complaint alleged that the defendants had deprived the students of freedom of speech, in violation of the First Amendment, by refusing to allow the students' club to meet on the same basis as other student groups because of the club's religious activities. The complaint prayed for declaratory and injunctive relief. The specific allegation concerning each of the named members of the board stated that the individual was a member of the board and was sued in that capacity. The District Court ultimately entered a final order ruling in favor of the students and against the defendants on the students' claim of denial of freedom of speech, but entered no injunction and granted no relief against any defendant in his individual capacity (563 F Supp 697). The school district did not challenge the District Court's judgment in any way and decided to comply with the judgment and to allow the club's meetings. However, an individual member of the school board filed a timely notice of appeal. In the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, no one raised any question about the individual school board member's standing to appeal. Concluding that the establishment clause of the First Amendment prevailed over the students' free-speech right to engage in religious activity, and reversing the District Court's judgment on the merits, the Court of Appeals held that the particular circumstances disclosed by the record and present at the high school in question led to the inexorable conclusion that the constitutional balance of interest tilted against permitting the student activity to be conducted within the school as a general activity program (741 F2d 538).

The United States and a special agent of the Internal Revenue Service petitioned the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois for enforcement of summonses that had been issued under 26 USCS 7602 by the agent to a bank. The summonses requested that the bank produce certain records pertaining to a taxpayer whose activities were being investigated by the Internal Revenue Service agent, but a bank officer, appearing in response to the summonses, had refused to produce any of the records requested. Finding that the summonses had not been issued in good faith because the special agent was conducting his investigation solely for the purpose of unearthing evidence of criminal conduct by the taxpayer, the District Court denied enforcement, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed (554 F2d 302).

A Delaware corporation with executive headquarters in Texas publicly announced its intent to make a tender offer to purchase shares of stock of a Washington corporation whose principal business, executive offices, and major assets were located in Idaho. The Texas-based corporation seeking the acquisition filed a schedule with the Securities and Exchange Commission as required by 13 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended by the Williams Act (15 USCS 78m), and filed documents with the Idaho Commission of Finance in an attempt to satisfy Idaho's takeover statute. After Idaho officials requested additional information and entered an order delaying the effective date of the tender offer, the Texas-based corporation filed an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas against the Idaho officials, praying for a declaration that the Idaho statute was invalid insofar as it purported to apply to interstate cash tender offers to purchase securities traded on a national exchange.
