The Idaho officials appeared specially to contest jurisdiction, venue, and the merits of the claim, but the District Court found four grounds for federal subject matter jurisdiction, held that personal jurisdiction over the Idaho defendants had been obtained pursuant to the Texas longarm statute, that venue, although improper under the general venue statute (28 USCS 1391(b)), could be sustained under the special venue provision of 27 of the Securities Exchange Act (15 USCS 78aa), and that the takeover statute was preempted by the Williams Act and placed an impermissible burden on interstate commerce (439 F Supp 420). On appeal, United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding, among other things, that venue was authorized by the terms of 27 of the Securities Exchange Act--providing that jurisdiction and venue may be had for actions brought to enforce "any liability or duty" created by the Act--because Idaho's enforcement attempt, by conflicting with the Williams Act, constituted a violation of a "duty" imposed by 28(a) of the Securities Exchange Act (15 USCS 78bb(a)), which provides that the jurisdiction of a state securities commission is not affected by the Act insofar as it does not conflict with the Act, and that venue was also proper under 28 USCS 1391(b), providing that when jurisdiction is not founded solely on diversity of citizenship, civil actions may be brought in the judicial district where all defendants reside, "or in which the claim arose," because the alleged invalid restraint against the Texas-based corporation had occurred in the Northern District of Texas (577 F2d 1256).

An Ohio state court, declaring that an insurance company was insolvent, directed that the company be liquidated. The Ohio superintendent of insurance was appointed to serve as liquidator. In the ensuing liquidation proceedings, the United States--which filed claims in excess of $ 10.7 million as an obligee on various immigration, appearance, performance, and payment bonds issued by the company as surety--asserted that those claims were entitled to first priority under 31 USCS 3713(a)(1)(A)(iii), which provides that a claim of the United States must be paid first when a person indebted to the United States is insolvent and an act of bankruptcy has been committed. Thereafter, the superintendent brought a declaratory judgment action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio against the United States. The superintendent argued that 3713(a)(1)(A)(iii) did not pre-empt an Ohio statute under which claims of federal, state, and local governments were entitled to only fifth priority--behind administrative expenses, specified wage claims, policyholders' claims, and claims of general creditors--in proceedings to liquidate an insolvent insurance company, because such statute fell within 2(b) of the McCarran-Ferguson Act (15 USCS 1012(b)), which provides that no federal statute will be construed to supersede a state statute enacted "for the purpose of regulating the business of insurance" unless the federal statute specifically relates to the business of insurance. The District Court, granting summary judgment for the United States, ruled that the Ohio statute did not involve the "business of insurance" pursuant to 2(b). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, reversing, expressed the view that the Ohio statute was exempt from federal pre-emption as a regulation of the "business of insurance" within the meaning of the McCarran-Ferguson Act, because the Ohio statute (1) transferred and spread the risk of insurer insolvency; (2) involved an integral part of the policy relationship; and (3) focused upon the protection of policyholders by diverting the scarce resources of the liquidating entity away from other creditors (939 F2d 341).

In the trial of a defendant who had allegedly strangled his fiancee with a cat leash, a Delaware trial court permitted an expert witness to state his opinion that hairs similar to those of the victim which had been found on the leash had been forcibly removed from the victim's head, overruling defense objections that the witness' inability to recall which of three possible methods of making such a determination had been the basis for his conclusion in this case precluded effective cross-examination. The Supreme Court of Delaware reversed the defendant's subsequent conviction on the ground that the admission of this testimony had violated the confrontation clause of the Sixth Amendment, by denying the defendant his right to effectively cross-examine a key prosecution witness.

Attorneys who regularly accepted court appointments to represent indigent defendants in minor felony and misdemeanor cases before the District of Columbia Superior Court sought an increase in the statutorily fixed fees they were paid for such work. When lobbying efforts failed, a group consisting of virtually all such attorneys agreed among themselves that they would not accept any new cases after a certain date if the District of Columbia had not passed legislation providing for an increase in their fees; and a trial lawyers' association to which the attorneys belonged supported and publicized their agreement. After the agreement went into effect, other available defense counsel were quickly overloaded, severely affecting the District's criminal justice system, and 2 weeks later the city council voted to increase the fees. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) subsequently filed a complaint against the trial lawyers' association, which complaint alleged that the association and its officers had entered into a conspiracy to fix prices and conduct a boycott and had thereby engaged in unfair methods of competition in violation of 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 USCS 45). An administrative law judge rejected various defenses, but recommended that the complaint be dismissed because District of Columbia officials regarded the net effect of the boycott as beneficial in providing better representation for indigent defendants; however, the FTC did not regard the boycott as harmless and issued a cease and desist order prohibiting the association from initiating any similar future boycotts (107 FTC 510). The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit vacated the FTC order and remanded for a determination whether the association possessed significant market power, as it held that (1) the attorneys' boycott contained an element of expression warranting protection under the Federal Constitution's First Amendment, (2) a restriction on this form of expression cannot be justified unless it is no greater than is essential to an important governmental interest, and (3) this test could not be satisfied by the application of a per se rule against price-fixing boycotts, but rather the FTC was required to prove that such conduct presented the evil against which the Sherman Act (15 USCS 1-7) was directed (272 App DC 272, 856 F2d 226).

A Liberian corporation and a Panamanian corporation operated ships which were used for Caribbean cruises. The ships were of foreign registry and were operated by crews subject to foreign ships' articles. A longshoremen's union, claiming that American residents, who were employed by the ships to do casual longshore work, were being paid substandard wages, picketed, in protest against such wages, near the ships while they were docked at American ports. Suing in the Circuit Court of Dade County, Florida, the corporations obtained injunctive relief against the picketing. The Florida District Court of Appeal for the Third Circuit affirmed (215 So 2d 51), and the Supreme Court of Florida denied review.

In an anti-trust suit a consent decree was entered directing the formation of two new companies, one to take over the motion-picture production and distribution assets, and the other the theater assets, of an existing corporation, which was to be dissolved upon the formation of the new companies. The decree provided that the owner of 24 per cent of the stock of the dissolved corporation may "either" sell his stock in one or the other of the two newly formed companies, "or" deposit such stock with a court-designated trustee. After the stockholder had chosen the latter alternative, the district court, without evidence or facts, amended the decree by ordering a compulsory sale.

The State of New York makes it a crime to possess a firearm without a license, whether inside or outside the home. An individual who wants to carry a firearm outside his home may obtain an unrestricted license to ‚Äúhave and carry‚Äù a concealed ‚Äúpistol or revolver‚Äù if he can prove that ‚Äúproper cause exists‚Äù for doing so. N. Y. Penal Law Ann. ¬ß400.00(2)(f ). An applicant satisfies the ‚Äúproper cause‚Äù requirement only if he can ‚Äúdemonstrate a special need for self-protection distinguishable from that of the general community.‚Äù E.g., In re Klenosky, 75 App. Div. 2d 793, 428 N. Y. S. 2d 256, 257. Petitioners Brandon Koch and Robert Nash are adult, law-abiding New York residents who both applied for unrestricted licenses to carry a handgun in public based on their generalized interest in self-defense. The State denied both of their applications for unrestricted licenses, allegedly because Koch and Nash failed to satisfy the ‚Äúproper cause‚Äù requirement. Petitioners then sued respondents‚Äîstate officials who oversee the processing of licensing applications‚Äîfor declaratory and injunctive relief, alleging that respondents violated their Second and Fourteenth Amendment rights by denying their unrestricted-license applications for failure to demonstrate a unique need for self-defense. The District Court dismissed petitioners‚Äô complaint and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Both courts relied on the Second Circuit‚Äôs prior decision in Kachalsky v. County of Westchester, 701 F. 3d 81, which had sustained New York‚Äôs proper-cause standard, holding that the requirement was ‚Äúsubstantially related to the achievement of an important governmental interest.‚Äù Id., at 96.

A union ordered a strike, or concerted cessation of work, on the part of a contractor's union employees doing carpentry work in a dwelling house, one of its objectives being to force the owner to cancel his installation contract with the supplier of the wall and floor coverings, who employed nonunion men. The strike was called prior to, but continued after, the effective date of 8 (b) (4) (A) of the National Labor Relations Act as amended by the Labor Management Relations Act, making secondary boycott an unfair labor practice. Interlocutory injunctive relief sought against the union under 10 (l) of the act was denied by a district court on the ground that the conduct complained of took place before the effective date of the statute. Nevertheless, the National Labor Relations Board found the union guilty of an unfair labor practice.

In Arizona, a person suspected of killing his son was taken to a police station, placed in custody, and advised of his Miranda rights, whereupon the suspect told the police that he did not wish to make any more statements without having a lawyer present, and police questioning ceased. After the suspect's wife asked to see her husband, the police permitted such a meeting in the presence of a police officer, who placed a tape recorder in plain sight on a desk and tape-recorded the subsequent incriminating statements of the suspect to his wife. At trial, an Arizona court refused to suppress the tape-recorded statements on the ground that the recording had been a product of police interrogation in violation of the suspect's Miranda rights, and the trial court expressed the view that the police actions had not been a ruse or subterfuge as an indirect means of avoiding the dictates of Miranda. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Arizona reversed the suspect's conviction for murder and child abuse, and expressed the view that the admission into evidence, at trial, of the tape-recorded conversation between the suspect and his wife violated the suspect's right not to incriminate himself under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution, because, in allowing the conversation to commence, the police did indirectly what they could not do directly--interrogate the suspect (149 Ariz 24, 716 P2d 393).

State and federal courts must enforce the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U. S. C. 11 et seq., with respect to all arbitration agreements covered by that statute. Here, the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, by misreading and disregarding the precedents of this Court interpreting the FAA, did not follow controlling federal law implementing that basic principle. The state court held unenforceable all predispute arbitration agreements that apply to claims alleging personal injury or wrongful death against nursing homes. The decision of the state court found the FAA's coverage to be more limited than mandated by this Court's previous cases. The decision of the State Supreme Court of Appeals must be vacated. When this Court has fulflled its duty to interpret federal law, a state court may not contradict or fail to implement the rule so established. See U. S. Costt, Art. VI, cl. 2.

In Ford v Wainwright (1986) 477 US 399, 91 L Ed 2d 335, 106 S Ct 2595, the United States Supreme Court held that the Federal Constitution's Eighth Amendment prohibits a state from inflicting the death penalty upon a prisoner who is insane. An accused was convicted in an Arizona state court of first-degree murder and sentenced to death. The accused was unsuccessful on direct review and in a series of state habeas corpus petitions. In addition, he filed three federal habeas corpus petitions, all of which were dismissed for failure to exhaust state remedies. In 1993, the accused (1) filed, in the United States District Court for the District of Arizona, his fourth federal habeas corpus petition; and (2) included a Ford claim that he was incompetent to be executed. The District Court dismissed the Ford claim as premature, but granted a writ of habeas corpus on other grounds. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed the grant, but explained that the court's instruction to enter a judgment denying the petition was not intended to affect any later litigation of the Ford claim (80 F3d 1301, 1996 US App LEXIS 6290). In 1997, the state obtained a warrant for the accused's execution. The accused, after unsuccessfully seeking state court relief, moved in the District Court to reopen his Ford claim. However, the District Court ruled that it lacked jurisdiction, under the restrictions in 28 USCS 2244(b), as amended by the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA), on "second or successive" federal habeas corpus applications. The accused then sought relief in the Court of Appeals, which (1) expressed the view that 2244(b) did not apply to a federal habeas corpus petition that raised only a Ford claim which had previously been dismissed as premature; and (2) ordered the case transferred back to the District Court (118 F3d 628, 1997 US App LEXIS 15347).

Challenging the constitutionality of provisions of Pennsylvania statutes governing the admission and commitment of a person 18 years of age or younger to a state mental health institution upon parental consent over the objection of such juvenile, five individuals who alleged that they were being held at a state mental health facility and that they had been admitted or committed pursuant to the challenged provisions, brought an action on behalf of themselves and a class in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. The District Court determined that the action was maintainable as a class action under Rule 23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure on behalf of "all persons eighteen years of age or younger who have been, are or may be admitted or committed to mental health facilities in Pennsylvania pursuant to the challenged provisions," notwithstanding that after the commencement of the action, state regulations had been promulgated which accorded significant procedural protection to those juveniles 13 years of age and older in regard to their admission and commitment to mental institutions. Thereafter, the District Court held that the challenged provisions violated the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause (402 F Supp 1039).

The National Park Service (NPS), a bureau of the United States Department of the Interior, issued regulations implementing the National Parks Omnibus Management Act of 1998 (the 1998 Act) (codified with certain exceptions in 16 USCS __ 5951-5966). One of these regulations (36 CFR _ 51.3) purported to render the Contract Disputes Act of 1978 (CDA) (41 USCS __ 601 et seq.)--which established rules to govern disputes arising out of certain government contracts--inapplicable to concession contracts with the NPS. A nonprofit trade association that represented concessioners doing business in the national parks--together with three such concessioners--brought suit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia against the Department of the Interior and related federal defendants. The plaintiffs alleged, among other matters, that _ 51.3 was facially violative of the 1998 Act. The District Court--in granting, in pertinent part, the defendants' motion to dismiss--upheld the regulation, on the asserted grounds that (1) the CDA was ambiguous as to its applicability to concession contracts, and (b) the NPS' interpretation was reasonable (142 F Supp 2d 54). The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed in pertinent part (350 US App DC 191, 282 F3d 818).

After granting certiorari to determine whether the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit had erred in affirming (424 F2d 951) the petitioner's conviction in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee of conspiracy to commit murder to avoid apprehension for the robbery of a federally insured bank, the United States Supreme Court determined that the record showed that the petitioner was neither charged with nor convicted of conspiracy to commit murder, and it dismissed the writ as improvidently granted.

A prison inmate who had sought to assure the safety of elderly prisoners during a prison riot was shot in the leg by a prison guard and seriously injured as he ran up a flight of stairs after the prison security manager, who had ordered prison guards to shoot low at any prisoner who climbed the stairs after him as he attempted to free a guard who had been taken hostage by rioters. The inmate sued the manager and others under 42 USCS 1983 on the claim that they had deprived him of his rights under the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments, and raised pendent state law claims for assault and battery and negligence, alleging that the riot had subsided by the time he was shot. The United States District Court for the District of Oregon directed a verdict for the prison officials, holding that their use of deadly force had been justified under the circumstances and could not be found to be not reasonably necessary. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded for a new trial with regard to the inmate's claim of cruel and unusual punishment, holding that an Eighth Amendment violation would be established if a prison official had deliberately shot the inmate when he knew or should have known that it was unnecessary or if the officials had acted with deliberate indifference to the inmate's rights (743 F2d 1372).

In a class action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana, challenging Indiana's practice of discontinuing unemployment benefits upon a determination of eligibility made without according a full hearing to the erstwhile beneficiary, a three-judge court enjoined Indiana to provide pre-termination hearings to beneficiaries. Thereafter, in a decision unrelated to the injunction, the only named representative of the class received full retroactive compensation (347 F Supp 218).

North Carolina appealed the District Court's remedial order to this Court, and we granted a stay pending appeal. See 580 U. S. __ (2017). The State now contends that "the remedial order should be vacated for the simple reason that the district court failed to meaningfully weigh any equitable considerations." Juris. Statement 22. We share that assessment and now vacate the order. Relief in redistricting cases is "'fashioned in the light of well-known principles of equity."' Reynolds v. Sims, 377 U. S. 533, 585 (1964). A district court therefore must undertake an "equitable weighing process" to select a fitting remedy for the legal violations it has identified, NAACP v. Hampton County Election Comm'n, 470 U. S. 166, 183, n. 36 (1985), taking account of "'what is necessary, what is fair, and what is workable,"' New York v. Cathedral Academy, 434 U. S. 125, 129 (1977). And in the context of deciding whether to truncate existing legislators' terms and order a special election, there is much for a court to weigh. Although this Court has never addressed whether or when a special election may be a proper remedy for a racial gerrymander, obvious considerations include the severity and nature of the particular constitutional violation, the extent of the likely disruption to the ordinary processes of governance if early elections are imposed, and the need to act with proper judicial restraint when intruding on state sovereignty. We do not suggest anything about the relative weight of these factors (or others), but they are among the matters a court would generally be expected to consider in its "balancing of the individual and collective interests" at stake. Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Bd. of Ed., 402 U. S. 1, 16 (1971).

In connection with the removal of a National Security Agency (NSA) employee from office, (1) 5 USCS 7532, which was originally passed in 1950, authorizes federal agency heads, including the Secretary of Defense, to suspend and remove an employee, under specified procedures, if such an action is necessary or desirable in the interests of national security; (2) the National Security Act of 1959 (the "1959 Act") (50 USCS 402 note), empowers the Secretary of Defense, or the Secretary's designee, to appoint NSA employees as may be necessary to carry out the functions of the NSA; and (3) the NSA Personnel Security Procedures Act of 1964 (the "1964 Act") (50 USCS 831-833), in 833(a), authorizes the Secretary of Defense to terminate the employment of any NSA employee whenever the Secretary (a) considers the action to be in the interests of the United States, and (b) determines that the procedures stated in other provisions of the law cannot be invoked consistently with national security. The Secretary of Defense has delegated his 1959 Act appointment authority to the NSA's Director, who has promulgated internal personnel regulations. After a NSA employee who was not a veteran disclosed to NSA officials that he had engaged in homosexual relationships with foreign nationals, the employee was notified of his proposed removal from office, under the NSA's regulations, on the ground that his conduct allegedly made impossible the employee's continued access to classified information, which access was essential to his NSA employment. Although the employee contested the decision administratively, the employee was eventually notified that his security clearance was being revoked, and the Director, because such clearance was a condition of NSA employment, removed the employee, under the purported authority of the 1959 Act. In response to the employee's request, under 7532, for a hearing before the Secretary of Defense, both the Director and the Secretary replied that the employee's removal (1) was "for cause," under the NSA's personnel regulations, and (2) was not pursuant to the Secretary's 7532 authority. The employee then brought suit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, and challenged his removal on grounds including a claim that (1) the 1959 Act's appointment authority did not include the authority to remove employees; and (2) thus, the NSA was required to apply 7532 procedures that allegedly guaranteed NSA employees a preremoval hearing before the Secretary or the Secretary's designee. The District Court, however, denied this claim, and granted summary judgment against the employee. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, reversing as to the optional applicability of 7532, and vacating the remainder of the District Court's decision, expressed the view that (1) the chronology of congressional action indicated that 7532, which predated the establishment of the NSA, controlled NSA dismissals on national security grounds; and (2) because the Director had disclaimed reliance on the 1964 Act's parallel removal scheme, remand to the NSA for compliance with 7532 was obligatory (261 App DC 96, 820 F2d 1275).

In 1938, a 17-year-old Negro of limited education and mental capacity, after expressly disavowing a desire for counsel, pleaded guilty in the Circuit Court of Kalamazoo County, Michigan, to a charge of murder. He was sentenced to solitary confinement at hard labor for life. In 1950, he filed a delayed motion for a new trial in the Circuit Court, asserting constitutional invalidity of his conviction and sentence because he did not have the assistance of counsel at the time of his plea and sentence.

Before September 1993, a Texas statutory provision specified that (1) an alleged victim's testimony about an alleged sexual offense could not support a conviction unless (a) such testimony was corroborated by other evidence, or (b) the victim made an "outcry"--that is, informed another person of the alleged offense--within 6 months of the alleged offense's occurrence; but (2) such testimony alone could support a conviction if the alleged victim was under 14 at the time of the alleged offense. Effective September 1, 1993, an amendment to the provision allowed the victim's testimony alone to support a conviction if the victim was under 18. In 1997, an accused was convicted on 15 counts of committing sexual offenses against his stepdaughter from 1991 to 1995, when she was 12 to 16 years old. Before the Court of Appeals of Texas, the accused argued that four of the convictions--with respect to offenses allegedly committed between June 1992 and July 1993--could not stand under the former version of the provision, because those convictions were based solely on the testimony of the victim, who was not under 14 at the time of the offenses and had not made a timely outcry. The Court of Appeals, in affirming the convictions, expressed the view that the amended version of the provision was applicable to the case, as this version (1) had not increased the punishment or changed the elements of the offense that the state had to prove, (2) had merely removed existing restrictions upon the competency of some classes of persons as witnesses, and (3) was thus a rule of procedure (963 SW2d 833). The Court of Criminal Appeals of Texas denied discretionary review.

Philadelphia‚Äôs foster care system relies on cooperation between the City and private foster care agencies. The City enters standard annual contracts with the agencies to place children with foster families. One of the responsibilities of the agencies is certifying prospective foster families under state statutory criteria. Petitioner Catholic Social Services has contracted with the City to provide foster care services for over 50 years, continuing the centuries-old mission of the Catholic Church to serve Philadelphia‚Äôs needy children. CSS holds the religious belief that marriage is a sacred bond between a man and a woman. Because CSS believes that certification of prospective foster families is an endorsement of their relationships, it will not certify unmarried couples‚Äîregardless of their sexual orientation‚Äîor same-sex married couples. But other private foster agencies in Philadelphia will certify same-sex couples, and no same-sex couple has sought certification from CSS. Against this backdrop, a 2018 newspaper story recounted the Archdiocese of Philadelphia‚Äôs position that CSS could not consider prospective foster parents in same-sex marriages. Calls for investigation followed, and the City ultimately informed CSS that unless it agreed to certify same-sex couples the City would no longer refer children to the agency or enter a full foster care contract with it in the future. The City explained that the refusal of CSS to certify same-sex couples violated both a non-discrimination provision in the agency‚Äôs contract with the City as well as the non-discrimination requirements of the citywide Fair Practices Ordinance. CSS and three affiliated foster parents filed suit seeking to enjoin the City‚Äôs referral freeze on the grounds that the City‚Äôs actions violated the Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses of the First Amendment. The District Court denied preliminary relief. It reasoned that the contractual non-discrimination requirement and the Fair Practices Ordinance were both neutral and generally applicable under Employment Div., Dept. of Human Resources of Ore. v. Smith, 494 U. S. 872, and that CSS‚Äôs free exercise claim was therefore unlikely to succeed. The Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed. Given the expiration of the parties‚Äô contract, the Third Circuit examined whether the City could condition contract renewal on the inclusion of new language forbidding discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. The court concluded that the City‚Äôs proposed contractual terms stated a neutral and generally applicable policy under Smith. CSS and the foster parents challenge the Third Circuit‚Äôs determination that the City‚Äôs actions were permissible under Smith and also ask the Court to reconsider that decision.

An individual was convicted in a California state court of sexually molesting a 5-year-old child. At trial, the individual objected, on the basis of a state evidentiary rule, to the testimony of the parent of another child who claimed to have been molested by the individual 20 years before. On direct appeal, the individual pursued his evidentiary objection, requesting the appellate court to find the error was a miscarriage of justice under the California Constitution. The California Court of Appeal found the error to be harmless and affirmed the conviction. The individual then petitioned for habeas corpus in Federal District Court, alleging that admission of the objected-to testimony constituted a denial of due process under the Federal Constitution. The District Court granted the petition and the Federal Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that the individual had exhausted his state remedies even though he had not claimed a violation of any federal constitutional right in the state proceedings (33 F3d 1037).

Having been informed by the victim of a burglary that she suspected a certain parolee, a police officer investigating the burglary left his card at the parolee's apartment with a note asking the parolee to call the officer so that the officer could discuss something with him. Shortly thereafter the parolee called the officer who suggested that the parolee meet with him at a state patrol office close to the parolee's apartment. Upon the parolee's arrival at the office, the officer took the parolee into a room, told the parolee that he was not under arrest, closed the door, and informed the parolee of his belief that the parolee had been involved in the burglary. After the officer falsely stated that the parolee's fingerprints had been found at the burglary scene, the parolee, within five minutes after coming to the office, confessed to the burglary. The officer then advised the parolee of his Miranda rights and took a taped confession. At the end of the taped conversation, about one-half hour after he had come to the office, the parolee left upon being informed that he was not being arrested but that the case was being referred to the district attorney. Subsequently, the parolee was convicted of first degree burglary in the Circuit Court of Umatilla County, Oregon, at a trial in which the parolee had been unsuccessful in moving to suppress his burglary confession as the fruit of questioning not preceded by Miranda warnings. The Court of Appeals of Oregon affirmed (22 Ore App 494, 539 P2d 1122), but the Supreme Court of Oregon reversed, finding that although the parolee had not been arrested or otherwise formally detained, the interrogation had taken place in a coercive environment requiring Miranda warnings (549 P2d 673).

Under Rule 54(b) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure the District Court entered a judgment in favor of the plaintiff upon a money claim, without adjudicating a counterclaim made by the defendant. With permission of the Court of Appeals, the District Court amended its judgment by adding a determination that there was no just reason for delay and an express direction for the entry of judgment, such certification being required by Rule 54(b) as a prerequisite of a final judgment upon one or more but less than all of the claims in a multiple claims action.

The Florida Supreme Court's denial of a writ of habeas corpus sought by one who attacked his conviction of crime in a Florida state court on the ground that he was deprived of due process of law in being denied the assistance of counsel at his trial, was reversed, on certiorari, by the United States Supreme Court, whose ruling stated in the opinion of Stewart, J. (speaking for a unanimous Court), is adequately reflected in headnote 7, infra.

Under a Mississippi statute giving the State Tax Commission of Mississippi exclusive authority to act as wholesale distributor of alcoholic beverages to licensed retailers in the state, the Commission promulgated Regulation 25, which allowed military post exchanges, ship stores, and officers' clubs to purchase liquor directly from distillers but required the distillers to collect and remit to the Commission their usual wholesale markups. The Commission refused to allow payment of the markups into an escrow fund pending judicial determination of their legality as applied to military purchases. The United States then sued in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi for declaratory and injunctive relief against the continued enforcement of Regulation 25, plus a judgment in the total amount paid to the Commission. A three-judge District Court granted summary judgment against the United States on the ground that the Twenty-first Amendment authorized application of Regulation 25 to Keesler Air Force Base and the Naval Construction Battalion Center, over which the United States has exclusive jurisdiction, and a fortiori also to Columbus Air Force Base and Meridian Naval Air Station, over which the United States exercises concurrent jurisdiction with the state (340 F Supp 903).

In an action brought by the plaintiff in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California for a judgment declaring him to be a citizen of the United States, the issue was whether the plaintiff, a native- born American who also had Japanese nationality under Japanese law, had lost his American citizenship under 401(c) of the Nationality Act of 1940 by entering the Armed Forces of Japan. The plaintiff alone testified at the trial, stating that he was inducted into the Japanese Armed Forces pursuant to the compulsory conscription law of that country, that rumors of harsh punishment of draft evaders by the secret police and the ruthlessness of the government in power made him afraid to take any action to avoid service, and that he did not seek aid of American officials.

Purporting to act for a class consisting of all Pennsylvania residents who had signed documents containing cognovit provisions for the entry of confessed judgments in Philadelphia County, the plaintiffs instituted an action against the county's prothonotary (Clerk of the Court of Common Pleas) and sheriff in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, alleging the unconstitutionality, as a matter of due process, of Pennsylvania statutes and rules whereby a confession of judgment, pursuant to a contractual cognovit provision, may be entered without notice or hearing by a prothonotary upon application by the creditor who, although required to mail notice to the debtor within 20 days after entry of judgment, may issue a writ of execution before the notice is mailed, and whereby the debtor, to obtain relief by striking or opening the judgment, must assert prima facie grounds for relief and must persuade the court to open the judgment. Allowing intervention by finance companies, the three-judge District Court, after a hearing, held that (1) the Pennsylvania system complied with due process insofar as there was an understanding and voluntary consent of the debtor in signing the cognovit document, (2) the plaintiffs had failed to prove lack of valid consent in the execution of bonds and warrants of attorney accompanying mortgages, (3) the plaintiffs could not maintain the class action on behalf of debtors having an income of more than $ 10,000, (4) the action could be maintained on behalf of natural persons who earned less than $ 10,000 and who signed consumer financing or lease contracts containing cognovit provisions, (5) there was no intentional waiver of known rights by members of such class in executing confession of judgment clauses, the Pennsylvania procedure thus violating due process as to such class, and (6) no judgment of confession could be entered as to a member of such class after a specified future date unless it was first shown that he had knowingly and voluntarily waived his rights when executing the cognovit document (314 F Supp 1091). The plaintiffs appealed from the District Court's failure to hold the Pennsylvania statutes and rules unconstitutional on their face.

The Internal Revenue Code (26 USC 147 as amended) requires that any person making a payment to another of $ 600 or more in any calendar year shall render a return thereof to the Commissioner of Internal Revenue. Treasury Regulations issued pursuant to this statute provide (1) that each of such payments be shown on an "Information Return" listing the payee's name, the amount and kind of payment, and the payor's name, but not verified or signed by the payor; and (2) that this form be accompanied by an "Annual Information Return," signed and verified by the payor, showing the total number of "Information Returns" filed by the payor. An indictment of a taxpayer under 145(a) of the Internal Revenue Code for his wilful failure to file a tax "return," and based upon his alleged failure to file a number of unverified "Information Returns," was dismissed by the District Court on the ground that only failure to file the verified "Annual Information Return," and not failure to file the unverified "Information Return," constituted such a failure to file a tax "return" as is punishable as a crime.

The defendant was convicted of contempt in the Circuit Court of Arlington County, Virginia, for refusing to obey a decision of that court ordering him to answer questions put to him by a legislative investigative committee of the Virginia General Assembly. On appeal the Supreme Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed without opinion.

An accused was charged with capital murder and scheduled for a jury trial in a Texas state court. When the jury was being selected, the prosecution, among other matters, assertedly used peremptory challenges to exclude 91 percent of the eligible African-American venire members. However, the state trial court, under then-existing law, denied a motion by the accused to strike the jury on the accused's theory that the prosecution's use of peremptory challenges had allegedly violated the equal protection clause of the Federal Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment. The accused was convicted of capital murder, after which the trial court sentenced him to death. While the accused's state-court appeal was pending, the United States Supreme Court decided Batson v Kentucky (1986) 476 US 79, 90 L Ed 2d 69, 106 S Ct 1712, which established a three-step process for evaluating a state criminal defendant's claim that a prosecutor has used a peremptory challenge in asserted violation of the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause. Under this process, such a defendant first must make a prima facie showing that the peremptory challenge has been exercised on the basis of race. Second, if that showing is made, the prosecutor must then offer a race-neutral basis for striking the juror in question. Third, in light of the parties' submissions, the trial court must determine whether the defendant has shown purposeful discrimination.

Petitioners Abbott and Gould, defendants in unrelated prosecutions, were charged with drug and firearm offenses, including violation of 18 U. S. C. ¬ß924(c), which prohibits using, carrying, or possessing a deadly weapon in connection with ‚Äúany crime of violence or drug trafficking crime,‚Äù ¬ß924(c)(1). The minimum prison term for a ¬ß924(c) offense is five years, ¬ß924(c)(1)(A)(i), in addition to ‚Äúany other term of imprisonment imposed on the [offender],‚Äù ¬ß924(c)(1)(D)(ii). Abbott was convicted on the ¬ß924(c) count, on two predicate drug-trafficking counts, and of being a felon in possession of a firearm. He received a 15-year mandatory minimum sentence for his felon-in-possession conviction and an additional five years for his ¬ß924(c) violation. Gould‚Äôs predicate drug-trafficking crime carried a ten-year mandatory minimum sentence; he received an additional five years for his ¬ß924(c) violation. On appeal, Abbott and Gould challenged their ¬ß924(c) sentences, resting their objections on the ‚Äúexcept‚Äù clause prefacing ¬ß924(c)(1)(A). That clause provides for imposition of a minimum five-year term as a consecutive sentence ‚Äú[e]xcept to the extent that a greater minimum sentence is otherwise provided by [¬ß924(c) itself] or by any other provision of law.‚Äù Abbott urged that the ‚Äúexcept‚Äù clause was triggered by his 15-year felon-in-possession sentence; Gould said the same of the ten years commanded by his predicate trafficking crime. The Third Circuit affirmed Abbott‚Äôs sentence, concluding that the ‚Äúexcept‚Äù clause ‚Äúrefers only to other minimum sentences that may be imposed‚Äù for ¬ß924(c) violations. Gould fared no better before the Fifth Circuit.

A product patent for an inoculant to increase the nitrogen-fixing efficiencies of leguminous plants, differing from previous inoculants usable for more than one variety of plants in containing strains of bacteria discovered by the patentee not to be mutually inhibiting, was held in an opinion by Douglas, J., in which five justices concurred to be invalid as lacking in invention.

In the Corporation Court of Houston, Texas, the petitioner was convicted of nine traffic offenses which were punishable by fines only, and he was fined a total of $ 425. He was unable to pay the fines because of indigency, and pursuant to a state statute and municipal ordinance, the Corporation Court ordered him imprisoned for 85 days, each day of imprisonment serving as a substitute for $ 5 of the fines. His petition for habeas corpus was denied by the County Criminal Court of Harris County, and the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed, rejecting the petitioner's contention that because he was too poor to pay the fines his imprisonment was unconstitutional (445 SW2d 210).

Police officers, investigating allegations that illegal gambling was being conducted out of a certain apartment, conducted a warrantless search of a communal trash bin in the basement of the apartment building and found evidence of gambling activity. The police subsequently applied for and obtained a warrant to search the apartment, based in part on the evidence found in the trash bin; and they found further incriminating evidence in the apartment, which led to felony charges against an occupant of the apartment. The occupant moved to quash the search warrant on the grounds (1) that the search of the trash bin had violated his rights under the Fourth Amendment, and (2) that, without the evidence found in that search, there was not sufficient evidence to support the search warrant. A magistrate agreed and granted that motion; and a Superior Court of California reached the same conclusion, and after being informed by the prosecution that it could not proceed without the evidence seized in the apartment, the Superior Court dismissed the charges. In reversing the Superior Court's judgment, the California Court of Appeal (1) concluded that the evidence found in the trash bin could not be used to support the search warrant, but (2) held that there was sufficient other evidence to establish probable cause in support of the warrant (175 Cal App 3d 634, 221 Cal Rptr 49). The Supreme Court of California denied petitions for review filed by both sides in the case. The United States Supreme Court granted the prosecution's petition for a writ of certiorari on the question whether the search of the trash bin violated the Fourth Amendment.

Relying upon 28 USCS 1251(a), conferring original and exclusive jurisdiction on the United States Supreme Court of all controversies between two or more states, and 28 USCS 1251(b), conferring original but not exclusive jurisdiction on the Supreme Court of all controversies between the United States and a state, California, in order to quiet title to certain lands along a portion of the Colorado River forming the boundary between the states of California and Arizona, moved for leave to file a bill of complaint in the Supreme Court against Arizona and the United States, both of whom had an interest in the lands in question and were indispensible parties to the action. Arizona and the United States contended that California's suit could not be brought in the Supreme Court because the United States had not given its consent to be sued by a state in a Supreme Court action to quiet title.

After a judge of the Court of Common Pleas of Hamilton County, Ohio, had summarily denied the request of out-of-state lawyers, not admitted to practice in Ohio, to appear pro hac vice to represent the defendants in a criminal prosecution, the lawyers commenced a mandamus action in the Supreme Court of Ohio, seeking to overturn the denial of admission and to remove the trial judge from the case. The Supreme Court of Ohio dismissed the mandamus action but removed the trial judge. Thereafter, the new trial judge ruled that the Ohio Supreme Court's dismissal of the mandamus action bound him to deny permission to the lawyers to represent the criminal defendants, although he did allow the lawyers to work with local counsel in preparing the case. The out-of-state lawyers then filed the instant action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio to enjoin further prosecution of the criminal case until the state trial court held a hearing on the pro hac vice application. The District Court held that the lawyers' interest in representing the criminal defendants was a constitutionally protected property right which the state courts had infringed without according the lawyers procedural due process (434 F Supp 481), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (574 F2d 874).

At a hearing conducted in connection with an alien's application for suspension of deportation, under 19(c) of the Immigration Act of 1917, as amended, the alien refused, on the ground of possible self incrimination, to answer questions regarding his Communist Party membership. The hearing officer denied the suspension, and the Board of Immigration Appeals affirmed, as did the United States Court of Appeals of the Ninth Circuit. (263 F2d 773.)

The Eighth Circuit correctly ruled that the allegations did not show respondents made misstatements relied upon by the public or that they violated a disclosure duty. The _ 78j(b) implied private right of action did not extend to aiders and abettors. Respondents had no role in preparing or disseminating the financial statements. Respondents had no duty to disclose and their deceptive acts were not communicated to the public. No member of the investing public had knowledge of respondents' deceptive acts during the relevant times. Thus, reliance could not be shown except in an indirect chain that was too remote for liability. The company, not respondents, misled its auditor and filed fraudulent financial statements. Nothing respondents did made it necessary or inevitable for the company to record the transactions as it did, thus, the investors' "scheme liability" theory failed. In 15 U.S.C.S. _ 78t(e), Congress amended the securities laws to provide for limited coverage of aiders and abettors, in actions to be brought by the Securities and Exchange Commission, but not by private parties. Concerns with the judicial creation of a private cause of action cautioned against its expansion.

Notwithstanding his plea of not guilty by reason of insanity, defendant was convicted in a Texas state court of the crime of felony theft and sentenced to life imprisonment as a habitual offender. The Court of Criminal Appeals of Texas affirmed. (172 Tex Crim 54, 353 SW2d 855.)

The state of Indiana and several of its officials and the Indiana Coal Association and several coal mine operators brought suits against the Secretary of the Interior in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, alleging that the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (30 USCS 1201 et seq.) contravened the commerce clause of the United States Constitution (Art I, 8, cl 3), the equal protection and due process guarantees of the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment, the Tenth Amendment, and the just compensation clause of the Fifth Amendment. The suits included challenges to the "prime farmland" provisions of the Act ( 507(b)(16), 508(a)(2)(C), 510(d)(1), 515(b)(7), (20), and 519(c)(2); 30 USCS 1257(b)(16), 1258(a)(2)(C), 1260(d)(1), 1265(b)(7), (20), and 1269(c)(2)), as well as 15 other substantive provisions applying to surface mining generally ( 515(b)(3), (5), 522(a), (c), (d), (e)(4), (5), 508(a)(2), (3), (4), (8), (10), 510(b)(1), (2), and 515(b)(19), (20); 30 USCS 1265(b)(3)(5), 1272(a), (c), (d), (e)(4), (5), 1258(a)(2), (3), (4), (8), (10), 1260(b)(1), (2), and 1265(b)(19), (20). Following a hearing, the District Court issued an order and opinion sustaining each of the plaintiffs' constitutional challenges and permanently enjoined the Secretary of the Interior from enforcing the challenged sections of the Act (501 F Supp 452).

An alien against whom an order of deportation had been entered by reason of his advocacy of the overthrow of the government by force and violence, was indicted for violation of 20(c) of the Immigration Act of 1917, as amended (8 USC 156(c)), making it a felony for an alien against whom such an order is outstanding, wilfully to fail or refuse to make timely application, in good faith, for travel or other documents necessary to his departure. The district court dismissed the indictment on the ground that the statute was unconstitutionally vague and indefinite.

With respect to some provisions of the Federal Power Act, as amended (FPA) (16 USCS 824 et seq.), 16 USCS 824(b) provided that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) had jurisdiction over "the transmission of electric energy in interstate commerce" and "the sale of electric energy at wholesale in interstate commerce." However, 824(b) also provided that FERC had no jurisdiction over facilities used for the generation of electric energy, over facilities used in local distribution or only for the transmission of electric energy in intrastate commerce, or over facilities for the transmission of electric energy consumed wholly by the transmitter. Moreover, 16 USCS 824(a) generally provided that federal regulation was to extend to only those matters which were not subject to regulation by the states.

The owner of a combination patent covering a fish-canning machine, but not covering the components thereof or the size of the cans serviced by the machine, instituted a suit for infringement in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California against the second-hand purchaser of certain machines, manufactured and originally sold under the patentee's authorization, and against the person retained by the secondhand purchaser to clean the machines and to resize some of the elements of the machines to adapt them for use with smaller cans than those serviced by the machines as originally constructed. The District Court held for the patentee (200 F Supp 841), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed, on the ground that the adaptation of the machines constituted "reconstruction" rather than "repair" (314 F2d 71).

A trust instrument, executed in Illinois, provided that during the settlor's life the trust income was to be paid to his three children; if any of the children died before the settlor, to the child's issue, if any, otherwise to the settlor's other children; and that upon his death the corpus was to be distributed in the same manner. However, no provision was made for distribution of the corpus and its accumulated income should the settlor survive all of his children and grandchildren.

The plaintiff, a manufacturer of shoes and customer of the defendant manufacturer of shoe machinery, brought, in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania, the present treble damage antitrust action based on defendant's monopolization of the shoe machinery market by offering its machines only for leasing but not for sale. In support of its action, plaintiff relied solely on a decree in favor of the United States in a former action against defendant as prima facie evidence under 15 USC 16(a). The District Court awarded damages, in the amount of $ 4,239,609. (245 F Supp 258.) On appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed the finding of liability but disagreed with the District Court on certain questions relating to the damage award. (377 F2d 776.)

An Air Force enlisted man who had been accepted in an officer training project and who had been assigned to an Air Force Base in Ohio "with duty at Arizona State University" was removed from the program, allegedly for engaging in civil rights activities on the campus. While he was seeking administrative relief through command channels, he was reassigned to an Air Force Base in Georgia to complete the remainder of his re-enlistment in a noncommissioned status. After exhausting those remedies, he was given permission by his superiors in Georgia to attend the same university in Arizona under a different program and at his own expense. Thereafter he filed his application for habeas corpus in the District Court for the District of Arizona, alleging that his enlistment contract had been breached and that he was being detained unlawfully. The respondents to the suit were the Secretary of the Air Force, the commander of the Georgia Air Force base (who had custody and control over the petitioner), and the commander of the Air Force ROTC program at Arizona State University, who was the only respondent present in Arizona, but who concededly had no control over the petitioner. The District Court denied the application, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed.

Section 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 USCS 78p(b)) provides that (1) profits realized by corporate insiders--defined as beneficial owners, directors, or officers of a corporation--from short-swing transactions in the corporation's securities are recoverable by the corporation, and (2) a suit to recover such short-swing profits may be "instituted" by (a) the issuer of the securities, or (b) "the owner of any security of the issuer." A person who held shares of a corporation's common stock brought suit under 16(b) in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York on behalf of the corporation against individuals and entities that allegedly had operated as a single beneficial owner of more than 10 percent of the corporation's common stock, so as to be covered by 16(b), and had profited from short-swing transactions in the corporation's stock. Less than 6 months after the plaintiff filed his complaint, the corporation was merged with a subsidiary of a second corporation and became the wholly owned subsidiary of the second corporation. As a result of this acquisition, the plaintiff, along with the other stockholders of the original corporation, received a combination of cash and stock in the second corporation in exchange for his stock in the original corporation. Accordingly, the plaintiff amended his complaint so as to claim to prosecute the 16(b) action on behalf of the second corporation as well as the original corporation. The defendants moved for summary judgment on the ground that the plaintiff no longer owned any security of the "issuer"--that is, the original corporation--and that he had thus lost standing to maintain the action. The District Court, in granting the defendants'motion, concluded that only the second corporation, as sole stockholder in the original corporation, could continue to prosecute the action. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, reversing on appeal, said that (1) 16(b) does not specifically bar the maintenance of suits by former shareholders, and (2) the remedial policy of 16(b) favored recognizing the plaintiff's continued standing after the merger (909 F2d 724).

The respondents applied to the Comptroller of the Currency for a certificate authorizing them to organize a national bank in a particular community. After receiving information obtained through a national bank examiner's field investigation, the Comptroller denied the application and notified the respondents that because the community already was adequately served by other banks, there was no need for the proposed national bank. In the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina, the respondents sought review of the Comptroller's decision. Holding that there was substantial basis for the Comptroller's decision and that it was neither capricious nor arbitrary, the District Court granted the Comptroller's motion for summary judgment (329 F Supp 1302). The Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit vacated the District Court's judgment on the ground that the Court of Appeals could not determine either what particular factors had been considered by the Comptroller or whether he had acted within permissible bounds of discretion in denying the application, and the Court of Appeals remanded the case for a trial de novo before the District Court (463 F2d 632).

The motion for leave to proceed in forma pauperis and the petition for writ of certiorari are granted. The judgment is vacated and the case is remanded for consideration in light of Coppedge v. United States, ante, p. 438.

In 1983, a Florida state court convicted a defendant of first-degree murder and sentenced him to death. A subsequently enacted Florida statute provide for lethal injection as a means of execution. Although the statute did not provide for any specific lethal-injection procedure, a Florida death row inmate's challenge to a particular three-drug sequence of injections was rejected by the Supreme Court of Florida in 2000. In December 2005, less than a month before the defendant's scheduled execution, the defendant challenged Florida's lethal-injection procedure by filing a postconviction petition in a Florida trial court, which dismissed his claim as procedurally barred. The Supreme Court of Florida affirmed ( 921 So. 2d 579, cert. denied, 546 U.S. ____, 126 S. Ct. 1441, 164 L. Ed. 2d 141). In an action brought in January 2006, pursuant to 42 U.S.C.S. _ 1983, in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Florida, the defendant (1) alleged that the injection procedure that would likely be used on him--the same three-drug procedure that had been at issue in the 2000 Florida Supreme Court decision--(a) caused a foreseeable risk of gratuitous and unnecessary pain, and (b) violated the prohibition of cruel and unusual punishments in the Federal Constitution's Eighth Amendment; and (2) sought an injunction to bar state officials "from executing [the defendant] in the manner they currently intend." However, the District Court, in dismissing the complaint, concluded that (1) the _ 1983 claim was the functional equivalent of a federal habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C.S. _ 2254; and (2) for procedural reasons, the  [**45]  petition was barred under 28 U.S.C.S. _ 2244(b). The United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit affirmed ( 437 F.3d 1084).

After an employer obtained a temporary restraining order in the Circuit Court of Duval County, Florida, prohibiting a strike in violation of a collective bargaining agreement provision forbidding work stoppages "because of a jurisdictional dispute," the union sought a writ of prohibition in the District Court of Appeal, First District. The Court of Appeal denied the writ (248 So 2d 179), but the Florida Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeal's decision on the ground that the National Labor Relations Board had exclusive jurisdiction of the case (279 So 2d 300).

Orders of the National Labor Relations Board requiring employers to permit distribution of union literature by nonemployee union organizers on employer's property were denied enforcement by the Courts of Appeals for the Fifth and Tenth Circuits (in Nos. 250 and 251, respectively); but a similar order was enforced by the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit in No. 422. In each case the Board had found that the employer's denial of access to his property by nonemployees was within the amended National Labor Relations Act's prohibition of employer interference, restraint, or coercion of employees in the exercise of rights guaranteed by the act.

The National Labor Relations Board originally adopted a practice of computing back pay on the basis of the entire period from an employee's discriminatory discharge to the date of offer of reinstatement. Subsequently the Board adopted a formula, called "the Woolworth formula," under which it computed back pay upon a quarterly basis, so that earnings made by the employee in one particular quarter had no effect upon the employer's back-pay liability for any other quarter. The Woolworth formula was applied to an employer, the income of whose employees, because of the seasonal nature of its business, was not constant. The objection that such application of the formula was oppressive was made by the employer in the Supreme Court for the first time.

While on parole from a federal rape conviction, the parolee was convicted of federal manslaughter and second degree murder offenses and sentenced to concurrent 10-year sentences for the homicides. Shortly after the parolee's incarceration under the homicide sentences, the United States Board of Parole (later renamed the Parole Commission) issued a parole violator warrant which was not executed, but which instead was lodged with prison officials as a detainer. The parolee requested that the warrant be executed immediately so that any imprisonment imposed for violation of his earlier parole could run concurrently with his homicide sentences, but the Board announced its intention to execute the warrant only upon the parolee's release from the homicide sentences. The parolee then instituted a habeas corpus action in a United States District Court in the Tenth Federal Judicial Circuit, seeking dismissal of the parole violator warrant on the ground that he had been improperly denied a prompt parole revocation hearing. The District Court dismissed the petition, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed.

An inmate at a state prison was tried and convicted in the Circuit Court for Allegany County, Maryland, of the first-degree murder of his cellmate. In the sentencing phase of the trial, the jury was provided with a verdict form, parts of which (1) presented jurors with a list of possible mitigating circumstances, accompanied by spaces in which they could check "yes" or "no" and preceded by a statement that the jury "unanimously find[s] that each of the following mitigating circumstances which is marked 'yes' has been proven to exist" by a preponderance of the evidence "and each mitigating circumstance marked 'no' has not been proven" by a preponderance of the evidence, and (2) asked the jury to affirm or deny that it "unanimously" found that the mitigating circumstances marked "yes" in the preceding section outweighed the aggravating circumstances marked "yes" in a previous section. The trial judge's instructions to the jury repeatedly emphasized that all jury determinations, including findings as to mitigating circumstances, had to be unanimous. The jury then (1) found that there was an aggravating circumstance in the case, (2) checked the spaces marked "no" after each mitigating circumstance listed on the verdict form and wrote "none" in the space for "other mitigating circumstances," and (3) returned a sentence of death. The inmate appealed his conviction and sentence, partly on the theory that the state's death penalty statute, as applied, was unconstitutionally mandatory because it required jurors to impose a death sentence if they unanimously found an aggravating circumstance but could not unanimously agree that any particular mitigating circumstance was present, even if some or all jurors believed that some mitigating circumstance was present. In affirming the death sentence, the Maryland Court of Appeals (1) agreed that jurors would be improperly prevented from giving due consideration to mitigating evidence if the statute and verdict form were construed as the inmate suggested; but (2) ruled that the statute and form were to be construed as requiring the jury to agree unanimously on all critical issues including the determination that any given mitigating circumstance was not established, so that the death penalty could not be imposed if even one juror adhered to the position that a mitigating circumstance existed and was not outweighed by the aggravating circumstances; and (3) directed that a jury unable to unanimously agree whether a particular mitigating circumstance existed should leave the verdict form blank as to that circumstance and proceed to the balancing stage, with each juror weighing the mitigating circumstances he or she found to exist (310 Md 33, 527 A2d 3).

Certain enlisted members of the United States Navy brought an action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia seeking payment of re-enlistment bonuses under the terms of the Variable Re-enlistment Bonus program as it existed at the time they agreed to extend their enlistments. The government claimed that (1) the terms of the program as it existed at the time the members began to serve their extensions controlled as to whether bonuses should be paid, and (2) no payment under the program should be made to any member who began to serve his extension after the Variable Re-enlistment Bonus program had been repealed. The District Court ordered that the bonuses be paid (365 F Supp 140), and the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed (533 F2d 1167).

Some police officers in California--who, as a result of an investigation of a gang-related driveby shooting, believed that at least one gang member (1) resided in a particular house, and (2) was armed and dangerous--obtained a warrant that authorized a broad search of the house for deadly weapons and evidence of gang membership. The police officers, understanding that the gang was composed primarily of illegal immigrants, notified the United States Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) of the intended search. An INS officer accompanied the police officers during the search. During the 2-to-3 hour duration of the search, occupants of the house (1) remained in handcuffs in the house's garage, (2) were guarded by one or two officers, and (3) were allowed to move around the garage. Also during this detention, (1) an officer asked for each occupant's name, date of birth, place of birth, and immigration status; and (2) the INS officer asked the detainees for their immigration documentation. One occupant, whose documentation had confirmed her permanent-resident status, brought against at least two of the officers under 42 U.S.C.S. _ 1983 a suit alleging that she had been detained for an unreasonable time and in an unreasonable manner in violation of the Federal Constitution's Fourth Amendment. The United States District Court for the Central District of California denied the officers' motion for summary judgment, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed in pertinent part and remanded ( 226 F.3d 1031).

Geraldine Tyler owned a condominium in Hennepin County, Minnesota, that accumulated about $15,000 in unpaid real estate taxes along with interest and penalties. The County seized the condo and sold it for $40,000, keeping the $25,000 excess over Tyler‚Äôs tax debt for itself. Minn. Stat. ¬ß¬ß281.18, 282.07, 282.08. Tyler filed suit, alleging that the County had unconstitutionally retained the excess value of her home above her tax debt in violation of the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause of the Eighth Amendment. The District Court dismissed the suit for failure to state a claim, and the Eighth Circuit affirmed.

The automobile in which two servicemen were riding, not in the performance of their duties, was struck at a highway intersection by an army truck, thereby causing the death of one and personal injuries to the other under circumstances which, in the case of persons not members of the armed forces of the United States, would have given rise to a right of action against the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act.

The State of Hawaii filed this original action against the Director of the Bureau of the Budget under Art. III, _ 2, of the Constitution, seeking to obtain an order requiring him to (1) withdraw his advice to federal agencies that _ 5 (e) of the Hawaii Statehood Act, which provides for the conveyance to the State of land "no longer needed by the United States," does not apply to lands obtained by the United States through purchase, condemnation or gift; (2) determine whether a certain tract of land in Hawaii acquired by the United States through condemnation was "needed by the United States"; and (3) convey this land, if not needed, to Hawaii. Held: The complaint is dismissed, because this is a suit against the United States which has not consented to the maintenance of such a suit against it. Pp. 57-58.

Under 502(g)(2) and 515 of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) (29 USCS 1132(g)(2), 1145), trustees of multiemployer pension plans are provided with a federal remedy to collect certain delinquent employer pension plan contributions. A company was a party to two multiparty employer collective bargaining agreements which obligated the company to make contributions to eight different employee benefit plans. As the expiration date of the agreements approached, the company notified both unions involved that, upon expiration, the company (1) would no longer be bound by the agreements and (2) was prepared to negotiate independently. After the agreements expired, the company ceased to make the contributions called for in the agreements, whereupon suits--consolidated in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California--were filed against the company by the trustees of the eight plans. These suits alleged that (1) federal jurisdiction existed under 502(g)(2) and 515 of ERISA; and (2) the company's unilateral decision to change the terms and conditions of employment, by discontinuing its pension plan contributions, constituted a breach of the company's duty to bargain in good faith and violated 8(a)(5) of the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) (29 USCS 158(a)(5)). The District Court, however, held that it lacked jurisdiction over the suits, and granted summary judgment in favor of the company, on the grounds that (1) 515 of ERISA did not apply to an employer's obligation under 8(a)(5) of the NLRA; and (2) the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) had exclusive jurisdiction over the trustees' claims. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed, expressing the view that the primary jurisdiction of the NLRB pre-empted a trust fund's suit in District Court, under 502(g)(2) and 515 of ERISA, to recover delinquent employer contributions accrued after a collective bargaining agreement had expired (779 F2d 497).

Petitioner, a Negro, was indicted for murder by an all-white grand jury and convicted by an all-white petit jury, notwithstanding a timely motion to quash the indictment. Although there were 12,511 adult Negroes in the county out of a total adult population of 34,821 and there were at least 25 Negro qualified male electors eligible for jury service, the venires for the term from which the grand and petit juries were selected did not contain the name of a single Negro and no Negro had served on a grand or petit criminal court jury in the county for 30 years.

A Virginia corporate scrap processor sued Maryland officials in the United States District Court for the District of Maryland, challenging the constitutionality of the Maryland junk automobile statute under which Maryland paid a bounty to scrap processors for the destruction of any vehicle formerly titled in Maryland, upon proof of ownership, permitting Maryland processors to prove ownership of a "hulk" by a simple indemnity agreement but requiring non-Maryland processors to prove ownership by a certificate of title, a police certificate vesting title, a bill of sale from a police auction, or a licensed wrecker's certificate. A three-judge District Court ruled that the statute violated the commerce clause of the United States Constitution (Art I, 8, cl 3) and denied the Virginia scrap processor the equal protection of the laws (391 F Supp 46).

A Federal Communications Commission examiner's award of a radio broadcast license to one of two mutually exclusive applicants therefor, each of whom sought to serve a different community, was overruled by the Commission; the Commission awarded the license to the other applicant in order to secure local competition in the community to be served by that applicant, such community having theretofore had only one local broadcasting station.

The Court having exercised original jurisdiction over this controversy between two sovereign States; the issues raised having been heard in an evidentiary proceeding before the Special Master appointed by the Court; the Court having heard argument on the Final Report of the Special Master and the exceptions filed by the state parties; the Court having issued its opinion on the issues raised in the exceptions, which is reported at 523 U.S. 767, 118 S. Ct. 1726, 140 L. Ed. 2d 993 (1998); and the Special Master having submitted his Report Upon Recommittal;

The petition for rehearing is granted. The order entered March 20, 1961, 365 U.S. 844, denying the petition for writ of certiorari is vacated and the petition for writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit is granted. Two of the children, Frank Southard and Bernice Little, filed an answer and also cross-petitioned against D. S. MacDonald, Jr., alleging that they had employed him as their attorney to represent them in the probate proceedings pending in the County Court of Bryan County on a contingent fee contract, after the death of their father, but during the life of their mother, involving a joint will of their deceased parents; that he had defrauded them as to the contingent fee contract, and also in securing a warranty deed from them covering 40 per cent of the land recovered for them from the estate of their parents.

South Carolina prison inmates who claimed that they had been unnecessarily beaten by prison guards during a prison uprising sought criminal arrest warrants against the guards from a state court magistrate. After the magistrate expressed his intent to issue the warrants, the state solicitor--as a result of a meeting with the legal advisor to the state's department of corrections, the prison warden, the county sheriff, and deputy attorney--wrote the magistrate a letter which requested that the warrants not be issued and stated that the solicitor intended to ask state officials to conduct an investigation concerning the charges made against the officers involved. The magistrate did not issue the warrants, and no investigation was conducted. The inmates subsequentely filed suit in the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina contending, among other claims, that the state correctional officials had conspired in bad faith to block the issuance of the arrest warrants and thereby violated 42 USCS 1983 and 1985(3). The District Court ultimately concluded that the state correctional officials denied the inmates their right to a meaningful ability to set in motion the governmental machinery, because the officials' activity stopped the machinery unlawfully, not in a proper way, as for example, upon a valid determination of lack of probable cause, and the court awarded the inmates compensatory and punitive damages. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed, concluding that even though a private citizen lacks a judicially cognizable interest in the prosecution or nonprosecution of another, that did not foreclose the inmates' right to seek an arrest warrant.

Petitioner veteran prevailed in an action for disability benefits against respondent Secretary of Veterans Affairs, and the veteran applied for an award of attorney fees and costs pursuant to the Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA). Upon the grant of a writ of certiorari, the veteran appealed the judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit which upheld the dismissal of the application as defective in content. The veteran's EAJA application failed to include the statutorily required allegation that the Secretary's position was not substantially justified, and the veteran's amendment of the application to include the allegation was not accomplished prior to expiration of the statutory period for filing the application. The veteran contended that the amendment cured the defect in the otherwise timely application, but the Secretary argued that no proper application was filed within the required time. The United States Supreme Court held that the curative amendment was permissible after the filing period expired and the veteran's application, as amended, qualified for consideration and determination on the merits.
