The required allegation that the Secretary's position was not substantially justified was merely a pleading burden to discourage irresponsible litigation, rather than an essential notice of the Secretary's well established burden of proving substantial justification. Further, the amendment was deemed timely under the relation-back doctrine since the amended application arose out of the conduct, transaction, or occurrence set forth in the initial application.

Under 18 USCS 922(d)(4), it is unlawful for a licensed firearms dealer to sell firearms to a person who has been adjudicated a mental defective or committed to a mental institution. Other federal firearms disabilities related to mental capacity or institutional commitment are contained in 18 USCS 922(g), 922(h), and 18 USCS Appx 1202(a)(1), 1202(a)(3). In 1982, after a customer, who had been involuntarily committed to a mental hospital for several days in 1971, answered affirmatively as to whether he had been committed to a mental hospital, a store in New Jersey refused to sell a firearm to the customer, in accordance with 922(d)(4). Under 18 USCS 925(c) (later amended) as it then read, certain former felons could apply to the United States Treasury's Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms for administrative relief, but no such relief was then available to former mental patients. When the Bureau therefore rejected the customer's request for a special exemption from federal firearms disabilities, the customer filed suit in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey, challenging the constitutionality of the federal firearms legislation. The District Court concluded that those portions of the federal firearms statutes which deprived the customer of his ability to purchase a firearm were unconstitutional under the Fifth Amendment, for (1) the statutory scheme violated equal protection principles due to the lack of a rational basis for singling out mental patients for permanent firearms-disability status, particularly as compared to convicts; and (2) the statutory scheme unconstitutionally created an irrebuttable presumption that one who had been committed, no matter what the circumstances, was forever mentally ill and dangerous (602 F Supp 682). After the United States Supreme Court noted probable jurisdiction of the Federal Government's appeal of the decision, and the case had been argued, Congress passed a statute (Firearm Owners' Protection Act, PL 99-308, 100 Stat 449) which (1) amended 18 USCS 925(c) to permit administrative relief by the Secretary of the Treasury from firearms disabilities to any person who was prohibited under the federal statutes from possessing, shipping, transporting, or receiving firearms or ammunition (100 Stat 449, 105); and (2) made this amendment applicable to any pending action, petition, or appellate proceeding (100 Stat 449, 110).

After the Secretary of Agriculture had issued an order requiring that milk distributors located in milk marketing areas pay nearby farmers higher prices for milk than were paid to farmers located a greater distance from such areas, farmers in the latter group brought suit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia and obtained a judgment invalidating the Secretary's order and granting injunctive relief. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed (131 App DC 109, 402 F2d 660).

In 2012 Alabama redrew the boundaries of the State's 105 House districts and 35 Senate districts. In doing so, while Alabama sought to achieve numerous traditional districting objectives-e.g., compactness, not splitting counties or precincts, minimizing change, and protecting incumbents-it placed yet greater importance on two goals: (1) minimizing a district's deviation from precisely equal population, by keeping any deviation less than 1% of the theoretical ideal; and (2) seeking to avoid retrogression with respect to racial minorities' "ability to elect their preferred candidates of choice" under ¬ß5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, 52 U. S. C. ¬ß10304(b), by maintaining roughly the same black population percentage in existing majority-minority districts. Appellants-Alabama Legislative Black Caucus (Caucus), Alabama Democratic Conference (Conference), and others-claim that Alabama's new district boundaries create a "racial gerrymander" in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause. After a bench trial, the three-judge District Court ruled (2 to 1) for the State. It recognized that electoral districting violates the Equal Protection Clause when race is the "predominant" consideration in deciding "to place a significant number of voters within or without a particular district," Miller v. Johnson, 515 U. S. 900, 913, 916, and the use of race is not "narrowly tailored to serve a compelling state interest," Shaw v. Hunt, 517 U. S. 899, 902 (Shaw II). In ruling against appellants, it made four critical determinations: (1) that both appellants had argued "that the Aots as a whole constitute racial gerrymanders," and that the Conference had also argued that the State had racially gerrymandered Senate Districts 7, 11, 22, and 26; (2) that the Conference lacked standing to make its racial gerrymandering claims; (3) that, in any event, appellants' claims must fail because race "was not the predominant motivating factor" in making the redistricting decisions; and (4) that, even were it wrong about standing and predominance, these claims must fail because any predominant use of race was "narrowly tailored" to serve a "compelling state interest" in avoiding retrogression under ¬ß5.

The Ninth Circuit had not discussed any specific facts or mentioned the reasoning of the other three courts that had rejected the Batson claim. The Batson issue turned largely on an evaluation of credibility. On federal habeas review, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 imposed a highly deferential standard for evaluating state-court rulings and demanded that state-court decisions be given the benefit of the doubt. The trial court had credited the prosecutor's race-neutral explanations, and the California Court of Appeal carefully reviewed the record at some length in upholding the trial court's findings. The state appellate court's decision was plainly not unreasonable. There was simply no basis for the Ninth Circuit to reach the opposite conclusion, particularly in such a dismissive manner.

The Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas convicted the defendant on 56 counts of forgery and 56 counts of theft, and sentenced him to 2 to 5 years of imprisonment on a single theft count and 5 years of probation on one of the forgery counts. Sentence was suspended on the remaining counts. The defendant appealed all 112 convictions to the Superior Court of Pennsylvania, which ruled that the statute of limitations barred the prosecution of 34 of the theft counts, including the count on which the defendant had received his sentence of imprisonment. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania affirmed the Superior Court's ruling on the statute of limitations, and also denied the Commonwealth's request that the case be remanded to the trial court for resentencing on the remaining 22 theft counts, the court holding that resentencing on the counts which were affirmed after an appeal by the Commonwealth was barred by the double jeopardy clause of the Fifth Amendment when the sentence of imprisonment on another count was vacated.

A driver was convicted in a Justice of the Peace Court in Mississippi of four misdemeanors--reckless driving, driving while his license was revoked, driving on the wrong side of the road, and driving while intoxicated--in connection with a traffic accident in which a passenger in the other vehicle was killed. The driver gave notice of appeal and the case was transferred to the Circuit Court for trial de novo as permitted under Mississippi law. While this appeal was pending, a grand jury indicted the driver for manslaughter, a felony, based on the same accident. The driver was arraigned on the appeals and the felony indictment simultaneously, and the five charges were set for trial together, but during the trial, the state elected not to press the misdemeanor charges. The jury convicted the defendant of manslaughter, and the trial judge sentenced him to 20 years in prison. The Mississippi Supreme Court affirmed and refused leave to pursue state postconviction remedies. The driver then brought the present habeas corpus action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi which granted the writ upon the recommendation of a magistrate on grounds that the manslaughter prosecution violated the double jeopardy clause because proof of manslaughter required proof of all the elements of reckless driving of which the driver had already been convicted, and on grounds that substitution of a felony charge covering the conduct for which the driver had already been convicted of four misdemeanors violated the due process clause. The Court of Appeals (693 F2d 132) for the Fifth Circuit affirmed, relying solely on the double jeopardy argument.

On dismissal of an indictment for violating the Federal Anti-Trust Act on the ground that women had improperly been excluded from the grand jury, defendant obtained orders for the return of documents produced before the grand jury in compliance with a subpoena, unsuccessfully challenged as being too sweeping, and restraining the United States from using any knowledge, information or evidence obtained from or contained in such documents.

Defendant, a labor union officer, was indicted and convicted in a Washington state court on a charge of embezzlement of union funds. His conviction was affirmed by the Supreme Court of Washington, the judges dividing equally. (56 Wash 2d 474, 349 P2d 387, adhered to on reh 56 Wash 2d 474, 353 P2d 429.) He attacked his conviction in the United States Supreme Court as invalid under the due process and equal protection clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. His attack was based primarily on voluminous and continuous adverse publicity circulated by news media in the vicinity of the place of the trial, it being alleged that this publicity prevented the selection of a fair grand jury and petit jury. As to the grand jury, it was claimed specifically that it was unfairly impaneled and instructed, and that a Washington statute permitting persons in custody to challenge grand jurors denied equal protection to persons not in custody, such as the defendant, who were investigated by grand juries.

The plaintiff, while a resident of Illinois, purchased from a British company licensed to do business in Illinois, Florida, and other states, a contract of insurance providing world-wide coverage against "all risks" of loss or damage to the property covered. Some months thereafter the plaintiff, having moved to Florida, instituted the present diversity of citizenship action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida to recover losses sustained in Florida and caused by deliberate acts of plaintiff's wife. The litigation presented three issues: (1) whether the "all risks" coverage of the policy included losses resulting from wilful injury to or appropriation of the injured property by the insured's spouse; (2) whether, as a matter of Florida law, a Florida statute invalidating contract provisions fixing the period of time for bringing suit under the contract was applicable to the insurance contract involved, the suit not having been brought within 12 months of the discovery of the loss, as required by the insurance policy; and (3) whether, as a matter of federal constitutional law, the Florida statute mentioned above could be applied to the insurance policy purchased in a sister state under the circumstances described above. The District Court entered judgment upon a verdict for the plaintiff and denied a motion for judgment non obstante veredicto. On appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed, sustaining the defense based upon the suit clause of the insurance contract on the ground that Florida could not apply its statute to the Illinois-made contract consistently with the requirement of due process. (265 F2d 522.)

A husband left Massachusetts, in which his wife had obtained a decree for separate support, went to Nevada, and there instituted a divorce suit in which the wife filed an answer admitting as true the allegations of the husband's complaint as to his Nevada residence, and a cross complaint for divorce. At the hearing both husband and wife appeared personally and were represented by counsel. The wife raised no question as to the husband's domicil. The Nevada court, after finding that it had jurisdiction of the parties and subject matter, entered a decree in favor of the wife. Shortly thereafter the parties returned to Massachusetts. The wife subsequently instituted contempt proceedings in a Massachusetts court against the husband for failing to abide by the terms of the Massachusetts decree for separate support. The husband set up the Nevada divorce obtained by the wife as a bar.

In a class action commenced March 3, 1972 in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, the plaintiff challenged the constitutionality of California Elections Code provisions requiring candidates in a primary election to pay a filing fee before having their names listed on the primary ballot. The plaintiff asserted that he wished to become a congressional candidate and that the state filing fee system barred indigents, such as himself, from seeking elective office and from voting for the candidates of their choice. On March 9, one day after oral argument and one day before the deadline for filing nomination papers, a three-judge Federal District Court granted a preliminary injunction requiring the state to allow the plaintiff and others similarly situated to place their names on the ballot without paying the required fee, so long as they were otherwise eligible and had deposited an affidavit of indigency (342 F Supp 1353).

Petitioner, alleged to have robbed five individuals on a single occasion in September, 1950, was, in October, 1954, convicted, on an indictment charging robbery of one of the individuals, in a prosecution in the County Court, Bergen County, New Jersey. Petitioner had previously been prosecuted on an indictment charging robbery of three of the other individuals, and had been acquitted; at both trials, only the fourth individual identified petitioner as one of the robbers, and petitioner relied upon the same alibi. Petitioner's conviction was affirmed by the Superior Court of New Jersey, Appellate Division (35 NJ Super 555) and by the Supreme Court of New Jersey (21 NJ 496, 122 A2d 628). Both state courts rejected claims that petitioner had been denied due process.

After having been convicted in an Oklahoma state court of felony murder (arising from an armed robbery), the defendant was subsequently convicted in the District Court, Tulsa County, Oklahoma, on a separate information charging the underlying offense of robbery with firearms, the trial court having rejected the defendant's claim that the second prosecution violated the double jeopardy clause of the Fifth Amendment. The Court of Criminal Appeals of Oklahoma affirmed (555 P2d 76).

Respondents were convicted separately of violating a Virginia statute that makes it a felony "for any person . . . , with the intent of intimidating any person or group . . . , to burn . . . a cross on the property of another, a highway or other public place," and specifies that "any such burning . . . shall be prima facie evidence of an intent to intimidate a person or group." When respondent Black objected on First Amendment grounds to his trial court's jury instruction that cross burning by itself is sufficient evidence from which the required "intent to intimidate" could be inferred, the prosecutor responded that the instruction was taken straight out of the Virginia Model Instructions. Respondent O'Mara pleaded guilty to charges of violating the statute, but reserved the right to challenge its constitutionality. At respondent Elliott's trial, the judge instructed the jury as to what the Commonwealth had to prove, but did not give an instruction on the meaning of the word "intimidate," nor on the statute's prima facie evidence provision. Consolidating all three cases, the Virginia Supreme Court held that the cross-burning statute is unconstitutional on its face; that it is analytically indistinguishable from the ordinance found unconstitutional in R. A. V. v. St. Paul, 505 U.S. 377, 120 L. Ed. 2d 305, 112 S. Ct. 2538; that it discriminates on the basis of content and viewpoint since it selectively chooses only cross burning because of its distinctive message; and that the prima facie evidence provision renders the statute overbroad because the enhanced probability of prosecution under the statute chills the expression of protected speech.

An individual was convicted in Florida state court on several felony counts, and his convictions were affirmed by the Third District Court of Appeal of Florida (358 So 2d 1109). The Supreme Court of Florida dismissed an application for a writ of certiorari, on the ground that the application was not filed timely (362 So 2d 1057), and a petition for rehearing and clarification was later denied. The defendant subsequently filed a petition for habeas corpus in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, contending that he had been denied his right to the effective assistance of counsel by the failure of his retained counsel to file the application for certiorari on time. The District Court denied the petition, stating that the failure to file a timely application for certiorari did not render counsel's action so grossly deficient as to render the proceedings fundamentally unfair. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed and remanded (649 F2d 290).

These two, consolidated cases presented the question whether federal courts have discretion to exceed the $ 30-per-day limit for expert witness fee awards prescribed by 28 USCS 1821. In the first case (No. 86-322), after a verdict was directed in favor of the defendant in an antitrust action brought in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, the defendant sought reimbursement of its litigation expenses, including substantial expert witness fees. The District Court (1) held that Rule 54(d) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure granted it discretion to exceed the $ 30-per-day limit for witness fee awards prescribed by 1821, and (2) awarded the defendant over $ 86,000 for its expert witness fees (102 FRD 73). En banc, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed and held that the limit of 1821 controlled (790 F2d 1193). In the second case (No. 86-328), after a judgment on the merits was entered in favor of the defendant in an employment discrimination action brought in the United States District Court for the Nothern District of Mississippi, the District Court declined to order the plaintiff to reimburse the defendant for expert witness fees in excess of the $ 30-per-day limit prescribed by 1821. En banc, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the District Court decision and held that the 1821 limit was dispositive (790 F2d 1174).

Certain organizations concerned with environmental protection petitioned the Department of Housing and Urban Development to prepare an environmental impact statement under 102(2)(C) of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 USCS 4332(2)(C))--which requires all federal agencies, "to the fullest extent possible," to include an environmental impact statement in every recommendation or report as to "major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment"--before the Department allowed a private real estate developer's statement of record as to a proposed subdivision adjacent to a state-designated "scenic" river in Oklahoma to become effective, such disclosure statement having been filed with the Department as required by the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act (15 USCS 1701 et seq.). The Disclosure Act requires that private real estate developers file statements of record as to new subdivisions and furnish property reports to prospective purchasers of lots, and provides that statements of record are to become effective within 30 days after being filed with the Department unless found to be incomplete or inaccurate. After the Department rejected the environmental protection organizations' request, the organizations instituted an action against Department officials in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Oklahoma, seeking a declaratory judgment and an injunction requiring that the defendants conduct an environmental study in compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act prior to registration of the developer's statement of record. The District Court entered judgment for the plaintiffs, ordering the preparation of an environmental impact statement and enjoining the Department from filing the developer's statement of record until a public hearing was held on the environmental impact study (382 F Supp 69). The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed the District Court's holding that a public hearing was necessary on the environmental impact statement, but affirmed the remainder of the District Court's judgment (520 F2d 240).

Assuming, without deciding, that the school's coach was speaking as a citizen about matters of public concern, the association could impose only those conditions on such speech that were necessary to managing an efficient and effective state-sponsored high school athletic league. Hard-sell tactics directed at middle school students could lead to exploitation, distort competition, and foster an environment in which athletics were prized more highly than academics. The association's rule discouraged precisely the sort of conduct that might lead to those harms, any one of which would detract from a high school sports league's ability to operate efficiently and effectively. Thus, the Supreme Court found that the First Amendment did not excuse the school from abiding by the same anti-recruiting rule that governed the conduct of its sister schools. As to the school's due process claim, even accepting the questionable holding that the association's closed-door deliberations were unconstitutional, any due process violation was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt because the school identified nothing investigators shared with the association's board that the school did not already know.

In 1968, the State of Georgia enacted a statute intended to stagger the terms of the three members of the Peach County Board of Commissioners of Roads and Revenues so that instead of having all three posts filled at four-year intervals, the single at-large member would be elected to a four-year term two years after the other two members were elected to four-year terms. Before the primary election in 1976 for the two Board seats not including the at-large post, an action was brought in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Georgia to enforce the requirements of 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (42 USCS 1973c), the state having failed to submit the voting change for approval either to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia or to the Attorney General, before implementing it. After the general election, a three-judge court found that the statute constituted a change in voting procedures subject to the provisions of 5, and that the change had been implemented without first being submitted for approval. The court enjoined further enforcement of the statute until such time as the state effected compliance with 5, but refused the challengers' request to set aside the 1976 elections and order new elections of all three members of the Board.

Defendant was born in Mexico in 1974 to his U.S. citizen father who was 16 years of age at the time, and his non-U.S. citizen mother. Defendant's father was issued a certificate of citizenship in 1999 because his mother, defendant's grandmother, was a U.S. citizen by birth. His father and grandmother brought defendant to the U.S. when he was two months old. In 1997, defendant was convicted of importation of marijuana and was deported. Defendant had since then repeatedly entered the U.S. and had been removed each time. Defendant asserted that ¬¨√ü¬¨√ü 1401(a)(7) and 1409 violated the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause on the basis of age and gender. The appellate court found that ¬¨√ü 1409's legitimation requirements for citizen fathers, but not for citizen mothers, did not offend principles of equal protection. Section 1401(a)(7) spoke plainly in terms of the residency of the citizen father; it provided no basis for imputing residency of a grandparent. Because the crime was a general intent crime, defendant's mistaken belief was not a defense. Defendant neither asked for, nor received, the Attorney General's permission to apply for reentry.

After a Texas state court's injunction against the production of minerals from certain oil leases was dissolved by an appellate court as having been illegally issued, the lease owners brought an action for damages under 42 USCS 1983 in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas against the corporation which had obtained the injunction, the corporation's sole owner, the judge who entered the injunction, and the individual sureties on the injunction bond, the lease owners claiming that the injunction had been corruptly issued as the result of a conspiracy between the judge and the other defendants, thus causing a deprivation of property without due process of law. The District Court dismissed the action, ruling that because the injunction was a judicial act within the jurisdiction of the state court, the judge was immune from liability in a 1983 suit, and that with the dismissal of the judge, the remaining defendants could not be said to have conspired "under color of" state law within the meaning of 1983, which provides for the liability of persons who, "under color of" state law, bring about a deprivation of constitutional rights. Ultimately, the Court of Appeals reversed the District Court's judgment insofar as it had dismissed claims against the defendants other than the judge, holding that there was no good reason in law, logic, or policy for conferring immunity on private persons who persuaded the immune judge to exercise his jurisdiction corruptly (604 F2d 976).

A court in which enforcement is sought of a National Labor Relations Board order requiring a plant owner to bargain collectively with a union representing plant guards may properly consider whether their status as employees entitled to the benefit of the National Labor Relations Act has been altered by the fact that after the order was issued guards were deputized as city policemen, although the issue, being nonexistent at the time of the Board's action, was not raised before the Board and 10e of the National Labor Relations Act provides that "no objection that has not been urged before the Board, its member, agent or agency, shall be considered by the court, unless the failure or neglect to urge such objection shall be excused because of extraordinary circumstances."

The plaintiff's mother and father were ceremonially married one year before the plaintiff was born, but the marriage was not valid because the father's divorce from his first wife had not been final. Eighteen years after the plaintiff was born, the plaintiff's father died intestate. Four months after the father's death, the United States Supreme Court decided Trimble v Gordon (1977) 430 US 762, 52 L Ed 2d 31, 97 S Ct 1459, which held that a total statutory disinheritance of children from a father's estate where the children were born out of wedlock and not legitimated by a subsequent marriage of their parents was unconstitutional. Shortly thereafter, while the estate of the plaintiff's father was still open, the plaintiff gave formal notice of her claim to a share of the estate, and she subsequently filed a formal complaint. Because state statutory law barred illegitimate children from inheriting from their fathers except under special circumstances, such as where their parents had subsequently married, a Texas trial court entered a take-nothing judgment against the plaintiff. The Court of Appeals of Texas affirmed, rejecting the plaintiff's equal protection challenge to the state law, and holding that Trimble v Gordon did not apply retroactively where a child's father died before the Trimble v Gordon decision was handed down and where suit was filed afterward (682 SW2d 697). The Supreme Court of Texas refused the plaintiff's application of error.

In United States v. Jones, we held that "the Government's installation of a GPS device on a target's vehicle, and its use of that device to monitor the vehicle's movements, constitutes a 'search."' 565 U. S., at __ (slip op., at 3) (footnote omitted). We stressed the importance of the fact that the Government had "physically occupied private property for the purpose of obtaining information." Id., at __ (slip op., at 4). Under such circumstances, it was not necessary to inquire about the target's expectation of privacy in his vehicle's movements in order to determine if a Fourth Amendment search had occurred. "Where, as here, the Government obtains information by physically intruding on a constitutionally protected area, such a search has undoubtedly occurred." Id., at _ n. 3 (slip op., at 6, n. 3). We reaffirmed this principle in Florida v. Jardines, 569 U. S. _, ___-__ (2013) (slip op., at 3-4), where we held that having a drug-sniffing dog nose around a suspect's front porch was a search, because police had "gathered ... information by physically entering and occupying the [curtilage of the house] to engage in conduct not explicitly or implicitly permitted by the homeowner." See also id., at __ (slip op., at 9) (a search occurs "when the government gains evidence by physically intruding on constitutionally protected areas"). In light of these decisions, it follows that a State also conducts a search when it attaches a device to a person's body, without consent, for the purpose of tracking that individual's movements. In concluding otherwise, the North Carolina Court of Appeals apparently placed decisive weight on the fact that the State's monitoring program is civil in nature. See Jones, __ N. C. App., at _ 750 S. E. 2d, at 886 ("the instant case . . . involves a civil SBM proceeding"). "It is well settled," however, "that the Fourth Amendment's protection extends beyond the sphere of criminal investigations," Ontario v. Quon, 560 U. S. 746, 755 (2010), and the government's purpose in collecting information does not control whether the method of collection constitutes a search. A building inspector who enters a home simply to ensure compliance with civil safety regulations has undoubtedly conducted a search under the Fourth Amendment. See Camara v. Municipal Court of City and County of San Francisco, 387 U. S. 523, 534 (1967) (housing inspections are "administrative searches" that must comply with the Fourth Amendment).

Upon receiving information that a child was being abused, the Baltimore City Department of Social Services (BCDSS) obtained a court order removing the child from the custody of his mother. The child was subsequently declared by a juvenile court to be a "child in need of assistance" under state law and was returned to the mother's custody subject to several conditions and the further orders of the court. When it appeared that the mother was violating the conditions of the custodial order and could not adequately care for the child, the court ordered removal of the child from her custody and directed her to produce the child. Upon her refusal to do so, she was held in contempt and imprisoned until such time as she produced the child or divulged his whereabouts. The court, rejecting the contention that the contempt order violated the mother's Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination, stated that the production of the child would purge the contempt and that the contempt order was issued not because of the mother's refusal to testify in any proceeding, but because of her refusal to obey the court's order. On appeal, the Court of Appeals of Maryland, vacating the juvenile court's judgment upholding the contempt order, found that the contempt order unconstitutionally compelled the mother to admit, through the act of producing the child, a measure of continuing control and dominion over his person under circumstances in which she had a reasonable apprehension that she would be prosecuted.

A court order, growing out of a proceeding under the Fair Labor Standards Act, enjoined in general terms violations of the wage, overtime, and record-keeping provisions of the Act, but did not prohibit the specific practices in violation of these provisions, on which the wage and hour administrator rested an application for an adjudication that the employer was guilty of civil contempt.

The petitioner, an interstate motor carrier certified by the Interstate Commerce Commission, transported shipments between points in Virginia, but routed them through its headquarters in West Virginia. The Virginia State Corporation Commission fined the carrier because of its failure to obtain a certificate for its intrastate operations. Upon the carrier's appeal, the Supreme Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed the order of the commission (with modifications not pertinent to the issue). (199 Va 797, 102 SE2d 339.)

An action challenging the constitutionality of a New York statute which makes it a crime (1) for anyone to sell or distribute contraceptives to minors under the age of 16, (2) for anyone other than a licensed pharmacist to distribute contraceptives to persons over 15, and (3) for anyone to advertise or display contraceptives, was instituted against state officials in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York by various individuals and organizations, including an out-of-state corporation which made mail-order sales of contraceptives in New York, advertised its products in periodicals in New York, and had been threatened with prosecution under the New York statute. A three-judge District Court held that the statute was unconstitutional under the First and Fourteenth Amendments (398 F Supp 321).

Separate federal grand jury indictments were returned against the defendant, charging that (1) the defendant, assuming leadership, and nine codefendants had conspired, in violation of 21 USCS 846, to distribute heroin and cocaine during a specified period, and (2) the defendant alone, in violation of 21 USCS 848, had conducted a "continuing criminal enterprise" in concert with five or more other persons with respect to whom the defendant occupied a position of organizer, supervisor, and manager, during the same specified period, to distribute and possess heroin and cocaine, and that as the result of such activity, the defendant had obtained a substantial income. The United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana denied the government's motion to try both indictments at the same trial, the defendant (and his codefendants in the conspiracy case) having objected on the ground that neither the parties nor the charges were the same. The defendant was first convicted of the conspiracy charge, receiving the maximum punishment of 15 years in prison and a fine of $ 25,000, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed the conviction. Thereafter, the defendant was convicted of the criminal enterprise charge, receiving the maximum sentence of life imprisonment and a fine of $ 100,000. The District Court rejected the defendant's contention that the conspiracy charged under 846 was a lesser included offense of the criminal enterprise charged under 848, and that thus prosecution for the latter offense was barred under the double jeopardy clause of the Fifth Amendment. The Court of Appeals affirmed the criminal enterprise conviction (532 F2d 1101).

Defendant refused to permit a Baltimore City health inspector, who had cause to suspect that defendant's home was infested with rats, to inspect his home without a warrant, and was convicted by a police justice for the Northern District of Baltimore under a Baltimore City Code provision making a house owner or occupier subject to a forfeiture of $ 20 for refusal to open his house to city health authorities having cause to suspect that a nuisance exists therein. On appeal, the Criminal Court of Baltimore, in a de novo proceeding, also found defendant guilty. The Maryland Court of Appeals denied certiorari.

A corporation which operated restaurants and other businesses filed a voluntary petition for reorganization under Chapter 11 of the Bankruptcy Code (11 USCS 1101 et seq.) in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the Eastern District of Missouri. During the reorganization attempt, the corporation obtained workers' compensation insurance from an underwriting company, but repeatedly failed to pay the premiums. When the reorganization failed, the Bankruptcy Court converted the case into a liquidation under Chapter 7 of the Bankruptcy Code (11 USCS 701 et seq.). The underwriting company, learning of the bankruptcy proceedings, sought to recover its premiums as an administrative expense under 11 USCS 503. Since essentially all of the corporation's assets were subject to a bank's security interest, which would ordinarily have priority over administrative expenses, the underwriting company sought to invoke 11 USCS 506(c), which provides that "[t]he trustee may recover" from property subject to an allowed secured claim the reasonable and necessary costs of preserving or disposing of such property. The Bankruptcy Court ruled in favor of the underwriting company. This ruling was affirmed (1) by the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, and (2) subsequently, by a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit (150 F3d 868). However, the Court of Appeals granted rehearing en banc and reversed, on the ground that 506(c) could not be invoked by an administrative claimant (177 F3d 719).

An individual, who had previously been convicted of a felony, was placed on probation after his conviction in a Wisconsin state court on various criminal charges. Under Wisconsin law, probationers are in the legal custody of the state department of health and social services and are subject to the rules and regulations established by that department. The probationer's apartment was searched pursuant to one such regulation which permits any probation officer to search a probationer's home without a warrant as long as the officer's supervisor approves and as long as there are "reasonable grounds" to believe contraband is present on the premises. Another regulation makes it a violation of the terms of probation to refuse to consent to a home search. The search was conducted by the supervisor of the probationer's probation officer and was based on information from a police detective that there were or might be guns at the probationer's apartment. A handgun was found during the search, and the probationer was charged with the felony of possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. At trial in the Circuit Court of Rock County, Wisconsin, the probationer's motion to suppress the evidence seized during the search was denied, and the probationer was convicted of the firearms violation. The conviction was affirmed by the Court of Appeals of Wisconsin (126 Wis 2d 183, 376 NW2d 62). The Supreme Court of Wisconsin affirmed the conviction and held (1) that the denial of the probationer's suppression motion was proper because probation diminishes a probationer's reasonable expectation of privacy so that a probation officer could, consistent with the Fourth Amendment, search a probationer's home without a warrant and with only reasonable grounds to believe contraband was present, (2) that the reasonable grounds standard in the state search regulation satisfied the reasonableness standard of the Federal Constitution, and (3) that the detective's tip established reasonable grounds within the meaning of the regulation (131 Wis 2d 41, 388 NW2d 535).

A defendant was convicted in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia of rape and of first-degree murder for killing the same victim in the perpetration of the rape, separate statutory offenses under the District of Columbia Code. The defendant was sentenced to two consecutive terms of imprisonment of 20 years to life for first-degree murder and of 15 years to life for rape. On appeal, the District of Columbia Court of Appeals affirmed the convictions and the sentences, rejecting the defendant's claim that his sentence for the offense of rape had to be vacated because that offense merged for purposes of punishment with the felony murder offense (379 A2d 1152).

Respondents Yassir Fazaga, Ali Malik, and Yasser Abdel Rahim, members of Muslim communities in California, filed a putative class action against the Federal Bureau of Investigation and certain Government officials, claiming that the Government subjected them and other Muslims to illegal surveillance under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 (FISA). FISA provides special procedures for use when the Government wishes to conduct foreign intelligence surveillance. Relevant here, FISA provides a procedure under which a trial-level court or other authority may consider the legality of electronic surveillance conducted under FISA and order specified forms of relief. See 50 U. S. C. ¬ß1806(f). The Government moved to dismiss most of respondents‚Äô claims under the ‚Äústate secrets‚Äù privilege. See, e.g., General Dynamics Corp. v. United States, 563 U. S. 478. After reviewing both public and classified filings, the District Court held that the state secrets privilege required dismissal of all respondents‚Äô claims against the Government, except for one claim under ¬ß1810, which it dismissed on other grounds. The District Court determined dismissal appropriate because litigation of the dismissed claims ‚Äúwould require or unjustifiably risk disclosure of secret and classified information.‚Äù 884 F. Supp. 2d 1022, 1028‚Äì1029. The Ninth Circuit reversed in relevant part, holding that ‚ÄúCongress intended FISA to displace the state secrets privilege and its dismissal remedy with respect to electronic surveillance.‚Äù 965 F. 3d 1015, 1052.

The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that respondent state inmate had fairly presented a federal ineffective assistance of counsel claim to the higher state courts as the state justices should have realized from the lower state trial court's opinion that the inmate's claim rested upon federal law. Certiorari was granted to determine whether the Ninth Circuit correctly interpreted the fair presentation requirement. Although the justices of the state supreme court had the opportunity to read the lower court opinions in the inmate's case, that opportunity did not mean that the inmate had fairly presented a federal claim when the appellate judges could have discovered that claim only by reading those opinions. To say otherwise would have required the state supreme court justices to read the lower court opinions, a requirement that federal habeas corpus law did not impose because it would have forced state appellate judges to alter their ordinary review practices, would have imposed a serious burden on them, and was unnecessary since litigants could easily indicate the federal law bases for their claims. Thus, the court held that ordinarily a state prisoner did not fairly present a claim to a state court if that court must read beyond a petition or a brief (or a similar document) that did not alert it to the presence of a federal claim in order to find material, such as a lower court opinion in the case, that did so. Moreover, the inmate had not demonstrated that state law used the words "ineffective assistance" to refer only to a federal law claim.

In the late 19th century, Utah Lake, a navigable body of water, was included within the boundaries of Utah Territory. After a portion of the Sundry Appropriations Act of 1888 ("the 1888 Act") (25 Stat 505) authorized the United States to select and reserve federal land as sites for reservoirs, the Federal Government in 1889 took several actions--whose nature and effect were to be disputed--with respect to Utah Lake. In a portion of the Sundry Appropriations Act of 1890 ("the 1890 Act") (predecessor to 43 USCS 662), Congress repealed the 1888 Act's reservoir-site provisions, but added that reservoir sites previously located or selected under the 1888 Act would remain segregated and reserved from entry or settlement. The Utah Enabling Act of 1894 (28 Stat 107) provided that Utah was to be admitted into the Union on an equal footing with the original states. Subsequently, Utah was admitted to statehood, and entered the Union in 1896. In 1976, a bureau of the Federal Government issued oil and gas leases for the lands underlying Utah Lake. The state of Utah then brought suit against the United States in the United States District Court for the District of Utah, and sought a judgment that the state, rather than the Federal Government, had title to the bed of Utah lake. The District Court, however, granted a summary judgment in favor of the United States, expressing the view that (1) as part of an 1889 reservoir-site selection, the United States had withdrawn the bed of Utah Lake pursuant to the 1888 Act; (2) because of this prior withdrawal, title to the lakebed did not pass to Utah, which otherwise would have been permitted, on an equal footing with the original states, to obtain title to the lands under navigable waters within the state upon Utah's entry into the Union; and (3) federal title to the bed of Utah Lake was not affected by Congress' subsequent passage of the Submerged Lands Act (43 USCS 1301 et seq.), which relinquished to the states title to some, but not all, federal submerged lands (624 F Supp 622). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed, (1) reaching similar conclusions as to reservoir-site selection, the equal footing doctrine, and the Submerged Lands Act; and (2) adding that the reservior-site selection was not affected by the 1890 Act, a provision as to reservoir sites in an 1891 act (predecessor to 43 USCS 663), or a provision as to reservoir sites in an 1897 act (predecessor to 43 USCS 664) (780 F2d 1515).

Federal statutes (1) prohibit persons who have been convicted of crimes punishable by more than a year in prison from possessing any firearm (18 USCS 922(g)(1)); (2) provide that persons violating 922(g)(1) must receive enhanced sentences if they also have three violent felony convictions (18 USCS 924(e)); and (3) state that a previous conviction does not provide the predicate for either the substantive offense or a sentence enhancement if the person's civil rights have been restored, "unless such . . . restoration of civil rights expressly provides that the person may not . . . possess . . . firearms" (18 USCS 921(a)(20)). An individual who had several previous felony convictions, including three convictions in Massachusetts state courts, was convicted in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts of violating 922(g)(1) on the basis of possession of several rifles and shotguns which were found at his home. The District Court initially imposed an enhanced sentence under 921(a)(20) based on the three Massachusetts convictions and one other felony conviction, but the court subsequently ruled that the Massachusetts convictions did not count because (1) the individual's civil rights had been restored by operation of Massachusetts law, under statutes which allowed him to possess rifles and shotguns but prohibited his possession of handguns outside his home or business, and (2) the fact that the present case involved rifles and shotguns made the restriction as to handguns irrelevant (941 F Supp 238, 1996 US Dist LEXIS 13540). The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reversed, holding that the Massachusetts convictions could be counted under 921(a)(20) because the individual, though not prohibited by the state from possessing the particular firearms found in his possession, remained subject to significant firearms restrictions.

Two railroad companies voluntarily merged. The Interstate Commerce Commission, whose approval was necessary, found that the merger was consistent with the public interest and that its terms were just and reasonable to each group of shareholders. It deemed itself without jurisdiction, however, to pass upon the claim of certain dissenting preferred stockholders that by the terms of the merged railroad's charter they were entitled to receive the equivalent of the par value of their stock and unpaid cumulative dividends, and remitted them to their remedies in the state courts, merely finding that, however settled, the claim did not involve enough to affect the solvency of the new company or jeopardize its operations.

An order of the Commissioner of Patents, disbarring an attorney on the ground of gross misconduct, is supported by findings that the attorney, in support of a client's patent application filed nineteen years before commencement of the disbarment proceedings, presented to the Patent Office an article published in a trade journal and naming as author an apparently disinterested labor leader, in the preparation of which the attorney had participated, and that he concealed from the Patent Office the fact that the article was prepared, and its publication under the labor leader's name was procured, by and on behalf of his client; and this is so even though the statements made in the article were true.

The issue presented is whether the districting plan adopted by the State of Alabama for its 2022 congressional elections likely violated ¬ß2 of the Voting Rights Act, 52 U. S. C. ¬ß10301. As originally enacted in 1965, ¬ß2 of the Act tracked the language of the Fifteenth Amendment, providing that ‚Äú[t]he right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged . . . on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.‚Äù In City of Mobile v. Bolden, 446 U. S. 55, this Court held that the Fifteenth Amendment‚Äîand thus ¬ß2‚Äîprohibits States from acting with a ‚Äúracially discriminatory motivation‚Äù or an ‚Äúinvidious purpose‚Äù to discriminate, but it does not prohibit laws that are discriminatory only in effect. Id., at 61‚Äì65 (plurality opinion). Criticism followed, with many viewing Mobile‚Äôs intent test as not sufficiently protective of voting rights. But others believed that adoption of an effects test would inevitably require a focus on proportionality, calling voting laws into question whenever a minority group won fewer seats in the legislature than its share of the population. Congress ultimately resolved this debate in 1982, reaching a bipartisan compromise that amended ¬ß2 to incorporate both an effects test and a robust disclaimer that ‚Äúnothing‚Äù in ¬ß2 ‚Äúestablishes a right to have members of a protected class elected in numbers equal to their proportion in the population.‚Äù ¬ß10301(b). In 1992, ¬ß2 litigation challenging the State of Alabama‚Äôs then-existing districting map resulted in the State‚Äôs first majority-black district and, subsequently, the State‚Äôs first black Representative since 1877. Alabama‚Äôs congressional map has remained remarkably similar since that litigation. Following the 2020 decennial census, a group of plaintiffs led by Alabama legislator Bobby Singleton sued the State, arguing that the State‚Äôs population growth rendered the existing congressional map malapportioned and racially gerrymandered in violation of the Equal Protection Clause. While litigation was proceeding, the Alabama Legislature‚Äôs Committee on Reapportionment drew a new districting map that would reflect the distribution of the prior decade‚Äôs population growth across the State. The resulting map largely resembled the 2011 map on which it was based and similarly produced only one district in which black voters constituted a majority. That new map was signed into law as HB1. Three groups of Alabama citizens brought suit seeking to stop Alabama‚Äôs Secretary of State from conducting congressional elections under HB1. One group (Caster plaintiffs) challenged HB1 as invalid under ¬ß2. Another group (Milligan plaintiffs) brought claims under ¬ß2 and the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. And a third group (the Singleton plaintiffs) amended the complaint in their ongoing litigation to challenge HB1 as a racial gerrymander under the Equal Protection Clause. A three-judge District Court was convened, and the Singleton and Milligan actions were consolidated before that District Court for purposes of preliminary injunction proceedings, while Caster proceeded before one of the judges on a parallel track. After an extensive hearing, the District Court concluded in a 227-page opinion that the question whether HB1 likely violated ¬ß2 was not ‚Äúclose.‚Äù The Court preliminarily enjoined Alabama from using HB1 in forthcoming elections. The same relief was ordered in Caster.

After giving interested parties an opportunity to submit their views in writing, the Federal Power Commission adopted regulations establishing "permissible" pricing provisions in the contracts of natural gas producers and providing that any contract containing other provisions "shall be rejected," so far as producer rates were concerned, and that any application for a certificate of public convenience and necessity "shall be rejected" if any contract submitted in support thereof contained forbidden provisions. Two independent natural gas producers thereafter applied to the Commission for certificates of public convenience and necessity, which the Commission rejected without a hearing because the applications disclosed price clauses not permissible under the regulations. (28 FTC 551; 29 FTC 378.)

The plaintiff, a railroad employee, was injured while shifting various railroad cars for his employer on tracks in a plant and descending, after attempting to help one of the brakemen assigned to assist him, on a ladder of a boxcar. In an action brought by plaintiff in a Virginia state court under the Federal Employers' Liability Act, his first cause of action charged defendant with negligence in requiring the shifting of the cars in such an accelerated time and with such inexperienced help that he was injured in attempting to carry out his instructions. In his second claim he alleged that the physician furnished him by defendant subsequent to his injury administered improper treatment, thus aggravating his injury, and that defendant was responsible for such negligence. At the close of the case the trial judge sustained the defendant's motion to strike petitioner's evidence and discharge the jury. On petition for writ of error, the Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals rejected the petition.

Defendant was convicted in a New York state court for selling "girlie" magazines to a minor in violation of a New York statute, in the meantime repealed, which prohibited the sale of magazines which would appeal to the lust of minors or their curiosity as to sex or to the anatomical differences between the sexes. His conviction was affirmed by the Appellate Term of the New York Supreme Court, First Judicial Department.

The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed a judgment of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, holding a witness before a grand jury in contempt, and the District Court's denial of the witness' motion to vacate the contempt judgment. (370 F2d 1019.)

After an 86-year-old white woman was allegedly raped, she described her assailant as a Negro youth, and the police found some fingerprints on the window through which the assailant had apparently entered her home. The defendant and several other Negro youths were taken to police headquarters, where they were questioned briefly and were fingerprinted. Several days later, the defendant was jailed and was fingerprinted again, and these fingerprints were found to match those on the window of the victim's home. In the Circuit Court of Lauderdale County, Mississippi, the defendant was convicted of rape, the court overruling his objection that the fingerprint evidence was inadmissible as the product of an unlawful detention. The Mississippi Supreme Court sustained the admission of the fingerprint evidence and affirmed the conviction (204 So 2d 270).

These separate‚àö¬∂[**2]‚àö¬∂ appeals, heard together, are from two orders of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York in the same case. In the first appeal, No. 28405, the defendants, Hughes Tool Company (Toolco) and Raymond M. Holliday, Toolco's chief financial officer, attack the validity of an order which granted default judgment in favor of the plaintiff, Trans World Airlines, Inc., because of the defendants' failure to produce Toolco's managing agent, Howard, R. Hughes, for examination and their failure to produce certain papers and documents, 32 F.R.D. 604 (S.D.N.Y.1963). In the second appeal, No. 28406, Toolco attacks an order which dismissed with prejudice its first five counterclaims against TWA and a group of additional defendants and an order of the same date which granted summary judgment in favor of TWA on the sixth counterclaim.

In a civil antitrust suit brought in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, the United States charged three carriers with violating 1-3 of the Sherman Act (15 USC 1-3) by transactions in which (1) two of the carriers formed the third carrier under an agreement that the third carrier would have the exclusive right to air traffic along the west coast of South America free from competition by the first carrier, and that the first carrier would be free from competition by the third carrier in other areas of South America and between the Canal Zone and the United States; (2) the first carrier and the second carrier conspired to monopolize and monopolized air commerce between the east coast of the United States and the west coast of South America and Buenos Aires; and (3) the first carrier used its 50 percent control of the third carrier to prevent it from securing authority from the Civil Aeronautics Board to extend its route from the Canal Zone to the United States. The trial court dismissed the complaint against the second carrier and the third carrier, holding that none of their respective practices violated the Sherman Act, but held that the first carrier had violated 2 of the Sherman Act by suppressing the third carrier's efforts to extend its route from the Canal Zone to the United States. (193 F Supp 18.)

Exemption 6 of the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (5 USCS 552(b)(6)) provides that FOIA disclosure requirements do not apply to "personnel and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy." A number of Haitian nationals had been involuntarily returned to Haiti after attempting to emigrate illegally to the United States. The United States State Department, in order to monitor compliance with an assurance by the Haitian Government that such returnees would not be subject to prosecution for illegal departure, conducted confidential interviews with a sample of such returnees, and all but one or two in the sample reported that they had not been harassed or prosecuted since their return. A Florida lawyer represented other Haitian nationals who were (1) seeking political asylum in the United States, and (2) attempting to prove, in immigration proceedings, that Haitians who emigrated illegally would face a well-founded fear of persecution if they returned. The lawyer and three of his clients made a series of FOIA requests, and the State Department's response included the release of 17 reports containing summaries of individual interviews with such returnees under the monitoring program, but the Department redacted--that is, deleted--the names and other identifying information from the reports before release. The lawyer and the clients then filed a FOIA suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, and sought the redacted information. Although the Department cited Exemption 6, the District Court's rulings included an order to produce the redacted information, as the court expressed the view that any invasion of privacy for the "mere" act of disclosure of names and addresses was (1) "de minimis" and little more than speculation, and (2) clearly outweighed by the public interest in the safe relocation of returned Haitians (725 F Supp 502). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, in affirming the District Court's order under somewhat different reasoning, expressed the view that (1) there were significant privacy interests at stake, where (a) the requesters wanted the redacted information in order to contact the returnees directly and to question them about their treatment by the Haitian Government, and (b) the returnees had been promised confidentiality; but (2) such privacy interests were outweighed by the public interest in learning whether the Federal Government (a) was adequately monitoring Haiti's compliance with its obligation not to persecute returnees, and (b) was honest to the public in stating that Haiti was adhering to its obligation; and (3) although the redacted information would not, in and of itself, tell the requesters anything about Haiti's treatment of returnees or the Federal Government's honesty, the indirect benefit of giving the requesters a means to locate the returnees and to cross-examine them provided a public value that required disclosure (908 F2d 1549).

In determining its federal income tax liability, a life insurance company for 2 years included the net valuation of unpaid premiums in its reserves, which reduces the company's taxable income, and in its assets and premium income, which increases the company's tax. As to another year, the company included the net valuation in its reserves, but not in its assets. The net valuation is that amount of the premium which a company must add to its reserves to insure that it will have sufficient funds to pay death benefits, and the remainder of the premium, called "loading," covers profits and expenses. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue assessed a deficiency because the insurance company did not, in any of the 3 years, include the entire unpaid premium, loading as well as net premium, in calculating assets and income. The Tax Court upheld the deficiency, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed, holding that the insurance company's reserve calculation was correct because it was required by state law and that in accord with normal accounting practices, the premiums could not be considered as either assets or income before they were actually collected (525 F2d 786).

The petitioners, both Negro ministers, were convicted in the Birmingham, Alabama, Recorder's Court for aiding and abetting a violation of the city criminal trespass ordinance. After a trial de novo they were again convicted in the Circuit Court. These convictions were affirmed by the Alabama Court of Appeals. (41 Ala App 319, 318, 134 So 2d 213, 215.) The Alabama Supreme Court denied writs of certiorari. (273 Ala 713, 704, 134 So 2d 214, 215.)

The defendant, a New York city policeman, signed a paper waiving immunity he would otherwise have had from prosecution under state law as to matters he might testify about before a grand jury. Provisions of the New York Constitution and the city charter required him to sign the waiver or lose his job. Twenty-two months later, long after he had resigned as a policeman, he was brought before a grand jury and asked whether he had ever accepted bribes while a policeman. He refused to answer the question claiming a federal constitutional and state privilege against self-incrimination. He was convicted of criminal contempt and his conviction was affirmed by the state appellate courts. The issue was whether his conviction deprived him of his liberty without due process.

Solely on the basis of the duration of relationship requirement of 42 USCS 416(c)(5) and (e)(2), which define "widow" and "child" so as to exclude from social security benefits a surviving wife or stepchild who had their respective relationships to a deceased wage earner for less than 9 months prior to his death, the Social Security Administration denied mother's insurance benefits to a widow and child's insurance benefits to the widow's daughter by a previous marriage, since the widow had been married to her deceased husband for less than 6 months at the time of his death. The widow and daughter, acting on behalf of a class of others similarly situated, challenged the constitutionality of 416(c)(5) and (e)(2) in an action brought in the Federal District Court for the Northern District of California against the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. Ordering the action certified as a class action on behalf of a plaintiff class of all otherwise eligible surviving spouses and stepchildren of deceased wage earners who were disqualified from receiving benefits by operation of the 9-month requirement, the three-judge District Court held that (1) it had jurisdiction under 28 USCS 1331, which gives the District Courts jurisdiction in civil actions arising under the Constitution or laws of the United States, notwithstanding that the third sentence of 42 USCS 405(h) provides that no action against the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare may be brought under 28 USCS 1331 to recover on any claim arising under Title II of the Social Security Act (42 USCS 401-431), and (2) the duration of relationship requirement was unconstitutional because the requirement presumed a fact which was not necessarily or universally true (373 F Supp 961).

Provisions of the California Elections Code (1) forbade the official governing bodies of political parties from endorsing candidates in party primaries, (2) restricted the organization and composition of such official governing bodies, (3) limited the term of office for a party's state central committee chair, and (4) required that the chair rotate between residents of northern and southern California. Various county central committees of the Democratic and Republican parties, and other groups and individuals active in partisan politics in California, brought an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California against state officials responsible for enforcing the Code. The plaintiffs contended that the provisions in question deprived political parties and their members of the rights of free speech and free association guaranteed by the Federal Constitution's First and Fourteenth Amendments. The District Court granted summary judgment for the plaintiffs as to the provisions in question, and the United States Court of Appeals affirmed (792 F2d 802). On appeal, the United States Supreme Court vacated and remanded (479 US 1024, 93 L Ed 2d 820, 107 S Ct 864) for further consideration in light of its decision in Tashjian v Republican Party of Connecticut (1986) 479 US 208, 93 L Ed 2d 514, 107 S Ct 544. After supplemental briefing, the Court of Appeals concluded that its previous decision was supported by the Tashjian decision, supra, and accordingly reinstated its judgment affirming the District Court's decision (826 F2d 814).

Defendant was convicted in the United States District Court of Alaska on a charge of transportation of a forged instrument in interstate commerce. His conviction was affirmed by the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. (324 F2d 914.)  Trial of petitioner over his objection by jury some of whose members were selected from panel in whose presence another jury in similar preceding case had announced verdict of his guilt is clearly erroneous.

A manufacturer of corn products, in order to assure adequate supplies of raw corn, engaged in the purchase and sale of corn futures, with resulting profits and losses. The manufacturer contended that the corn futures constituted capital assets, and, consequently, that profits and losses from their sale were entitled to preferential tax treatment under the capital assets provisions of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939.

After being informed that the defendant had been involved in a robbery, police officers went to his home. He was not at home, but a 15-year-old girl who identified herself as his wife allowed the officers to enter and search her belongings. When several rings taken by the robbers were found, the officers "staked out" the house and awaited the defendant's return. Upon his arrival late that night, the officers arrested him as he alighted from his car, which was parked outside the house and was 15 or 20 feet away from it, and they then conducted a second search of the house without requesting permission to do so. No warrant was ever obtained. In making the second search, the officers discovered under a couch a jewelry case stolen in the robbery. The evidence discovered through the second search was admitted at the defendant's robbery trial in a California state court on the ground that the search was incident to the defendant's arrest; the defendant was convicted of robbery; the California Court of Appeal affirmed; and the California Supreme Court denied review.

A union representing most stage actors and actresses in the United States unilaterally established in 1928 a licensing system for the regulation of theatrical agents. The essential elements of the regulations have remained unchanged, requiring, among other things, that a licensed agent renounce any right to take a commission on an employment contract under which an actor or actress receives so-called "scale" wages. Agents are also required to pay franchise fees to the unions which are deposited in the general treasury and not segregated from other union funds. The union has also entered into collective bargaining agreements with theatrical producers specifying minimum wages and other terms and conditions of employment. Eventually, a group of agents who refused to accept the regulations or apply for franchises brought suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York contending that the union's regulation of theatrical agents violated the antitrust provisions of 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act (15 USCS 1, 2). The District Court dismissed the complaint, finding that the union's creation and maintenance of the agency franchise system was fully protected by the antitrust exemption for unions and their members arising under 6 and 20 of the Clayton Act (15 USCS 17, 29 USCS 52) and 4, 5, and 13 of the Norris-LaGuardia Act (29 USCS 104, 105, 113) (478 F Supp 496). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed, deciding that the central feature of the union's franchising system--the union's exaction of an agreement by agents not to charge commissions on certain types of work--was immune from antitrust challenge. Furthermore, the Court of Appeals suggested that if the exaction of franchise fees by the union exceeded its expenses in administering the franchise system, the fees could not legally be collected. However, the Court of Appeals concluded that the fees were sufficiently low that a remand on this point would not have served any useful purpose (622 F2d 647).

A Florida prisoner, who had pleaded guilty to a state robbery charge and who had received a 99-year sentence, (1) filed a federal habeas corpus petition in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, and (2) alleged that his guilty plea had not been entered knowingly and voluntarily. However, the District Court adopted a Magistrate Judge's recommendation and, in a ruling, dismissed this petition as assertedly barred by the limitations period in another AEDPA provision (28 U.S.C.S. _ 2244(d)).

The Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, as amended (ADA) (42 USCS 12101 et seq.) is made inapplicable to very small businesses by 42 USCS 12111(5), which provides that the ADA applies to only employers that have 15 or more employees. A bookkeeper, whose employment at a medical clinic--which was a professional corporation owned by four physician-shareholders who practiced medicine at the clinic and constituted its board of directors--had been terminated, brought, against the clinic, an action alleging unlawful discrimination on the basis of disability in violation of the ADA. The United States District Court for the District of Oregon, adopting a magistrate judge's findings and recommendation, granted the clinic's motion for summary judgment, which was based on an assertion that the clinic had fewer than 15 employees, where the accuracy of this assertion depended on whether the four shareholder-directors were counted as employees (2000 US Dist LEXIS 8574). A divided panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed (271 F3d 903).

Under Article VII-A, Title 3, of the New York Tax Law, a town proceeded to foreclose a lien for delinquent taxes on the real estate of a long-time resident. In accordance with the statute, the taxpayer was given no notice except by mail, posting notice at the post office and publication in two local newspapers. She filed no answer; judgment of foreclosure was entered; and a deed to her property was delivered to the town. A few days later, she was adjudged insane and committed to a hospital for the insane. Subsequently, appellant was appointed committee of her person and property, and he filed a motion in the trial court where the judgment of foreclosure had been entered to have the default opened, the judgment vacated and the deed set aside. He alleged that, prior to entry of the judgment of foreclosure, the taxpayer was well known by town officials to be financially able to meet her obligations but mentally incompetent to handle her affairs or to understand the meaning of any notice served upon her and that no attempt had been made to have a committee appointed for her person or property.

A witness summoned before a congressional committee confessed to having run a gambling business in Maryland. This confession was used to convict him in the Maryland state courts of conspiring to violate the state's anti-lottery laws, as against his objection that use of committee testimony was forbidden by 18 USC 3486, which provides that no testimony given by a witness in congressional inquiries "shall be used as evidence in any criminal proceeding against him in any court."

In Flora v United States, 357 US 63, 2 L ed 2d 1165, 78 S Ct 1079, the Supreme Court held, Whittaker, J., dissenting, that under 28 USC 1346(a)(1) a taxpayer is required to pay the full amount of an income tax deficiency assessment before he can maintain an income tax refund suit in a Federal District Court. A petition for rehearing was granted in 360 US 922, 3 L ed 2d 1538, 79 S Ct 1430.

Petitioner Miguel Luna Perez, who is deaf, attended schools in Michigan‚Äôs Sturgis Public School District (Sturgis) from ages 9 through 20. When Sturgis announced that it would not permit Mr. Perez to graduate, he and his family filed an administrative complaint with the Michigan Department of Education alleging (among other things) that Sturgis failed to provide him a free and appropriate public education as required by the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). See 20 U. S. C. ¬ß1415. They claimed that Sturgis supplied Mr. Perez with unqualified interpreters and misrepresented his educational progress. The parties reached a settlement in which Sturgis promised to provide the forward-looking relief Mr. Perez sought, including additional schooling. Mr. Perez then sued in federal district court under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) seeking compensatory damages. Sturgis moved to dismiss. It claimed that 20 U. S. C. ¬ß1415(l) barred Mr. Perez from bringing his ADA claim because it requires a plaintiff ‚Äúseeking relief that is also available under‚Äù IDEA to first exhaust IDEA‚Äôs administrative procedures. The district court agreed and dismissed the suit, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed.

Each of the plaintiffs, who had been convicted by courts-martial, after having exhausted his available military remedies without obtaining relief, brought suit in the Court of Claims to recover back pay, alleging that the court-martial infringed on his constitutional rights. The Court of Claims rendered judgments for the plaintiffs, because the plaintiffs' constitutional rights to a fair trial were denied in one case by a violation of paragraph 153(a) of the Manual for Courts-Martial, which states that the court-martial cannot base a conviction upon the uncorroborated testimony of a purported accomplice, if such testimony is self-contradictory, uncertain, or improbable (181 Ct Cl 210, 383 F2d 1009), and in the other case by a denial of the plaintiff's right to discovery under the Jencks Act (180 Ct Cl 131, 377 F2d 586).

On April 15, 2013, brothers Dzhokhar and Tamerlan Tsarnaev planted and detonated two homemade pressure-cooker bombs near the finish line of the Boston Marathon, killing three and wounding hundreds. Three days later, as investigators began to close in, the brothers fled. In the process, they murdered a Massachusetts Institute of Technology campus police officer, carjacked a graduate student, and fought a street battle with police during which Dzhokhar inadvertently ran over and killed Tamerlan. Dzhokhar eventually abandoned the vehicle and hid in a covered boat being stored in a nearby backyard. He was arrested the following day. Dzhokhar was indicted for 30 crimes, including 17 capital offenses. To prepare for jury selection, the parties proposed a 100-question screening form, which included several questions regarding whether media coverage may have biased prospective jurors. The District Court declined to include a proposed question that asked each prospective juror to list the facts he had learned about the case from the media and other sources. According to the District Court, the question was too ‚Äúunfocused‚Äù and ‚Äúunguided.‚Äù Following three weeks of in-person questioning, a jury was seated. The jury found Dzhokhar guilty on all counts, and the Government sought the death penalty. At sentencing, Dzhokhar sought mitigation based on the theory that Tamerlan had masterminded the bombing and pressured Dzhokhar to participate. In an attempt to show Tamerlan‚Äôs domineering nature, Dzhokhar sought to introduce the statements of Ibragim Todashev, who had alleged during an FBI interview that, years earlier, Tamerlan had participated in a triple homicide in Waltham, Massachusetts.
