According to Garland L. Bonin, the Commissioner of Public Welfare, the sudden rise in the ADC case load resulted from the Supreme Court's decision in King v. Smith, 392 U.S. 309, 88 S. Ct. 2128, 20 L. Ed. 2d ‚àö¬∂[*338]‚àö¬∂ 1118 (1968). This ruling had the effect of compelling Louisiana to make ADC payments to families previously excluded from receiving such grants under the man in the house policy, pursuant to which payments had been‚àö¬∂[**2]‚àö¬∂ withheld from families in which the parent and a member of the opposite sex were not married but either lived together as man and wife and maintained a common household, or had continuous intimate relations even if they did not maintain a common household.

Upon trial in a Tennessee state court, the defendants were convicted of committing murder in the perpetration of a rape, and were sentenced to death by electrocution. After the Court of Criminal Appeals of Tennessee had affirmed the judgment of conviction but reversed and remanded on the issue of punishment on the ground that the death sentence was unconstitutional, the Governor of Tennessee commuted the defendants' death sentences to terms of 99 years imprisonment. Subsequently, the Court of Criminal Appeals, on rehearing, held that the Governor's commutation was valid, and affirmed the convictions and sentences, as modified by the commutation (491 SW2d 624). The defendants then petitioned for federal habeas corpus relief, alleging that their constitutional rights were violated by the illegal commutation of their sentences. The United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee dismissed for failure to exhaust state remedies, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed (see 519 F2d 1402), holding that since the death sentences had been vacated at the time of the Governor's commutation order, there were no viable death sentences to commute and therefore the commutation was invalid.

Title 8 U. S. C. ¬ß1229b(a) authorizes the Attorney General to cancel the removal of an alien from the United States who, among other things, has held the status of a lawful permanent resident (LPR) for at least five years, ¬ß1229b(a)(1), and has lived in the United States for at least seven continuous years after a lawful admission, ¬ß1229b(a)(2). These cases concern whether the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA or Board) should impute a parent‚Äôs years of continuous residence or LPR status to his or her child. That issue arises because a child may enter the country lawfully, or may gain LPR status, after one of his parents does‚Äîmeaning that a parent may satisfy ¬ß1229b(a)(1) or ¬ß1229b(a)(2), while his child, considered independently, does not. In In re Escobar, 24 I. & N. Dec. 231, the BIA concluded that an alien must meet ¬ß1229b(a)‚Äôs requirements on his own. But the Ninth Circuit found the Board‚Äôs position unreasonable, holding that ¬ß1229b(a)(1) and ¬ß1229b(a)(2) require imputation. See MercadoZazueta v. Holder, 580 F. 3d 1102; Cuevas-Gaspar v. Gonzales, 430 F. 3d 1013. Respondent Martinez Gutierrez illegally entered the country with his family in 1989, when he was 5 years old. Martinez Gutierrez‚Äôs father was lawfully admitted to the country two years later as an LPR. But Martinez Gutierrez was neither lawfully admitted nor given LPR status until 2003. Two years after that, he was apprehended for smuggling undocumented aliens across the border. Admitting the offense, he sought cancellation of removal. The Immigration Judge concluded that Martinez Gutierrez qualified for relief because of his father‚Äôs immigration history, even though Martinez Gutierrez could not satisfy ¬ß1229b(a)(1) or ¬ß1229b(a)(2) on his own. Relying on Escobar, the BIA reversed. The Ninth Circuit then granted Martinez Gutierrez‚Äôs petition for review and remanded the case to the Board for reconsideration in light of its contrary decisions. Respondent Sawyers was lawfully admitted as an LPR in October 1995, when he was 15 years old. At that time, his mother had already resided in the country for six consecutive years following a lawful entry. After Sawyers was convicted of a drug offense in August 2002, the Government began removal proceedings. The Immigration Judge found Sawyers ineligible for cancellation of removal because he could not satisfy ¬ß1229b(a)(2). The BIA affirmed, and Sawyers petitioned the Ninth Circuit for review. There, he argued that the Board should have counted his mother‚Äôs years of residency while he was a minor toward ¬ß1229b(a)(2)‚Äôs 7-year continuous-residency requirement. The Court of Appeals granted the petition and remanded the case to the BIA.

The Federal Election Commission (FEC) brought a civil enforcement action seeking to establish a violation of a provision of the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) (2 USCS 441(b)). Following an adverse judgment in the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, the FEC filed, in its own name, a petition for a writ of certiorari in the United States Supreme Court, without having sought or obtained the authorization of the Solicitor General before filing the petition. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and invited the United States to submit a brief addressing the question whether the FEC had statutory authority to represent itself in the Supreme Court in this case. The United States in its brief argued that the FEC lacked the statutory authority to represent itself in the Supreme Court in this case, but that the Solicitor General had authorized the FEC's petition by way of a subsequent letter which was dated more than 120 days after the statutory deadline (28 USCS 2101(c)) for filing of petitions for certiorari had passed. The brief in response filed by the FEC asserted that the FEC had independent statutory authority to represent itself before the Supreme Court in this case..

As a result of a friendly takeover during August 1978, a publicly held corporation became a wholly owned subsidiary of a larger corporation. In connection with the takeover, the subsidiary engaged the services of an investment banking firm and a law firm. The investment banking firm charged the subsidiary a total of $ 2,225,586, the law firm charged the subsidiary a total of $ 505,069, and the subsidiary, in connection with the takeover, spent $ 150,962 for miscellaneous items, such as accounting, printing, proxy solicitation, and Securities and Exchange Commission fees. On its federal income tax return for its short taxable year ending in August 1978, the subsidiary claimed a deduction for the investment banking expenses but did not deduct the legal or miscellaneous expenses. After the Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed the claimed deduction, the subsidiary, asserting the right to deduct the investment expenses, the legal expenses, and the miscellaneous expenses, sought redetermination in the United States Tax Court. In a decision that was based primarily on the long-term benefits that accrued to the subsidiary from the takeover, the Tax Court ruled that the expenses were capital in nature and therefore not deductible under 162(a) of the Internal Revenue Code (26 USCS 162(a)) on the 1978 return as ordinary and necessary business expenses (93 TC 67). Rejecting the subsidiary's contention that, because the disputed expenses did not create or enhance a separate and distinct additional asset, they could not be capitalized and therefore were deductible under 162, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed the Tax Court judgment (918 F2d 426).

The inmate and another person were convicted of kidnaping, assault, and sexual assault after they forced a prostitute to perform fellatio and sexual intercourse, and choked her, beat her, and shot her when she tried to flee. The inmate sought postconviction relief in an Alaska court, claiming that he received ineffective assistance of counsel because his counsel did not seek restriction-fragment-length-polymorphism DNA testing on sperm found in a condom at the scene of the crime; however, the state court denied relief. After the state court denied relief, the inmate filed an action in federal district court, seeking an order requiring an Alaska district attorney's office to give him access to evidence that was introduced at his trial so he could have DNA tests conducted at his expense. The U.S. Supreme Court held that the court of appeals erred when it found that the inmate had a right under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to have access to the evidence he sought. The issue of access to DNA evidence postconviction was best left to Congress and state legislatures, and there was nothing inadequate about the procedures Alaska provided to inmates.

In August 1996, two former employees of the University of Minnesota, an arm of the state of Minnesota, filed age-discrimination complaints in the United States District Court for the District of Minnesota against the university's board of regents under the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) (29 USCS 621 et seq.) and Minnesota's human rights act. The charges alleged that the university had discriminated against the employees in December 1994. In September 1996, the university filed answers setting forth, among other matters, an affirmative defense that the suits were barred in whole or in part by the Federal Constitution's Eleventh Amendment. In July 1997, the university moved to dismiss the employees' federal and state claims, but the employees urged the Federal District Court to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state claims pursuant to a provision of the federal supplemental jurisdiction statute (28 USCS 1367(a))--which generally grants Federal District Courts jurisdiction over all nonfederal claims that are so related to claims in an action within such courts' original jurisdiction that such nonfederal claims form part of the same case or controversy--if the federal claims were upheld. On July 11, 1997, the Federal District Court granted the university's motion to dismiss.

Regulations governing eligibility for disability benefits under Titles II and XVI of the Social Security Act (42 USCS 401-431, 1381-1383c) establish a "sequential evaluation" process. Eligibility is initially determined by a state agency acting under the authority and control of the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and the agency's decisions are reviewable by the Social Security Administration (SSA), which may return a case to the agency for correction. A disappointed claimant is then afforded a three-stage administrative review process, the completion of which results in the exhaustion of the claimant's administrative remedies, and the claimant may then seek judicial review within 60 days of notice of the action taken, as provided in 42 USCS 405(g). A class action was brought in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York against the Secretary and the SSA Commissioner by named individuals, seeking relief on behalf of all individuals residing in New York who had applied for or received disability benefits, who had been found to have a severe mental impairment, and who had been denied disability benefits or whose benefits had been terminated, pursuant to an allegedly unpublished and unlawful policy of the Secretary. The plaintiffs claimed that the failure to make the policy known to claimants denied the individual plaintiffs and class members due process of law. Holding that the policy in question was illegal, the District Court also (1) held that the class included claimants who had not exhausted administrative remedies as well as those who had not complied with the 60-day requirement for judicial review, (2) ordered the Secretary to reopen the decisions denying or terminating benefits and to redetermine eligibility, and (3) awarded interim relief (578 F Supp 1109). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed, holding that the District Court had jurisdiction over the claims of class members who had failed to exhaust their administrative remedies and the claims of those who failed to seek judicial review within the 60-day period (742 F2d 729, rehearing denied 755 F2d 331).
On Petition for Writ of Certiorari to the District Court of Appeal of Florida, First District.

The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected all the claims of two environmental groups who were challenging standards promulgated by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to air pollution. (657 F2d 298). Notwithstanding their lack of success on the merits, the groups filed a request for attorney's fees incurred in the action, relying on 307(f) of the Clean Air Act (42 USCS 7607(f)), which permits the award of attorney's fees in certain proceedings whenever the court determines that such an award is appropriate. The Court of Appeals agreed with the groups that it was appropriate for them to receive fees where they contributed to the goals of the Act (672 F2d 33, 684 F2d 972).

Two Negro candidates for the school board in East Baton Rouge Parish, Louisiana, brought suit in the United States District Court for the District of Louisiana to enjoin the Louisiana secretary of state from effectuating a state statute requiring that in all primary, general, or special elections, the nomination papers and ballots designate the race of candidates for elective office. A three-judge Federal District Court denied injunctive relief on the ground that the statute was constitutional. (206 F Supp 700.)

An employer which provided protection services at a plant, under a contract which expired June 30, 1967, entered into a consent election agreement specifying as the appropriate unit all guards at the plant. On February 28, 1967, the United Plant Guard Workers (UPG) won the election; on March 8, 1967, the National Labor Relations Board Regional Director certified the UPG; and on April 29, 1967, the UPG entered into a 3-year collective bargaining agreement with the employer. Another employer, having been informed of these developments, successfully bid for a contract to provide such protection services at the plant beginning July 1, 1967. The new employer began hiring in June under terms different from those specified in the collective bargaining agreement. It hired 27 of the former employer's guards on condition that they sign membership cards of the American Federation of Guards (AFG), and brought in 15 of its own guards from other locations. On June 29, 1967, it recognized the AFG, and on July 12, 1967, it rejected the UPG's bargaining demand. The NLRB found the plant to be the appropriate unit; held that the new employer violated 8(a)(2) of the amended National Labor Relations Act by unlawfully recognizing and assisting the AFG; and held that it violated 8(a)(5) of the amended Act by failing to recognize and bargain with the UPG and by refusing to honor the UPG's collective bargaining agreement with the former employer (182 NLRB No. 50). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit enforced the NLRB's order insofar as it related to unlawful assistance and refusal to bargain, but it refused enforcement of that part of the NLRB's order which required the new employer to recognize the UPG's collective bargaining agreement with the former employer (441 F2d 911).

Under 706(e) of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e-5(e)), a complainant alleging employment discrimination must file his or her charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) within 180 days of the occurrence of the alleged unlawful act, or within 300 days if the proceedings are initially instituted with a state or local employment discrimination agency. Section 706(c) (42 USCS 2000e-5(c)) provides that no employment discrimination charge may be filed with the EEOC until 60 days have elapsed from initial filing of the charge with a state or local agency, unless that agency's proceedings "have been earlier terminated." The combined effect of these two provisions has been described in a United States Supreme Court decision as requiring a complainant to file his or her charge with the state or local agency, or to have the EEOC refer the charge to that agency, within 240 days, unless that agency terminates its proceedings before 300 days, in which case the complaint is timely if it is filed not more than 300 days after the alleged unlawful act. A complainant in Colorado, alleging that her employer had discharged her because of her sex in violation of Title VII, filed an employment discrimination charge with the EEOC 290 days after her discharge. The EEOC notified the Colorado Civil Rights Division (CCRD) that the EEOC would initially process the charge, pursuant to a work-sharing agreement between the EEOC and the CCRD. The CCRD notified the complainant that it had waived its right to initial processing but that it retained jurisdiction to act on the charge after the conclusion of the EEOC's proceedings. The EEOC issued an administrative subpoena for information relevant to the complainant's charge. The employer refused to comply, maintaining that the EEOC lacked jurisdiction to investigate the charge because the charge had not been timely filed. The EEOC brought an action in the United States District Court for the District of Colorado seeking judicial enforcement of the subpoena. The District Court concluded that the charge had not been timely filed, and accordingly dismissed the enforcement action. The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, affirming the District Court's judgment, held that (1) the extended 300-day federal filing period was applicable, even though the charge had not been filed with the CCRD within Colorado's own 180-day statute of limitations, but (2) the complainant's charge had not been filed during the 300-day period because the CCRD had not "terminated" its proceedings within the meaning of 706(c), and thus the 60-day deferral period had not expired until after the 300-day limit (803 F2d 581).

By will probated in 1831, Stephen Girard left a fund to the City of Philadelphia in trust for the erection, maintenance and operation of a "college," providing that it was to admit "as many poor white male orphans, between the ages of six and ten years, as the said income shall be adequate to maintain." The college was established and is now being operated by a Board appointed under a Pennsylvania statute.

A naturalized American citizen was convicted of a conspiracy to violate the Espionage Act of 1917. Subsequently his citizenship was canceled on the ground of fraud in its procurement, and, after the required hearings, his deportation was ordered by the Attorney General under an act of Congress permitting the deportation of "aliens" so convicted.

Upon trial in the Municipal Court of Lorain, Ohio, the defendant was convicted of violating city gambling ordinances, which convictions were based on evidence seized by city policemen, who, without a warrant, had entered the defendant's upstairs apartment unannounced and against the defendant's protest, had observed a dice game in progress, had placed everyone present under arrest, and had seized the articles used in the game, the downstairs portion of the building, which housed a cigar store and a storeroom, also being searched, with resultant discovery and seizure of numbers game paraphernalia. The police officers had acted on a suspicion that a crime was being committed, based on tips from persons who had stopped the officers on the street and on the officers' observation of cars parked near the building and of men entering the apartment. The trial court denied the defendant's motion to suppress the evidence thus seized. Although the Court of Common Pleas reversed the conviction based on the possession of the numbers game paraphernalia that had been found in the lower portion of the building, the convictions based on the evidence seized in the defendant's apartment were affirmed by the Court of Appeals, and the Supreme Court of Ohio dismissed an appeal.

The accused was approached by two plainclothes police officers as he and a companion entered a parking lot. The officers were driving in an unmarked police vehicle. The accused was carrying a brown paper grocery bag in a manner later described by the officers as "gingerly." One of the officers left the police vehicle and, without identifying himself, asked the accused to "come here a minute." The accused did not respond and kept walking. When the officer identified himself as a police officer, the accused threw the grocery bag he was carrying onto the hood of his car and turned to face the officer, who was approaching him. The officer asked the accused what the bag contained. The accused did not answer, whereupon the officer rebuffed the accused's attempt to protect the bag, pushed his hand away, and opened the bag. Drug paraphernalia found in the bag provided probable cause for the arrest of the accused and sufficient evidence to support his subsequent conviction, in an Ohio state court, for drug abuse. The Supreme Court of Ohio, upholding the warrantless search of the bag as a search incident to arrest, recognized that the accused was not arrested until after the contraband was discovered in the search of the bag, but nonetheless held the search constitutional because its fruits justified the arrest that followed (45 Ohio St 3d 255, 544 NE2d 239).

Upon finding it likely that the plaintiffs would prevail on their claim that a New York welfare statute was violative of the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, a three-judge Federal District Court in the Southern District of New York issued a preliminary injunction against the enforcement of the statute, and found it unnecessary to determine the plaintiffs' claims that the state welfare program was in conflict with federal welfare statutes (303 F Supp 339).

A selective service registrant who, while enrolled in a Boston music school, was given a II-S student classification and hence deferred from military service, in November 1967 surrendered his draft card to a minister at a public gathering in protest against United States involvement in the war in Vietnam. Shortly thereafter, his local draft board, pursuant to the regulations, declared him "delinquent" for failing to have his draft card in his possession and at the same time reclassified him I-A--available for military service. He appealed his reclassification to the Selective Service Appeal Board, and while this appeal was pending filed suit in the United States District Court for Connecticut seeking an injunction against any possible induction into the Armed Forces on the ground that his delinquency reclassification was invalid, but the District Court, relying on 10(b)(3) of the Military Selective Service Act of 1967, which precludes judicial review of draft classifications "except as a defense to a criminal prosecution," dismissed the suit for want of jurisdiction (284 F Supp 749), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (406 F2d 636). While the appeal to the Court of Appeals was pending, the Appeal Board upheld the reclassification and the local board then ordered the registrant to report for induction, which order was stayed pending decision in the instant case.

In an action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, brought against certain police officers under 42 USCS 1983, the father of a boy who had been shot and killed by the officers while the boy was attempting to escape arrest, sought to recover damages and to obtain a declaratory judgment that Missouri statutes authorizing the police to use deadly force in apprehending a person who has committed a felony, following notice of the intent to arrest, were unconstitutional. The District Court initially held that a defense of good faith had been established, and denied both forms of relief, but on appeal only from the denial of declaratory relief, the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit held that such relief was available and remanded the case for consideration of the constitutional issue (502 F2d 588). On remand, the plaintiff filed an amended complaint, making no claim for damages, and the District Court upheld the Missouri statutes (404 F Supp 643). However, the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the statutes were unconstitutional (547 F2d 1007).

An employee was 62 years old when she lost her job. The employee, claiming that she had been discharged because of her age in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) (29 USCS 621 et seq.), filed suit against her employer in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee. In a pretrial deposition, the employee testified that she had removed and copied several of the employer's confidential documents during her final year of employment. A few days after these deposition disclosures, the employer sent the employee a letter (1) declaring that her actions had been in violation of her job responsibilities; (2) advising her once again that she was terminated; and (3) reciting that if the employer had known of her misconduct, then the employer would have discharged her at once for that reason. However, for purposes of summary judgment, the employer conceded its discrimination against the employee. The District Court, granting summary judgment for the employer, stated that the employee's misconduct had been the grounds for her termination and that neither backpay nor any other remedy was available to her under the ADEA (797 F Supp 604). The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed on the same rationale (9 F3d 539).

The petitioner was convicted by a Federal court of bribing a Federal revenue agent, after a trial in which the prosecutor, over the petitioner's objections, was allowed to ask the latter's character witnesses whether they ever heard that on a specified date, which was 27 years before trial, the defendant had been arrested for receiving stolen goods. While the circuit court of appeals held the cross-examination permissible, the writer of the opinion expressed the wish that the Supreme Court adopt the Illinois rule under which questions as to previous convictions, prosecutions or arrests are improper unless they relate to offenses similar to those for which the defendant is on trial.

The plan permitted participants to direct the investment of their contributions. One of _ 1132(a)'s authorized civil actions allowed participants to bring actions on behalf of a plan to recover for violations of the obligations defined in 29 U.S.C.S. _ 1109(a). And, 29 U.S.C.S. _ 1132(a)(2) encompassed appropriate claims for "lost profits" as fiduciaries were chargeable with any profit which would have accrued to the plan if there had been no breach of trust, including profits forgone because the fiduciary failed to purchase specific property which it was his duty to purchase. The "entire plan" language from a prior case upon which the Fourth Circuit relied and which appeared nowhere in 29 U.S.C.S. __ 1109, 1132(a)(2), did not apply to defined contribution plans such as the one at issue. Therefore, although _ 1132(a)(2) did not provide a remedy for individual injuries distinct from plan injuries, that provision did authorize recovery for fiduciary breaches that impaired the value of plan assets in a participant's individual account. Accordingly, the Fourth Circuit's judgment was vacated.

Under the Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938, the Civil Aeronautics Board consolidated 45 route applications of 25 air lines into one area proceeding. After hearings, it made findings of fact as to what new routes should be established and which of the applicants could best serve these routes. It entered orders authorizing certificates of convenience and necessity for several new routes in the area. One applicant was authorized to engage in air transportation along certain of these routes which were different from those described in its applications. Its applications requested authority to transport on "the routes detailed herein, or such modification of such routes as the Board may find public necessity and convenience require" and also contained prayers for general relief.

A truck buyer brought against the seller, which had made with the buyer a retail installment sales contract, a suit in which the buyer (1) alleged a TILA violation; and (2) sought to recover $24,192.80, which was twice the amount of the contractual finance charges. When a Federal District Court held that the buyer's damages were not capped at $1,000, a jury awarded damages of $24,192.80. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed ( 319 F.3d 119).

On the day following a California police officer's encounter with a known marijuana dealer, including the purchase from the dealer of a package of marijuana, other police officers observed an encounter between the dealer and the defendant husband, which occurred under identical surrounding circumstances except that the officers did not see any substance passing between the two men. The officers following the defendant lost contact with him when he made a U-turn in the middle of a block. Without securing a search warrant, the officers, among them one having information that the defendant husband was selling from his apartment marijuana possibly secured from the dealer, obtained from the building manager a passkey to defendants' apartment, and entered the apartment, where they found the defendant husband in the living room. The defendant wife emerged from the kitchen, and one of the officers, after identifying himself, observed through the open doorway of the kitchen a package of marijuana on a scale atop the kitchen sink. The officers then arrested both defendants and searched the apartment, finding additional marijuana in the kitchen cupboard and atop the bedroom dresser. The defendants were convicted in the Superior Court of Los Angeles County of possessing marijuana. Their convictions were affirmed by the California District Court of Appeal on the grounds that there was probable cause for the arrests, that the officers' entry into the apartment was for the purpose of arrest and was not unlawful, and that the search, being incident to the arrests, was likewise lawful and its fruits admissible in evidence against the defendants. (195 Cal App 2d 246, 15 Cal Rptr 767.)

Defendant's appeal from a judgment of conviction in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York was dismissed by the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit on the ground that the appeal was not timely filed. Upon defendant's motion, the District Court reduced the sentence; the following day defendant filed a second notice of appeal, but again the Court of Appeals granted the government's motion to dismiss.

A defined benefit pension plan, established and maintained by an employer pursuant to a collective bargaining agreement, included a provision that limited otherwise defined, vested benefits to the amounts that could be provided by the assets of the pension fund. The employer decided to close the plant employing the persons covered by the plan, and subsequently terminated the plan when the assets in the fund were sufficient to pay only about 35 percent of the vested benefits, such termination occurring after the enactment of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (29 USCS 1001 et seq.), but before the effective date of certain provisions of the Act that would have required significant changes in at least the vesting provisions of the plan. In view of Title IV of the Act (29 USCS 1301 et seq.), which requires the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation to guarantee payment of all "nonforfeitable" benefits of an employer's terminating plan (29 USCS 1322(a)) and gives the Corporation a statutory right to reimbursement from the employer for the amount by which the plan's guaranteed benefits exceed the plan's assets (29 USCS 1362(b)), the employer filed an action for declaratory and injunctive relief against the Corporation in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, seeking a declaration that it had no liability under the Act for any failure of the plan to pay all of the vested benefits in full, and an order enjoining the Corporation from taking actions inconsistent with that declaration. Granting summary judgment for the employer, the District Court accepted the employer's contentions that the limitation of liability clause in the plan was valid on the date of termination and that the clause prevented the benefits at issue from being characterized as "nonforfeitable" (436 F Supp 1334). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed, holding that the limitation of liability clause merely affected the extent to which the benefits could be collected, without qualifying the employees' rights against the plan (592 F2d 947).

The Pregnancy Discrimination Act (42 USCS 2000e) was enacted by Congress in 1978 to provide that the prohibition against sex discrimination in employment in 703(a) of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 included a prohibition against discrimination on the basis of pregnancy. In order to comply with the Act, an employer amended its health insurance plan for its employees to cover pregnancy-related conditions of female employees to the same extent as other medical conditions. The plan also provided coverage of the pregnancy-related conditions of the spouses of male employees, but not to the extent of that provided to female employees. One of the employer's male employees filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), alleging that the employer unlawfully refused to provide full insurance coverage for his wife's hospitalization caused by her pregnancy. Later, the employees' union filed a similar charge on behalf of other individuals. The employer then commenced an action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, challenging EEOC guidelines that considered the employer's plan unlawful, and seeking both declaratory and injunctive relief. The EEOC later filed a civil action against the employer, alleging discrimination on the basis of sex against male employees in its provision of hospitalization benefits. Concluding that the Pregnancy Discrimination Act extended only to female employees, and not to the spouses of male employees, the District Court held that the employer's plan was lawful and enjoined enforcement of the EEOC guidelines relating to pregnancy benefits for employees' spouses, and dismissed the EEOC's complaint (510 F Supp 66). On appeal of the two consolidated cases, a divided panel of the United States Court of Appeals reversed, reasoning that the plan contained a distinction based on pregnancy that results in less medical coverage for male employees with spouses than for female employees with spouses, and was impermissible under the statute (667 F2d 448). The court reaffirmed the panel's conclusion after rehearing the case en banc (682 F2d 113).

A state senator was indicted on federal charges arising from his alleged acceptance of money for using his public office to block the extradition of a criminal defendant from the state, and for agreeing to introduce state legislation which would enable four persons to obtain master electricians' licenses which they had been unable to gain through existing examination processes. Prior to trial in the United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee, the senator moved to suppress all evidence relating to his legislative activities. The District Court granted the motion, holding that the senator, by virtue of his office, had an evidentiary privilege cognizable under Rule 501 of the Federal Rules of Evidence, which provides that "the privilege of a witness ... shall be governed by the principles of the common law as they may be interpreted by the courts of the United States in the light of reason and experience." The District Court reasoned that this privilege was equivalent to that granted to members of Congress under the speech or debate clause of the Constitution (Art I, 6, cl 1), and was limited to prohibiting the introduction of any evidence of the senator's legislative acts and underlying motivations. On review, the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ultimately accepted the existence of such a privilege, and determined that certain evidence should in fact be suppressed, but ruled that other items of evidence were insufficiently related to the legislative process to be protected by the privilege (587 F2d 284).

After a prison inmate who had a violent past and had stated that he would "not do federal time" escaped, a reliable informant told a federal agent that the informant had seen a person who the informant thought was the inmate at the private residence of another individual, the agent and the informant drove to an area near the home, and the agent observed outside the home a man who resembled the inmate. Subsequently, police officers--who had obtained a no-knock warrant to enter and search the home and had been told by the informant that the resident might have guns and drugs hidden in his garage--executed the warrant by simultaneously (1) announcing that they had a search warrant, and (2) breaking a single garage window, through which the officers pointed a gun. The search resulted in the resident being indicted under 18 USCS 922(g)(1) for being a felon in possession of firearms. The United States District for the District of Oregon, granting the resident's motion to suppress evidence regarding his possession of the firearms, expressed the view that the police officers had violated the Federal Constitution's Fourth Amendment and 18 USCS 3109--which provides that a police officer may break a door or window of a house, or any part of a house, or anything therein, to execute a search warrant, if, after notice of the officer's authority and purpose, the officer is refused admittance or when necessary to liberate the officer or a person aiding the officer in the execution of the warrant--because there were insufficient exigent circumstances to justify the officers' destruction of property in their execution of the warrant. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, affirming, expressed the view that the standard for justification of a no-knock entry was heightened when property was destroyed (91 F3d 1297).

Two defendants were charged with federal drug offenses in the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina. The prosecutions arose after a truck driven by one of the defendants was stopped by a highway patrol officer working with an agent of the Drug Enforcement Administration and detained for about 15 minutes until the agent, who had pursued the other defendant in another vehicle, arrived on the scene and within 5 minutes determined that the truck contained material resembling marijuana. Subsequent chemical tests showed that the material was in fact marijuana. The District Court denied a motion to suppress the contraband and the defendants were convicted. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed, concluding that the investigative stops failed to meet the requirement of brevity and that the length of the detentions transformed them into de facto arrests without probable cause (712 F2d 65).

The 1968 Communist Party candidates for President and Vice President of the United States, various Minnesota voters who alleged a desire to vote for those candidates, and the Communist Parties of the United States and of Minnesota, brought an action in the United States District Court for the District of Minnesota seeking a declaration that the Communist Control Act of 1954 (50 USC 841-842) was constitutionally invalid, and praying for a temporary restraining order and permanent injunction requiring the Secretary of State of Minnesota to include the names of the plaintiff candidates on the November 1968 ballot. Without deciding the merits of the claims, the three- judge District Court ordered that the names of the plaintiff candidates be placed on the November 1968 ballot (290 F Supp 642). After the election, the District Court held that the prayer for injunctive relief, which referred only to the 1968 election and requested no injunction as to future conduct, had been rendered moot by the passing of that election. As to the prayer for a declaratory judgment striking down the Communist Control Act, the court found no present case or controversy, and therefore dismissed the complaint (300 F Supp 1145).

A taxpayer inherited an approximately 233,000 estate in Arkansas from his mother, who died intestate. Under Arkansas law, the taxpayer was the sole heir to the estate. At the time of the mother's death, (1) the taxpayer was insolvent, (2) the taxpayer owed the Federal Government approximately 325,000 on unpaid tax assessments, and (3) the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) had valid tax liens against all of the taxpayer's "property and rights to property" pursuant to 26 USCS 6321. After petitioning for the position, the taxpayer was appointed as administrator of the decedent's estate by the Pulaski County Probate Court in August 1994. The taxpayer resigned as administrator in February 1995, after filing in the Probate Court and county land records a written disclaimer of all interests in the estate. Under Arkansas law, (1) such a disclaimer created the legal fiction that the disclaimant predeceased the decedent, (2) the disclaimant's share of the estate passed to the person next in line to receive that share, and (3) the disavowing heir's creditors could not reach property thus disclaimed. The Probate Court declared valid the taxpayer's disclaimer in March 1995. The estate then passed to the taxpayer's daughter, who succeeded the taxpayer as administrator and established a trust with the funds from the estate, of which trust she and, during their lifetimes, her parents were the beneficiaries. The trust was spendthrift, and under state law, its assets were shielded from creditors seeking to satisfy the debts of the trust's beneficiaries. When the taxpayer revealed to the IRS his beneficial interest in the trust, the IRS in April 1996 (1) filed a notice of federal tax lien against the trust as the taxpayer's nominee, (2) served a notice of levy on accounts held in the trust's name by an investment bank, and (3) notified the trust of the levy. The trust then filed a wrongful levy action against the United States in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas. The Federal Government counterclaimed against the trust, the trustee, and the trust beneficiaries, seeking to (1) reduce to judgment the tax assessments against the taxpayer, (2) confirm the government's rights to seize the trust's assets in collection of those debts, (3) foreclose on the tax liens, and (4) sell the trust property. On cross-motions for summary judgment, the District Court ruled in the government's favor (1997 US Dist LEXIS 6755). The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed, reading the United States Supreme Court's precedents to convey that state law determines whether a given set of circumstances creates a right or interest, but federal law dictates whether that right or interest constitutes "property" or the "righ[t] to property" under 6321 (152 F3d 892, 1998 US App LEXIS 20084).

The plaintiff, a private university which refused to admit Negroes as students, instituted an action in the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina, seeking to enjoin the Internal Revenue Service--pursuant to its decision to no longer allow tax-exempt status under 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (26 USCS 501(c)(3)) for private schools maintaining racially discriminatory admissions policies--from revoking its ruling letter declaring that the plaintiff qualified for tax-exempt status, and from withdrawing advance assurance to the plaintiff's donors that contributions to the plaintiff would constitute charitable deductions for the donors under 26 USCS 170(c)(2). The plaintiff contended that the Service's threatened action was outside its lawful authority and would violate the plaintiff's First Amendment, due process, and equal protection rights. The District Court granted a preliminary injunction against the Service pending a decision on the merits, holding that the suit was not precluded by the Anti-Injunction Act of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (26 USCS 7421(a)), which provides in general that no suit for the purpose of restraining the assessment or collection of any tax shall be maintained in any court by any person, whether or not such person is the person against whom such tax was assessed (341 F Supp 277). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed, holding that the suit was barred by the Anti-Injunction Act (472 F2d 903, reh den 476 F2d 259).

A woman failed to pay real estate taxes on her interest in certain land in West Virginia. The land was then sold to West Virginia under procedures which afforded notice of sale to the landowner only through posting of a delinquency list on the county courthouse door and publication of the list in local newspapers. Although West Virginia law entitled the woman to redeem her interest at any time within 18 months of the state's purchase, the woman failed to redeem, and West Virginia thereafter transferred the interest to an individual in a sale, the only notice of which was, as authorized under state law, by way of publication in two local newspapers. Some two years after the state's sale, the woman brought an action to quiet title in the Circuit Court of Kanawha County, West Virginia, naming the individual who purchased from the state as a defendant. The Circuit Court ruled against the woman, and its judgment was affirmed by the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia (221 SE2d 171). Subsequently, the woman appealed to the United States Supreme Court, and it noted probable jurisdiction (426 US 946, 49 L Ed 2d 1182, 96 S Ct 3164).

The former stockholders of a company, who had agreed to merge that company into another company and to exchange their stock in the first company for stock in the second company, subsequently concluded that financial statements of the second company on which they had allegedly relied had misrepresented that company's financial condition. The stockholders accordingly filed an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, which action alleged that the second company, the accounting firm which had prepared the financial statements, and certain individuals had committed violations of the federal securities laws and Georgia common law. On January 30, 1985, the jury found in favor of the accounting firm and a director of the second firm, but returned a verdict against the other defendants and awarded the stockholders more than $ 2 million in damages; the stockholders immediately made an oral motion for prejudgment interest on that award, but were told to submit their motion in writing within 10 days; and the judgment was filed and entered. On February 11, 1985, the stockholders filed a motion for prejudgment interest; on March 1, 1985, the stockholders filed a notice of appeal from the judgment in favor of the accounting firm and the director; on July 1, 1985, the District Court, ruling on the motion for prejudgment interest, entered an order stating that the judgment would be amended to reflect the addition of prejudgment interest; on July 9, 1985, the District Court filed an amended judgment adding prejudgment interest to the judgment; and on July 31, 1985, the stockholders filed a new notice of appeal which failed to include the accounting firm as a party. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit dismissed the stockholders' appeal as to the accounting firm for lack of jurisdiction, on the grounds that (1) the motion for prejudgment interest constituted a motion to alter or amend the judgment under Rule 59(e) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure; (2) all notices of appeal filed prior to the disposition of that motion were therefore ineffective under Rule 4(a)(4) of the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure; and (3) no "unique circumstances" sufficient to validate a premature appeal were shown by the stockholder's alleged reliance on (a) orders of the District Court which appeared to treat the judgment of January 30 as final and appealable, (b) the District Court clerk's requirement of a filing fee for the July 31 notice which should not have been necessary if a Rule 59 motion had been made, or (c) the Court of Appeals' failure to originally notify the stockholders that jurisdiction was questionable (825 F2d 1521).

Upon investigating an attorney in connection with his real estate settlement activities, particularly in connection with a transaction for a "Lot 13T," a bi-county fraud unit, acting pursuant to state warrants, conducted simultaneous searches of the attorney's law office and another office he maintained for a corporation of which he was the sole shareholder. The attorney was thereafter charged with the Maryland crime of false pretenses, based on his misrepresentation to the purchaser of Lot 13T, and was convicted of such offense in the Circuit Court of Frederick County, Maryland, at a trial in which the court, rejecting the attorney's contentions that his Fifth and Fourth Amendment rights had been violated, permitted the state to introduce into evidence a number of documents, including documents pertaining to a lot other than Lot 13T, which had been seized during the office searches. The attorney's conviction was affirmed by the Court of Special Appeals of Maryland (24 Md App 128, 331 A2d 78).

A disbarment proceeding for professional misconduct was brought against the petitioner, a member of the New York Bar, on a charge of refusing to honor a subpoena duces tecum in that he refused to produce the demanded financial records and refused to testify at the judicial inquiry. The petitioner's sole defense was that the production of the records and his testimony would tend to incriminate him. The Appellate Division, Second Department, of the New York Supreme Court, ordered the petitioner disbarred, holding that the constitutional privilege against self-incrimination was not available to him as a lawyer.

A class action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, instituted by the head of a household receiving assistance under the Food Stamp Act of 1964 (7 USCS 2011 et seq.), presented the question of the validity of regulations of the Secretary of Agriculture (7 CFR 271.3(c)) and parallel regulations of the State of Iowa which (1) provide that transportation allowances received by food stamp recipients from the state to defray the cost of commuting to a training school must be included as "income" in determining the price to be paid for food stamps, (2) allow a standardized 10% deduction as to the transportation allowance, and (3) prohibit a specific educational deduction for commuting expenses, even if they equal the transportation allowance. The three-judge District Court held that there was no rational basis for treating as income a transportation allowance which was fully expended for its intended purpose, and that both the federal and the state regulations were invalid as conflicting with the Food Stamp Act and as discriminating against recipients of such allowances in violation of equal protection guarantees explicit in the Fourteenth Amendment and implicit in the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment (402 F Supp 398).

A pharmaceutical contractor entered into three contracts with the Defense Supply Agency of the Department of Defense and one contract with the Veterans' Administration for the sale of pharmaceutical products to the government. All four contracts were negotiated, rather than awarded after formal advertising. As required by 10 USCS 2313(b) and 41 USCS 254(c), each contract contained a standard access-to-records clause granting the Comptroller General the right to examine any directly pertinent records involving transactions related to the contract. Relying on these clauses, the Comptroller General issued a formal demand to the supplier for access to all books, documents, papers, and other records directly pertinent to the government contracts. The contractor refused to comply with the Comptroller General's request and commenced an action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, seeking a declaratory judgment that the access demand exceeded statutory authority. The United States intervened and counterclaimed to enforce the Comptroller General's demand. The District Court granted partial summary judgment for each party and permitted access to all records directly pertaining to the pricing and cost of producing items furnished under the contracts while barring access to records with respect to research and development, marketing and promotion, distribution, and administration, except to the extent that such data may be included in the cost items to which access was provided. The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed (214 App DC 418, 665 F2d 1236).

A reapportionment plan for the Texas House of Representatives provided for 150 representatives to be selected from 79 single-member districts and 11 multimember districts. Under the plan, the population of the smallest district (71,597) was approximately 9.9 percent smaller than that of the largest district (78,943). The plan was challenged in the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas. A three-judge District Court was convened and held that the reapportionment plan was unconstitutional because of the state's failure to justify the population variations among the districts, and that in two counties the use of multimember districts unconstitutionally diluted the votes of Negroes and Mexican-Americans, respectively (343 F Supp 704).

In 1985, a corporation filed a complaint in the Circuit Court of McDowell County, West Virginia, seeking a declaratory judgment to remove an alleged cloud on title to an interest in oil and gas development rights in a West Virginia tract of land. The defendants--including a second corporation with which the first, complaining corporation had a royalty arrangement involving the tract--filed a counterclaim for slander of title and alleged that the first corporation (1) knew that the second corporation had good title to the oil and gas; and (2) had acted in bad faith in advancing a claim--on the basis of a supposedly worthless quitclaim deed obtained from a third company--in an effort to renegotiate the royalty arrangement. The second corporation also introduced evidence purporting to show that (1) the first corporation was a large company in its own right and a wholly owned subsidiary of an even larger company; (2) the anticipated gross revenues from oil and gas development--and therefore the amount of royalties involved--were substantial; and (3) the first corporation had supposedly engaged in similar nefarious activities in business dealings in other parts of the country. The jury awarded $ 19,000 in actual damages and $ 10 million in punitive damages against the first corporation on the slander of title counterclaim. The first corporation, in support of motions for judgment notwithstanding the verdict and for remittitur, argued to the effect that the punitive damages award violated the due process clause of the Federal Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment, but the trial court denied the motions without opinion. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, in upholding the jury's verdict, expressed the view that (1) the defendants against whom punitive damages had been awarded after the United States Supreme Court's punitive damages, due process decision in Pacific Mut. Life Ins. Co. v Haslip (1991) 499 US 1, 113 L Ed 2d 1, 111 S Ct 1032, fell into the three categories of (a) "really stupid" defendants, (b) "really mean" defendants, and (c) "really stupid" defendants who could have caused a great deal of harm by their actions but who actually caused minimal harm; and (2) the punitive damages award in the case at hand satisfied the "reasonable relationship" test required in the circumstances, where, under the jury's verdict, (a) the type of fraudulent action intentionally undertaken by the first corporation could potentially cause millions of dollars in damages to other victims, (b) the first corporation's conduct had been reprehensible, and (c) an award of the magnitude in question was necessary to discourage the first corporation from continuing its pattern and practice of fraud, trickery, and deceit (187 W Va 457, 419 SE2d 870).

Anticipating completion of the Trans Alaska Pipeline, seven of its eight owners filed tariffs with the Interstate Commerce Commission setting out the rules and rates governing transportation of oil over the pipeline. Acting pursuant to 15(7) of the Interstate Commerce Act (49 USCS 15(7)), which provides that the Commission may suspend the operation of any filed schedule stating a new individual or joint rate, fare, or charge, the Commission found that protests lodged against the tariffs gave it reason to believe that the proposed rates were not just and reasonable. The Commission suspended the initial rates, stated that it would not suspend interim tariffs which specified rates no higher than rates estimated by the Commission as likely to be lawful rates, and stated that any interim tariffs must provide for refunds of any amounts later determined to be in excess of lawful rates. On a petition for review, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit determined that the Commission had the statutory authority to suspend initial tariffs and the ancillary authority to set out maximum interim rates and to condition a decision not to suspend tariffs on a requirement that carriers whose tariffs were allowed to go into effect be prepared to make refunds of any amounts collected which were later determined to be unlawful (557 F2d 775).

The sole question in the present case was whether the United States District Court for the Southern District of California had jurisdiction to issue a writ of habeas corpus ad prosequendum directing a New York City prison official to deliver petitioner, a prisoner of that city, to California for trial on an indictment pending in the District Court. Both the District Court and the Court of Appeals held that such jurisdiction exists. (277 F2d 433.)

Together, the Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act of 2000 (DD Act) and the Protection and Advocacy for Individuals with Mental Illness Act (PAIMI Act) offer States federal money to improve, inter alia, medical care for persons with developmental disabilities or mental illness. As a condition of funding, a State must establish a protection and advocacy (P&A) system ‚Äúto protect and advocate [those individuals‚Äô] rights.‚Äù 42 U. S. C. ¬ß15043(a)(1). A participating State may appoint either a state agency or a private nonprofit entity as its P&A system, but if a state agency it must have authority to litigate and freedom from the control of other state agencies or officers. Virginia has appointed an independent state agency, petitioner Virginia Office for Protection and Advocacy (VOPA), authorizing it to litigate to secure disabled individuals‚Äô rights, free of executive-branch oversight; to operate independently of Virginia‚Äôs attorney general; and to employ its own lawyers to sue on its behalf. While investigating patient deaths and injuries at state mental hospitals, VOPA asked respondents‚Äîstate officials in charge of those hospitals‚Äîto produce relevant patient records. Respondents refused, asserting that a state-law privilege shielded the records from disclosure. VOPA then filed suit in Federal District Court, seeking a declaration that respondents‚Äô refusal to produce the records violated the DD and PAIMI Acts and an injunction requiring respondents to produce the records and refrain in the future from interfering with VOPA‚Äôs right of access. Respondents moved to dismiss on the ground that they are immune from suit under the Eleventh Amendment, but the court held that the suit was permitted by the doctrine of Ex parte Young, 209 U. S. 123, which normally allows federal courts to award prospective relief against state officials for violations of federal law. The Fourth Circuit reversed, finding that Ex parte Young did not apply because the suit was brought by a state agency.

A Mexican-American employee who was denied a promotion filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission alleging national origin discrimination, and received a right to sue letter from the Commission. The employee brought a class action against his employer under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e et seq.) in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas. The District Court certified a class including Mexican-American employees and Mexican-American applicants for employment who had not been hired. The District Court found that the employer had not discriminated against the employee in hiring, but that it had discriminated against him in its promotion practices. With regard to the class, the court conversely found no discrimination in promotion practices, but concluded that the employer had discriminated against Mexican-Americans in its hiring practices at the facility in question. (463 F Supp 315). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit held that the District Court's class certification was proper under its "across-the-board" rule, under which it is permissible for an employee complaining of one employment practice to represent another complaining of another practice, if the plaintiff and the members of the class suffer from essentially the same injury. On the merits, the Court of Appeals upheld the employee's promotion claim, but held that the District Court's findings were insufficient to support recovery on behalf of the class (626 F2d 369). Eventually, on remand from the United States Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals vacated its ruling as to the employee's promotion claim, but approved the District Court's class certification (647 F2d 633).

The question presented in this case was whether under the income tax provisions of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 in effect in 1967 and 1968, an estate's net long-term capital gain to which the alternative tax under 26 USCS 1201(b) was applicable could be reduced by the amount of the capital gain that had been set aside to a charity pursuant to the terms of the decedent's will. During 1967 and 1968, the executors of an estate, in accordance with the decedent's will, set aside for a charity portions of the estate's long-term capital gains from the sales of securities, and in their fiduciary income tax returns for those years, the executors sought to use the alternative tax and excluded the portions of long-term gain set aside for the charity from the long-term capital gains to which the alternative tax was applicable. However, the District Director of Internal Revenue disallowed the exclusion, without which the alternative tax was higher than the normal tax computed with the capital-gains deduction authorized by 26 USCS 1202. Additional amounts due under the normal tax were assessed and paid, and the executors then instituted a refund action in the United States District Court for the Central District of California. The District Court sustained the executors' position, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed (563 F2d 400).

One convicted of illegally selling narcotics and given a cumulative sentence composed of consecutive sentences on four counts filed a motion in a District Court seeking suspension of sentence and probation on three of the counts.

The question presented‚Äîwhether 11 U. S. C. ¬ß363(m) of the Bankruptcy Code is jurisdictional‚Äîarises in the context of the Chapter 11 bankruptcy of Sears, Roebuck and Co. Sears sold most of its pre-bankruptcy assets to respondent Transform Holdco LLC, including the right to designate to whom a lease between Sears and petitioner MOAC Mall Holdings LLC should be assigned. MOAC leases space to tenants at the Minnesota Mall of America. The agreement with Transform required Sears to assign the lease to any assignee duly designated by Transform. When Transform later designated the Mall of America lease for assignment to its wholly owned subsidiary, MOAC filed an objection with the Bankruptcy Court, arguing that Sears had not shown ‚Äúadequate assurance of future performance by the assignee‚Äù as the Code requires, ¬ß365(f )(2)(B). The Bankruptcy Court disagreed with MOAC‚Äôs adequate-assurance argument and issued an order authorizing the lease assignment (Assignment Order). The Code contemplates that interested parties like MOAC may appeal such an order, but the effect of a successful appeal is limited by ¬ß363(m), which states that ‚Äú[t]he reversal or modification on appeal of an authorization under [¬ß363(b) or ¬ß363(c)] of a sale or lease of property does not affect the validity of a sale or lease under such authorization to an entity that purchased or leased such property in good faith . . . unless such authorization and such sale or lease were stayed pending appeal.‚Äù Fearing the implications of ¬ß363(m) on an appeal, MOAC sought to stay the Assignment Order. The Bankruptcy Court denied the stay, reasoning that an appeal of the Assignment Order did not qualify as an appeal of an authorization described in ¬ß363(m), and emphasizing Transform‚Äôs explicit representation that it would not invoke ¬ß363(m) against MOAC‚Äôs appeal. After the Assignment Order became effective, Sears assigned the lease to Transform‚Äôs designee, and MOAC appealed the Assignment Order. The District Court sided with MOAC on the adequate-assurance issue. Transform filed for rehearing, arguing that ¬ß363(m) deprived the District Court of jurisdiction. The District Court determined that Second Circuit precedent bound it to treat ¬ß363(m) as jurisdictional and dismissed the appeal. The Second Circuit affirmed.

Pursuant to a wiretap authorization issued under Title III of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 (18 USCS 2510-2520), government agents intercepted all conversations over a particular telephone suspected of being used in furtherance of a conspiracy to import and distribute narcotics. Forty percent of the calls were clearly narcotics related, many of the remaining calls were short, such as wrong number calls, or ambiguous in nature, and several were between the telephone registrant and her mother. Upon cessation of the interceptions, several people were indicted on narcotic charges. Several of the defendants moved prior to the trial to suppress all the intercepted conversations, and the United States District Court for the District of Columbia ordered suppression of the intercepted conversations and all derivative evidence on the ground that the agents had failed to comply with the minimization requirement of 18 USCS 2518(5), providing that wiretapping authorized under Title III of the Act must be conducted so as to minimize the interception of communications not subject to interception under the Title (311 F Supp 223). On a second appeal, following an initial remand, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed the District Court's second suppression order, holding that (1) suppression was not appropriate, and (2) while the presence or absence of a good faith attempt to minimize on the part of the agents was one factor to be considered in assessing whether the minimization requirement had been satisfied, the decision as to suppression had to be based ultimately on the reasonableness of the actual interceptions, not on whether the agents subjectively intended to minimize their interceptions (516 F2d 751). Subsequently, the defendants were convicted of narcotic charges at a non-jury trial on stipulated evidence consisting primarily of the intercepted conversations and their convictions were affirmed on appeal (551 F2d 467).

In wrongful death actions brought against a foreign corporation in a Texas District Court by the survivors and representatives of four United States citizens who died when a helicopter owned by the foreign corporation crashed in Peru, the corporation moved to dismiss the actions for lack of in personam jurisdiction over it. The motion was denied, and after a consolidated jury trial, judgment was entered against the corporation. The Texas Court of Civil Appeals reversed, holding that in personam jurisdiction over the corporation was lacking (616 SW2d 247), but this was in turn reversed by the Texas Supreme Court (638 SW2d 870).

Under 26 USCS 6321, a federal lien attaches to all property and rights to property belonging to any taxpayer who fails to pay federal taxes owed by the taxpayer. When a husband failed to pay income tax liabilities assessed against him by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the Federal Government filed a lien that sought to attach, under 6321, the husband's properties that included a piece of real property in Michigan that the husband and his wife held under Michigan law as tenants by the entireties. After the notice of the lien was filed, the husband and wife executed a quitclaim deed that purported to transfer to the wife the husband's interest in the real property. Subsequently, when the wife was attempting to sell the property, the IRS agreed to release the lien with a stipulation that half of the net proceeds of the sale be held in escrow, pending determination of the Federal Government's interest in the property. In an action by the wife to quiet title to the escrowed proceeds, the United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan, granting the government's motion for summary judgment, held that the lien entitled the government to half of the property's value. On appeal by both parties, the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, remanding to the District Court to consider an alternative claim by the government, expressed the view that the lien did not attach to the property because under Michigan law, the husband had no separate interest in property held as a tenant by the entirety (140 F3d 638). After the District Court, on remand, awarded the IRS a share of the proceeds of the sale (65 F Supp 2d 651), both parties again appealed, with the government again asserting that its lien attached to the husband's interest in the entireties property. The Court of Appeals, affirming the District Court's decision concerning the government's alternative claim, held that the Court of Appeals' earlier decision in the instant case was the law of the case on the issue of whether the lien under 6321 attached (233 F3d 358).

A Nebraska taxpayer owned shares in two mutual funds that derived a portion of their income from interest earned on repurchase agreements involving debt securities issued by the United States Government and its agencies (federal securities). In such transactions, the holder of federal securities (seller-borrower) would transfer specified federal securities to the mutual funds in exchange for cash, and at a subsequent time the mutual funds would transfer the securities back to the seller-borrower, who would pay the mutual funds an amount equal to the original cash transfer plus interest at an agreed-upon rate, which bore no relation to the yield on the underlying federal securities. After deducting administrative costs, the mutual funds distributed this interest to the taxpayer according to his proportionate ownership of shares in the mutual funds. Nebraska had concluded in a previous revenue ruling that the interest income derived from the repurchase agreements and distributed to the taxpayer was subject to the state income tax. The taxpayer brought a declaratory judgment action in the District Court of Lancaster County, Nebraska, seeking to have the revenue ruling declared invalid as contrary to 31 USCS 3124(a), which exempts income from obligations of the United States Government from state taxation, and to the supremacy clause (Art VI, cl 2) of the Federal Constitution. The state court granted the relief requested, and the Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed (244 Neb 82, 504 NW2d 800).

In a suit in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Washington to enjoin a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation and to prevent an individual from complying with SEC subpoenas that had been issued to him, some parties expressly requested notice of the subpoenas issued by the SEC to third parties. The District Court denied the request for notice of subpoenas issued to third parties, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed (704 F2d 1065).

The inmate drove a vehicle from which a co-defendant shot and killed a victim, but the inmate contended at trial that there was no evidence that the inmate was aware that the co-defendant intended to shoot the victim. The inmate argued that a jury instruction failed to clarify that the inmate must have knowledge of the murder, rather than any crime, in order to be convicted as an accomplice to the murder, in view of the prosecutor's argument that accomplice liability was premised on "in for a dime, in for a dollar." The U.S. Supreme Court held that the jury was properly instructed that, in order to find the inmate guilty as an accomplice, the inmate must have had knowledge that his conduct would promote or facilitate the commission of the murder. The instruction properly quoted the accomplice-liability statute, Wash. Rev. Code _ 9A.08.020 (2008), in requiring that the inmate have knowledge of the crime with which the inmate was charged as an accomplice. Further, there was no reasonable likelihood that the prosecutor's arguably improper closing statement influenced the jury, since both the prosecution and the defense focused on the inmate's knowledge of the shooting.

After this Court held that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 was unconstitutional as applied to state and local governments because it exceeded Congress‚Äô power under ¬ß5 of the Fourteenth Amendment, see City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U. S. 507, Congress passed the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000 (RLUIPA) pursuant to its Spending Clause and Commerce Clause authority. RLUIPA targets two areas of state and local action: land‚Äìuse regulation, RLUIPA ¬ß2, 42 U. S. C. ¬ß2000cc, and restrictions on the religious exercise of institutionalized persons, RLUIPA ¬ß3, ¬ß2000cc‚Äì1. It also provides an express private cause of action for ‚Äúappropriate relief against a government,‚Äù ¬ß2000cc‚Äì2(a), including, inter alia, States, their instrumentalities and officers, and persons acting under color of state law, ¬ß2000cc‚Äì5(4)(A). Petitioner Sossamon, a Texas prison inmate, sued respondents, the State and prison officials, seeking injunctive and monetary relief under RLUIPA for prison policies that prevented inmates from attending religious services while on cell restriction for disciplinary infractions and that barred use of the prison chapel for religious worship. Granting respondents summary judgment, the District Court held that sovereign immunity barred Sossamon‚Äôs claims for monetary relief. The Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding that the statutory phrase ‚Äúappropriate relief against a government‚Äù did not unambiguously notify Texas that its acceptance of federal funds was conditioned on a waiver of sovereign immunity to claims for monetary relief.

The present action was brought in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York by a bakery company against a labor union, the plaintiff alleging that the union instigated its members to strike or not to report for work on January 2, 1960, in violation of the no-strike clause contained in the collective bargaining contract between the parties. In this contract the parties agreed on arbitration of "all complaints, disputes, or grievances arising between them involving questions of interpretation or application of any cause or matter covered by this contract or any act or conduct or relation between the parties hereto, directly or indirectly." Upon application of the union the District Court granted a stay of the action pending completion of arbitration, holding that the employer's claim was an arbitrable matter under the contract. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed. (294 F2d 399.)

A New York statute provides that a person who teaches or advocates, or is knowingly a member of an organization which teaches or advocates, the overthrow of the government by force or violence shall be disqualified from employment or continued employment in the public school system. It directs the Board of Regents to list, after notice and hearing, organizations which it finds to engage in these activities, and to issue regulations that membership in such an organization shall constitute prima facie evidence of disqualification. An action for a declaration that the statute was invalid and for an injunction restraining the Board from enforcing the statute was decided in favor of the Board by the highest court of New York.

A former Congressman was convicted in the United States District Court for the District of Maryland on seven counts of violating the federal conflict of interest statute, 18 USC 281, and on one count of conspiring to defraud the United States in violation of 18 USC 371. At the trial, there was evidence admitted, as well as argument by counsel, relating to the authorship, content, and motivation of a speech which the defendant allegedly made on the floor of the House of Representatives in pursuance of a conspiracy designed to give assistance, in return for compensation, to certain savings and loan associations which had been indicted on mail fraud charges. The Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit set aside the conviction on the conspiracy count, holding that the government's allegations with respect to the defendant's having conspired to make this speech were barred by Article 1 6 of the Federal Constitution, which provides that Senators and Representatives shall not be questioned in any other place for any speech or debate in either House; and the Court of Appeals, finding that the evidence adduced under the unconstitutional aspects of the conspiracy count had infected the entire prosecution, ordered a new trial on the other counts. (337 F2d 180.)

California's mobile home residency law (MRL) (1) limited the bases on which a mobile home park owner could terminate a mobile home owner's rental of space in the park; (2) generally prohibited park owners from requiring the removal of a mobile home when it was sold; (3) prohibited park owners from charging transfer fees for such sales; and (4) prohibited park owners from disapproving of a purchaser who was able to pay the rent. Following enactment of the MRL, a California city enacted a mobile home rent control ordinance which set back existing rents to the level of 2 years earlier and required park owners to obtain the approval of the city council for any rent increases.
