The student was suspended from school after he refused the principal's direction to take down a banner that he unfurled at a school-sponsored and school-supervised event. The principal directed the student to take the banner down because the banner appeared to advocate illegal drug use in violation of school policy. The school board upheld the student's suspension. The Ninth Circuit found a First Amendment violation because the school officials punished the student without demonstrating that his speech gave rise to a risk of substantial disruption. The Court, however, held that the school officials did not violate the First Amendment by confiscating the pro-drug banner and suspending the student. The Court concluded that the "substantial disruption" rule of Tinker was not the only basis for restricting student speech. Considering the special characteristics of the school environment and the governmental interest in stopping student drug abuse, the Court held that schools were entitled to take steps to safeguard those entrusted to their care from speech that could reasonably be regarded as encouraging illegal drug use.

In a government civil antitrust suit in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, it was held that Ford Motor Company, the nation's second largest automobile manufacturer, had violated the antimerger provisions of the Clayton Act by acquiring, from the nation's second largest independent spark plug manufacturer, the latter's tradename, its only spark plug plant in this country, a battery plant, and extensive rights to its nationwide distribution organization for spark plugs and batteries. In addition to ordering the car manufacturer to divest the tradename and the spark plug plant, the court enjoined the car manufacturer for 10 years from manufacturing spark plugs; ordered it for 5 years to buy half of its total annual requirement of spark plugs from the divested plant under the divested tradename; prohibited it for 5 years from using its own tradenames on plugs; required it for 10 years to continue its policy of selling spark plugs to its dealers at prices no less than its prevailing minimum suggested jobbers' selling price; and ordered it to condition its divestiture sale on the purchaser's assuming the existing wage and pension obligations, and to offer employment to any employee displaced by a transfer of nonplug operations from the divested plant (286 F Supp 407; 315 F Supp 372).

A disabled veteran, whose sole income came from veterans' and other benefits paid by the Federal Government, was ordered by the Circuit Court for Washington County, Tennessee, to pay $ 800 per month to his ex-wife for child support. The veteran refused to pay the full amount, on the ground that $ 90 of his monthly benefits were specifically designated as Veterans' Dependents' Benefits and that only the Veterans' Administration (VA) or other federal agencies providing aid could order him to contribute additional sums for child support. When his ex-wife petitioned to have him held in contempt, the veteran invoked the supremacy clause of the Federal Constitution (Art VI, cl 2) and sought a ruling from the Circuit Court (1) that it lacked jurisdiction over his disability benefits and (2) that a Tennessee statute which purportedly allowed the Circuit Court to consider those benefits in setting the veteran's child support obligations was null and void. The Circuit Court, however, held the veteran in contempt and upheld the validity of the Tennessee statute. In affirming that ruling, the Tennessee Court of Appeals (1) found that the Circuit Court's order did not undermine any substantial federal interest because Congress had intended those benefits to support the beneficiary's dependents as well as the beneficiary himself, and accordingly (2) rejected the veteran's contention that the federal agencies providing his benefits had exclusive jurisdiction to allocate child support payments therefrom. The Supreme Court of Tennessee denied the veteran's application for permission to appeal, and the veteran appealed to the United States Supreme Court with respect to state court jurisdiction over his veterans' benefits.

The National Labor Relations Board has a practice of excluding from collective bargaining units only those confidential employees with a "labor nexus" while rejecting any claim that all employees with access to confidential information are beyond the reach of the definition of "employee" in 2(3) of the National Labor Relations Act (29 USCS 152(3)). In keeping with this practice, the Board--finding that the personal secretary to a corporation's general manager and chief executive officer, did not assist and act in a confidential capacity to persons who formulate, determine, and effectuate management policies in the field of labor relations--ruled that the secretary was protected by the Act (29 USCS 151 et seq.) and that her discharge following her signing of a petition for reinstatement of a fellow employee constituted an unfair labor practice. The Board also ordered reinstatement of the secretary (236 NLRB 1616). The employer sought review in the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit and the Board cross-petitioned for enforcement. Ultimately, that court refused to enforce the Board's order, holding that all secretaries working in a confidential capacity, without regard to labor relations, must be excluded from the coverage of the Act (603 F2d 25), and that the evidence in the record failed to support a finding that the secretary in question did not come within the court's broader definition of confidential secretary (627 F2d 766). In another case, the National Labor Relations Board, reviewing an employer's refusal to bargain with a unit of employees which the employer contended included confidential employees not subject to the National Labor Relations Act, accepted the view that none of the challenged employees was a confidential employee under the Board's labor nexus test, and issued a bargaining order after finding that the employer's refusal to bargain violated the Act (244 NLRB 485). On the employer's petition for review and the Board's cross-petition for enforcement, the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals once again denied enforcement, noting that the Board's labor nexus test which the court had rejected in its earlier decision had also been utilized in the case before it. (631 F2d 734).

In an individual's action seeking monetary and injunctive relief under California laws designed to curb false advertising (Bus. & Prof. Code, _ 17500 et seq.) and unfair competition (Bus. & Prof. Code, _ 17200 et seq.), in which plaintiff alleged that defendant corporation, in response to public criticism and to induce consumers to continue to buy its products, made false statements of fact about its labor practices and about working conditions in factories that made its products, the trial court sustained defendant's demurrer without leave to amend on the ground the statements were constitutionally protected noncommercial speech. (Superior Court of the City and County of San Francisco, No. 994446, David A. Garcia, Judge.) The Court of Appeal, First Dist., Div. One, No. A086142, affirmed.

New York's Superintendent of Insurance, as liquidator of a private corporation, instituted an action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleging that the defendants had violated the federal securities laws--including 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and the Securities and Exchange Commission's Rule 10b- 5, which outlaw the use of any manipulative or deceptive device or contrivance in connection with the purchase or sale of any security--by the use of a fraudulent scheme whereby the corporation was deceived into selling its United States Treasury bonds at full market price, with the proceeds thereof not being received by the corporation, but instead being fraudulently used by the defendants to purchase the corporation's stock pursuant to the alleged scheme. The District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a cause of action under federal law (300 F Supp 1083), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (430 F2d 355).

A defendant pleaded guilty to federal drug charges and was sentenced by the United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. At sentencing, the District Court failed to inform the defendant of his right to appeal his sentence. In a later motion for postconviction relief, the defendant alleged that such failure violated the express terms of Rule 32(a)(2) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which provided that "[t]here shall be no duty on the court to advise the defendant of any right of appeal after sentence is imposed following a plea of guilty or nolo contendere, except that the court shall advise the defendant of any right to appeal the sentence" (Rule 32(a)(2), which was effective at the time of the defendant's sentencing, was later succeeded by Rule 32(c)(5), which likewise imposed on the District Court the duty to advise the defendant at sentencing of any right to appeal). The District Court (1) rejected the defendant's claim that any Rule 32 violation, without regard to prejudice, was enough to vacate a sentence, and (2) expressed the view that the defendant was not entitled to relief because he actually knew of his right to appeal when he was sentenced. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed, expressing the view that (1) the Rule 32(a)(2) violation was subject to harmless-error review, and (2) because the defendant was aware of his right to appeal, the rule's purpose had been served (order reported at 142 F3d 430, 1998 US App LEXIS 5222).

In unrelated Texas state court trials, the petitioners were convicted of various primary charges and were given increased punishments on the basis of provisions of the state's habitual criminal statutes. Through allegations in the indictment and through the introduction of evidence respecting the petitioners' prior convictions, the jurors in each trial were fully informed of such convictions, but the jurors were instructed that such matters were not to be considered in passing upon the petitioners' guilt or innocence on the primary charges. The petitioners challenged the validity of permitting the jurors to be informed about the prior convictions before the petitioners' guilt on the primary charges was determined. Of the three petitioners, one unsuccessfully appealed to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit (343 F2d 723) from a Federal District Court's denial of habeas corpus, and the other two unsuccessfully appealed their convictions to the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals (387 SW2d 411; 389 SW2d 304).

The corporation also received at its home office directly from Illinois customers orders which were filled by shipment directly to the customer.

An individual whose conviction and imprisonment on charges of rape and crime against nature were affirmed by the Tennessee Court of Criminal Appeals (521 SW2d 591) was denied review by the Supreme Court of Tennessee, and he filed an unsuccessful petition for post-conviction relief in the Knox County Criminal Court. The prisoner subsequently filed a petition in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee for a writ of habeas corpus under 28 USCS 2254, alleging four specified grounds for relief. The District Court, although concluding that it could not consider two of the claims because the prisoner had not exhausted his state remedies for those grounds, granted the writ. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed, concluding that the District Court properly found that the prisoner's constitutional rights had been seriously impaired and specifically rejecting the state's argument that the District Court should have dismissed the petition because it included both exhausted and unexhausted claims (624 F2d 1100).

Retired employees who had received workers' compensation awards subsequent to their retirement brought two separate suits in New Jersey state court to challenge the validity of provisions in their employers' pension plans reducing or offsetting a retiree's pension benefits by an amount equal to a workers' compensation award for which the retiree is eligible. The defendant employers independently removed the suits to the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey. There, both District Court judges ruled that the pension offset provisions in the employers' pension plans were invalid under New Jersey law, concluding that Congress had not intended the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (29 USCS 1001 et seq.) to preempt such a state law, held that the pension offset provisions were prohibited by 203(a) of the Act (29 USCS 1053(a)), the Act's antiforfeiture provision, and struck down a contrary regulation of the federal Treasury Department authorizing the use of such offset provisions. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit consolidated the appeals from these two decisions and reversed, holding that the pension offset provisions did not cause a forfeiture of vested pension rights that is forbidden by 203(a) of the Act and that the New Jersey statute forbidding the use of such provisions had been preempted by the Act (616 F2d 1238).

This case involved the status of a woman as the decedent's "widow" entitled to death benefits under the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act. She had married the decedent in 1921, and they lived together until 1925, when he deserted her. They never lived together again, and he never contributed anything to her support. In 1940 she entered into an attempted remarriage with another, from whom she was later divorced in 1949. She then refused a request from her first husband to resume the marital relationship. The term "widow," as defined in the act (33 USC 902(16)), includes a wife who, at the time of the decedent's death, was "living apart for justifiable cause or by reason of his desertion."

The United States condemned for use by the Army a laundry plant for a definite term, to be extended from year to year at the election of the Secretary of War. Having no other means of serving its customers, the laundry suspended business for the duration of the Army's occupancy. In the District Court the owner was awarded an annual rental, an amount, with interest, for damages to the plant and machinery beyond ordinary wear and tear, and interest on the rental due for the first term from the day on which the Army took possession, and on the rental for each year thereafter from the beginning of the year until paid. No compensation was awarded for diminution in the value of the business due to the destruction of its "trade routes."

This suit by appellants to enjoin appellees from alleged violations of the Fourteenth Amendment in refusing to admit Negroes to the University of Tennessee must be dismissed as moot, since appellants' requests for admission to the University have been granted and there is no suggestion that any person "similarly situated" will not be afforded similar treatment. Pp. 517-518.

A North Carolina statute and a Nebraska constitutional amendment provide that no one be denied an opportunity to obtain or retain employment because he is or is not a member of a labor organization, and prohibits employers from entering into contracts or agreements obligating themselves to exclude persons from employment because they are or are not labor union members.

In the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas, an accused pleaded guilty to attempted possession of marijuana with intent to distribute it, in violation of 21 USCS 841(a) and 846. Under the circumstances, 21 USCS 841(b)(1)(B) required a sentence of 5-40 years in prison. The District Court (1) concluded that the accused's activities concerning the importation of cocaine were part of the same continuing conspiracy as was involved in the accused's attempted possession of marijuana; (2) took into account such cocaine activities of the accused as "relevant conduct" under 1B1.3 of the Federal Sentencing Guidelines (18 USCS Appx); (3) as a result, used a higher base offense level and sentence range--292-365 months--than the court would have otherwise used under 2D1.1 of the Guidelines; and (4) after some adjustments, including a downward departure under 5K1.1 of the Guidelines for the accused's "substantial assistance" to the government, sentenced him to 144 months in prison. Subsequently, the accused was indicted in the same district for conspiring and attempting to import cocaine, in violation of 21 USCS 952(a) and 963. The accused moved to dismiss and argued that he had already been punished for these offenses, for his activities concerning the importation of cocaine had been considered as "relevant conduct" at his prior sentencing. The District Court then dismissed the indictment on the ground that punishment for the cocaine offenses would violate the prohibition of the double jeopardy clause of the Federal Constitution's Fifth Amendment against multiple punishments. However, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, in reversing on appeal, expressed the view that (1) the use of relevant conduct to increase the punishment of a charged offense does not punish the offender for the relevant conduct; and (2) under this standard, the double jeopardy clause did not bar the accused's prosecution on the cocaine charges (25 F3d 250).

The Interstate Commerce Commission, by terminating its investigation proceedings, approved the proposed discontinuance of a railroad's portion of the operation of certain interstate train runs, such railroad's portion of the operation having been confined to two states, while a second railroad continued the runs by operation in three other states (331 ICC 447). Thereafter, the Commission, in separate proceedings, similarly approved the second railroad's proposed termination of other interstate train runs which connected with the runs involved in the first proceeding (333 ICC 720). Suits to review the Commission's actions were instituted in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois by various cities, state agencies, and other interested parties. The District Court dismissed such suits on the ground that the Commission's decisions were not subject to judicial review (294 F Supp 1103, 1106), but the United States Supreme Court reversed (24 L Ed 2d 340). Thereafter, the District Court remanded the proceedings involving the first railroad back to the Interstate Commerce Commission, holding that under the provisions of 13a(1) of the Interstate Commerce Act--requiring that a carrier proposing discontinuance or change of train operation or service must give notice of the proposed discontinuance or change to the governor of each state in which the train operated, and must post such notice in every station, depot, or other facility served by the train--the railroad's compliance with the statutory requirements as to only the states in which it operated the train runs was inadequate, since the notice requirements should also have been met as to the other states involved in the continued operation of the runs by the second railroad. The District Court also remanded the proceedings involving the second railroad to the Commission, because of the close relationship with the first proceedings. (312 F Supp 442.)

An indictment charging a husband and wife with conspiring to commit an offense against the United States, in violation of the federal conspiracy statute (18 USC 371), was dismissed by the United States District Court for the Southern District of California on the ground that it did not state an offense, since a husband and wife are legally incapable of conspiring.

The jurisdiction of a three-judge district court of a suit to enjoin, on grounds of alleged repugnancy to the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, the enforcement of an Illinois statute requiring the licensing of persons engaged in the business of cashing checks or money orders, is not affected by the fact that the Supreme Court of Illinois has not yet decided whether the statute's exemption of the American Express Company is unconstitutional.

At defendants' trial in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts on a charge of bank robbery, a government witness, on cross- examination, testified that an FBI agent who interviewed him prior to the trial wrote down a statement. The government attorney denied that he had such a statement in his possession, stating that the only document in his possession was an interview report of the agent, which, because not a "statement" within the meaning of the Jencks Act (18 USC 3500), the government was not required to produce. At the conclusion of an inquiry conducted by the trial judge in the absence of the jury to determine the nature of the report as producible under the Jencks Act (that is, whether the report was signed or otherwise approved by the witness or was a substantially verbatim recital of an oral statement of the witness to the agent recorded contemporaneously with the making of the statement), the judge refused to order the government to deliver the report to the defendants, and also denied their motion to strike the testimony of the witness. Defendants were convicted and their conviction was affirmed by the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. (269 F2d 688.)

At defendant's trial in the Superior Court of Los Angeles County, California, on a charge of armed robbery, the court admitted in evidence, over defendant's objection, several articles which had been found by police officers in a search made without a warrant during his absence with the consent of the hotel clerk, of his hotel room in Pomona, California, two days before defendant was arrested in Las Vegas, Nevada. He was convicted; his conviction was affirmed by the District Court of Appeals of California (205 Cal App 2d 108, 22 Cal Rptr 718); and the Supreme Court of California denied further review (205 Cal App 2d 116).

A New York statute limits the use of the word "savings," or its variants, to those types of state financial institutions which are mutual in character as distinguished from stockholder-owned. Under this statute national banks were prohibited from using the word in their advertising or business.

Idaho sought to levy corporate income taxes on a parent corporation which was incorporated in New Jersey and maintained its headquarters and commercial domicile in New York. The parent corporation's primary Idaho business was the operation of a silver mine. The case involved three types of intangible income--dividend payments, interest payments, and capital gains from the sale of stock--that the parent corporation received from subsidiary corporations having no other connection with Idaho. The Idaho State Tax Commission assessed tax deficiencies against the parent corporation. On the parent corporation's petition for review, the state district court upheld the Commission's unitized treatment of the subsidiaries but overruled the Commission's determination that the disputed dividends, interest, and capital gains constituted "business" income. The Commission appealed to the Supreme Court of Idaho, which held that the trial court had erred by excluding from "business" income the parent corporation's receipt of dividends, interest, and capital gains as a result of its owning stock in the other corporations, and also held, in response to the parent corporation's constitutional arguments, that this tax treatment did not violate the commerce clause of the Federal Constitution (Art I, 8, cl 3) or the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment (99 Idaho 924, 592 P2d 39). The United States Supreme Court vacated and remanded the case for reconsideration in light of an earlier decision of the United States Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court of Idaho then reinstated is previous opinion.

Plaintiff, a mate on a barge undergoing repairs in his employer's repair yard, was ordered to do carpentry work on a raft used in chipping, painting, and welding on the employer's vessels; the raft was not being used to service the barge on which the plaintiff was employed. Plaintiff was injured when, while he was standing on a catwalk on a lighter alongside which the raft lay, and attempting to move the raft into position for boarding, the catwalk gave way. In an action under the Jones Act, instituted in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York, the jury returned a verdict in plaintiff's favor, and judgment was entered thereon. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed (263 F2d 147).

The motion for leave to proceed in forma pauperis and the petition for writ of certiorari are granted. California, 372 U.S. 353: Two defendants were tried and convicted in a California state court on charges of felonies. A single public defender was appointed to represent them. At the commencement of the trial, the defender moved for a continuance, but this motion was denied. On appeal, the District Court of Appeal affirmed their convictions after denying their request for appointment of counsel under a California rule of criminal procedure authorizing such denial where after an independent investigation of the record the appellate court determines that appointment of counsel would be helpful to neither the defendant nor the court. (187 Cal App 2d 802, 10 Cal Rptr 188.) Their petition for a hearing was denied by the Supreme Court of California. (187 Cal App 2d 813, 10 Cal Rptr 214.)

S. C. ¬ß541(a). Section 541 is intended to include within the estate any property made available by other provisions of the Bankruptcy Code. The filing of a petition also automatically ‚Äúoperates as a stay, applicable to all entities,‚Äù of efforts to collect prepetition debts outside the bankruptcy forum, ¬ß362(a), including ‚Äúany act to obtain possession of property of the estate or of property from the estate or to exercise control over property of the estate,‚Äù ¬ß362(a)(3). Here, each respondent filed a bankruptcy petition and requested that the city of Chicago (City) return his or her vehicle, which had been impounded for failure to pay fines for motor vehicle infractions. In each case, the City‚Äôs refusal was held by a bankruptcy court to violate the automatic stay. The Seventh Circuit affirmed, concluding that by retaining possession of the vehicles the City had acted ‚Äúto exercise control over‚Äù respondents‚Äô property in violation of ¬ß362(a)(3).

At defendant's trial in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York, on charges of having knowingly received and possessed goods stolen in interstate commerce, the presiding judge, acting according to his convictions in protecting the rights of the accused, declared a mistrial on his own motion and with neither approval nor objection by the defendant's counsel. At a subsequent trial, the defendant was convicted, and the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the conviction. (282 F2d 43.)

So far as pertinent to the issue in the present case, the United States District Court issued two orders: (1) the first one denied plaintiffs' motion to vacate a previous order dismissing the complaint and granting them leave to file an amended complaint, and granted them further leave to amend their complaint; and (2) about two years later, an order dismissing the cause of action after plaintiffs had elected to stand on their complaint. The plaintiffs appealed from the second order. The Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit dismissed the appeal as untimely (246 F2d 281), holding that the first order of the District Court constituted the final judgment in the case.

A man accused of beating, scalding, and setting fire to a woman who subsequently died of her injuries was charged with murder and was convicted in a Louisiana trial court. During the penalty phase of the trial, the prosecutor, in closing arguments, repeatedly advised the jurors that their decision as to whether the accused should be sentenced to death would be reviewed by others and was not the final decision. The accused was then sentenced to death, and the Supreme Court of Louisiana affirmed the accused's conviction and sentence. The United States Supreme Court granted certiorari and remanded the case for reconsideration in light of intervening precedent; but, after the Supreme Court of Louisiana reaffirmed the accused's sentence, the United States Supreme Court, in 1984, denied a further petition for certiorari, at which point the accused's conviction and sentence became final. After unsuccessfully seeking state collateral relief, the accused filed a federal habeas corpus petition in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, which petition contended that the prosecutor's closing argument, by diminishing the jury's sense of responsibility for the capital sentencing decision, had violated the Federal Constitution's Eighth Amendment under the rule of Caldwell v Mississippi (1985) 472 US 320, 86 L Ed 2d 231, 105 S Ct 2633. The District Court denied relief on the grounds that (1) the prosecutor's comments in the case at hand were significantly different from those condemned in the Caldwell case, and (2) there was no reasonable probability that the sentence would have been different in the absence of the prosecutor's comments. A panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed (848 F2d 582). While a rehearing en banc was pending, the United States Supreme Court held in Teague v Lane (1989) 489 US 288, 103 L Ed 2d 334, 109 S Ct 1060, that a rule of constitutional law established after a petitioner's conviction has become final may not be used to attack the conviction on federal habeas corpus, unless the rule falls within one of two narrow exceptions. Subsequently, the Court of Appeals, en banc, affirmed the denial of the accused's petition, as the Court of Appeals determined that (1) the Caldwell decision announced a new rule within the meaning of Teague v Lane, and (2) this rule did not fall within the exception to the Teague doctrine for watershed rules of criminal procedure that guarantee the accuracy of a criminal proceeding (881 F2d 1273).

The plaintiff was required, as a condition precedent to his employment on the teaching faculty of the University of Maryland, to sign a loyalty oath certifying that he was not engaged in one way or another in the attempt to overthrow the government of the United States, or the state of Maryland, or any political subdivision of either of them, by force or violence. He refused to execute this oath and brought suit before a three-judge Federal District Court in the District of Maryland, seeking a declaratory judgment that the oath was unconstitutional. The District Court ordered the complaint dismissed. (258 F Supp 589.)

The Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) sought to deport eight resident aliens who belonged to a group that the Federal Government characterized as an international terrorist and communist organization. In 1987, the aliens filed suit in the United States District Court for the Central District of California against the United States Attorney General, the INS, and various immigration officials, in which suit it was alleged, among other matters, that the INS was selectively enforcing immigration laws against the aliens in violation of the Federal Constitution's First and Fifth Amendments. Ultimately, the District Court (1) preliminarily enjoined deportation proceedings against six of the aliens, on the ground that these aliens were likely to prove that (a) the INS had selectively enforced routine status requirements against those aliens, and (b) the possibility of deportation, combined with the chill to First Amendment rights while the proceedings were pending, constituted irreparable injury; and (2) granted judgment to the federal parties, on other grounds, with respect to the two other aliens (883 F Supp 1365, 1995 US Dist LEXIS 3294). The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed the District Court's judgment as to the six aliens and reversed as to the two others (70 F3d 1045, 1995 US App LEXIS 31415). On remand, the District Court (1) denied the Attorney General's request that the injunction as to the six aliens be dissolved, and (2) entered an injunction in favor of the two others. While the Attorney General's appeal of this decision was pending, Congress passed the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) which, among other matters, repealed the old judicial-review scheme set forth in 8 USCS 1105a and instituted a more restrictive scheme in 8 USCS 1252. The Attorney General, filing motions in both the District Court and the Court of Appeals, argued that 1252(g)--which barred judicial review of the Attorney General's decision to commence proceedings, adjudicate cases, or execute removal orders against any alien under the IIRIRA "except as provided in this section"--deprived those courts of jurisdiction over the selective-enforcement claim. The District Court denied the motion, and the Attorney General's appeal from that denial was consolidated with the appeal already pending. The Court of Appeals affirmed the existence of jurisdiction under 1252 and affirmed the District Court's judgment on the merits (119 F3d 1367, 1997 US App LEXIS 17744, reh, en banc, den 132 F3d 531, 1997 US App LEXIS 36154).

A suit instituted in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas challenged the constitutionality of a Texas statute reapportioning the Texas House of Representatives in a combination of single- member, multi-member, and floterial districts. The three-judge District Court held that the provisions relating to the floterial districts were unconstitutional, but upheld the provisions with regard to the other districts, notwithstanding that the plaintiffs' evidence as to inequalities in representation showed, among other things, that the population per representative varied from 54,385 to 71,301, or from 14.84 percent over- represented to 11.64 percent underrepresented. The District Court entered a decree permitting the 1966 election to proceed under the statute, with a proviso that if the legislature did not adopt corrective legislation by August 1, 1967, the counties in the floterial districts would be reconstituted as multi-member districts and all of the representatives assigned to those counties would be elected at large. (252 F Supp 404.)

An investor, who was a veteran of two unsuccessful oil and gas investment ventures, invested approximately $ 310,000 with an oil and gas producer in a drilling venture involving leaseholds acquired by and held in the name of the producer. The investor then contacted a number of friends, family members, and business associates about the venture, all of whom, because of the investor's involvement, decided to invest about $ 7,500 in the venture, although most of them had not met or spoken to the producer or personally toured the leaseholds. The investor helped each of his contacts complete a subscription-agreement form which the producer had prepared. Each form stated that the venture interests were being sold without benefit of registration under the Securities Act of 1933 (15 USCS 77a et seq.), in reliance on a Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) rule then in effect, and the interests were never registered with the SEC. The contacts' investment checks were made payable to the producer's company, and the investor received no commission in connection with the purchases. When the drilling venture failed and the investment interests proved to be worthless, the investor and the contacts brought suit against the producer in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, seeking rescission of their investment agreements on grounds that such agreements constituted the unlawful sale of unregistered securities under 12(1) of the Securities Act of 1933 (15 USCS 77l(1)). The producer, in response, (1) asserted that the investor's claim was barred by the equitable defense of in pari delicto, and (2) moved to realign the investor as a third-party defendant, on grounds that the investor was a "seller" of the venture interests to the contacts within the meaning of 12(1). The District Court denied the producer's motion to realign and, after a bench trial, granted judgment for the investor and the contacts on their 12(1) rescission claims, making no specific mention of the producer's in pari delicto defense against the investor. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding that (1) the in pari delicto defense was not available in an action under 12(1), since that section created a strict liability offense rather than liability based on intentional misconduct, and (2) the investor was not a "seller" under 12(1), since there was no evidence that the investor sought or received any financial benefit in return for his advice to the contacts (787 F2d 985). The Court of Appeals denied rehearing en banc (794 F2d 1016).

The New York City Board of Estimate--which managed city property, granted city contracts, exercised zoning authority, and shared with the City Council the power to modify and approve budgets proposed by the mayor--was composed of the following officials, who became members of the Board by law upon their election to office: (1) the city's mayor, the comptroller, and the city council president, each of whom was elected citywide and cast two votes on the Board, except that the mayor did not participate in the Board's budget decisions; and (2) the presidents of the city's five boroughs, each of whom cast one vote. Registered voters from Brooklyn, the most populous of the boroughs, filed an action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York against the city, the Board, and the Board members, in which action the voters (1) alleged that the composition of the Board violated the "one person, one vote" rule established under the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, because giving equal voting power to the presidents of boroughs with widely varying populations diluted the voting rights of Brooklyn residents; and (2) sought declaratory and injunctive relief. The District Court granted summary judgment for the defendants, on the ground that the Board was not subject to the "one person, one vote" rule because (1) it did not exercise legislative authority, and (2) its members were not elected as such but were in effect appointed after their election to separate offices (551 F Supp 652). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed and remanded for further proceedings, as it held that the Board must conform to the "one person, one vote" rule because all of its members are ultimately selected by popular vote (707 F2d 686). On remand, the District Court held that the Board should be evaluated on the basis of the maximum population deviation between the largest and smallest districts--a 132.9 percent deviation between Brooklyn and Staten Island--without any modification to account for the three at-large members (592 F Supp 1462); and in a separate decision, the District Court (1) ruled that none of the explanations offered by the city required or justified this gross deviation from equal representation, and (2) granted summary judgment in favor of the plaintiff voters (647 F Supp 1463). The Court of Appeals, affirming, rejected the city's argument that discrepancies between election districts should be analyzed by applying the so-called Banzhaf Index, which focuses not on population but on calculating the power of individual voters to cast the deciding vote in the election of a representative who can cast the deciding vote on the governmental body in question (831 F2d 384).

The motion for leave to proceed in forma pauperis and the petition for a writ of certiorari are granted. The judgment is vacated and the case is remanded to the Supreme Court of Illinois for further consideration in light of Douglas v. California, 372 U.S. 353: Two defendants were tried and convicted in a California state court on charges of felonies. A single public defender was appointed to represent them. At the commencement of the trial, the defender moved for a continuance, but this motion was denied. Thereafter the defendants dismissed the defender and renewed motions for separate counsel and for a continuance. These motions were also denied. On appeal, the District Court of Appeal affirmed their convictions after denying their request for appointment of counsel under a California rule of criminal procedure authorizing such denial where after an independent investigation of the record the appellate court determines that appointment of counsel would be helpful to neither the defendant nor the court. (187 Cal App 2d 802, 10 Cal Rptr 188.) Their petition for a hearing was denied by the Supreme Court of California. (187 Cal App 2d 813, 10 Cal Rptr 214.)

A corporation which was incorporated in Delaware, and which was engaged in the sale of oil and chemical products in Iowa, extracted oil and gas not only from various states but also on the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS)--an area generally defined by the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA) (43 USCS 1331 et seq.) as all those submerged lands three or more geographical miles from the United States coastline. As the corporation was operated as a "unitary business"--a business carried on partly within and partly without the state, where the portion of the business carried on within the state depended on or contributed to the business outside the state--Iowa's corporate income tax apportionment formula would ordinarily have caused the corporation's Iowa income, for tax purposes, to have been based upon the ratio of the corporation's Iowa gross sales to the corporation's total gross sales. In Moorman Mfg. Co. v Bair (1978) 437 US 267, 57 L Ed 2d 197, 98 S Ct 2340, reh den 439 US 885, 58 L Ed 2d 201, 99 S Ct 233, the United States Supreme Court held that this Iowa apportionment formula did not violate the Federal Constitution's due process clause (Fourteenth Amendment) or commerce clause (Art I, 8, cl 3). For several years, however, the corporation filed Iowa tax returns in which the corporation adjusted the Iowa formula to exclude a figure which, the corporation stated, reflected income earned from the OCS. After auditing the returns, the Iowa department of revenue rejected the adjustment and determined that the corporation's tax payment was deficient. The corporation, which claimed that the adjustment was required by the allegedly pre-emptive effect of the OCSLA, challenged the deficiency determination, but the challenge was successively rejected in (1) an administrative hearing before the department, (2) an appeal to the Polk County District Court of Iowa, and (3) a further appeal to the Iowa Supreme Court (414 NW2d 113)--with both courts concluding that, based upon an examination of the text and history of the OCSLA, the OCSLA did not pre-empt Iowa's corporate income tax apportionment formula.

A corporation against which the National Labor Relations Board had filed an unfair labor practice charge requested that the Board make available copies of all potential witnesses' statements prior to the hearing on the charge. The request was denied on the ground that the Freedom of Information Act (5 USCS 552), under which the request was made, exempted from disclosure "investigatory records compiled for law enforcement purposes" to the extent that their production would "interfere with enforcement proceedings" (5 USCS 552(b)(7)(A)). The corporation then filed an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama seeking disclosure, and the court ruled that the exemption did not apply since the Board had not claimed that release of the documents would pose any unique or unusual danger of interference with the particular enforcement proceeding. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed (563 F2d 724).

Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (42 USCS 1973), as amended in 1982 in order to make clear that proof of discriminatory intent is not required, (1) prohibits voting procedures which result in a denial or abridgment of the right to vote on account of race, and (2) states that a violation is established where it is shown that members of a protected class have less opportunity than others "to participate in the political process and to elect representatives of their choice." In Texas, judges of the district courts--the state's trial courts of general jurisdiction--are elected at-large from election districts consisting of one or more entire counties, with varying numbers of judges elected from each district. Various individuals, together with organizations representing African-American and Hispanic voters, filed suit in the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas against various state officials. The plaintiffs alleged in part that (1) the at-large electoral scheme for state district court judges diluted the voting strength of minorities in violation of 2, and (2) this dilution could be remedied by alternative electoral schemes using electoral subdistricts or modified at-large structures. The District Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs on the statutory vote-dilution claim, but a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed (902 F2d 293). After rehearing en banc, the Court of Appeals again reversed the judgment of the District Court, as (1) the en banc majority held that the results test in 2 is inapplicable to judicial elections, because Congress' reference to voters' opportunity to elect "representatives" of their choice evidenced a deliberate decision to exclude the election of judges from scrutiny under that test, while (2) other judges, concurring in the judgment, expressed the view that (a) 2 does apply to judicial elections generally, but (b) elections for "single-member offices" such as the judgeships at issue, whose holders exercise individual authority within a jurisdiction that is coextensive with their electoral constituency, are exempt from vote dilution challenges under 2 (914 F2d 620).

The Illinois Election Code, Ill. Rev. Stat., c. 46, _ 10 -- 2, requires that a petition to form, and to nominate candidates for, a new political party be signed by at least 25,000 qualified voters, including at least 200 from each of at least 50 of the 102 counties in the State. Alleging that 52% of the State's registered voters reside in Cook County alone, 87% in the 49 most populous counties, and only 13% in the 53 least populous counties, appellants sued to enjoin enforcement of the requirement of at least 200 signatures from each of at least 50 counties.

An employer was brought before the National Labor Relations Board on an unfair labor practice charge based on a union's complaint that the employer had violated its duty to bargain collectively under 8(a)(5) of the National Labor Relations Act (29 USCS 158(a)(5))--which includes the duty to provide relevant information needed by a labor union for the proper performance of its duties as an employee bargaining representative--by refusing to disclose information about employee aptitude tests requested by the union in order to prepare for grievance arbitration. The grievance in question related to the rejection of some bargaining unit employees for job openings based on their scores in the employer's psychological aptitude testing program. The employer had in fact supplied the union with much of the requested information, but had refused to disclose the actual test questions, the actual employee answer sheets, and the scores linked with the names of the employees who received them, in order to protect the future integrity of the tests and the privacy interests of the examinees. The employer offered to turn over the scores of any employees who would sign a waiver releasing the employer's psychologist from his pledge of confidentiality, but the union declined to seek such releases. Concluding that all of the items requested were relevant to the grievance and would be useful to the union in processing it, the National Labor Relations Board ordered the employer to turn over all requested materials directly to the union, subject to certain restrictions on the union's use of the information (218 NLRB 1024). The Board rejected the employer's suggestion, which had earlier been accepted by an administrative law judge, that the tests be turned over to an industrial psychologist for independent evaluation in order to preserve test secrecy. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ordered enforcement of the Board's order without modification (560 F2d 722.)

Under the Coal Lands Acts of 1909 (30 USCS 81) and 1910 (30 USCS 83-85), all land patents issued pursuant to the Acts reserved to the United States all rights to the coal contained in the subject properties. In order to encourage the development of coalbed methane (CBM) gas as an energy source, (1) the United States Department of the Interior issued a 1981 opinion concluding that the reservation of coal under the Acts did not encompass CBM gas, and (2) energy companies relying on that opinion entered into leases with landowners holding title under the Acts to produce CBM gas. An Indian tribe, which had received equitable title to the United States' coal rights in patented lands that had formerly been part of the tribe's reservation, (1) filed an action in the United States District Court for the District of Colorado against the royalty owners and producers under the gas leases covering those lands and against various federal agencies; and (2) sought a declaration that the reservation of coal under the Acts included the CBM gas, which therefore belonged to the tribe. The District Court, holding that the plain meaning of the term "coal" was limited to the solid rock substance and did not include the CBM gas, granted summary judgment for the defendants (874 F Supp 1142). However, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, upon rehearing en banc, agreed with a decision by a panel of the Court of Appeals (119 F3d 816), and held, reversing the District Court's decision, that (1) the Acts' use of the term "coal" was ambiguous, (2) ambiguities in land grants must be resolved in favor of the sovereign, and (3) the Acts' reservation of coal therefore included the CBM gas (151 F3d 1251).

A suit was brought by the United States in a California Federal district court for injunctive and other equitable relief, against a number of corporations for alleged violation of the Sherman Act by conspiring to acquire control of local transportation companies in numerous cities located in widely different parts of the United States, and to restrain and monopolize interstate commerce in motor busses, petroleum supplies, tires and tubes sold to those companies. Defendant sought dismissal on the ground that such court was not a convenient forum for trial, but that a Federal district court sitting in Chicago would be the most convenient to them. In support of the claim, it was shown that a criminal prosecution against defendant and their officers growing out of substantially the same transactions had, pursuant to Rule 21 (b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, been transferred from the district court in California to the Illinois district court.

The petitioner, a captain in the Air Force, was convicted by a court- martial on March 8, 1968, of wilfully disobeying a lawful order, and was sentenced to one year's confinement at hard labor. He was then ordered confined to his quarters at Cannon Air Force Base, New Mexico, and the court- martial's judgment was forwarded for review by the convening authority, which approved the sentence, ordering that pending completion of appellate review, the petitioner be confined in the United States Disciplinary Barracks, Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. The petitioner's attorneys appealed the merits of the conviction to the Air Force Board of Review, and also sought habeas corpus relief from the United States District Court for the District of New Mexico, arguing that (1) both his confinement at the Cannon Air Force Base and his proposed transfer to Fort Leavenworth constituted an attempt to "execute" his sentence in violation of Article 71(c) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, and (2) since no finding had been made that restraint was necessary to prevent his flight from the jurisdiction, as was required by Article 13 of the Code, the civilian court should require his complete release. While the Air Force Board of Review affirmed the court-martial's judgment, the Court of Military Appeals agreed to review the case. The District Court, refusing to apply the principle that the petitioner must exhaust his military remedies before seeking habeas corpus relief from civilian courts, found that the military court system did not provide the petitioner with an adequate remedy for testing the validity of his confinement pending appeal, and on the merits granted the petitioner part of the relief he requested, refusing to review the legality of his confinement at Cannon Air Force Base, but finding that his incarceration at Fort Leavenworth would constitute an "execution" of his sentence in violation of Article 71(c). On appeal by both sides, the Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed the District Court's grant of partial relief, holding that the District Court could not properly grant the petitioner any form of relief until he had first challenged the validity of his confinement before the appellate tribunals within the military system (402 F2d 441). Shortly thereafter, recognizing that since his sentence was scheduled to expire on December 26, 1968 (the sentence having been reduced to 9 1/2 months for good behavior), he might be released from custody before the United States Supreme Court had an opportunity to pass upon his claims for relief pending his appeal, and in order to avoid the possibility of mootness, the petitioner promptly requested the Court of Appeals to stay its mandate and order his release pending the Supreme Court's decision on petition for certiorari. The Court of Appeals agreed to stay its mandate, but refused to require the military to release the petitioner from custody at the Cannon Air Force Base. The petitioner then applied to Mr. Justice White, an individual Justice of the Supreme Court sitting as a circuit justice, for temporary release from all confinement pending the Supreme Court's action on his certiorari petition, and after such application was denied, a similar one was made to Mr. Justice Douglas, another individual Justice of the Supreme Court, who ordered that the petitioner "be placed in a non-incarcerated status" until the full court had an opportunity to pass on the issues raised in a considered manner (21 L Ed 2d 554, 89 S Ct 478), and pursuant to such order the petitioner was released from confinement on Christmas Eve, two days before his sentence was scheduled to expire.

The present controversy arises from a long-standing dispute between the coastal states and the federal government over their respective rights to exploit the oil and other natural resources of off-shore submerged lands. In United States v California (1947) 332 US 19, 91 L ed 1889, 67 S Ct 1658, the Supreme Court of the United States held that, as against California, the United States possessed paramount rights in such lands underlying the Pacific Ocean seaward of the low-water mark on the coast of California and outside of inland waters. In 1950, the Court made like holdings with respect to submerged lands in the Gulf of Mexico similarly lying off the coasts of Louisiana and Texas. United States v Louisiana, 339 US 699, 94 L ed 1216, 70 S Ct 914; United States v Texas, 339 US 707, 94 L ed 1221, 70 S Ct 918. By the Submerged Lands Act of 1953 (43 USC 1301 et seq.) the United States relinquished to the coastal states all of its rights in all lands beneath navigable waters within a three-mile limit and, in excess of that limit, within state boundaries as they existed at the time a state became a member of the Union, or as theretofore approved by Congress. The limit of the grant was three leagues. The United States, invoking the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of the United States, brought the present suit against Louisiana, Texas, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida, seeking, among other relief, a declaration that it was entitled to exclusive possession over the lands, minerals, etc., underlying the waters of the Gulf of Mexico more than three geographic miles seaward from the coast of each state. The defendant states claimed a right to the submerged lands within three leagues of their coast, Alabama filing a cross bill to establish such right. The claim of Florida is discussed in an opinion appearing p. 1096, infra. The present opinion deals with the claims of Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama.

Two taxpayers in Arkansas assumed a deed of trust and note obligating them to pay "a reasonable attorney's fee" in the event of default and the placing of the note in the hands of an attorney for collection. Subsequently they defaulted and the mortgagee brought suit to foreclose the deed of trust in the Chancery Court, Fort Smith District, Sebastian County, Arkansas, which fixed the attorney's fee at $ 1,250 and granted the mortgagee's claim for the attorney's fee priority over federal tax liens which were filed after the commencement of the foreclosure suit but before the decree of foreclosure. The Supreme Court of Arkansas affirmed on the ground that the claim for an attorney's fee became choate before the United States filed its tax liens. (235 Ark 267, 357 SW2d 653.)

A patent for an improved antiperspirant cosmetic in which to acid-reacting salts are added certain types of the reactive amino chemical group, particularly urea, the addition resulting in an improved compound which checks perspiration but, differently from the previously known antiper-spirants, neither irritates the skin nor corrodes the clothing, was held, in an opinion by Black, J., to be invalid as lacking in invention because merely applying to a new cosmetic use the publicly available knowledge that urea would inhibit acidic corrosion.

An amendment of the Georgia Constitution revoked an exemption from taxation granted to a Georgia corporation by a provision of the act under which it was incorporated. Injunctive and declaratory relief against the state revenue commissioner, who was threatening to collect ad valorem taxes from the corporation, was denied by the state courts solely on the ground that the action was, in effect, an unconsented suit against the state. Plaintiff's suit for injunctive relief in a federal district court was dismissed on the same ground.

Decedent had been employed as an operator of one of a fleet of motorboats carrying sightseers on a river during the summer months only. His employment had terminated in December, after he had helped to lay the boats up for the winter. He was reemployed the next March and injured in April while helping to paint, clean and waterproof the boats, preparing them for navigation. At that time, none of the boats was afloat, none had a captain or crew, and the work being done was of the kind that, in the case of larger vessels, would customarily be done exclusively by shore-based personnel. Held: At the time of his injury, decedent was not a "seaman" within the purview of the Jones Act

Petitioners are primarily nonprofit organizations that provide health insurance to their employees. Federal regulations require petitioners to cover certain contraceptives as part of their health plans, unless petitioners submit a form either to their insurer or to the Federal Government, stating that they object on religious grounds to providing contraceptive coverage. Petitioners allege that submitting this notice substantially burdens the exercise of their religion, in violation of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, 107 Stat. 1488, 42 U. S. C. ¬ß2000bb et seq. Following oral argument, the Court requested supplemental briefing from the parties addressing "whether contraceptive coverage could be provided to petitioners' employees, through petitioners' insurance companies, without any such notice from petitioners." Post, p. Both petitioners and the Government now confirm that such an option is feasible. Petitioners have clarified that their religious exercise is not infringed where they "need to do nothing more than contract for a plan that does not include coverage for some or all forms of contraception," even if their employees receive cost-free contraceptive coverage from the same insurance company. Supplemental Brief for Petitioners 4. The Government has confirmed that the challenged procedures "for employers with insured plans could be modified to operate in the manner posited in the Court's order while still ensuring that the affected women receive contraceptive coverage seamlessly, together with the rest of their health coverage."
The Second Circuit's judgment was affirmed in a unanimous decision.

The two admiralty cases involved in the present litigation presented the question whether under the Rivers and Harbors Act of 1899 shipowners who by their alleged acts of negligence caused their vessels to sink in inland waterways may be held responsible, after having abandoned the vessels, for their removal or the expenses of the United States for such removal. In one of the cases, the United States brought suit against the parties responsible for the sinking for a declaration of their responsibility for removing the sunken vessels; in the other, the United States, having itself removed the sunken vessel, sought reimbursement for its removal expenses. The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana granted summary judgment for the defendants under the theory that the relief requested by the United States was not available under the Act. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed and remanded the case to the trial court for a determination whether the acts of the various defendants constituted negligence. (367 F2d 971.)

While a state grand jury was investigating alleged sales of Negro votes in Bibb County, Georgia, the petitioner, an elected sheriff, issued to the local press written statements, one of them after he was cited for contempt of court, accusing the judges who had formulated the instructions to the jury of race agitation and an attempt at judicial intimidation of Negro voters and leaders, and comparing the calling of the grand jury to the activities of the Ku Klux Klan. The Superior Court found him guilty of contempt on three counts. On writ of error, the Georgia Court of Appeals affirmed the convictions on two counts and reversed the conviction on another count. (103 Ga App 305, 119 SE2d 261.) The Georgia Supreme Court, without opinion, declined to review the convictions so affirmed.

Skinner, 251 La. 300, ‚àö¬∂[**705]‚àö¬∂ 204 So. 2d 370 (1967). We granted certiorari to consider several alleged errors occurring during the course of the state court proceedings.

In this case, the Court of Appeals held that respondent, who was convicted of rape and other serious crimes, is entitled to relief under the federal habeas statute because the Supreme Court of Nevada unreasonably applied clearly established Supreme Court precedent regarding a criminal defendant's constitutional right to present a defense. At his trial, respondent unsuccessfully sought to introduce evidence for the purpose of showing that the rape victim previously reported that he had assaulted her but that the police had been unable to substantiate those allegations. The state supreme court held that this evidence was properly excluded, and no prior decision of this Court clearly establishes that the exclusion of this evidence violated respondent's federal constitutional rights. The decision of the Court of Appeals is therefore reversed.

The Internal Revenue Code (26 USCS 1-9602) imposes no current tax on certain stock-for-stock exchanges; but 26 USCS 356(a)(1) provides that if such an exchange, made pursuant to a corporate reorganization plan, is accompanied by additional consideration in the form of cash or other property--commonly referred to as "boot"--then the recipient may be taxed on his or her gain up to the value of the boot. Although boot is thus generally treated as a capital gain, 356(a)(2) of the Code (26 USCS 356(a)(2)) provides an exception where the exchange "has the effect of the distribution of a dividend," in which case the boot must be treated as a dividend and is thus taxed as ordinary income to the extent that gain is realized. A taxpayer who was the sole owner of a small company entered into a merger agreement with a corporation whereby the taxpayer transferred his shares in the company to a wholly owned subsidiary of the corporation in exchange for 300,000 shares of the corporation's common stock--0.92 percent of the shares then outstanding--plus a cash "boot" of $ 3,250,000; in agreeing to this exchange, the taxpayer rejected an alternative offer of 425,000 shares--1.3 percent--of the corporation's stock. In calculating his federal income taxes for that year, the taxpayer treated the boot as long-term capital gain; but the Commissioner of Internal Revenue decided that the boot should be taxed as ordinary income, and therefore assessed a deficiency of $ 972,504.74, on the theory that the boot should be treated as though it were made by the acquired company in a hypothetical redemption of its own stock immediately prior to the exchange, in which case it would have the effect of a dividend within the meaning of 356(a)(2). On review, the United States Tax Court ruled in favor of the taxpayer, as it (1) held that boot, in such cases, should be treated as though there were a pure stock-for-stock exchange followed immediately by a postreorganization redemption by the acquiring corporation of a portion of the taxpayer's shares therein, and (2) found that, under the facts of this case, such a redemption should be treated as capital gain pursuant to 302(b)(2) of the Code (26 USCS 302(b)(2))--which provides that a stock redemption is treated as payment for the stock, and thus not as a dividend, if the stockholder involved relinquishes more than 20 percent of his or her share of the corporation's voting stock and retains less than 50 percent of the total voting stock (86 TC 138). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed (828 F2d 221).

Pursuant to its Revised Constitution, which had been approved by the Secretary of the Interior, the Tribal Council of the Jicarilla Apache Tribe enacted an ordinance imposing a severance tax on oil and gas production on the tribal land, the tax applying to any oil and natural gas severed, saved, and removed from tribal lands, but not applying to oil and gas consumed by lessees of the Tribe to develop their leases or received by the Tribe as in-kind royalty payments, and the ordinance was approved by the Secretary. Subsequently, several individuals and corporations who, pursuant to long-term leases previously signed with the Tribe, extracted and produced oil and gas from the Tribe's reservation lands and who paid royalties to the Tribe brought actions in the United States District Court for the District of New Mexico to enjoin enforcement of the tax by either the tribal authorities or the Secretary. The District Court consolidated the cases and permanently enjoined enforcement of the tax, ruling that the Tribe lacked the authority to impose the tax, that only state and local authorities had the power to tax oil and gas production on Indian reservations, and that the tax violated the commerce clause of the United States Constitution (Art I, 8, cl 3). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed, holding that the taxing power is an inherent attribute of tribal sovereignty that had not been divested by any treaty or act of Congress (617 F2d 537).

Two previously competing companies formed a joint venture to refine and sell gasoline in the western United States under the two companies' original brand names. The joint venture set a single price for both companies' brands of gasoline. A class of service station owners who sold the companies' gasoline, bringing suit against the companies in the United States District Court for the Central District of California, alleged that the companies had engaged in price fixing that either (1) was per se illegal under _ 1 of the Sherman Act (15 U.S.C.S. _ 1); or (2) violated _ 1 under the quick-look doctrine, which had been applied to business activities that were so plainly anticompetitive that courts needed to undertake only a cursory examination before imposing antitrust liability.

Ten clergymen were convicted in the Municipal Court of Tallahassee, Florida, of unlawful assembly for their refusal to disperse from the Tallahassee municipal airport during a civil rights demonstration. The clergymen appealed their convictions directly to the Supreme Court of Florida, which ruled that it lacked jurisdiction, and ordered the appeal transferred to the Circuit Court of the Second Judicial District, Leon County, Florida (134 So 2d 228), which affirmed the convictions.

A member of the United States House of Representatives instituted an action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, challenging the constitutionality, under Article I, 1, and Article I, 6, cl 1, of the Federal Constitution, of provisions of the Postal Revenue and Federal Salary Act of 1967 (2 USCS 351-361), and of the 1975 Executive Salary Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act (2 USCS 31), relating to increases in salaries paid members of Congress. The District Court dismissed the complaint (428 F Supp 302).

So far as pertinent here, 2(a) of the Clayton Act, as amended by the Robinson-Patman Act, prohibits price discrimination where its effect may be to injure competition, and enumerates four situations, not involved in the present case, which justify price differentials. Section 2(b) authorizes the Federal Trade Commission to issue an order terminating price discrimination, unless justification is affirmatively shown, provided, however, that nothing therein contained shall prevent a seller rebutting the prima facie case by showing that his lower price was made in good faith to meet an equally low price of a competitor.

In an action against the United States to recover damages under the Federal Tort Claims Act (28 USC 1346, 2671 et seq.) for injuries resulting from the negligent operation of a government automobile by a government employee, the United States filed a third-party complaint, asking that if it should be held liable to the plaintiff, it should have indemnity from the employee.

In 1958, the petitioner loaned the sum of $ 15,000,000 to a predecessor of a Cuban national bank, which bank was an agency of the Cuban Government. The loan was secured by a pledge of United States Government bonds, held by the petitioner, a New York bank. On January 1, 1959, the Castro government came to power in Cuba. That government renewed the loan in 1959, and in 1960 it repaid $ 5,000,000 of the loan, following which the New York bank released collateral equal to the value of the portion repaid. However, allegedly pursuant to decrees of the Castro government, the Cuban militia seized all of the Cuban branches of the New York bank in the latter part of 1960, following which the New York bank retaliated by selling the remaining collateral it held securing the $ 10,000,000 loan, and by applying the proceeds of the sale to the repayment of the principal and unpaid interest. The sale of the collateral realized a sum conceded by the New York bank to be in excess of $ 1,800,000 over and above the amount which was required to pay off the principal and unpaid interest on the loan. The Cuban national bank then sued the New York bank in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York to recover the excess amount of $ 1,800,000, and the New York bank, by way of setoff and counterclaim, asserted the right to recover damages, claimed by the New York bank to be equal to or greater than the excess amount, because of the expropriation of its property in Cuba. The District Court granted summary judgment in favor of the New York bank, holding that, as a result of the Hickenlooper Amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1964 (22 USCS 2370(e)(2)), the act of state doctrine did not apply, and that the taking of the New York bank's property in Cuba violated customary international law (270 F Supp 1004). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed and remanded, holding (1) that the Hickenlooper Amendment was not applicable under the circumstances of the case, because, inter alia, none of the expropriated property had ever been brought into the United States, (2) that the act of state doctrine, barring inquiry by United States courts into the legality of acts of foreign governments committed within their own territories, thus prevented the court from inquiring into the validity of the expropriation, and (3) that the New York bank therefore had no right to apply the excess amount to the losses it suffered because of the expropriation (431 F2d 394). On certiorari, the United States Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment and remanded the case for reconsideration in light of a letter which had been submitted to it after the Court of Appeals' decision by a legal adviser to the Department of State, which letter advised the Supreme Court that the executive branch did not believe that the act of state doctrine should be applied to bar consideration of a defendant's counterclaim or setoff against the Government of Cuba in the instant or in like cases, the Department of State justifying its position by relying on the Bernstein exception to the act of state doctrine, which exception had, in past cases, been generally interpreted to provide that where the executive branch, responsible for the conduct of foreign affairs, represents to the judicial branch that the application by the judicial branch of the act of state doctrine in a particular case would not advance the interests of American foreign policy, then the courts could ignore the limitations of the doctrine and proceed to examine the validity of the acts of a foreign sovereign government under applicable principles of customary international law (400 US 1019, 27 L Ed 2d 630, 91 S Ct 581). On remand, the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit concluded that the Bernstein exception should be limited to the facts of Bernstein v N. V. Nederlandsche-Amerikaansche Stoomvaart- Maatschappij (210 F2d 375), and decided that, in spite of the Department of State's letter, it was still precluded by the act of state doctrine from considering the validity of the Cuban expropriation (442 F2d 530).

In condemnation proceedings in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon, it was held that the compensable value of certain riparian land, taken from the condemnees by the United States Government as part of a comprehensive river development plan, did not include the land's special value as a port site. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the land's value as a port site was compensable. (367 F2d 186.)

1950, Montana, Wyoming and North Dakota signed the Yellowstone River Compact, which spelled out how the states would share water. In 2007, Montana sued Wyoming, alleging farmers and other water users along the Powder and Tongue rivers were being harmed by Wyoming's excessive water use. Attorneys for Wyoming argued that much of the water used by the state's residents and businesses was not covered by the 1950 agreement. Special Master Barton Thompson issued an interim report, finding that Montana had grounds to sue over Wyoming's expanded use of water since 1950. However, Thompson rejected Montana's claim that Wyoming should be held liable for increased water use due to irrigation improvements. Meanwhile, North Dakota, also a member of the Yellowstone compact, was named as a second defendant in the original lawsuit. But Montana officials have said its inclusion was a formality and that they have no disagreement with their eastern neighbor.

Under the Postal Reorganization Act, the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) applies to "tort claims arising out of [Postal Service] activities." 39 U.S.C. _ 409(c). The FTCA, in turn, waives sovereign immunity in certain cases involving negligence committed by federal employees in the course of their employment, 28 U.S.C. _ 1346(b)(1), making the United States liable "in the same manner and to the same extent as a private individual under like circumstances," _ 2674. However, the sovereign immunity bar remains as to, inter alia, "any claim arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter." _ 2680(b). Consequently, the United States may be liable if postal workers commit torts under local law, but not for claims defined by the exception. Petitioner Dolan filed an FTCA suit against the Postal Service for injuries she suffered when she tripped and fell over mail left on her porch by postal employees. The District Court dismissed the suit, and the Third Circuit affirmed, both concluding that, although the FTCA generally waives sovereign immunity as to federal employees' torts, Dolan's claims were barred by _ 2680(b)'s exception.

As against a claim by a clan of an Alaskan Indian tribe of a right, under the Fifth Amendment, to compensation for the sale by the federal government of Alaskan timber, five members of the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Reed, J., held that the sale did not amount to a compensable taking. The majority rested its decision on the grounds, first, that no federal statute had recognized the Indians' right to unrestricted possession, occupancy, and use of the land; and second, that the history of the tribe did not indicate that it had a proprietary interest in the land which survived the conveyance of Alaska to the United States.

Two New York corporations marketed an investment program involving commodity-futures trades on the London Metals Exchange. The corporations employed a British corporation with its offices in London as a broker to handle trades on that Exchange. An individual who was a citizen and a resident of the United Kingdom represented the British company in soliciting the New York corporations' business. When the United States Internal Revenue Service disallowed income tax deductions claimed by the participants in the investment program, some of the participants sued the New York corporations in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, charging that they were fraudulently induced to participate in the investment program, in violation of various federal securities laws.
