The New York corporations impleaded the British corporation and its representative, contending that the New York corporations' liability, if any, was caused by the British parties' improper trading activities. After the United States Supreme Court handed down a decision recognizing an implied private cause of action under the Commodity Exchange Act (7 USCS 1 et seq.), the plaintiffs amended their complaints to allege violations of this statute. The District Court held that it lacked personal jurisdiction over the British parties, because (1) the Commodity Exchange Act was silent about service of process for private causes of action and (2) the requirements of the Louisiana long-arm statute were not met. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed (795 F2d 415).

Alien members of the Communist Party were detained, pending final determination of their deportability. One of them had been released on bail, but was rearrested without a new warrant. In reliance on the discretion conferred upon the Attorney General by 23 of the Internal Security Act of 1950, their release on bond was refused solely on the ground that they had been active in the Communist movement. In habeas corpus proceedings the aliens raised various objections.

The lessee of a parcel of land in the State of Louisiana posted "No Trespassing" signs on the land and employed a staff of persons who prohibited strangers from entering the land and using a system of manmade canals, which had been constructed with private funds, and which traversed the land and joined surrounding naturally navigable waterways. When several persons asserted a right under federal law to enter the property, travel the canals, and engage in commercial fishing and shrimping activities without obtaining the lessee's permission, the lessee brought an action in a Louisiana state court seeking permanent injunctions against those persons from trespassing on the land and making use of the canals. The trial court granted the lessee's motion for summary judgment based on affidavits and a deposition, and the Court of Appeal of Louisiana for the Third Circuit affirmed, holding that no general public right of use of the canal system arose by reason of the authority over navigation conferred upon Congress by the commerce clause of the Constitution (Art I, 8, cl 3), and that any factual dispute between the litigants as to whether the canal system had destroyed the navigability of the surrounding natural waterways was immaterial, so that summary judgment was proper as a matter of law.

The Wartime Suspension of Limitations Act provides for the suspension, until three years subsequent to a Presidential proclamation of termination of hostilities, of the running of the limitations periods normally applicable to wartime offenses involving "fraud . . . in any manner" against the government. The indictments herein charged violations, in 1945 and 1946, of the False Claims Act by attempts to obtain payments from the Commodity Credit Corporation in amounts based upon knowingly false certifications of certain wool purchases which had not, in fact, been made, and knowingly and falsely certifying that wool was purchased at a higher price than was actually paid. The indictments were dismissed by the District Court on the ground that the offenses charged were not within the scope of the Wartime Suspension of Limitations Act, and were, consequently, barred by the applicable three-year statute of limitations.

In each of these cases, an employer allegedly fired a long-time employee simply for being homosexual or transgender. Clayton County, Geor- gia, fired Gerald Bostock for conduct “unbecoming” a county employee shortly after he began participating in a gay recreational softball league. Altitude Express fired Donald Zarda days after he mentioned being gay. And R. G. & G. R. Harris Funeral Homes fired Aimee Ste- phens, who presented as a male when she was hired, after she in- formed her employer that she planned to “live and work full-time as a woman.” Each employee sued, alleging sex discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The Eleventh Circuit held that Title VII does not prohibit employers from firing employees for being gay and so Mr. Bostock’s suit could be dismissed as a matter of law. The Second and Sixth Circuits, however, allowed the claims of Mr. Zarda and Ms. Stephens, respectively, to proceed.
Held: An employer who fires an individual merely for being gay or transgender violates Title VII. Pp. 4–33.

After protracted school desegregation litigation instituted in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia as a class action by Negro parents and guardians against the School Board of Richmond, Virginia, the plaintiffs, on March 10, 1970 filed, in addition to a motion for further relief, an application for the award of attorney's fees; this application was renewed on July 2, 1970. After having approved, on April 5, 1971, a noninterim plan for achievement of a unitary school system in Richmond, the District Court, on May 26, 1971, awarded plaintiffs, in exercise of its equity powers, counsel fees in the amount of $ 43,355 for services rendered from March 10, 1970 to January 29, 1971 (53 FRD 28). While the school board's appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit was pending, 718 of the Emergency School Aid Act (20 USCS 1617) became law; this statute grants authority to a federal court to award the prevailing party in a school desegregation case, upon the entry of a final order, a reasonable attorney's fee when appropriate. The Court of Appeals, sitting en banc, reversed, with one of the judges dissenting, on the grounds that (1) in the absence of a statute authorizing the award of attorneys' fees in a school desegregation case, the award was not justified under the circumstances of the instant case, and (2) 718 was not applicable because there were no orders pending or appealable on either May 26, 1971, when the District Court made its fee award, or on July 1, 1972, when 718 became effective (472 F2d 318).

The inmate contended that the trial court's findings were adopted in whole from findings prepared ex parte by the prosecution, which included a factual finding that the inmate's attorneys were advised by an expert that further investigation of the inmate's brain damage would be a waste of time. The U.S. Supreme Court held that the statutory presumption of correctness of the state court's findings was improperly applied based solely on the ground that the findings were fairly supported by the record, since there was no consideration of other exceptions to the presumption under former 28 U.S.C.S. ¬¨√ü 2254(d). The inmate essentially argued that the state court's process was deficient which implicated exceptions to the presumption of correctness that the inmate did not receive a full and fair evidentiary hearing in state court based on an inadequate factfinding procedure, hearing, and proceeding. Further, while it was admitted that the state court adopted the prosecution's findings of fact verbatim, it remained to determine the precise nature of what transpired during the state-court proceedings in order to determine whether an exception to the presumption of correctness was applicable.
The petition for a writ of certiorari is granted and the judgments are affirmed. City of Greenwood v. Peacock, ante, p. 808.

Defendant pleaded guilty to violations of the Mann Act; the violations were laid in two counts, each of which referred to a different woman transported in interstate commerce for the purpose of prostitution; he was sentenced to consecutive terms on each of the two counts.

Although investigators and witnesses concluded that Curtis Campbell caused an accident in which one person was killed and another permanently disabled, his insurer, petitioner State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company (State Farm), contested liability, declined to settle the ensuing claims for the $ 50,000 policy limit, ignored its own investigators' advice, and took the case to trial, assuring Campbell and his wife that they had no liability for the accident, that State Farm would represent their interests, and that they did not need separate counsel. In fact, a Utah jury returned a judgment for over three times the policy limit, and State Farm refused to appeal. The Utah Supreme Court denied Campbell's own appeal, and State Farm paid the entire judgment. The Campbells then sued State Farm for bad faith, fraud, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The trial court's initial ruling granting State Farm summary judgment was reversed on appeal. On remand, the court denied State Farm's motion to exclude evidence of dissimilar out-of-state conduct. In the first phase of a bifurcated trial, the jury found unreasonable State Farm's decision not to settle. Before the second phase, this Court refused, in BMW of North America, Inc. v. Gore, 517 U.S. 559, 134 L. Ed. 2d 809, 116 S. Ct. 1589, to sustain a $ 2 million punitive damages award which accompanied a $ 4,000 compensatory damages award. The trial court denied State Farm's renewed motion to exclude dissimilar out-of-state conduct evidence. In the second phase, which addressed, inter alia, compensatory and punitive damages, evidence was introduced that pertained to State Farm's business practices in numerous States but bore no relation to the type of claims underlying the Campbells' complaint. The jury awarded the Campbells $ 2.6 million in compensatory damages and $ 145 million in punitive damages, which the trial court reduced to $ 1 million and $ 25 million respectively. Applying Gore, the Utah Supreme Court reinstated the $ 145 million punitive damages award.

Petitioner was tried on charges alleging that he distributed cocaine and trafficked in cocaine, in violation of Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 94C, __ 32A and 32E(b)(1), and the prosecution offered certificates signed by state laboratory analysts which stated that evidence that was connected to petitioner was cocaine. Petitioner objected to admission of the certificates, claiming that their admission violated his right under the Sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution to confront the analysts who signed the certificates, but the trial court overruled the objection and admitted the certificates under Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 111, _ 13. The U.S. Supreme Court held that admission of the certificates violated petitioner's Sixth Amendment right to confront the witnesses against him. The certificates were affidavits, which fell within the core class of testimonial statements covered by the Confrontation Clause, and they were made under circumstances which would have led an objective witness reasonably to believe that they were made for use in a criminal trial. Although petitioner could have subpoenaed the analysts, that right was not a substitute for his right to confront them.

Michelle Cochran and Axon Enterprise, Inc.‚Äîrespondents in separate enforcement actions initiated in the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC)‚Äîeach filed suit in federal district court challenging the constitutionality of the agency proceedings against them. When, as in the enforcement actions against Cochran and Axon, a Commission elects to institute administrative proceedings to address statutory violations, it typically delegates the initial adjudication to an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) with authority to resolve motions, hold a hearing, and then issue a decision. As prescribed by statute, a party objecting to the Commission proceedings makes its claims first within the Commission itself, and then (if needed) in a federal court of appeals. But the parties here sidestepped that review scheme and brought their claims in district court, seeking to enjoin the administrative proceedings. Cochran and Axon asserted that the tenure protections of the agencies‚Äô ALJs render them insufficiently accountable to the President, in violation of separation-of-powers principles. Axon also attacked as unconstitutional the combination of prosecutorial and adjudicatory functions in the FTC. Each suit premised jurisdiction on district courts‚Äô ordinary federal-question authority to resolve ‚Äúcivil actions arising under the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States.‚Äù 28 U. S. C. ¬ß1331. Cochran‚Äôs and Axon‚Äôs suits initially met the same fate: dismissal for lack of jurisdiction. The district court in Cochran‚Äôs case held that the review scheme specified in the Securities Exchange Act‚Äî‚Äúadministrative review followed by judicial review in a federal court of appeals‚Äù‚Äî ‚Äúimplicitly divest[s] district courts of jurisdiction‚Äù over ‚Äúchallenges to SEC proceedings,‚Äù including Cochran‚Äôs constitutional ones. Likewise, the district court in Axon‚Äôs case found that the FTC Act‚Äôs comparable review scheme displaces ¬ß1331 jurisdiction for claims concerning the FTC‚Äôs adjudications. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court‚Äôs dismissal of Axon‚Äôs constitutional challenges to the FTC proceeding, concluding that the claims were the type that fell within the FTC Act‚Äôs review scheme. But the en banc Fifth Circuit disagreed as to the equivalent SEC question, finding that Cochran‚Äôs claim would not receive ‚Äúmeaningful judicial review‚Äù in a court of appeals; that the claim was ‚Äúwholly collateral to the Exchange Act‚Äôs statutory-review scheme‚Äù; and that the claim fell ‚Äúoutside the SEC‚Äôs expertise.‚Äù

Petitioner, a man in his thirties, was tried and convicted in a Pennsylvania state court for larceny, and was sentenced to imprisonment for 2 1/2 to 5 years. He conducted his own defense, appointment of counsel having been neither requested by petitioner nor offered by the court. At the trial, considerable hearsay and otherwise incompetent evidence prejudicial to petitioner was admitted; the prosecuting witness, being recalled for further cross-examination, was made a witness for petitioner, to the latter's detriment; petitioner was prevented from proving a fact clearly relevant to his defense; and the trial judge, advising petitioner of his privilege against self-incrimination, made reference in the presence of the jury to petitioner's criminal record. Petitioner's subsequent application to the State Supreme Court for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming a denial of federal constitutional right on his trial, was denied.

Under some provisions adopted as part of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (110 Stat 3009-546), although 8 USCS 1252(a)(1) generally authorizes Federal Courts of Appeals to consider petitions challenging final orders that command removal of aliens from the United States, 8 USCS 1252(a)(2)(C) provides that "no court shall have jurisdiction to review any final order of removal against any alien who is removable by reason of" conviction of certain crimes, including any aggravated felony. Each of three aliens--who were (1) lawful permanent residents of the United States, and (2) subject to administratively final orders of removal because they had been convicted of aggravated felonies--filed a petition for review pursuant to 1252(a)(1) in the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit and a petition for a writ of habeas corpus pursuant to 28 USCS 2241 in a United States District Court in order to challenge the United States Board of Immigration Appeals' determination that, as a matter of law, the alien was ineligible to apply for a discretionary waiver of deportation under the repealed 212(c) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 USCS 1182(c)). The petitions for review were consolidated by the Court of Appeals, which, in dismissing these petitions for lack of jurisdiction, expressed the view that the aliens nevertheless could pursue their claims in a 2241 action in the District Court (232 F3d 328).

During the pendency of actions brought by the Administrator of the Office of Price Administration against sellers of commodities to recover damages for sales in excess of maximum prices established under the Emergency Price Control Act, various OPA functions were transferred to the Secretary of Commerce by Executive Order No. 9841. The Attorney General promptly moved to substitute the United States as party plaintiff, relying upon Executive Order No. 9842, which was incorporated by reference in Executive Order No. 9841 and directed the Attorney General to conduct litigation against violators of price control in the name of the United States. The courts below held that the suits could not be maintained in the name of the United States.

An injunction was obtained by the state of Ohio in state court requiring an individual who was the chief executive of a corporation to clean up a hazardous waste site. When the individual failed to comply with his obligation under the injunction, the state obtained the appointment in state court of a receiver who was directed to take possession of all property and other assets of the individual and the corporation and to implement the judgment entry by cleaning up the site. The receiver took possession of the site but had not completed his task when the individual filed a personal bankruptcy petition. The state filed a complaint in the Bankruptcy Court seeking a declaration that the individual's obligation under the judgment order to clean up the site was not dischargeable in bankruptcy because it was not a "debt," or a "liability on a claim," within the meaning of the Bankruptcy Code, and also seeking an injunction against the bankruptcy trustee to restrain him from pursuing any action to recover assets of the individual in the hands of the receiver. The Bankruptcy Court ruled against the state (29 BR 816) as did the District Court. The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed, holding that the state essentially sought from the individual only a monetary payment and that such a required payment was a liability on a claim that was dischargeable under the bankruptcy statute (717 F2d 984).

Operators of bleached craft pulp mills in California who discharged pollutants into the Pacific Ocean were granted variances from certain effluent limitations of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) by the California State Water Resources Control Board in connection with proposed National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permits under 402 of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972 (33 USCS 1342). As authorized under 402(d)(2) of the statute (33 USCS 1342(d)(2)), however, the EPA denied the variances and vetoed the permits to the extent that they exempted the mill operators from effluent limitations. Thereafter, the mill operators brought a direct review action in the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, but the Court of Appeals dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, holding that although 509(b)(1)(F) of the statute (33 USCS 1369(b)(1)(F)), providing for review in the Courts of Appeals of EPA actions "in issuing or denying any permit under section 402," authorized direct review in the relevant Courts of Appeals for states in which the EPA itself administers the NPDES permit program, 509(b)(1)(F) did not apply since California was a state authorized to administer its own NPDES permit-issuing program, and the EPA, in the case at bar, had done no more than veto a permit proposed by the authorized state authority (599 F2d 897).

A company headquartered in California filed, with the Commission's DG-Competition, an antitrust complaint against a second company, also headquarted in California. This complaint alleged that the second company had violated EU competition law with respect to the European market. While the complaint apparently was still in the investigative stage, the first company requested, from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, a discovery order under _ 1782(a), allegedly in connection with the complaint, to direct the second company to produce some documents that had been produced in previous antitrust litigation involving the second company. However, the District Court denied the request, as assertedly unsupported by applicable authority.

The National Labor Relations Board certified unions as the collective bargaining representatives for lay teachers employed in certain Catholic high schools located in Illinois and Indiana, but the schools declined to recognize the unions or to bargain with them, and the unions filed unfair labor practice complaints with the Board. In the unfair labor practice proceedings, the schools challenged the Board's exercise of jurisdiction over religious schools on both statutory and constitutional grounds, but the Board, relying upon its policy of declining jurisdiction only when schools are completely religious, not just religiously associated as the high schools involved in the unfair labor practice proceeding were found to be, held that it had properly exercised its statutory jurisdiction, and upon finding that the schools had violated the National Labor Relations Act (29 USCS 151 et seq.), ordered that the schools cease their unfair labor practices and bargain collectively with the unions (224 NLRB 1221 and 224 NLRB 1226). On review, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit denied enforcement of the Board's orders, ruling that the Board's standard for exercising its discretion in extending its jurisdiction to religiously affiliated schools was not a workable guide and that the First Amendment free exercise and establishment clauses foreclosed the Board's jurisdiction (559 F2d 1112).

A member of a labor union instituted an action for declaratory and injunctive relief in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, challenging the constitutionality under the due process clause of a Louisiana statute, and the actions thereunder of the defendants, state officials. The challenged statute created a Labor- Management Commission of Inquiry to investigate criminal violations in the field of labor-management relations upon referral by the governor, to hold public hearings for determining whether there was probable cause to believe that violations of the criminal laws had occurred, and to make public findings and recommendations to appropriate authorities with regard to the institution of criminal prosecutions, including conclusions as to specific individuals, the statute also limiting the right of a witness, who could be compelled to attend, or his counsel, to examine other witnesses and to call witnesses. The complaint contained allegations that the commission was an executive trial agency performing an accusatory function designed to publicly find the plaintiff and others guilty of violations of criminal laws without trial or procedural safeguards, allegedly for the purpose of injuring the plaintiff and destroying the labor union of which he was a member, and that the defendants, acting in concert with others and in connection with the administration of the statute, had engaged in a course of conduct designed publicly to brand the plaintiff and others as criminals, including the filing of allegedly baseless criminal charges against the plaintiff. The three- judge District Court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a cause of action, holding that the Act was constitutional, and that the other matters alleged were merely potential defenses to the pending criminal charges against the plaintiff (286 F Supp 537).

Defendants' petition, based on 28 USC 1443, to remove to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia criminal trespass prosecutions pending against them in the Superior Court of Fulton County, Georgia, alleged that defendants had been arrested on various dates in the spring of 1963 when they sought to obtain service at privately owned restaurants open to the general public in Atlanta, Georgia, and that their arrests were effected for the sole purpose of racial discrimination. On its own motion and without a hearing, the District Court remanded the cases to the state court. Pending defendants' appeal to the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 was enacted; this Act, as interpreted by the United States Supreme Court, prohibited trespass prosecutions of the kind involved in the instant case, even though the prosecutions were instituted prior to the passage of the Act. The Court of Appeals therefore returned the case to the District Court, with directions that defendants be given an opportunity to prove that their prosecutions had resulted from orders to leave public accommodations for racial reasons, and, upon such proof, to dismiss the prosecutions. (342 F2d 336.)

Pre-1988 Medicaid eligibility rules for married applicants often required both spouses to deplete their combined resources before a spouse who was institutionalized, as in a nursing home, became eligible for benefits. In order to prevent the pauperization of the "community spouse"--that is, the spouse remaining at home--the Medicare Catastrophic Coverage Act of 1988 (MCCA) (42 USCS 1396r-5 et seq.) (1) directed that, in any month in which one spouse was institutionalized, no income of the community spouse was to be deemed available to the institutionalized spouse ( 1396r-5(b)(1)); (2) required states to set a "minimum monthly maintenance needs allowance" (MMMNA) for the community spouse ( 1396r-5(d)(3)); and (3) prescribed that, if the community spouse's posteligibility income was insufficient to yield income equal to or above the MMMNA, the shortfall--called the "community spouse monthly income allowance" (CSMIA)--could be deducted from the institutionalized spouse's income and paid to the community spouse ( 1396r-5(d)(1)(B)). In determining the institutionalized spouse's Medicaid eligibility, a portion of the couple's resources--called the "community spouse resource allowance" (CSRA)--was to be reserved for the benefit of the community spouse ( 1396r-5(c)(2)). Under 1396r-5(e)(2)(C), a couple could obtain a higher CSRA by establishing that the standard CSRA was inadequate to raise "the community spouse's income" to the MMMNA. An administrative hearing for such a purpose was authorized by 1396r-5(e)(2)(A)(v). To calculate the CSRA at such a hearing, some states used an "income-first" method, under which the state considered whether the community spouse's income, including potential CSMIA transfers from the institutionalized spouse, would suffice to enable the community spouse to meet monthly needs once the institutionalized spouse qualified for Medicaid. Other states used a "resources-first" method that excluded such potential income transfers from consideration. After entering a Wisconsin nursing home, a wife applied for Medicaid. The Green County, Wisconsin, department of human services (1) determined (using figures as subsequently corrected somewhat) that the wife and her husband could retain $ 74,822 in assets--$ 72,822 as the husband's standard CSRA and $ 2,000 as the wife's personal allowance; (2) found that, as of the date of the application, the couple possessed resources exceeding their $ 74,822 limit by $ 14,513; and (3) concluded that the wife would not be eligible for Medicaid until the couple's spending reduced their resources by the $ 14,513 amount. The wife sought a hearing before Wisconsin's department of health and family services in order to obtain a higher CSRA for the husband, on the grounds that the husband's monthly income fell below the applicable MMMNA. The hearing examiner, applying a Wisconsin statute that adopted the income-first rule, concluded that he lacked authority to increase the CSRA. Wisconsin's Department of Industry, Labor and Human Relations affirmed the hearing examiner's decision, and the Circuit Court for Green County affirmed. However, the Wisconsin Court of Appeals--in reversing the Circuit Court's order and in directing a remand--concluded that (1) the MCCA mandated the resources-first method, and (2) Wisconsin's income-first statute thus conflicted with the MCCA (2000 WI App 150, 237 Wis 2d 810, 615 NW2d 647).

Relying upon 307(b)(1) of the Clean Air Act (42 USCS 7607(b)(1)), providing for direct review in the various Federal Courts of Appeals of locally and regionally applicable actions taken by the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) under specific enumerated provisions of the Act, and of "any other final action of the Administrator under [the] Act," a corporation which built a power generating facility in Lake Charles, Louisiana, brought an action in the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit to obtain review of the decision of a Regional Administrator of the EPA that the EPA's "new source" performance standards regarding air pollution were applicable to the corporation's waste-heat boilers at the facility. Because of its uncertainty regarding the proper forum for judicial review, the corporation also filed a complaint for injunctive relief against the Administrator in the United States District Court for the Western District of Louisiana. Notwithstanding that it had filed its petition in the Court of Appeals, the corporation argued in the Court of Appeals that such court did not have jurisdiction to review the decision of the Administrator since the decision, an admittedly "final" one, was not an action taken under any of the provisions specifically enumerated in 307(b)(1) and could not be characterized as falling within the phrase "any other final action of the Administrator." Concluding that the Administrator's decision did not fall within the meaning of "any other final action" under 307(b)(1), the Court of Appeals dismissed the corporation's petition for lack of jurisdiction (587 F2d 237).

A Negro boy of fifteen was convicted in a state court of murder upon evidence which included a confession. The case was brought to the Supreme Court by a contention of denial of due process, in that the confession was obtained by duress.

In granting an injunction against a strike called by a union against a railroad in connection with a controversy, then pending before the National Railroad Adjustment Board, resulting from orders of the railroad which, in effect, eliminated the jobs of two of five-men way-freight crews and changed the home or away-from-home terminals of the remaining crews, the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas imposed conditions requiring that the railroad either restore the situation which existed prior to the orders, or pay the employees adversely affected by the orders the wages they would have received had the orders not been issued. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit sustained the injunction but vacated the conditions, holding that the District Court had no power to attach them. (266 F2d 335.)

Jurisdiction to adjudicate the prisoner's claims was proper even though it was his second habeas application as the 28 U.S.C.S. _ 2244 limit on second or successive petitions did not govern where a 28 U.S.C.S. _ 2254 application raising a Ford incompetency claim was filed as soon as that claim was ripe. Review was without deference as the state court's failure to provide procedures mandated by case law after the prisoner made a substantial showing of incompetency was an unreasonable application of clearly established case law. The state court failed to provide the prisoner with the required minimum process where it conveyed untrue information to counsel, provided an inadequate opportunity to submit expert evidence in response to a report filed by court-appointed experts, and made its determination without holding a final competency hearing. The prisoner's severe delusions could have rendered him incompetent to be executed even though he could identify the stated reason for his execution. Thus, the prisoner's submission that his documented delusions prevented him from comprehending the meaning and purpose of the punishment to which he had been sentenced should have been considered.

Upon trial in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, the defendant was convicted of federal automobile theft offenses, the District Court having denied the defendant's pretrial and posttrial motions to dismiss the indictment on the ground that he had been denied a speedy trial in violation of the Sixth Amendment because 22 months had elapsed between his arrest and indictment and a further period of 12 months had elapsed between his indictment and trial. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding that absent a showing of actual prejudice, the 22-month pre-indictment delay was not to be counted for purposes of the defendant's Sixth Amendment motions (502 F2d 1233).

In a suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio by a former supervisor of elementary education against school officials for refusal to renew her contract of employment because of her activities in support of a school desegregation plan, in violation of 42 USCS 1983 and 1985, the District Court granted summary judgment for the defendants and dismissed the complaint on the ground that res judicata barred her claim because she had earlier obtained a state-court judgment awarding reinstatement and damages against the school board for breach of contract. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (703 F2d 564).

A Negro who had been employed by a brewing company, and who--under the provisions of a multiemployer collective bargaining agreement for the California brewery industry providing greater benefits in hiring and layoffs to workers classified as "permanent" employees than to workers classified as "temporary" employees--had been classified as a "temporary" employee because he could not meet the requirement for "permanent" classification of having worked at least 45 weeks in a single calendar year, brought a class action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California against brewing companies, unions, and an association of California brewers, claiming, among other things, that the defendants had discriminated against him and other Negroes in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e et seq.) because the 45-week requirement operated to preclude blacks from achieving, or from gaining a reasonable opportunity of achieving, "permanent" status. The District Court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a claim on which relief could be granted, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded, finding that the 45-week rule was not a "seniority system" or part of a "seniority system" within the meaning of 703(h) of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e-2(h)), which provides--as an exception to Title VII's prohibition against unlawful practices, procedures, or tests that operate to "freeze" the status quo of prior discriminatory employment practices--that it is not an unlawful employment practice for an employer to apply different standards of compensation, or different terms, conditions, or privileges of employment under a "bona fide seniority system" if such differences are not the result of an intention to discriminate because of race (585 F2d 421).

Inquiries as to thefts of property of a corporation were conducted by the head of a detective agency, together with two of its employees and a member of the state police force detailed to assist in the investigation, in which they obtained confessions from suspects by physical force and violence. Thereupon they were indicted for violations of 19 and 20 of the Criminal Code (now 18 USC 241, 242). The pertinent provisions of 19 prohibit a conspiracy to injure a citizen in the free enjoyment of any right or privilege secured to him by the Federal Constitution, and those of 20 penalize a person who under color of state law wilfully subjects any inhabitant of a state to the deprivation of any rights, privileges, or immunities so secured or protected. As to the charges under 20, the head of the agency was convicted and the other defendants were acquitted. As to all defendants a mistrial was declared under 19, the jury being unable to agree on a verdict. Upon a new indictment under 19 all the defendants were convicted, but on appeal the judgment was reversed by the Court of Appeals.

The validity of a notice of appeal received at the office of the Clerk of a District Court within the thirty days prescribed by 28 USC 2107 for filing a notice of appeal is not vitiated by the fact that the $ 5 fee required by 28 USC 1917 to be paid "upon the filing" of a notice of appeal was not received by the clerk until three or four days after the expiration of the thirty-day period prescribed by 28 USC 2107.

The parents of a child with a disability brought, under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) (20 U.S.C.S. __ 1400 et seq.), an action to require a public school board to pay for their son's private school tuition. The parents prevailed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York (86 F. Supp. 2d 354) and the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (297 F. 3d 195). Subsequently, the parents sought to recover $29,350 in fees that they had paid for services rendered by an educational consultant during the IDEA proceedings. The District Court (1) under 20 U.S.C.S. _ 1415(i)(3)(B)--which authorized a court to award "reasonable attorneys' fees as part of the costs" to parents who prevailed in an IDEA action--granted the parent' request in part, and (2) awarded them $8,650 (2003 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 12764).

Under Illinois statutes, organizers of a new political party must (1) canvass the electoral area where they wish to run candidates; (2) when running candidates for statewide office, obtain the signatures of 1 percent of the voters at the last statewide election or 25,000 voters, whichever is less; and (3) when running candidates solely for offices within a political subdivision of the state, circulate petitions containing a complete list of candidates for all offices to be filled in the subdivision at large, and obtain signatures (a) from 5 percent of the voters at the last election in the subdivision or 25,000 voters, whichever is less, or (b) if the subdivision is divided into separate districts from which some officers are elected, from 5 percent of the voters at the last election in each district or 25,000 voters, whichever is less. Also, an Illinois statute provides that new political parties may not bear the same name as any established party. A group of citizens sought (1) to expand the Harold Washington Party (HWP), which was already an established party in the city of Chicago, throughout Cook County--which was divided into one Chicago city district and one suburban district, each of which was large enough to require 25,000 signatures on new-party nominating petitions--and (2) to run candidates for at-large, city-district, and suburban-district county board seats in 1990. The citizens gathered 44,000 signatures from the city district, but only 7,800 signatures from the suburban district. Interested voters filed objections to the HWP petitions with the county electoral board, but the electoral board ruled that (1) the citizens were not barred from running for county offices under the HWP name because of the fact that a party of the same name already existed in the city, especially since the most recent HWP mayoral candidate had authorized the county candidates to use the party name; (2) the failure to collect 25,000 signatures from the suburban district disqualified the HWP from running candidates for suburban-district county board seats, but not for city-district and at-large seats; and (3) the HWP's failure to designate candidates for county judicial offices did not disqualify the entire HWP slate for county offices. The Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois (1) affirmed the electoral board's ruling as to use of the HWP name, but (2) held that either the lack of sufficient signatures in the suburban district or the failure to designate judicial candidates was sufficient grounds to disqualify the entire HWP slate of candidates. On review, the Supreme Court of Illinois held, in a brief written order, that (1) the citizens were prohibited from using the HWP name, and (2) the failure to obtain sufficient signatures in the suburban district disqualified the entire slate of candidates.

On a state prisoner's petition for habeas corpus, the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts set aside his conviction of armed robbery and ordered his release because of introduction, at the state trial, of evidence obtained by an unlawful search and seizure. (252 F Supp 851.) The Court of Appeals for the First Circuit affirmed. (368 F2d 142.)

Shareholders of an investment company brought a derivative action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York against several members of the company's board of directors and its registered investment advisor, alleging that the defendants had violated their duties under the Investment Company Act (15 USCS 80a-1 et seq.) and the Investment Advisers Act (15 USCS 80b-1 et seq.) in connection with the company's purchase of certain commercial paper. Five members of the company's board of directors, who were neither affiliated with the investment advisor nor defendants in the derivative suit, acting as a quorum pursuant to the company's bylaws, concluded that continuation of the derivative action was contrary to the best interests of the company and its shareholders, and moved the District Court to dismiss the action. The District Court held that under the so-called "business judgment rule," a quorum of truly disinterested and independent directors has the authority to terminate a derivative suit which they conclude, in good faith, is contrary to the company's best interests (404 F Supp 1172), and eventually entered summary judgment against the plaintiffs, finding no evidence that the directors who voted to terminate the suit had acted other than independently and in good faith (426 F Supp 844). Thereafter, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed, holding that because of the Investment Company Act, disinterested directors of an investment company lack the power to foreclose the continuation of nonfrivolous litigation brought by shareholders against majority directors for breach of their fiduciary duties (567 F2d 1208).

A form of mixed train and truck transportation known as "Plan II TOFC/COFC service" enables a carrier to transport a trailer and its contents over rail on a flatcar (trailer-on-flatcar, TOFC, or "piggyback" service), or similarly to transport a container (container-on-flatcar, or COFC), and then to haul the trailer or container on the highway, without unloading or reloading the shipment. Under a provision of the Staggers Rail Act (49 USCS 10505(f)), the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) is authorized to exempt from state regulation transportation provided by a rail carrier as a part of a continuous intermodal movement. Pursuant to this provision, the ICC adopted in 1981 a regulation exempting Plan II service from state regulation. In 1982, three interstate railroads petitioned the Railroad Commission of Texas (RCT) to apply this exemption to their Texas intrastate TOFC/COFC service. The RCT granted a partial exemption that covered the rail but not the truck portions of the intrastate service. The railroads petitioned the ICC to review this decision, and the ICC held that the RCT's assertion of regulatory jurisdiction over the truck portions of the intrastate service was inconsistent with the 1981 regulation. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed, holding that the truck portions of the intrastate service were to be classified as "transportation provided by a motor carrier" within the meaning of 49 USCS 10521(b)(1) and thus not subject to ICC exemption from state control (770 F2d 452).

The National Labor Relations Board, in certification proceedings instituted by a union, found that a bus company possessed sufficient control over the employees of a company which had contracted to provide cleaning and maintenance services at terminals operated by the bus company, to qualify as a joint employer with the cleaning company, and directed a representation election within the unit consisting of such employees. The United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, in a suit filed by the bus company, enjoined the election on the ground that the Board's findings established, as a matter of law, that the cleaning company was the sole employer of the employees in question, and the Board, therefore, had violated the National Labor Relations Act by attempting to conduct a representation election where no employment relationship existed between the employees and the purported employer. (205 F Supp 686.) The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed. (309 F2d 397.)

In an action brought by the widows of passengers killed in the crash, outside of Louisiana's territorial waters, of a helicopter used in connection with oil drilling operations, the United States District Court for the Western District of Louisiana accepted admiralty jurisdiction, found that the deaths were caused by the negligence of the operating company, and awarded damages equal to the pecuniary loss suffered by the two families. The District Court held, however, that the law did not authorize recovery for the two families' loss of society (360 F Supp 1140). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed, holding that the families were entitled to claim damages for loss of society (545 F2d 422).

After the plaintiff's conviction in a New York state court for violating a New York statute prohibiting the distribution in quantity of anonymous handbills in political campaigns had been reversed on state law grounds, he sought declaratory and injunctive relief in a three-judge Federal District Court in the Eastern District of New York on the ground that, on its face, the statute was repugnant to the guaranties of free expression secured by the Federal Constitution, since the statute suffered from impermissible overbreadth by prohibiting the distribution of anonymous handbills both within and outside the protection of the First Amendment. Applying the doctrine of abstention, the District Court, one judge dissenting, dismissed the case and remitted the plaintiff to the New York state courts to institute a declaratory judgment action there or to assert his constitutional challenge as a defense in any future criminal prosecution for violation of the statute. (261 F Supp 985.)

A manufacturer of components used in naval vessels brought a diversity action in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey against a corporation with whom it had entered into a series of contracts, seeking damages and reformation with regard to the contract. Among the claims asserted in the manufacturer's complaint was a $ 19 million claim for the outstanding balance due on contracts already performed. Counterclaims were then filed by the defendant corporation. The facts underlying most of the claims and counterclaims were in dispute, but as to the manufacturer's $ 19 million claim, the sole dispute concerned the application of a release clause contained in the agreement. The District Court granted summary judgment for the manufacturer on the $ 19 million claim, and assessed prejudgment interest at the prevailing rate. The manufacturer then moved for certification of the District Court's order as a final judgment under 54(b) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, which provides that when more than one claim is presented in an action, whether as a claim or counterclaim, a District Court may direct the entry of a final judgment as to one or more but fewer than all of the claims upon an express determination that there is no just reason for delay. Determining that there was "no just reason for delay" under Rule 54(b), the District Court expressly directed entry of final judgment for the manufacturer. While acknowledging that Rule 54(b) certification was not to be granted as a matter of course, the District Court identified the relevant factors in the case before it: among other things, the court found that certification would not result in unnecessary appellate review, that the claims finally adjudicated were separate, distinct, and independent of any of the other claims or counterclaims involved, that the nature of the claims was such that no appellate court would have to decide the same issues more than once if there were subsequent appeals, that the manufacturer would suffer severe daily financial loss from nonpayment of the judgment as a result of the difference between the current interest rates and the statutory prejudgment rate, and that the solvency of the parties was not a significant factor since each appeared to be financially sound. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit concluded that the District Court had abused its discretion by granting Rule 54(b) certification and dismissed the case for want of an appealable order, the Court of Appeals reasoning that the matter should remain in status quo since nonfrivolous counterclaims were pending, and since the manufacturer had not made a showing of unusual or harsh circumstances (597 F2d 35).

Amounts owing to a subcontractor from a contractor were claimed by the United States, under federal tax liens, and by a performance-bond surety in whose favor the subcontractor had made an "assignment" of all sums to become due for performance of the subcontract, as security for any indebtedness or liability thereafter incurred by the subcontractor to the surety. The contractor thereupon instituted in the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas, San Antonio Division, an interpleader action, in which he impleaded the surety and the government. The District Court ruled that the claim of the surety had priority, since the "assignment" antedated the filing of notice of the federal tax lien, and constituted the surety a "mortgagee" within the meaning of 3672(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939, which provides that a federal tax lien shall not be valid as against any mortgagee until notice thereof has been filed by the Collector (140 F Supp 60). The District Court's judgment was affirmed by the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit (239 F2d 384).

A grand jury indicted a company and two company officers on two counts of conspiracy to defraud the United States and nine counts of tax fraud. The defendants each pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to defraud the government, and all other counts were dismissed. Thereafter, the government moved for disclosure of all grand jury materials to attorneys in the Justice Department's Civil Division, their paralegal and secretarial assistants, and certain Defense Department experts, for use in preparing and conducting a possible civil suit against the defendants under the False Claims Act (31 USCS 231 et seq.) The officers and company opposed the disclosure and made an allegation of grand jury misuse for civil purposes. The United States District Court for the Southern District of California granted the requested disclosure. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that Civil Division attorneys could obtain disclosure only by showing particularized need under Rule 6(e)(3)(C)(i) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure and that the District Court had not applied a correct standard of particularized need (642 F2d 1184).

The Nationality Act of 1940, as amended by the Second War Powers Act of 1942, sought to make American citizenship more easily available to aliens who served honorably in the United States Armed Forces during World War II by (1) exempting such aliens from residency, language proficiency, and various other naturalization requirements, and (2) authorizing representatives of the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) to receive and grant naturalization petitions outside the United States. An American vice consul in the Philippines was given such authorization in August 1945; however, after the Philippine government expressed concern that the country would be drained of essential manpower, the vice consul was notified in October 1945 that his authority had been revoked, and such authority was not given to any other official in the Philippines until August 1946. The Nationality Act expired on December 31, 1946, and a successor statute--applicable, under 8 USCS 1421(e), to all petitions filed after September 26, 1961--excluded Filipino veterans from the liberalized naturalization program (8 USCS 1440). Fourteen Filipino veterans who (1) were eligible for naturalization under the Nationality Act, (2) had been present in the Philippines between October 1945 and August 1946, and (3) had not taken affirmative steps to be naturalized before the Nationality Act expired subsequently claimed that they were nevertheless entitled to naturalization under the Nationality Act, and they filed petitions to that effect in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California after September 26, 1961. Similar petitions were filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California by two other Filipino veterans, one of whom had begun the petition process while in civilian employment in the United States but had not completed the process before the Nationality Act expired. All of these petitions were denied by the District Courts. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded the District Court decisions on the grounds that (1) the revocation of the vice consul's authority violated the mandatory language of the Naturalization Act, and (2) granting naturalization to these veterans was an appropriate equitable remedy (one decision reported at 796 F2d 1091).

A city, after having consolidated with two neighboring cities and having annexed an additional incorporated area, submitted jointly with the United States Attorney General an electoral plan to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia for a declaratory judgment approving the plan under 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (42 USCS 1973c) as not having the purpose or effect of denying or abridging the right to vote on account of race. The plan provided for the election to the city council of nine members who were required to be elected by a majority vote. Under the submitted plan, four members would be elected from four single-member districts, two members would be elected from two larger districts, each comprised of two of the smaller districts, and three members would be elected at-large, one each residing in one of the two larger districts, and the third at-large seat to be occupied by the mayor with no residency requirement. One-third of the council seats were to be elected from black majority districts, with blacks comprising 40.56% of the population of the enlarged city, and 35% of the voting age population. The District Court held that the plan could not be approved under 5 of the Act because it insufficiently neutralized the adverse impact upon minority voting strength that resulted from the expansion of the city's borders, concluding that it was necessary in order for the plan to be approved that the majority vote requirement be eliminated for the two non-mayoral at-large council seats.

One who was convicted in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts of 75 counts of making false claims against the government was committed to the Attorney General pursuant to 18 USC 4208(b) pending a study to be used "as a basis for determining the sentence to be imposed," and more than three months after the commitment order the court suspended sentence and placed the defendant on probation. The defendant's appeal within 10 days from the order placing him on probation was dismissed as untimely by the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, on the ground that the time for appeal expired 10 days after entry of the commitment order. (307 F2d 839.)

Pursuant to 1(14)(a) of the Interstate Commerce Act (49 USCS 1(14)(a)), which authorizes the Interstate Commerce Commission, "after hearing," to establish compensation to be paid by a railroad for the use of cars not owned by it, the Commission issued a tentative draft, based on information compiled by railroads, of incentive per diem charges on standard boxcars, which charges were designed to spur prompt return of cars to their owners, and to make acquisition of new cars financially attractive to the railroads.The Commission gave all interested parties 60 days in which to file written statements of position, submissions of evidence, or other relevant observations, but denied certain railroads' requests for an oral hearing before the Commission promulgated its final incentive per diem rate schedule.Two of the railroads instituted an action in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida to set aside the rate schedule, contending that the Commission, in restricting the railroads to only written submissions of evidence and arguments, had failed to comply with the applicable hearing provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (5 USCS 551 et seq.).The District Court held that in view of the language of 1(14)(a) of the Interstate Commerce Act, the Commission's rule-making procedure was subject to 556 and 557 of the Administrative Procedure Act, which govern when rules are required by statute "to be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing," and which require that interested parties be allowed to present oral evidence and to cross-examine witnesses, except where parties will not be prejudiced by restriction to written submissions--the District Court concluding that the railroads had been prejudiced by the Commission's determination to receive only written submissions in the instant case (322 F Supp 725).

The validity of a federal statute requiring a request in writing as a prerequisite to the delivery of nonsealed mail from abroad containing Communist propaganda material was attacked in No. 491 in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and in No. 848 in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, Southern Division. After the institution of the suits each plaintiff was notified by the post office that none of his mail would be detained. In No. 491 a three-judge District Court dismissed the complaint as moot. (229 F Supp 913.) In No. 848 a like District Court reached the merits and held that the statute was unconstitutional under the First Amendment. (236 F Supp 405.)

The Nazi Government of Germany confiscated the value or proceeds of many Jewish life insurance policies issued before and during the Second World War. After the war, even a policy that had escaped confiscation was likely to be dishonored, whether because insurers denied its existence or claimed it had lapsed from unpaid premiums, or because the German Government would not provide heirs with documentation of the policyholder's death. Responsibility as between the government and insurance companies is disputed, but the fact is that the proceeds of many insurance policies issued to Jews before and during the war were paid to the Third Reich or never paid at all. These confiscations and frustrations of claims fell within the subject of reparations, which became a principal object of Allied diplomacy after the war. Ultimately, the western allies placed the obligation to provide restitution to victims of Nazi persecution on the new West German Government, which enacted restitution laws and signed agreements with other countries for the compensation of their nationals. Despite a payout of more than 100 billion deutsch marks as of 2000, however, these measures left out many claimants and certain types of claims. After German reunification, class actions for restitution poured into United States courts against companies doing business in Germany during the Nazi era. Protests by defendant companies and their governments prompted the United States Government to take action to try to resolve the matter. Negotiations at the national level produced the German Foundation Agreement, in which Germany agreed to establish a foundation funded with 10 billion deutsch marks contributed equally by the German Government and German companies to compensate the companies' victims during the Nazi era.  [***384]  The President agreed that whenever a German company was sued on a Holocaust-era claim in an American court, the Government would (1) submit a statement that it would be in this country's foreign policy interests for the foundation to be the exclusive forum and remedy for such claims, and (2) try to get state and local governments to respect the foundation as the exclusive mechanism. As for insurance claims in particular, both countries agreed that the German Foundation would work with the International Commission on Holocaust Era Insurance Claims (ICHEIC), a voluntary organization whose mission is to negotiate with European insurers to provide information about and settlement of unpaid insurance policies, and which has set up procedures to that end. The German agreement has served as a model for similar agreements with Austria and France. Meanwhile, California began its own enquiry into the issue, prompting state legislation designed to force payment by defaulting insurers. Among other laws, California's Holocaust Victim Insurance Relief Act of 1999 (HVIRA) requires any insurer doing business in the State to disclose information about all policies sold in Europe between 1920 and 1945 by the company or any one "related" to it upon penalty of loss of its state business license. After HVIRA was enacted, the State issued administrative subpoenas against several subsidiaries of European insurance companies participating in the ICHEIC. Immediately, the Federal Government informed California officials that HVIRA would damage the ICHEIC, the only effective means to process quickly and completely unpaid Holocaust era insurance claims, and that HVIRA would possibly derail the German Foundation Agreement. Nevertheless, the state insurance commissioner announced that he would enforce HVIRA to its fullest. Petitioner insurance entities then filed this suit challenging HVIRA's constitutionality. The District Court issued a preliminary injunction against enforcing HVIRA and later granted petitioners summary judgment. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding, inter alia, that HVIRA did not violate the federal foreign affairs power.

A labor union member who twice had been an unsuccessful candidate for union office formally advised the union that he would be a candidate in the union's upcoming election and requested that the union provide him with mailing labels containing the names and addresses of voting union members so that he could arrange, at his own expense, to mail campaign literature to the members prior to the union's nominating convention. The union denied the request because a union rule prohibited such preconvention mailing. Subsequently, the member filed an action under 401(c) of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959 (LMRDA) (29 USCS 481(c))--which requires a labor union to comply with all reasonable requests, from any bona fide candidate for union office, to distribute, at the candidate's expense, campaign literature from the candidate to all union members in good standing. The United States District Court for the District of Maryland, entering a preliminary injunction against the union's denial of the member's request, held that (1) the clear language of 401(c) required the court to focus on the reasonableness of the member's request rather than on the reasonableness of the union rule under which the request had been denied, (2) the request was reasonable, and (3) a union rule whose application resulted in the rejection of such a request was invalid. The United Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, holding that the question whether the member's request should have been granted depended entirely on whether the request was reasonable, affirmed the District Court's judgment (857 F2d 216, adhered to on rehearing en banc 889 F2d 58).

A deputy sheriff in Nevada, investigating a report of an assault, approached a suspect and asked him if he had any identification on him. After the suspect repeatedly refused to identify himself, he was arrested and charged with obstructing the discharge of the deputy sheriff's official duty. The suspect was convicted in a Nevada trial court, which agreed that the suspect's refusal to identify himself, as required by Nevada's "stop and identify" statute, had constituted such an obstruction.

These two consolidated cases presented issues as to the validity of the state of Washington's business and occupation (B & O) tax on business activities within the state, including manufacturing and wholesale selling. In the first case (No. 85-2006), 71 commercial enterprises filed 53 separate actions in the Thurston County Superior Court for refunds of B & O taxes paid to the state. The enterprises challenged the state's "multiple activities" exemption, under which local manufacturers were exempted from the manufacturing tax for the portion of their output that was subject to the wholesale tax, in other words, for their in-state sales, but sales by local manufacturers to out-of-state purchasers remained subject to the manufacturing tax. The Superior Court joined the actions, found that the exemption did not violate the Federal Constitution's commerce clause (Art I, 8, cl 3), and granted the state taxation department's motion for summary judgment. The Supreme Court of Washington affirmed (105 Wash 2d 328, 715 P2d 128). In the second case (No. 85-1963), an out-of-state manufacturer sued in the Superior Court for a refund of B & O taxes paid for its wholesaling activities within Washington, on the grounds that its business did not have a sufficient nexus with Washington to justify the collection of the tax, and that the tax was not fairly apportioned to reflect the amount of business conducted in the state. This manufacturer had no office, property, or employees in Washington but solicited business in the state under the direction of out-of-state executives and an in-state independent contractor. The Superior Court denied the tax refund, holding that (1) the manufacturer had a sufficient nexus with the state, since the manufacturer's in-state sales representatives helped the manufacturer establish and maintain its market in the state, and (2) the tax was fairly apportioned. The Washington Supreme Court affirmed (105 Wash 2d 318, 715 P2d 123).

At a robing room conference during the trial of an accused in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York on a conspiracy count and four counts of violating the federal bank robbery statute, the trial judge told defense counsel that if the accused were convicted he would give "the absolute maximum sentence," or a life sentence plus sentences for years, so that the accused would not be eligible for parole and would be imprisoned for life. Upon being told of these remarks and being advised by counsel that the likelihood of conviction was great, the accused pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 22 1/2 years in prison. In later proceedings in the same court, the judgment of conviction was set aside on the ground that the plea of guilty was not entered voluntarily (214 F Supp 560), and the counts of a new indictment for the same offenses were dismissed as twice putting the accused in jeopardy. (216 F Supp 850.)

An accused pleaded guilty to federal charges of conspiring to distribute 5 or more kilograms of cocaine and of distributing cocaine, but reserved the right to contest at sentencing the drug quantity attributable under the conspiracy count. Before accepting the plea, the Federal District Court judge (1) made the inquiries required by Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure; (2) told the accused that she faced a mandatory minimum of 1 year in prison for distributing cocaine, but a 10-year minimum for conspiracy if the government could show the required 5 kilograms; and (3) explained that, by pleading guilty, she would be waiving her right at trial to remain silent. The judge put the accused under oath and asked her "Did you do that?" The accused indicated that she had done some of the proffered conduct and confirmed her guilty plea. At her sentencing hearing, three codefendants testified that she had sold 1 1/2 to 2 ounces of cocaine twice a week for 1 1/2 years, and another person testified that petitioner had sold her 2 ounces of cocaine. The accused put on no evidence and argued that the only reliable evidence showed that she had sold only 2 ounces of cocaine. The District Court (1) ruled that as a consequence of accused's guilty plea, she had no right, at the sentencing hearing, to remain silent about her crime's details; (2) found that the codefendants' testimony put her over the 5-kilogram threshold, thus mandating the 10-year minimum; and (3) noted that her failure to testify was a factor in persuading the court to rely on the codefendants' testimony. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed (122 F3d 185).

The ordinance violated the Tonnage Clause. The Clause's prohibition embraced all taxes and duties regardless of their name or form, and even though not measured by tonnage, which operated to impose a charge for the privilege of entering, trading in, or lying in a port. The ordinance taxed no other form of personal property and its amount depended upon the ship's capacity. It raised revenue for general municipal services, which argued in favor of applying the Clause. The ordinance applied almost exclusively to oil tankers and was closely correlated with cargo capacity. Entry into port automatically established a tax situs in the City. Whatever words the City used to describe the tax imposed on mobile homes, trailers, and recreational vehicles, it in fact taxed those vehicles only when they were a form of real property like a home. The ship tax differed from the tax on other oil-related property under Alaska Stat. _ 43.56.210 (2008), in that it was a purely municipal tax with no effective electorate-related check upon the City's vessel-taxing power.

The issue in the present case was whether the Federal Power Commission has authority, under the Natural Gas Act, to issue an order directing a pipeline company, after termination of its contract to purchase from a producer gas produced in a Louisiana field and delivered into Texas over a transmission line part of which was constructed by the pipeline company, to continue purchasing gas at a price, higher than the contract rate, set by the producer and approved by the Commission. Upon the producer's petition, the Commission found that the pipeline company, by ceasing to take gas from the producer's field, had abandoned its facilities used for this purpose, as well as the service rendered by these facilities, contrary to the provisions of 7(b) of the Natural Gas Act, which forbids such abandonment without prior consent of the Commission. Accordingly, the Commission ordered the pipeline company to renew operation of its facilities used to purchase gas from the producer, and directed that the purchases were to be at the producer's new rate and in volumes consistent with the terms of the contract previously in force. (31 FPC 1079, 1086.) The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit upheld the Commission's order. (350 F2d 689.)

The present class action was instituted in a Florida state court by four nonunion employees, who sought declaratory and injunctive relief against an "agency shop" arrangement in a collective labor contract under which employees, without being required to join the contracting union, were required to pay, as a condition of employment, an initial service fee and monthly service fees to the union. The trial court dismissed the action on the ground that the arrangement did not violate the Florida right-to-work law. (41 LRRM 2300.) The Florida Supreme Court reversed, holding that state law forbids the "agency shop" clause involved and that the state courts have jurisdiction to afford a remedy. (141 So 2d 269.)

In a companion case to Textile Workers Union of America v Lincoln Mills of Alabama, supra, p. 972, the United States Supreme Court affirmed a judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit (233 F2d 104), affirming a judgment of the United States District Court for the District of Maine (131 F Supp 767), granting, in an action by a labor union, specific performance of a grievance arbitration provision in a collective bargaining contract between the union and an employer. Five members of the Court, in an opinion by Douglas, J., rested the affirmance on the grounds stated in the majority opinion in the Textile Workers Union Case, and held, further, that in an action under 301 of the Labor Management Relations Act of 1947 to compel arbitration, an order granting the relief sought is appealable.

After the United States Supreme Court had reversed the defendant's conviction and had remanded the case to the state courts for a determination whether the defendant had been the victim of systematic exclusion of Negroes from the grand and petit juries (377 US 129, 12 L ed 2d 190, 84 S Ct 1152), the Circuit Court of Green County, Alabama, found that no such exclusion had occurred, and the Alabama Supreme Court affirmed (280 Ala 509, 195 So 2d 800).

After a circuit court of appeals has heard and determined an appeal in an antitrust case certified to it by this Court under the Act of June 9, 1944 (because of want at the time of a quorum of Justices of this Court qualified to participate in the consideration of the case), the circuit court of appeals has jurisdiction to issue a writ of mandamus to compel the district court to comply with its mandate -- even though the term during which the circuit court of appeals issued its mandate to the district court has expired and even though it be assumed arguendo that all further appeals in the case would come to this Court.

A taxpayer, engaged in the car and truck rental business, elected to compute the depreciation allowance on its cars (retained for less than 3 years) and its trucks (retained for more than 3 years) in accordance with the declining balance method which is authorized, as a means of computing the "reasonable allowance" for depreciation of business assets, by 167 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. Treasury Regulations, issued in 1956, operated to bar use of the declining balance method in respect of assets having less than 3 years of useful life to the taxpayer in his trade or business, and also provided that the declining balance method should not be so applied as to permit depreciation of an asset below a reasonable salvage value. In an action in the United States District Court for the District of Delaware, in which the taxpayer sought refund of taxes paid, the validity of these Regulations was challenged. The District Court ruled in favor of the taxpayer (165 F Supp 261), but the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed (268 F2d 604).

In settlement of a lawsuit brought in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York by a leather-goods manufacturer against alleged trademark infringers who manufactured and distributed imitations of its goods, the alleged trademark infringers agreed to the entry of a permanent injunction prohibiting them from further activity which would infringe the trademark of the leather-goods manufacturer. After submission of an affidavit by counsel for the leather-goods manufacturer, the District Court (1) found probable cause to believe that the trademark infringers had engaged in conduct in violation of the injunction, and (2) appointed counsel for the leather-goods manufacturer as special counsel to represent the United States in an investigation and possible prosecution of a criminal contempt action. Subsequently, the District Court signed an order directing the alleged trademark infringers to show cause why they should not be cited for contempt for violating the permanent injunction. The alleged trademark infringers filed, but were denied, motions opposing the order to show cause and the appointment of an interested party's counsel as special prosecutors (592 F Supp 734). The alleged trademark infringers were convicted of criminal contempt or of aiding and abetting the criminal contempt. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit (1) rejected the contention that the appointment of the leather-goods manufacturer's counsel as special prosecutors violated the alleged trademark infringers' right to be prosecuted by an impartial prosecutor, (2) suggested that an interested party's attorney would often be the only source of information about contempts occurring outside the court's presence, (3) stated that the supervision of contempt prosecutions by a judge would generally be sufficient to prevent the danger that a special prosecutor would use the threat of prosecution as a bargaining chip in civil negotiations, (4) stated that the authority to prosecute encompasses the authority to engage in necessary investigative activity, and (5) affirmed the alleged trademark infringers' convictions (780 F2d 179).

The United States brought suit against 10 corporations and 5 directors, asserting that interlocking directorates between banks and insurance companies violated 8 of the Clayton Act (15 USCS 19), which forbids a person from serving simultaneously on the boards of directors of two or more competing corporations, other than banks, that meet certain specifications. The United States District Court for the Northern District of California granted summary judgment for the corporations and dismissed the government's suits (422 F Supp 686). The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the fourth paragraph of 8 barred all interlocking directorates between banks and competing nonbanking corporations (656 F2d 428).

In a class action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia against an employer and certain unions for racially discriminatory employment practices in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e et seq.), the District Court found that the employer had engaged in racial discrimination as to various matters, including the refusal to hire black applicants for certain positions, which applicants were one of the plaintiff classes represented in the action. The District Court ordered the employer to notify the members of such class of their right to priority consideration for employment, but the court refused to grant any other specific relief sought, which included an award of backpay and seniority status retroactive to the dates when the individual class members had been discriminatorily refused employment.
