On appeal by the plaintiffs claiming inadequacy of the relief ordered, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed in part, reversed in part, and vacated in part, holding that the District Court had erred in failing to award backpay to the job-applicant class, but had properly denied seniority relief as being barred by 703(h) of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (42 USCS 2000e-2(h)), which provides that it shall not be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to apply different conditions of employment pursuant to a bona fide seniority system (495 F2d 398).

In the United States District Court for the Southern District of Alabama, an action was brought for the purpose of requiring the defendant, an Alabama county school board, to cease maintaining a racially segregated, dual public school system, which included approximately 42 percent Negro students and 58 percent white students. The metropolitan area of the county was divided by a major north-south highway, and most of the Negro elementary school students in the metropolitan area lived on the east side of the highway and attended all-Negro or nearly all-Negro schools. A desegregation plan was approved by the District Court, but the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, holding the District Court's plan deficient in faculty and staff desegregation and in student assignment, (1) directed that faculty and staff members be reassigned in such a manner that the ratio of Negro and white faculty and staff members in each school would be substantially the same as that for the entire school system, and (2) required additional desegregation of students, but treated the eastern part of the county's metropolitan area in isolation from the rest of the school system and required no bus transportation of students for purposes of desegregation, with the result that more than 90 percent of the students in each of nine elementary schools in the eastern part of the metropolitan area would be Negro (430 F2d 883; 430 F2d 889).

Under the Rules of Decision Act (_ 34 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, R. S. _ 721, 28 U. S. C. _ 725), as applied in Erie R. Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64, a federal court, in a diversity of citizenship case arising in South Carolina and turning on a question of state law on which there has been no decision by the highest court of the State, need not follow a decision on the question by a South Carolina county court of common pleas, whose decisions are not reported and, under state practice, are binding only on the parties to the particular case and do not constitute precedents in any other case in that court or in any other court of the State. Pp. 153-162.

The representative of an employer conducted an investigatory interview with one of the employer's workers regarding the employee's suspected theft of food from the employer. During the interview the employee requested that the union shop steward or some other union representative be called to the interview, but her several requests for such representation were denied. An unfair labor practice proceeding was brought, and the National Labor Relations Board held that the employer's denial of the employee's request for union representation at the interview, which interview the employee reasonably believed might result in disciplinary action, constituted an unfair labor practice under 8(a)(1) of the National Labor Relations Act (29 USCS 158(a)(1)) since the denial of representation at the interview interfered with, restrained, and coerced the individual right of employees, protected by 7 of the Act (29 USCS 157), to engage in concerted activities for mutual aid or protection (202 NLRB 446). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, holding that the Board's present construction of 7 of the Act, contrary to its prior construction, was impermissible, refused to enforce the Board's order which directed that the employer cease and desist from requiring an employee to take part in an investigatory interview without union representation if the employee requested representation and reasonably feared disciplinary action (485 F2d 1135).

Under _ 8c of the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937, the Secretary of Agriculture promulgated an order regulating the marketing of milk in the Boston area. As amended in 1941, the order provided for fixing uniform prices to be paid to all producers and required that, in computing such uniform prices, certain amounts should be deducted for special payments to cooperative marketing associations. Claiming that this deduction and these payments to cooperatives unlawfully diverted funds which belonged to producers, certain producers who were not members of any cooperative sued to enjoin the Secretary from carrying out the provisions therefor. Held: The provisions for such deduction and for such payments to cooperatives are invalid, because they are not authorized by the Act

An employer engaged in interstate commerce filed suit in a state court for temporary and permanent injunctions against a labor union responsible for peaceful picketing of some of the employer's retail stores, presumably to compel its factory employees to join the union. After the state court had denied the union's motion to dismiss the action on the ground that the National Labor Relations Board had exclusive jurisdiction of the subject matter of the suit, the union sought an injunction in the federal District Court requiring the employer to withdraw the suit commenced in the state court.

Several persons purchased automobiles from various dealers, financing their purchases through standard retail installment contracts that were assigned to a finance company. As required by the Truth in Lending Act (15 USCS 1601 et seq.) and implementing Regulation Z of the Federal Reserve Board (12 CFR Part 226), the front page of each contract disclosed and explained certain features of the agreement, but no mention was made on the disclosure page that a clause in the body of the contract gave the creditor a right to accelerate payment of the entire debt upon the buyer's default. The buyers then commenced four separate suits against the finance company in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon, alleging, among other things, that the finance company had violated the Act and Regulation Z by failing to disclose on the front page of the contract that the creditor retained the right to accelerate payment of the debt. In two of the suits, the District Court held that facial disclosure of the acceleration clauses was mandated by the provision of the Act compelling publication of "default, delinquency, or similar charges payable in the event of late payments" (15 USCS 1638(a)(9) and 1639(a)(7)). On a consolidated appeal of such two cases and the two other suits in which buyers prevailed on other grounds, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit agreed with the District Court that the Act imposed a general acceleration clause disclosure requirement, basing its decision on the principle that under Regulation Z the creditor must disclose whether a rebate of unearned interest will be made upon acceleration and also disclose the method by which the amount of unearned interest will be computed if the debt is accelerated, the Court implicitly rejecting the contrary administrative interpretation of the pertinent statutory and regulatory provisions (588 F2d 753).

After rent control had terminated in an area, the United States brought an action under the Housing and Rent Act of 1947 to obtain, in addition to statutory damages, restitution of overceiling rentals charged by a landlord in violation of the act.

The Clean Air Act (42 USCS 1857 et seq.) authorizes the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency to promulgate certain "emission standards" for hazardous air pollutants. The emission of an air pollutant in violation of an applicable emission standard is prohibited by 112(c)(1)(B) of the Act (42 USCS 1857c-7(c)(1)(B)). An individual was indicted for violating this section for failing to comply with the administrator's "work practice" regulation specifying procedures to be followed in connection with asbestos emissions during building demolitions ( 40 CFR 61.22(d)(2)(i)). The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan dismissed the indictment on the ground that the cited regulation was not an "emission standard" within the meaning of 112(c). The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed, holding that 307(b) of the Act (42 USCS 1857h-5(b))--which provides (in subparagraph (1)) that a petition for review of the Administrator's action in promulgating an emission standard may be filed only in the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, and (in subparagraph (2)) that judicial review of such action by the Administrator is not subject to review in a civil or criminal enforcement proceeding--precluded an individual from questioning in a criminal proceeding whether a regulation ostensibly promulgated under the Act was in fact an emission standard (545 F2d 1).

An information filed in the United States District Court for the District of Montana charged the defendant with knowingly fishing on a portion of a river in Montana reserved for use by the Crow Indians, in violation of 18 USCS 1165. The case was submitted to the District Court on an agreed statement of facts, which showed that the defendant had been fishing while standing on land owned by Montana within the exterior boundaries of the Crow Reservation. After considering the stipulated facts and reviewing the applicable treaties, the District Court dismissed the information for failure to state an offense (395 F Supp 205). On the government's appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that (1) it had jurisdiction under 18 USCS 3731, (2) the defendant had violated 18 USCS 1165, and (3) the double jeopardy clause of the Fifth Amendment did not bar the appeal, because no further factual proceedings were required in the District Court after its legal conclusions were found to be erroneous (548 F2d 822).

In the district court, respondents introduced evidence that petitioners issued certificates of conformance falsely stating that their work was completed in compliance with U.S. Navy specifications for generator sets needed in the construction of Navy guided missile destroyers and that petitioners presented invoices for payment to the prime contractor shipyards. Respondents, however, did not introduce the invoices that the shipyards submitted to the Navy. The district court found respondents' evidence legally insufficient under the FCA, but the Sixth Circuit held that claims under 31 U.S.C.S. _ 3729(a)(2), (3) did not require proof of an intent to cause a false claim to be paid by the Government; instead, proof of an intent to cause such a claim to be paid by a private entity using Government funds was sufficient. Contrary to the Sixth Circuit, the Court held that under _ 3729(a)(2) respondents were required to prove that petitioners intended that the false statement be material to the Government's decision to pay or approve the false claim. Similarly, under _ 3729(a)(3) respondents were required to show that petitioners agreed to make use of the false statement to achieve this end.

An order disbarring an attorney under former Rule 2, paragraph 5, of the Rules of the Supreme Court of the United States, under which disbarment in a state was ground for disbarment from practice in the Supreme Court unless the attorney showed good cause to the contrary, will be set aside upon rehearing, where, after the entry of the order of disbarment, the Supreme Court has adopted new Rules, which, in Rule 8, adds the provision that "no order of disbarment will be entered except with the concurrence of a majority of the justices participating," and a majority of the justices participating on rehearing find no ground for disbarment.

After earlier proceedings in a private antitrust action, wherein the United States Supreme Court entered a mandate directing entry of judgment for the plaintiff (395 US 642, 23 L Ed 2d 599, 89 S Ct 1871), the plaintiff filed an application in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon for allowance of attorneys' fees for services performed during the appellate stages of the litigation, both in the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and in the Supreme Court. The District Court denied the application, ruling that the allowance of such attorneys' fees was not authorized under 4 of the Clayton Act, which provides for recovery of treble damages "and the cost of suit, including a reasonable attorney's fee." The Court of Appeals on the plaintiff's appeal and on his simultaneously filed applications for such attorneys' fees, concluded that the Supreme Court's mandate, by not mentioning attorneys' fees, precluded an award of such fees.

After an individual was killed while doing sandblasting work on a vessel berthed in the navigable waters of the United States, the individual's mother filed an action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia against the shipbuilding corporation for which the individual's employer had been a subcontractor. This action invoked federal admiralty jurisdiction and alleged that (1) the individual's fatal injuries had been caused by the corporation's negligence, and (2) the mother was entitled to damages under general maritime law. However, the District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, as the court expressed the view that general maritime law provided no cause of action for death of a nonseaman in state territorial waters resulting from negligence (1998 US Dist LEXIS 20374). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, in reversing and in ordering a remand, expressed the view that while the United States Supreme Court had not yet recognized a maritime cause of action for wrongful death resulting from negligence, such an action was appropriate (210 F3d 209). The Court of Appeals subsequently denied a suggestion for rehearing en banc (215 F3d 420).

A newspaper filed a request under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (5 USCS 552) for certain documents from the United States Department of State. The request was for documents indicating whether two Iranian nationals living in Iran held valid U.S. passports, or for any other records indicating whether either individual was an American citizen. The State Department denied the newspaper's request stating that the release of the requested information would be a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy, and was therefore exempt from disclosure under Exemption 6 of the FOIA (5 USCS 552(b)(6)), which exempts from disclosure "personnel and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy." The newspaper brought an action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia to enjoin the Department from withholding the requested documents. The District Court granted the newspaper's motion for summary judgment. The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit affirmed, holding that the citizenship status of the Iranian nationals was less intimate than information normally contained in personnel and medical files, and accordingly was not contained in "similar files" for purposes of Exemption 6. In view of this finding, the Court of Appeals ruled that there was no need to consider whether disclosure of the information would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy. (647 F2d 197).

Nonunion employees of a railroad brought a suit in a Nebraska state court against the railroad and labor organizations representing various groups of employees of the railroad to enjoin the enforcement of a union shop agreement entered into between the railroad and the labor organizations. Under the terms of the union shop agreement all employees of the railroad, as a condition of their continued employment, must become members of the specified union within sixty days and thereafter maintain that membership. The Nebraska trial court issued an injunction and the Supreme Court of Nebraska affirmed, holding that the union shop agreement violated the First Amendment, in that it deprived employees of their freedom of association, and violated the Fifth Amendment, in that it required the members to pay for many things besides the cost of collective bargaining, and that, therefore, there was no valid federal law to supersede the "right to work" provision of the Nebraska Constitution, which outlawed union shop agreements. The federal law referred to is 2 Eleventh of the Railway Labor Act as amended (64 Stat 1238), which provides that notwithstanding the law of "any state," a carrier and a labor organization may make an agreement requiring all employees within a stated time to become members of the labor organization, provided there is no discrimination against any employee and provided further that membership is not denied nor terminated "for any reason other than the failure of the employee to tender the periodic dues, initiation fees, and assessments (not including fines and penalties) uniformly required as a condition of acquiring or retaining membership."

In an action in a California state court where certain employers sought injunctive relief against a union's strike activities allegedly in violation of collective bargaining agreements, the state court issued a temporary restraining order which, under California law, would expire after 15 days. Two days after the issuance of the restraining order, the union and the individual defendants removed the case to the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, and filed a motion to dissolve the restraining order. About two weeks later, the District Court, after a hearing, denied the motion to dissolve, and when the union resumed its strike activities some six months later, the District Court held the union in criminal contempt on the grounds that (1) the court's denial of the motion to dissolve the temporary restraining order gave the order continuing force and effect, and (2) 28 USCS 1450--which provides that upon removal of a state court action to a Federal District Court, all injunctions, orders, and other proceedings had in such action prior to removal shall remain in full force and effect until dissolved or modified by the District Court--served to continue the restraining order in effect until affirmatively dissolved or modified by the court. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that under either state law or Rule 65(b) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, the temporary restraining order against the union had expired long before the date of the alleged contempt, and 1450 did not operate to indefinitely prolong the restraining order (472 F2d 764).

Having rejected a claim under the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act on the ground that the claimant's disability was not related to the conditions of his employment, a deputy commissioner subsequently awarded compensation to the claimant on his conclusion that the employment conditions had in fact materially aggravated and hastened the disabling condition. The United States District Court for the Middle District of Florida upheld the award, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed on the ground that the deputy commissioner had no authority to change his mind in the absence of changed conditions or new evidence clearly demonstrating mistake in the initial determination (442 F2d 508).

The United States initiated condemnation proceedings in a federal District Court to acquire approximately 50 acres of land owned by a city, that had been used as a sanitary landfill. The city claimed that it was entitled to recover all of the costs incurred in acquiring a substitute site and developing it as a landfill, but the District Court found no basis for departing from the normal market value standard for determining just compensation and accordingly entered judgment based on the jury's finding of fair market value of the condemned property (529 F Supp 220). The Court of Appeals reversed and remanded (706 F2d 1356).

The United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri, sitting as a three-judge court, held that a 1967 Missouri reapportionment statute creating congressional districts varying in population from about 420,000 to about 445,000 did not meet the federal constitutional requirement that, as nearly as practicable, one man's vote in a congressional election should be worth as much as another's (279 F Supp 952).

A steel tubing company brought an antitrust suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois against a competing corporation, that corporation's wholly owned subsidiary, and a supplier of tubing mills. The jury found that the parent corporation and its wholly owned subsidiary had conspired to violate 1 of the Sherman Act (15 USCS 1), but that the supplier was not part of the conspiracy. The jury also found that the parent company, but not the subsidiary, had interfered with the tubing company's contractual relationship with the supplier, that the subsidiary, but not the parent, had interfered with the tubing company's contractual relationship with a potential customer and had slandered the tubing company, and that the supplier had breached its contract to supply a tubing mill. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit

The National Labor Relations Board found that the respondent employer had violated 8(a)(5) of the National Labor Relations Act by refusing to bargain collectively with the representative of its maintenance employees as regards the replacement of these employees by those of an independent contractor doing the same work. The Board ordered the employer to resume its maintenance operations, reinstate the employees with back pay, and bargain with the union. On appeal, the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit granted the Board's petition for enforcement. (116 App DC 198, 322 F2d 411.)

A judgment of the Circuit Court of the City of St. Louis enjoined a labor union from continuing a strike against a public utility seized by the governor of the state under a statute authorizing him to seize a public utility affected by a work stoppage. Although noting that the injunction had expired by its own terms, the Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed, holding valid the statutes authorizing seizure by the governor, making a strike after seizure unlawful, and giving the state courts power to enforce the provisions of the statute by injunction. (317 SW2d 309.)

The Secretary of Labor cited a railway company for a violation of the Occupational Safety and Health Act (29 USCS 651 et seq.), and the railway company contested the citation. The Secretary then filed a complaint, and the railway company filed an answer. A union representing the employees of the railway company properly moved to intervene in the proceedings. At the hearing, the Secretary moved to vacate the citation on the ground that he did not have jurisdiction over the relevant safety conditions and that the Federal Railway Administration had the proper jurisdiction. The Administrative Law Judge granted the Secretary's motion and vacated the citation despite the union's objection. Subsequently, the Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission directed review of the Administrative Law Judge's order. The Secretary objected to this action, alleging that part of the citation involved matters beyond the reach of the Act and that additional portions of the citation did not warrant litigation because of the state of the evidence. Some 6 years later, the Commission rejected the Secretary's contention and remanded the case to the Administrative Law Judge for consideration of the objections raised by the union. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed the Commission's holding that it could review the Secretary's decision to withdraw a citation.

When a Pennsylvania local police officer observed a motorist driving erratically and ignoring a red light, the officer stopped the motorist's vehicle. After smelling alcohol and observing the motorist's stumbling movements, the officer administered field sobriety tests, including asking the motorist to recite the alphabet, and inquired about alcohol. The motorist failed the sobriety tests, whereupon the officer arrested the motorist, placed the motorist in a police car, and gave the motorist Miranda warnings. Later, at a Pennsylvania trial in which the motorist's statements and conduct prior to arrest were admitted into evidence, the motorist was convicted of driving under the influence of alcohol. On appeal, the Superior Court of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia Office, reversed, on the ground that certain of the motorist's statements prior to arrest had been elicited through custodial interrogation and should have been suppressed for lack of Miranda warnings (365 Pa Super 106, 528 A2d 1385). The Pennsylvania Supreme Court denied the state's appeal application (542 A2d 1365).

A defendant, when he was 19 years old, pleaded guilty to the charge of carrying a pistol without a license in violation of a provision of the District of Columbia Code. He was placed on probation for 2 years under the Federal Youth Corrections Act of 1950 (18 USCS 5005 et seq.). At the end of the 2-year probationary period, he was unconditionally discharged from the Youth Corrections Act program. 9 years after that conviction, the defendant again was tried and convicted of carrying a pistol without a license under the same provision of the District of Columbia Code, and the defendant was sentenced as a felon, rather than as a misdemeanant, under a recidivist provision of the District of Columbia Code. The defendant contended that the earlier conviction could not properly provide the basis for his being sentenced as a recidivist because that conviction had been expunged under the Youth Corrections Act following his successful completion of the 2-year probationary term. The District of Columbia Court of Appeals rejected this assertion and affirmed the sentence (440 A2d 1008).

A license granted for the exhibition of a motion picture was rescinded by the appropriate New York authorities on the ground that the picture was "sacrilegious" within the meaning of a statute requiring the denial of a license if a film was "sacrilegious." Against various constitutional objections the statute was upheld by the state courts. The Supreme Court unanimously reversed.

In 2017, Abdulkadir Masharipov carried out a terrorist attack on the Reina nightclub in Istanbul, Turkey, on behalf of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization. Masharipov killed Nawras Alassaf and 38 others. Alassaf‚Äôs family then brought this suit under 18 U. S. C. ¬ß2333, an Antiterrorism Act (ATA) provision that permits U. S. nationals who have been ‚Äúinjured . . . by reason of an act of international terrorism‚Äù to file a civil suit for damages. Instead of suing ISIS directly under ¬ß2333(a), the plaintiffs (respondents here) invoked ¬ß2333(d)(2) to sue three of the largest social-media companies in the world‚ÄîFacebook, Twitter (petitioner here), and Google (which owns YouTube)‚Äîfor aiding and abetting ISIS. The parties today agree on the basic aspects of these platforms: Billions of people from around the world have signed up for them and upload massive amounts of content each day. Defendants profit from that content by placing advertisements on or near it and use ‚Äúrecommendation‚Äù algorithms that match content, advertisements, and users based on information about the use, advertisement, and content being viewed. As the parties represent things, the algorithms here match any content with any user who is more likely to view that content, and the platforms perform little to no front-end screening on any content before it is uploaded. Plaintiffs, however, allege that for several years the companies have knowingly allowed ISIS and its supporters to use their platforms and ‚Äúrecommendation‚Äù algorithms as tools for recruiting, fundraising, and spreading propaganda; plaintiffs further allege that these companies have, in the process, profited from the advertisements placed on ISIS‚Äô tweets, posts, and videos. The District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, but the Ninth Circuit reversed.

It is provided in 28 USCS 1500 that the United States Court of Federal Claims (known until 1992 as the United States Claims Court, which in turn succeeded in 1982 to the trial functions of the former Court of Claims) "shall not have jurisdiction of any claim for or in respect to which the plaintiff or his assignee has pending in any other court any suit or process against the United States or any person who, at the time when the cause of action alleged in such suit or process arose, was, in respect thereto, acting or professing to act, directly or indirectly under the authority of the United States." A corporation was sued by thousands of plaintiffs alleging injury from exposure to asbestos fibers and dust released from products made by either the corporation or a company that the corporation had acquired. In 1979, the corporation filed a complaint against the United States in what was then the Court of Claims and sought recovery on a theory of alleged breach of implied warranties in contracts between the corporation and the United States, with respect to (1) the corporation's alleged conformance to government specifications in the inclusion of asbestos in products which the corporation had supplied to government shipyards; and (2) the government's alleged sale of some of the asbestos fiber used in the corporation's products. At the time that the complaint was filed, the corporation had pending, in the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania, a third-party complaint against the United States (1) seeking indemnification or contribution for any damages that the corporation might have to pay to the estate of a particular individual; and (2) alleging that any asbestos products to which the individual had been exposed had been supplied to the government in accordance with specifications in government contracts. The District Court, however, granted the corporation's voluntary motion to dismiss the third-party complaint in 1980. In 1981, the corporation (1) filed a second complaint against the United States in what was then the Court of Claims; (2) sought payment for amounts that the United States had allegedly recouped, under a federal employees' compensation statute, from asbestos claimants who had been paid by the corporation; and (3) asserted that the recoupments were takings of the corporation's property without due process and just compensation, contrary to the Federal Constitution's Fifth Amendment. At the time that the 1981 complaint was filed, the corporation had pending in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York an action against the United States, which action included a takings claim for the government's allegedly improper recoupment, under the same federal statute, of money paid by the corporation for claimants covered by the statute. The New York action was dismissed 5 days later, however, and the corporation's unsuccessful attempts at appealing the dismissal ended in 1983. In 1989, what was by then the Claims Court dismissed the corporation's 1979 and 1981 complaints pursuant to 1500, on the ground that when the corporation had filed the complaints, the corporation had had the same claims pending in other courts (17 Cl Ct 146). On appeal, a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit initially reversed, on the ground that 1500 was inapplicable, because no other claim had been pending elsewhere when the Claims Court had entertained and acted upon the government's motion to dismiss (911 F2d 654). On rehearing en banc, however, the Court of Appeals--having previously vacated the panel opinion--affirmed the dismissals (962 F2d 1013).

Partners operating eight finance offices in Alabama, and using the reserve method of accounting permitted by 166(c) of the 1954 Internal Revenue Code, formed eight new corporations and transferred the assets of the eight partnership offices, including the accounts receivable, to the corporations, in exchange for shares of the corporations. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue determined that the partnership should have included in income the amount of the bad debt reserve applicable to the accounts receivable that had been transferred. Tax deficiencies were computed, and the partners, having paid them, brought suit for refunds in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama. The District Court allowed recovery, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed (414 F2d 627).

After a prime contractor refused to pay a subcontractor the money which the subcontractor claimed was due for a painting job, the controversy was submitted to arbitration. The subcontractor and the prime contractor each appointed an arbitrator, and these two arbitrators selected a third arbitrator, who was supposedly neutral. After the arbitration award was made, the subcontractor discovered that the prime contractor had been a regular customer of the third arbitrator and had paid him several thousand dollars in fees for services as an engineering consultant, including services on the projects involved in the arbitration. Suing the sureties on the prime contractor's bond, the subcontractor challenged the arbitration award, but the United States District Court for the District of Puerto Rico, finding that the arbitration proceedings were fair and impartial, refused to set aside the award, and the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit affirmed. (382 F2d 1010.)

The defendants, in close association, engaged in a fraudulent scheme to obtain money from a woman, whom one of the defendants married, and left after the purpose of the scheme was accomplished. While the marriage lasted, the husband obtained from the victim a check drawn by her on a Los Angeles bank and indorsed it for collection to a Texas bank. After a trial, at which the victim, who in the meantime had obtained a divorce, testified, both defendants were convicted of the substantive offense of violating, the husband as a principal and the other defendant as an abettor, the mail fraud statute and the National Stolen Property Act, and of a conspiracy to commit these offenses.

This is a companion case to Kinsella v Singleton, supra, p. 268, and McElroy v United States ex rel. Guagliardo, infra, p. 282. Petitioner, a civilian employee of the United States Army attached to an army installation in France, was tried by a general court-martial for the capital offense of premeditated murder, and was convicted of unpremeditated murder, a noncapital offense. While serving his sentence at a federal prison, he filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania, claiming that Article 2(11) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, subjecting to court-martial jurisdiction persons employed by the Armed Forces, was unconstitutional as applied to him because depriving him of a civil trial affording all of the protections of Article 3 and the Fifth and Sixth Amendments of the Federal Constitution. The writ was dismissed (161 F Supp 112), and the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed. (261 F2d 204.)

The principal question in the instant case was whether an employer commits an unfair labor practice under 8(a) of the amended National Labor Relations Act by extending a 20-year seniority credit to strike replacements and strikers who returned to work. Finding the employer's practices illegal, the National Labor Relations Board directed the employer to cease and desist from these practices and to take affirmative action in regard to reinstatement and backpay of employees. The Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit denied the Board's petition for enforcement and remanded the case for further findings. (303 F2d 359.)

After the issuance of an unfair labor practice complaint charging an employer with refusal to bargain collectively with its employees' certified bargaining agent, the District Court for the Southern District of New York granted the National Labor Relations Board a temporary injunction, the effect of which was to require the employer to bargain with the agent pending the Board's resolution of the unfair labor practice charge. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, applying a different standard from those used by the District Court in determining whether the Board was entitled to injunctive relief, reversed and set aside the temporary injunction. (366 F2d 847.) Pending certiorari, Mr. Justice Harlan granted the Board's application for a stay of the Court of Appeals' mandate. (17 L ed 2d 45, 87 S Ct 5.)

The plaintiff, a former fireman on defendant's steam locomotives, filed suit in a state court to recover under the Federal Employers' Liability Act for injuries, alleging that after thirty years of service he had been forced to cease work by silicosis caused by continuous inhalation of silica dust which arose from sand materials emitted in excessive amounts by the locomotives' faultily adjusted sanding apparatus.

An employee filed an action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida under 42 USCS 1983 alleging that her employer, a Florida university, had denied her employment opportunities solely on the basis of her race and sex. The District Court granted the defendant Florida Board of Regents' motion to dismiss because the employee had not exhausted available administrative remedies. On appeal, a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed, and remanded the case for further proceedings (612 F2d 946). The full Court of Appeals then granted the Board's petition for rehearing and, vacating the panel decision, held that a 1983 plaintiff could be required to exhaust administrative remedies if certain minimum conditions were met, and remanded the case to the District Court to determine whether exhaustion would be appropriate in the instant case (634 F2d 900).

An animal-rights protester, who had attempted to approach the Vice President of the United States and to unfurl a banner when the Vice President spoke at a military base, was (1) seized by two military police officers as the protester approached a fence separating the public from the speaking platform, and (2) allegedly shoved or thrown into a military van. The protester filed an action against defendants including one of the officers in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California and claimed in part that the defendant officer had violated the protester's rights under the Federal Constitution's Fourth Amendment by using excessive force to arrest him. The District Court, while granting defense motions for summary judgment with respect to all other claims on the basis of qualified immunity, ruled that the defendant officer was not entitled to summary judgment on the claim of excessive force. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, in affirming, observed that (1) its two-part analysis for qualified immunity questions first required a determination as to whether the law governing the officer's conduct was clearly established, with a lack of such clarity automatically entitling the officer to immunity; (2) since the law regarding excessive force was clearly established, analysis proceeded to the question whether a reasonable officer could have believed that the officer's conduct was lawful; (3) this inquiry and the merits of the Fourth Amendment claim were identical, since both concerned the objective reasonableness of the officer's conduct in light of the circumstances the officer faced at the scene; and (4) this issue was properly left to the jury (194 F3d 962).

Petitioners are primarily nonprofit organizations that provide health insurance to their employees. Federal regulations require petitioners to cover certain contraceptives as part of their health plans, unless petitioners submit a form either to their insurer or to the Federal Government, stating that they object on religious grounds to providing contraceptive coverage. Petitioners allege that submitting this notice substantially burdens the exercise of their religion, in violation of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, 107 Stat. 1488, 42 U. S. C. ¬ß2000bb et seq. Following oral argument, the Court requested supplemental briefing from the parties addressing "whether contraceptive coverage could be provided to petitioners' employees, through petitioners' insurance companies, without any such notice from petitioners." Post, p. Both petitioners and the Government now confirm that such an option is feasible. Petitioners have clarified that their religious exercise is not infringed where they "need to do nothing more than contract for a plan that does not include coverage for some or all forms of contraception," even if their employees receive cost-free contraceptive coverage from the same insurance company. Supplemental Brief for Petitioners 4. The Government has confirmed that the challenged procedures "for employers with insured plans could be modified to operate in the manner posited in the Court's order while still ensuring that the affected women receive contraceptive coverage seamlessly, together with the rest of their health coverage."

A lessee of coal mining rights in Federal lands sought to prevent the Secretary of Interior from leasing similar rights in other near-by Federal lands to a competing company, which, after applying for such a lease, had established mines on partially exhausted state-owned lands and desired the Federal lands to prolong its business. The lessee alleged that the proposed lease was in violation of a regulation of the Secretary which instructed the General Land Office to make favorable recommendation on new leases only in cases where there has been furnished a satisfactory showing that an additional coal mine is needed and that there is an actual need for coal which cannot otherwise be reasonably met. The Secretary, however, took the view that the regulation prevented a lease only to a newcomer, but not to an existing mine for the purpose of enabling it to continue an established business.

A state prisoner sentenced as a recidivist in Virginia filed a petition for habeas corpus in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, naming the superintendent of the Virginia State Penitentiary as the only respondent, and alleging that his third-offender sentence was based in part upon a larceny conviction which was invalid because his federal constitutional right to counsel had been denied him at the trial on the larceny charge. The District Court dismissed the petition, but the Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit granted a certificate of probable cause and leave to appeal in forma pauperis. Shortly before the appeal was argued, the prisoner was paroled by the Virginia Parole Board under a parole order which placed him in the custody and control of the parole board, and directed him to live with his aunt and uncle in Georgia, required him to obtain his parole officer's permission to leave the community, change his residence, or own or operate a motor vehicle, and required him to make monthly reports to his parole officer, to permit the officer to visit his home or place of employment at any time, and to follow the officer's instructions and advice. When he was placed on parole, the prisoner moved to add the members of the Virginia Parole Board as respondents. The Court of Appeals refused to permit the parole board members to be added as respondents, on the ground that they did not have physical custody of the prisoner's person and therefore were not proper parties, and dismissed the petition for habeas corpus, holding that the case was moot as to the prison superintendent because he no longer had custody or control of the prisoner. (294 F2d 608.)

Petitioner Gerald Groff is an Evangelical Christian who believes for religious reasons that Sunday should be devoted to worship and rest. In 2012, Groff took a mail delivery job with the United States Postal Service. Groff‚Äôs position generally did not involve Sunday work, but that changed after USPS agreed to begin facilitating Sunday deliveries for Amazon. To avoid the requirement to work Sundays on a rotating basis, Groff transferred to a rural USPS station that did not make Sunday deliveries. After Amazon deliveries began at that station as well, Groff remained unwilling to work Sundays, and USPS redistributed Groff‚Äôs Sunday deliveries to other USPS staff. Groff received ‚Äúprogressive discipline‚Äù for failing to work on Sundays, and he eventually resigned. Groff sued under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, asserting that USPS could have accommodated his Sunday Sabbath practice ‚Äúwithout undue hardship on the conduct of [USPS‚Äôs] business.‚Äù 42 U. S. C. ¬ß2000e(j). The District Court granted summary judgment to USPS. The Third Circuit affirmed based on this Court‚Äôs decision in Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison, 432 U. S. 63, which it construed to mean ‚Äúthat requiring an employer ‚Äòto bear more than a de minimis cost‚Äô to provide a religious accommodation is an undue hardship.‚Äù 35 F. 4th 162, 174, n. 18 (quoting 432 U. S., at 84). The Third Circuit found the de minimis cost standard met here, concluding that exempting Groff from Sunday work had ‚Äúimposed on his coworkers, disrupted the workplace and workflow, and diminished employee morale.‚Äù 35 F. 4th, at 175.

When a company asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to renew the required federal licenses for five of the hydroelectric dams--which impounded river water, ran it through turbines, and returned the water to the riverbed after passing it around part of the river--that the company operated on a Maine river to generate power for the company's paper mill, the company (1) applied for certifications under _ 401 from Maine's department of environmental protection, but (2) filed the application under protest on the basis of the company's assertion that the dams did not cause any "discharge" into the river.

The Federal Trade Commission enjoined a large manufacturer of shoes from entering into franchise contracts with retail shoestore operators which obligated the manufacturer to give to the dealer, but not to the manufacturer's other customers, valuable services, and in return required the dealers not to purchase conflicting lines of shoes from the manufacturer's competitors. On review, the Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit set aside the Commission's order on the ground that the manufacturer's practice was not an unfair method of competition in violation of 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act. (339 F2d 45.)

Ellis Island lies in New York Harbor about 1,300 feet from the New Jersey shore. There was a longstanding dispute between the states of New Jersey and New York concerning their boundary in the harbor area. Eventually, the two states entered into a boundary compact that was consented to by Congress in 1834 (4 Stat 708), pursuant to the Federal Constitution's compact clause (Art I, 10, cl 3). At that time, Ellis Island comprised about 3 acres. The compact included provisions that (1) in Article First, established a general boundary line--as to which Ellis Island was later held to be on the New Jersey side--that applied except as otherwise mentioned in the compact; and (2) in Article Second, provided that New York would retain its "present jurisdiction" over Ellis Island. Meanwhile, New York had (1) in 1800, ceded, with a reservation for the service of judicial process, "jurisdiction" over Ellis Island to the United States; and (2) in 1808, granted all of the state's property interest in the island to the United States. The Federal Government used Ellis Island for military purposes until the 1890's, when the location became a major immigration station. From about 1890 to 1934, the Federal Government, in connection with these immigration operations, enlarged the surface area by adding about 24.5 acres of filled land on the submerged lands around Ellis Island. Also, in 1904, New Jersey conveyed to the United States all of the state's property interest in about 48 acres that surrounded Ellis Island. The immigration station was closed in 1954, but the Federal Government retained control of the location and eventually developed it as a national historic site. However, for such purposes as taxation, zoning, environmental protection, and elections, both New Jersey and New York asserted rival claims of sovereign authority over the filled land which the Federal Government had added. In 1993, New Jersey (1) invoked the United States Supreme Court's original jurisdiction under Art III, 2, cl 2 of the Constitution; and (2) sought leave to file a bill of complaint against New York concerning these rival claims to the filled land. The Supreme Court (1) granted New Jersey's petition (511 US 1080, 128 L Ed 2d 458, 114 S Ct 1828), and (2) appointed a special master (513 US 924, 130 L Ed 2d 273, 115 S Ct 309). In 1997, the special master submitted to the Supreme Court a final report and a supplement (520 US ____, 138 L Ed 2d 209, 117 S Ct 2451). The special master (1) concluded that the filled land was subject to the sovereign authority of New Jersey; (2) rejected New York's claims that (a) the state had obtained sovereign authority over the filled land by prescription and acquiescence, and (b) laches barred New Jersey's complaint; (3) determined that the original 1834 area of Ellis Island followed the mean low-water mark; (4) recommended that the area covered by a particular pier which had existed in 1834 be treated as part of the original island; and (5) further recommended that the Supreme Court, in the interest of practicality, convenience, and fairness, adjust the boundary line between the two states so as to place all of the main immigration building and the land immediately surrounding it within New York.

The District Court for the District Columbia dismissed "with prejudice" an indictment charging the defendant with various crimes under the District of Columbia Code, on finding that the government had not acted promptly enough in bringing the case to trial. The United States appealed pursuant to the District of Columbia Code 23-105, to the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which, without making any determination of its jurisdiction under 23-105, certified the case to the United States Supreme Court pursuant to the Federal Criminal Appeals Act (18 USC 3731).

An Alaskan borough brought suit against the Secretary of Interior in the United States District Court for the District of Alaska, seeking a declaration that 401(a) of the Wildlife Refuge Revenue Sharing Act (16 USCS 715s(a))--which was amended in 1964 to add the word "minerals" to the list of refuge sources, the revenues from which were to be distributed according to a formula provided in 401(c) of the Act (16 USCS 715s(c)) whereby 25 percent of the revenues are to be paid to the counties in which a wildlife refuge lies and the remaining funds are used by the Department of Interior for public purposes--governed the distribution of oil and gas revenues from a national wildlife refuge lying within the borough (a "county" for purposes of 401(c)). The state of Alaska subsequently filed suit in the District Court against the Secretary and various federal officials, seeking a declaration that 35 of the Mineral Leasing Act of 1920 (30 USCS 191)--which provides a formula for distributing revenues from oil and gas leases on public land in Alaska whereby 90 percent of the revenues are paid to the state and 10 percent to the United States Treasury--governed the distribution of the oil and gas revenues from the refuge. The District Court consolidated the suits and granted summary judgment for the state of Alaska, holding that the term "minerals" in the Wildlife Refuge Revenue Sharing Act referred only to oil and gas found on land acquired for wildlife refuges and that distribution of oil and gas revenues from leases on public land reserved for wildlife refuges continues to be governed by 35 of the Mineral Leasing Act (436 F Supp 288). The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed, finding that the legislative history of the 1964 amendment was largely ambiguous and that the addition of the word "minerals" could not be deemed to have repealed the Mineral Leasing Act by implication without a clear showing that this was the intent of Congress (612 F2d 1210).

Shortly after his arrest in connection with a robbery, the 18-year-old accused was taken to an interrogation room for questioning by two police detectives. When the detectives informed him that he had a right to his counsel's presence at the interrogation, the accused responded "Uh, yeah. I'd like to do that." Despite this response, the detectives continued with their questioning, and when they subsequently asked the accused whether he wished to talk to them without a lawyer being present, the accused responded "Yeah and no, uh, I don't know what's what, really," and "All right. I'll talk to you then." The accused then told the detectives that he knew in advance about the planned robbery but claimed that he was not a participant. After considerable probing by the detectives, the accused confessed that "I committed it," but he then returned to his earlier story that he only knew about the planned crime. Upon further questioning, the accused again insisted for a lawyer saying "I wanta get a lawyer," and this time the detectives honored the request and terminated the interrogation. At his trial for armed robbery in an Illinois Circuit Court, the accused moved to suppress his incriminating statements, but the trial judge denied the motion, and the accused was subsequently convicted. In affirming the accused's conviction, the Illinois Appellate Court acknowledged that the accused's first request for counsel when he said "Uh, yeah. I'd like to do that" appears clear and unequivocal, but it concluded that when the request is considered with other statements, the accused was undecided about exercising his right to counsel and never made an effective request for counsel (113 Ill App 3d 305, 69 Ill Dec 339, 447 NE2d 556). The Supreme Court of Illinois affirmed, holding that the accused's responses to continued police questioning rendered his initial request for counsel ambiguous and that the officers therefore were not required to terminate their questioning (102 Ill 2d 365, 80 Ill Dec 784, 466 NE2d 236).

The decedent transferred certain property to a trust, giving his wife a life interest in the property and a special power of appointment. A few days later, the wife transferred different property to a similar trust. The plan to create the two trusts was devised by the decedent, and he selected the property to be included in each trust. After the death of the decedent, who had been predeceased by his wife, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue determined that the two trusts were reciprocal and that the amount of the wife's trust was includible in the decedent's gross estate for federal estate tax purposes under 811(c)(1)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939, which provided that certain transferred property in which a decedent retained a life interest was to be included in his gross estate. After paying a deficiency, the decedent's estate sought a refund in the Court of Claims, which granted the refund, holding that the amount of the wife's trust was not includible in the decedent's gross estate, since the two trusts were not created either in consideration of one another or with the motive of avoiding estate taxes (183 Ct Cl 745, 393 F2d 939).

A state prisoner's petition for habeas corpus alleging that his federal constitutional rights were violated by denying him assistance of counsel at his trial on a charge of burglary was dismissed by a Nebraska state court. The Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed on the ground that habeas corpus was not available to determine claims of this kind. (177 Neb 404, 129 NW2d 107.)

Prior to the defendant's jury trial in a Wisconsin state court for the misdemeanor of resisting arrest, the defendant filed a motion requesting that venue be changed to a different county because the local news media's massive coverage of the defendant's activities had resulted in community prejudice against the defendant. The motion was denied by the trial judge on the ground that a Wisconsin statute, which expressly authorized a change of venue in a felony case, did not permit a change of venue in a misdemeanor case. Affirming the defendant's conviction, the Wisconsin Supreme Court held not only that the trial judge had correctly construed Wisconsin law as precluding the possibility of a change of venue in misdemeanor cases, but also that Wisconsin law, as so construed, was constitutionally valid (41 Wis 2d 312, 164 NW2d 266, 34 ALR3d 787).

Defendant was convicted, in a Florida state court, of violating a Florida vagrancy statute which made it a misdemeanor to be found "wandering or strolling around from place to place without any lawful purpose or object." The Supreme Court of Florida affirmed the conviction. The evidence merely showed that defendant, at the time of his arrest, was sitting on a bench, using it for that purpose in the precise place where the bench had been placed. (202 So 2d 852.)

The City of San Antonio‚Äîacting on behalf of a class of 173 Texas municipalities‚Äîwas awarded a multi-million dollar judgment in Federal District Court against a number of popular online travel companies (OTCs) over the calculation of hotel occupancy taxes. To prevent execution on that judgment pending appeal, the OTCs obtained supersedeas bonds securing the judgment. See Fed. Rule Civ. Proc. 62. On appeal, the Court of Appeals determined that the OTCs had not underpaid on their taxes. In accordance with Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 39(d), the OTCs filed with the circuit clerk a bill of costs seeking appellate docketing fees and printing costs, which were taxed without objection. The OTCs then filed a bill of costs in the District Court seeking more than $2.3 million in costs‚Äîprimarily for premiums paid on the supersedeas bonds that are listed in Rule 39(e) as ‚Äútaxable in the district court for the benefit of the party entitled to costs.‚Äù San Antonio objected and urged the District Court to exercise its discretion to decline to tax all or most of those costs. The District Court held that it had no discretion to deny or reduce those costs under Circuit precedent. The Court of Appeals affirmed, reasoning that the District Court lacked discretion to deny or reduce appellate cost awards.

Two individuals working in a movie theater and a third person working in a bookstore which shared common ownership with the theater were convicted in the State Court for Fulton County, Georgia, of distributing obscene material in violation of a Georgia statute. The trial court fined all three and sentenced them to jail terms, but placed them on immediate probation. After the convictions were affirmed on appeal, the court required the probationers, as a condition of their probation, to make monthly installment payments on their fines. After three months had elapsed and none of probationers had made any of the required payments, county probation officers moved for revocation of their probation. At the revocation hearing, the probationers admitted that they had failed to make the installment payments, but offered evidence of their inability to make these payments out of their own earnings and also stated that they had expected their employer to pay the fines for them. However, the court decided to revoke the probations unless the probationers made up their arrearages within five days. Unable to do so, the probationers moved for a modification of the conditions of their probations, but the motion was denied, and the court ordered the probationers to serve the remaining portions of their jail sentences. This revocation decision was upheld on appeal by the Georgia Court of Appeals against claims that it was unconstitutional under the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to imprison a probationer solely because of his inability to make installment payments on fines (150 Ga App 582, 258 SE2d 171).

In a government civil antitrust suit charging a violation of 7 of the Clayton Act by one natural gas company's acquisition of the stock and assets of another gas company, in that such acquisition substantially lessened competition in the sale of natural gas in California--a market of which the defendant was the sole out-of-state supplier at the time of the acquisition--the United States Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the United States District Court for the District of Utah dismissing the complaint, and directed the District Court to order divestiture without delay (376 US 651, 12 L Ed 2d 12, 84 S Ct 1044). On remand, the District Court denied intervention to the State of California, to a large industrial user of natural gas purchasing from the defendant's sources, and to a natural gas distributor whose sole supplier of natural gas had been the acquired company and would be the new company. The United States Attorney General then settled the case with the defendant, but on direct appeal by those who were denied intervention, the Supreme Court once again reversed and remanded with directions to allow each appellant intervention as a matter of right, to have a de novo hearing on the type of divestiture envisioned in the prior opinion, and to order a divestiture without delay (386 US 129, 17 L Ed 2d 814, 87 S Ct 932). On remand, the District Court chose as the best-qualified applicant to acquire the new company formed to compete with the defendant, the only gas pipeline operator among the various applicants, and, under a plan approved by the court, the defendant was to receive five million shares of the new company's nonvoting preferred stock, convertible into common stock at the end of 5 years, and the new company was to assume approximately 170 million dollars of the defendant's system-wide bond and debenture indebtedness, and the court awarded 21.8 percent of the new gas reserves in the San Juan Basin to the new company, and also gave the new company more than 50 percent of the net additions to the reserves developed since the illegal merger (291 F Supp 3).

A conviction of possessing and operating an illegal distillery was obtained in the United States District Court for Massachusetts after a still was found during a search under a warrant issued on the basis of a government investigator's detailed affidavit based on his own observations, information received by other government investigators, and reports made to the affiant describing the results of their observations and investigations. The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reversed on the ground that the affidavit was insufficient to establish probable cause because it failed to indicate which of the facts alleged were hearsay and which were within the affiant's own knowledge. (324 F2d 864.)

In a diversity action instituted in the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania, plaintiff sought recovery for the death of her decedent who was killed in an accident involving a truck which, together with its driver, defendant had leased; plaintiff's decedent had been hired by the truck driver to assist in the operation of the truck. The action was tried to the jury on the theory of the defendant's negligence, and judgment went for plaintiff. (161 F Supp 875.) The Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed, finding that under applicable state law the decedent was defendant's employee and that the state workmen's compensation act provided the exclusive remedy. (257 F2d 445.) The Court of Appeals viewed the decedent's employee status as established as a matter of law as a consequence of the jury's affirmative answer to a special interrogatory asking whether it found that an unforeseen contingency arose which made it reasonably necessary for the protection of the defendant's interest that the truck driver engage the decedent.

A 17-year old male pleaded guilty to second degree murder and was sentenced to a 10-year prison term in accordance with the Youth Corrections Act (18 USCS 5005 et seq.), under which he was to be segregated from adult prisoners and receive rehabilitative treatment. While in prison, the defendant was found guilty of assaulting a federal officer with a dangerous weapon, whereupon the defendant was given an additional sentence to run consecutively with his term under the Act. The sentencing judge further found that the defendant would "not benefit any further" under the Act and sentenced him as an adult. Subsequently, the defendant was convicted of a second assault charge and received another consecutive sentence. At this point, the Bureau of Prisons classified the defendant as an adult offender and, although his Youth Corrections Act sentence had not expired, placed the defendant with the adult prison population. The defendant then filed a petition for a writ of a habeas corpus on the grounds that the Bureau had no authority to treat him as an adult offender during the remainder of his Youth Corrections Act sentence, and the writ was granted by the United States District Court for the Southern District of Illinois. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed, holding that the Act forbids the reevaluation of a sentence under the Act by a second judge, even if the second judge makes an explicit finding that further treatment under the Act would not benefit the offender (642 F2d 1077).

"I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will uphold and defend the Constitution ‚àö¬∂[**1100]‚àö¬∂ of the United States of America and the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and that I will oppose the overthrow of the government of the United States of America or of this Commonwealth by force, violence or by any illegal or unconstitutional method." Mrs. Richardson sought declaratory and injunctive relief against enforcement of the oath as a bar to her resuming employment with Boston State Hospital, and also sought damages for pay withheld by reason of her having refused to subscribe to the oath.

An action under the Jones Act was instituted in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Alabama to recover for injuries sustained by a Greek seaman while aboard a Greek-flag ship in the Port of New Orleans. The ship, which with sister ships was regularly engaged in runs between United States ports and foreign countries, was managed by a Greek corporation; however, more than 95 percent of the stock of such corporation was owned by a Greek citizen who was a lawful permanent resident alien, and who managed the corporation out of New York. The seaman's contract of employment had been entered into in Greece, and provided for adjudication by a Greek court of all claims arising thereunder. The District Court sitting without a jury rendered judgment for the seaman (273 F Supp 248), and the Court of Appeals affirmed (412 F2d 919).

The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 (43 USCS 315 et seq.) granted the United States Secretary of the Interior authority to (1) divide the federal public rangelands into grazing districts, (2) specify the amount of grazing permitted in each district, (3) issue leases or permits to graze livestock, and (4) charge reasonable fees for use of the land. In 43 USCS 315b, the Act (1) gave preference, in respect to permits, to (a) landowners engaged in the livestock business, (b) bona fide occupants or settlers, or (c) owners of water or water rights; and (2) provided that (a) grazing privileges would be adequately safeguarded, but (b) the creation of a grazing district or the issuance of a permit did not create any right, title, interest, or estate in or to the lands. A group of nonprofit ranching-related organizations with members who held grazing permits brought, against defendants including the Secretary, an action challenging 10 of the new federal grazing regulations issued by the Secretary in 1995. The United States District Court for the District of Wyoming found 4 of the 10 regulations unlawful (929 F Supp 1436). As to the four regulations, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, reversing in part, upheld three--(1) 43 CFR 4100.0-5, which changed the definition of "grazing preference;" (2) 43 CFR 4110.1(a), which permitted those who were not "engaged in the livestock business" to qualify for grazing permits; and (3) 43 CFR 4120.3-2(b), which granted the United States title to all future range improvements (167 F3d 1287).

An accused and his codefendant were tried by a jury in the United States District Court for the District of Arizona for narcotics and weapons offenses. As instructed by Rule 24(b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, the District Court allotted 10 peremptory challenges to the codefendants that could be used jointly in the selection of 12 jurors. When a prospective juror indicated on his questionnaire and in his discussion with the trial judge that he would favor the prosecution, the codefendants challenged the juror for cause, but the District Court declined to excuse the juror. After two unsuccessful objections to the for-cause ruling, the accused used a peremptory challenge to remove the juror. Subsequently, the codefendants exhausted all of their peremptory challenges. When jury selection was completed, the District Court read the names of the jurors to be seated and asked if the prosecutor or defense counsel had any objections to any of those jurors. Counsel for the accused responded: "None from us." At the conclusion of the trial, the accused was convicted on all counts. On appeal, the accused contended that (1) the District Court abused its discretion in refusing to strike the juror for cause, and (2) this error forced the accused to use a peremptory challenge on the juror. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit expressed the view that (1) the District Court's refusal to strike the juror for cause was an abuse of discretion; (2) the error did not violate the Federal Constitution's Sixth Amendment, because the juror was removed and the impartiality of the jury ultimately seated was not challenged; (3) the District Court's mistake resulted in a violation of the accused's due process rights under the Constitution's Fifth Amendment, since the District Court's error in denying the for-cause challenge forced the accused to use a peremptory challenge curatively, thereby impairing his right to the full complement of peremptory challenges to which he was entitled under federal law; and (4) such an error required automatic reversal (146 F3d 653, 1998 US App LEXIS 10899).

The Federal Government initiated an action to enjoin a distributor of generic drugs from distributing in interstate commerce a number of generic drug products that contain eight specified active ingredients. The term "generic drug" is used to describe a product that contains the same active ingredients but not necessarily the same excipients, such as coatings, binders, and capsules, as a so-called "pioneer drug" that is marketed under a brand name. In this case, the government alleged that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had never approved new drug applications with respect to any of these products. Section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USCS 355) requires FDA approval of any new drug introduced into interstate commerce. The United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida held that a generic drug product containing the same active ingredients as the previously approved pioneer drug is a "new drug" only if there is a reasonable possibility that the differences in excipients between the generic product and the pioneer will make the generic product less safe and effective, and the court found clear evidence in support of the general proposition that differences in excipients may affect the safety and effectiveness of drug products (498 F Supp 288). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit vacated the District Court's injunction and remanded with instructions to dismiss the complaint, holding that the statutory prohibition against the sale of a "new drug" without prior approval does not apply to a drug product having the same active ingredients as the previously approved drug product, regardless of any differences in excipients (654 F2d 1114).

The defendant was convicted in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas for violating 26 USC 5851 by knowingly possessing a sawed-off shotgun which had not been registered with the Secretary of the Treasury or his delegate, as required by 26 USC 5841. The District Court rejected the defendant's contention that 5851 violated his constitutional privilege against self-incrimination. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the defendant's conviction. (372 F2d 651.)

A California state prisoner, challenging a disciplinary action that had been imposed on him approximately 6 months previously, appealed the action pursuant to California's prisoner-grievance system. The prison's appeals coordinator rejected the grievance as time-barred under the applicable state regulations, because the grievance had not been filed within 15 working days of the action being challenged. The prisoner subsequently brought suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California under 42 U.S.C.S. _ 1983 against some California correctional officials. The District Court, in granting the officials' motion to dismiss, said that the prisoner had not fully exhausted his administrative remedies as required by a provision of the Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (PLRA) (42 U.S.C.S. _ 1997e(a)), which provides that no federal action may be brought by a prisoner with respect to prison conditions "until such administrative remedies as are available are exhausted."

The defendant was convicted of "assault with malice aforethought with intent to murder; repetition of offense," upon trial in the Eighth Judicial District Court, Hunt County, Texas, the indictment also having alleged, pursuant to the state recidivist statutes, a prior Texas conviction for burglary and three prior Tennessee convictions for forgery. The prosecution, in the jury's presence, offered in evidence two records of one of the Tennessee convictions, the first of such records showing that the defendant had not been represented by counsel in the Tennessee case, and the second record omitting any reference to absence of counsel but not showing a waiver of counsel. The trial court admitted the second record into evidence, but subsequently instructed the jury not to consider prior offenses for any purpose, apparently because the evidence failed to establish grounds for application of the recidivist statutes, and the punishment imposed by the jury was not enhanced under such statutes. The Court of Criminal Appeals of Texas affirmed the conviction. (397 SW2d 79.)

An indigent, married, pregnant woman, who desired but had been refused an abortion, 23 other individuals (nine physicians licensed in Georgia, seven nurses, five clergymen, and two social workers), and two nonprofit Georgia corporations that advocated abortion reform instituted an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia, seeking a declaratory judgment that the Georgia abortion statutes were unconstitutional and an injunction against the statutes' enforcement.A three-judge District Court was convened, which court held that all the plaintiffs had standing to sue, but that only the pregnant woman's case presented a justiciable controversy.While the District Court held invalid those portions of the statutes which limited legal abortions to specific situations requiring a showing that (1) a continuation of the pregnancy would endanger the life or seriously and permanently injure the health of the pregnant woman, or (2) the fetus would very likely be born with a grave, permanent, and irremediable mental or physical defect, or (3) the pregnancy resulted from forcible or statutory rape, as well as (4) certain other procedural or evidentiary aspects of the statute, and granted declaratory relief accordingly, it held that the state's interest in the protection of health and potential human existence justified state regulation of the abortion procedures.It therefore upheld the remainder of the statutes and denied injunctive relief (319 F Supp 1048).From this judgment, the plaintiffs took a direct appeal to the United States Supreme Court pursuant to 28 USCS 1253, and an alternative appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

A black federal employee filed suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York to redress racially discriminatory employment practices. The suit was filed 42 days after the employee had been informed of a final decision of the General Services Administration that his complaint as to these practices was without merit. Since 717(c) of the Civil Rights Act of 1967, as added by 11 of the Equal Employment Opportunity Act of 1972 (42 USCS 2000e-16(c)), requires the filing of such suit within 30 days of the receipt of notice of final agency action, the employee proceeded on the theory that the judicial remedy afforded by 717(c) was designed merely to supplement other putative judicial relief. The District Court dismissed the complaint as not timely filed. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (507 F2d 1300).

After 25 cars had been coupled together on one track in the defendant's railroad yard, the twenty-sixth car, when added, failed to couple. After three or four other cars had been added, the first 25 cars began rolling down the track. The plaintiff, when attempting to stop them, as was his duty, fell under a car and, as result of injuries so received, lost his leg. The plaintiff obtained a judgment of the District Court for $ 80,000. The Court of Appeals set the judgment aside on the grounds that (1) the trial court's charge to the jury failed to make it clear that the jury could find for the plaintiff only if it inferred "bad condition of the couplers and consequent violation of defendant's statutory duty," and (2) that the charge deprived the railroad of the defense that the failure of the cars to couple was due to the fact that the couplers had not been properly opened.

Once a person turns 65 or has received federal disability benefits for 24 months, he becomes ‚Äúentitled‚Äù to benefits under Part A of Medicare. 42 U. S. C. ¬ß¬ß426(a)‚Äì(b). Part A provides coverage for, among other things, inpatient hospital treatment. See ¬ß1395d(a).
