Medicare pays hospitals a fixed rate for such treatment based on the patient‚Äôs diagnosis, regardless of the hospital‚Äôs actual cost and subject to certain adjustments. ¬ß¬ß1395ww(d)(1)‚Äì(5). One such adjustment is the ‚Äúdisproportionate share hospital‚Äù (DSH) adjustment, which provides higherthan-usual rates to hospitals that serve a higher-than-usual percentage of low-income patients. To calculate the DSH adjustment, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) adds together two statutorily described fractions: the Medicare fraction‚Äîwhich represents the proportion of a hospital‚Äôs Medicare patients who have low incomes‚Äîand the Medicaid fraction‚Äîwhich represents the proportion of a hospital‚Äôs total patients who are not entitled to Medicare and have low incomes. Together those fractions produce the ‚Äúdisproportionatepatient percentage,‚Äù which determines whether a hospital will receive a DSH adjustment, and how large it will be. Not all patients who qualify for Medicare Part A have their hospital treatment paid for by the program. Non-payment may occur, for example, if a patient‚Äôs stay exceeds Medicare‚Äôs 90-day cap per spell of illness, see ¬ß1395d, or if a patient is covered by a private insurance plan, see ¬ß1395y(b)(2)(A). Such limits on Medicare‚Äôs coverage prompt the question raised here: whether patients whom Medicare insures but does not pay for on a given day are patients ‚Äúwho (for such days) were entitled to [Medicare Part A] benefits‚Äù for purposes of computing a hospital‚Äôs disproportionate-patient percentage. ¬ß1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I). A 2004 HHS regulation says yes: If the patient meets the basic statutory criteria for Medicare (i.e., is over 65 or disabled), then the patient counts in the denominator and, if poor, in the numerator of the Medicare fraction. See 69 Fed. Reg. 49098‚Äì49099. Respondent Empire Health Foundation challenged that regulation as inconsistent with the statute. The Ninth Circuit agreed. That court focused on the statute‚Äôs use of two different phrases: ‚Äúentitled to [Medicare Part A] benefits‚Äù and ‚Äúeligible for [Medicaid] assistance.‚Äù The Ninth Circuit read the latter phrase to mean that a patient qualifies for Medicaid and the former phrase to mean that a patient has an absolute right to payment from Medicare. The Court granted certiorari to resolve a conflict between the Ninth Circuit and two other Circuit Courts, which had approved of HHS‚Äôs regulation

Following the denial of a pretrial motion to suppress, the prosecution--at the defendant's trial in the Court of Common Pleas, Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania, on a charge of carrying a concealed deadly weapon and a firearm without a license--introduced in evidence a revolver that had been seized from the defendant by a police officer. The seizure occurred when the officer noticed a bulge under the defendant's jacket after the defendant had been directed by the officer to get out of his car, which had been stopped for the purpose of issuing a traffic summons because the automobile was being operated with an expired license plate. The defendant was convicted, and the conviction was affirmed by the Superior Court of Pennsylvania (232 Pa Super 486, 335 A2d 516). However, the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania reversed on the ground that the police officer's order to the defendant to get out of his car was an impermissible seizure under the Fourth Amendment because the order had been issued as a matter of routine rather than on the basis of objective observable facts supporting a suspicion that the driver posed a threat to the officer's safety, the revolver thus being the fruit of an unconstitutional search (370 A2d 1157).

In one count of a three-count complaint in an action brought by an employer against an international union and one of its locals in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana, the employer, invoking the court's jurisdiction under 301 of the Taft-Hartley Act (29 USC 185), which gives federal courts jurisdiction of suits for violation of contracts between an employer and a labor organization, sought injunctive relief against the union's breach of the provisions of a collective bargaining agreement between the parties by repeated strikes and work stoppages over work assignments and docking employees for reporting late to work, which the agreement required to be arbitrated. The District Court dismissed this count of the complaint on the ground that it sought injunctive relief which federal courts are without jurisdiction to grant, by virtue of 4 of the Norris-La Guardia Act (29 USC 104), which bars federal courts from issuing injunctions in any case involving any labor dispute. (187 F Supp 225.) The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed the order of dismissal for the same reasons. (290 F2d 312.)

A father, charged with various sexual offenses against his minor daughter, subpoenaed a state child welfare agency's records which pertained to the daughter, and in which he hoped to find a medical report, names of witnesses, and other exculpatory evidence. The agency, however, refused to comply with the subpoena, invoking a state law which protected the confidentiality of its records and allowed access only to certain specified persons and agencies, including courts of competent jurisdiction. After examining the records in chambers and finding no medical report, the Court of Common Pleas of Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, refused to order the disclosure of the records. The father was subsequently convicted before the Court of Common Pleas, but the Superior Court of Pennsylvania vacated the conviction and remanded for further proceedings, holding (1) that the withholding of the records violated the father's rights under the confrontation clause of the Sixth Amendment; (2) that the Court of Common Pleas on remand must examine the records in chambers, release any verbatim statements by the daughter, and then make the full record available to defense counsel for the limited purpose of arguing the relevance of the statements; and (3) that a new trial should be ordered unless the error was found to be harmless (324 Pa Super 557, 472 A2d 220). The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, referring also to the compulsory process clause of the Sixth Amendment, affirmed and remanded, but directed that defense counsel be granted access to the entire record on remand in order to search for any evidence that might be useful to the defense (509 Pa 357, 502 A2d 148).

After the City Council of Cuyahoga Falls, Ohio (hereinafter City), passed a site-plan ordinance authorizing construction of a low-income housing complex by respondents -- a nonprofit corporation dedicated to developing affordable housing and related parties -- a group of citizens filed a formal petition requesting that the ordinance be repealed or submitted to a popular vote. Pursuant to the City's charter, the referendum petition stayed the site plan's implementation until its approval by the voters. An Ohio court denied respondents an injunction against the petition, and the city engineer, on advice from the city law director, denied their request for building permits. The voters eventually passed the referendum, thus repealing the ordinance. Subsequently, the Ohio Supreme Court declared the referendum invalid under Ohio's Constitution, the City issued the building permits, and construction commenced. While the state litigation was still pending, respondents filed a federal suit against the City and its officials, seeking an injunction ordering the City to issue the building permits, as well as declaratory and monetary relief. They claimed that by submitting the site plan to voters, the City and its officials violated the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, as well as the Fair Housing Act. The District Court, inter alia, denied the City's summary judgment motion. After the Ohio Supreme Court invalidated the referendum, thus reducing the federal action to a claim for damages for the construction delay, the District Court granted the City and its officials summary judgment. In reversing, the Sixth Circuit found that respondents had produced sufficient evidence to go to trial on the allegation that the City, by allowing the petition to stay the site plan's implementation, gave effect to the racial bias reflected in the public's opposition to the project; that respondents had stated a valid Fair Housing Act claim because the City's actions had a disparate impact based on race and family status; and that a genuine issue of material fact existed as to whether the City had engaged in arbitrary and irrational government conduct in violation of substantive due process.

Respondent Lorenzo Johnson was convicted as an accomplice and co-conspirator in the murder of Taraja Williams, who was killed by a shotgun blast to the chest in the early morning hours of December 15, 1995, in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. After his conviction was affirmed in state court, Johnson exhausted his state remedies and sought a writ of habeas corpus in Federal District Court pursuant to the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA), 28 U. S. C. ¬ß2254. The District Court denied habeas relief but the U. S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed, holding that the evidence at trial was insufficient to support Johnson's conviction under the standard set forth in Jackson v. Virginia, 443 U. S. 307 (1979). We have made clear that Jackson claims face a high bar in federal habeas proceedings because they are subject to two layers of judicial deference. First, on direct appeal, "it is the responsibility of the jury-not the court-to decide what conclusions should be drawn from evidence admitted at trial. A reviewing court may set aside the jury's verdict on the ground of insufficient evidence only if no rational trier of fact could have agreed with the jury." Cavazos v. Smith, 565 U. S. 1, __ (2011) (per curiam) (slip op., at 1). And second, on habeas review, "a federal court may not overturn a state court decision rejecting a sufficiency of the evidence challenge simply because the federal court disagrees with the state court. The federal court instead may do so only if the state court decision was 'objectively unreasonable."' Ibid. (quoting Renico v. Lett, 559 U. S. ___ (2010) (slip op., at 5)).

The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed a criminal conviction upon the defendant's appeal from a Federal District Court's judgment (see 506 F2d 1398). The defendant petitioned the United States Supreme Court for a writ of certiorari, but died before the Supreme Court took any action on the petition.

Oral arguments in proceedings before the Federal Trade Commission for alleged violations of certain provisions of the Robinson-Patman Act were heard by the full Commission of five members, but two Commissioners retired before the decision and a new Commissioner, appointed to fill one of the vacancies, declined to participate in the decision because he had not heard the oral arguments. A cease and desist order was entered, all three of the participating Commissioners having concurred as to one of the alleged violations of the Robinson-Patman Act, but only two of the participating Commissioners having concurred in another alleged violation of the act. On petition for review, a three-judge panel of the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit entered an order, sustained on rehearing by the full court, which enforced that portion of the Commission's order that was concurred in by all three of the participating Commissioners, but which refused to enforce that part of the Commission's order that was concurred in by only two of the Commissioners. The Court of Appeals held that absent statutory authority to the contrary, it was necessary that three members of the five-member Commission concur in order to enter a binding order on behalf of the Commission. (358 F2d 224.)

In the instant cases, one of the questions presented was whether conscientious objection to a particular war, rather than objection to all war, relieved the objector from military service responsibilities under the provision of 6(j) of the Military Selective Service Act of 1967 exempting registrants "conscientiously opposed to participation in war in any form," and under administrative regulations incorporating the same standards for conscientious-objector discharges of servicemen. Another issue presented was whether limitation of conscientious-objector status only to those who objected to all wars violated the religious clauses of the First Amendment. In No. 85, conscientious objector status was administratively denied to a draft registrant who, on the basis of a humanist approach to religion and fundamental principles of conscience, objected to participation in the Vietnam war as being unjust, but not to participation in a war of national defense or a war sponsored by the United Nations as a peace-keeping measure. The registrant was subsequently convicted in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York for wilful failure to report for induction, the District Court having determined that there was a basis in fact to support the denial of the conscientious-objector exemption, since the registrant's objection ran only to a particular war. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the conviction (420 F2d 298). In No. 325, the Army denied an application for a conscientious-objector discharge which had been made by a soldier after completion of basic training and receipt of orders for Vietnam duty, and which was based on objection to the Vietnam war but not to all wars. Such objection was founded on the soldier's duty under the Catholic faith to forswear participation in an "unjust" war. The United States District Court for the Northern District of California denied habeas corpus relief to the soldier, finding a basis in fact for the Army's rejection of the application for discharge, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed on the ground that objection to the Vietnam war, but not to all wars, did not qualify the soldier for discharge (418 F2d 908).

After its judgment upholding state public school Bible readings and prayer recitations was vacated by the Supreme Court of the United States (374 US 487, 10 L ed 2d 1043, 83 S Ct 1864), the Supreme Court of Florida reaffirmed its judgment. ((Fla) 160 So 2d 97.)

The holder of a United States patent brought a patent infringement suit in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon against a Canadian corporation, predicating venue on the provision of 28 USCS 1391(d) that "an alien may be sued in any district." The court dismissed the complaint on the ground of improper venue, holding that 28 USCS 1400(b) is the exclusive provision governing venue in patent infringement litigation. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed (442 F2d 420).

In 2016, Congress passed the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act (PROMESA), 48 U. S. C. ¬ß2101 et seq., to deal with a fiscal crisis in Puerto Rico brought about by soaring public debt. PROMESA establishes a system for overseeing Puerto Rico‚Äôs finances, while also enabling the Commonwealth to gain bankruptcy protections similar to those available under the Federal Bankruptcy Code. See Financial Oversight and Management Bd. for Puerto Rico v. Aurelius Investment, LLC, 590 U. S. ___, ___. The statute creates the Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico‚Äîpetitioner in this case‚Äîas an ‚Äúentity within the territorial government‚Äù of Puerto Rico. ¬ß2121(c)(1). Under PROMESA, the Board approves the Commonwealth‚Äôs fiscal plans and budgets, supervises its borrowing, and represents Puerto Rico in so-called Title III cases‚Äîjudicial debt-restructuring proceedings modeled on federal bankruptcy proceedings. Beginning in 2016, respondent Centro de Periodismo Investigativo, Inc. (CPI)‚Äîa nonprofit media organization that has reported on Puerto Rico‚Äôs fiscal crisis‚Äîasked the Board to release various documents relating to its work. When CPI‚Äôs requests went unfulfilled, it sued the Board in the United States District Court for Puerto Rico, citing a provision of the Puerto Rican Constitution interpreted to guarantee a right of access to public records. The Board moved to dismiss on sovereign immunity grounds, but the District Court rejected that defense. The First Circuit affirmed. The court began by citing Circuit precedent that Puerto Rico enjoys sovereign immunity, and it assumed without deciding that the Board shares in that immunity. But it then held that PROMESA‚Äîparticularly its jurisdictional provision, Section 2126(a)‚Äîclearly abrogates the Board‚Äôs immunity.

In the circumstances of this case, whatever the towage contract provided, the owner of a tow was not liable to a third party for the negligence of employees of a towing company, where such employees were in fact acting as employees of the towing company and not as employees of the owner of the tow.

Petitioner claimant sued respondent United States Department of Labor, alleging violations of the Privacy Act of 1974. The district court granted summary judgment in favor of the claimant and awarded $ 1,000 in statutory damages under 5 U.S.C.S. _ 552a(g)(4). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed, finding that the claimant failed to raise a triable issue of fact about damages. The claimant petitioned for review. When the claimant filed for black lung benefits, the Government disclosed the claimant's Social Security number beyond the limits set by 5 U.S.C.S. _ 552a of the Privacy Act of 1974. The claimant provided no proof of actual damages; the claimant submitted no corroboration for his claim of emotional distress. The claimant argued that 5 U.S.C.S. _ 552a(g)(4)(A) entitled any plaintiff adversely affected by an intentional or willful violation to the $ 1,000 minimum on proof of nothing more than a statutory violation. The Supreme Court disagreed with the claimant and determined that plaintiffs needed to prove some actual damages to qualify for a minimum statutory award of $ 1,000. The Court found that the "entitlement to recovery" necessary to qualify for the $ 1,000 minimum was not shown merely by an intentional or willful violation of the Act producing some adverse effect, and the statute guaranteed $ 1,000 only to plaintiffs who suffered some actual damages.

Both school districts adopted plans whereby, after place of residence and availability of space were considered, school assignments were made on the basis of race to ensure that schools were racially balanced. The U.S. Supreme Court first held that the cases were not moot, even though the plans were not currently being applied to children of the association's members or the student, since it was not absolutely clear that application of the racial guidelines could not reasonably be expected to recur. Further, the Court held that the districts, which did not operate legally segregated schools, denied students equal protection by classifying students by race and relying upon the classification in school assignments. The districts failed to establish a compelling interest in racial diversity since their plans relied on racial classification in a nonindividualized, mechanical way as a decisive factor, and racial imbalance in the schools was not unconstitutional by itself. Further, the minimal effect the classifications actually had on assignments indicated that other means would be effective to achieve the districts' goals and that the use of racial classifications was unnecessary.

The Economic Stabilization Act of 1970 (84 Stat 799 as amended, 12 USCS 1904 note), since expired, authorized the President to issue orders and regulations to stabilize wages and salaries. By Executive Order, the President created the Pay Board to oversee wage and salary controls imposed under the Act. The State of Ohio enacted a statute providing for a 10.6% wage and salary increase for almost 65,000 state employees. The state applied to the Pay Board for approval of the increases, but the Board denied the application for an exemption to the extent that it exceeded salary increases of 7%. Two state employees then obtained a writ of mandamus from the Supreme Court of Ohio, compelling state officials to pay the full increases provided in the Ohio statute (34 Ohio St 2d 252, 63 Ohio Ops 2d 392, 298 NE2d 129). The United States subsequently filed the instant action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio to enjoin the state and its officials from paying wage and salary increases in excess of the 7% authorized by the Board. The District Court certified to the Temporary Emergency United States Court of Appeals the question of the applicability of the Stabilization Act to state employees. The Court of Appeals, enjoining the payment of wage and salary increases in excess of the amount authorized by the Board, construed the Act as applying to state employees and as such upheld its constitutionality (487 F2d 936).

I join the Court's dismissal of this appeal for failure to docket within the prescribed time. I do so despite the fact that the Court apparently has not consistently enforced the provisions of its Rule 13 (1) and, on occasion, has permitted appeals despite untimely docketing.

Defendant was convicted of a drug offense and pro se moved for a new trial, but the motion was recharacterized as a motion for habeas corpus relief under 28 U.S.C.S. _ 2255 and denied. Upon the grant of a writ of certiorari, defendant appealed the judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit which determined that a subsequent _ 2255 motion was properly denied as lacking appellate court approval. Defendant contended that the recharacterization of his pro se motion for a new trial as a _ 2255 motion was insufficient to justify denial of his subsequent _ 2255 motion on the ground that it was a second or successive habeas corpus petition filed without appellate court approval. The government first argued that a writ of certiorari was not available to review the denial of authorization to file the second petition and, in any event, the recharacterization was not appealed and thus became the law of the case. The United States Supreme Court first held that defendant was appealing the determination that his motion for a new trial was a first habeas corpus petition, rather than any denial of authorization to file a second petition, and thus the Supreme Court had jurisdiction over the appeal. Further, defendant's pro se motion for a new trial was improperly recharacterized as a _ 2255 motion, regardless of whether defendant appealed the recharacterization, since the lower court did not inform defendant of its intent to recharacterize, warn defendant concerning restrictions on second or successive petitions, nor provide defendant with an opportunity to withdraw or amend the filing.

A person accused of assault and battery was placed in the Charleston County, South Carolina jail. The accused retained counsel who, after a bond hearing, allegedly told the police not to question the accused further. While still in custody, the accused was informed that he was a suspect in a murder. After receiving Miranda warnings, the accused indicated that he understood his rights and signed "waiver of rights" forms. The police then interrogated the accused about the murder. The accused did not request his attorney's presence at any time during the interrogation. The accused was brought to trial, and the trial court denied his motion to suppress the statements he had given to the police. The jury found the accused guilty and sentenced him to death. The Supreme Court of South Carolina upheld the conviction on direct appeal (277 SC 452, 290 SE2d 1), and the United States Supreme Court, in 1982, denied certiorari (459 US 932, 74 L Ed 2d 191, 103 S Ct 242). After unsuccessfully petitioning for collateral relief in the state courts, the accused filed a petition in United States District Court for federal habeas corpus relief, which petition was denied. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, affirming on appeal in 1988, held that the accused's statements to the police were not obtained in violation of the accused's federal constitutional rights or in violation of the United States Supreme Court's prophylactic rule requiring the police, during continuous custody, to refrain from initiating any further questioning once an accused invokes the right to counsel (846 F2d 255). Approximately 1 month later, on the same day that the Court of Appeals denied rehearing petitions by the accused, the United States Supreme Court handed down its decision in Arizona v Roberson (1988) 486 US 675, 100 L Ed 2d 704, 108 S Ct 2093, holding that the Federal Constitution's Fifth Amendment forbids police to initiate interrogation of a suspect as to a second, unrelated offense without providing counsel, where the suspect has previously cut off interrogation by requesting counsel. On a motion by the accused for reconsideration, a panel of the Court of Appeals denied rehearing on the ground that the accused's interrogation, although contrary to the Roberson guidelines, had been conducted in strict accordance with established law at the time, and that the accused was not entitled to the retroactive benefit of the Roberson decision (864 F2d 24). The accused's petition for a rehearing en banc was denied.

The present action was brought in a Wisconsin state court by an attorney admitted to practice law in Wisconsin; the purpose of the action was to recover dues paid by the plaintiff to the Wisconsin state bar under compulsion of the bylaws of that organization, it being alleged in the complaint that the order of the Supreme Court of Wisconsin integrating the Wisconsin bar, in so far as it coerced the plaintiff to support the state bar, was unconstitutional on the ground, among others, that it violated the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The state court dismissed the action on the ground, among others, that the complaint did not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. The Supreme Court of Wisconsin, determining the constitutional issue raised on its merits, affirmed. (10 Wis 2d 230, 102 NW2d 404.)

Attorneys who represented the Republic of Cuba in legal matters, including litigation, instituted an action against the Attorney General of the United States in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, seeking a judgment declaring that their activities did not subject them to the requirements of registration under the amended Foreign Agents Registration Act (22 USC 611). The District Court denied the Attorney General's motion for judgment on the pleadings, but certified to the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit the question whether persons requested to register under the act may have their rights adjudicated by a declaratory judgment suit. The Court of Appeals held that the doctrine of sovereign immunity required that the case be dismissed as an unconsented suit against the United States. (115 App DC 210, 318 F2d 181.)

The Northern Cheyenne Allotment Act of 1926 (44 Stat 690) establishes the Northern Cheyenne Reservation and provides for the allotment of agricultural and grazing lands to individual tribal members. Section 3 of the Act reserved mineral deposits underlying reservation lands for the tribe's benefit, but also provided that 50 years after approval of the Act such deposits "shall become the property of the respective allottees or their heirs," and further provided that "unallotted lands" were subject to Congress' control and management for the benefit of the Indians. By the Act of July 24, 1968 (82 Stat 424), Congress amended 3 of the 1926 Act, terminating the grant of mineral rights to allottees and reserving the mineral rights in perpetuity for the tribe's benefit. However, the 1968 Act expressly conditioned the termination of allottees' rights on the tribe's bringing an action in the United States District Court for the District of Montana against the allottees and obtaining a judgment that the allottees had not been granted vested mineral rights by the 1926 Act. The tribe instituted such action in the specified District Court, which held that the 1926 Act did not grant the allottees vested rights in the mineral deposits (349 F Supp 1302), but the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed (505 F2d 268).

After an adult bookstore located in a borough's commercial zone introduced a coin-operated mechanism which permitted customers to watch a live dancer, usually nude, performing behind a glass panel, complaints were filed against the bookstore operators charging that the exhibition of live dancing violated the borough's zoning ordinance which governed uses permitted in a commercial zone. The bookstore operators were found guilty in a municipal court, and were also found guilty on appeal in the Camden, New Jersey, County Court. In response to the bookstore operators' defense based on the First and Fourteenth Amendments, the court recognized that live nude dancing was protected by the First Amendment, but ruled that First Amendment guarantees were not involved. The Superior Court of New Jersey, Appellate Division, affirmed the bookstore operators' convictions, and the Supreme Court of New Jersey denied further review.

The Federal Trade Commission issued a cease-and-desist order against the respondent retail department store for violations of the Fur Products Labeling Act, finding that many of respondent's retail sales were falsely "invoiced." As to misbranding, the commission found that three of the six disclosure requirements contained in 4(2) of the act had been violated, but included also the three disclosure requirements not shown to be violated in the scope of its decree. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit eliminated the prohibitions relating to invoicing on the ground that a retail sales slip was not an "invoice" within the meaning of the act and struck from the order the prohibition against misbranding through omission of the three categories as to which no violations were found. (254 F2d 18.)

This case presented the question whether union signatory subcontracting clauses that are sought or negotiated in the context of a collective bargaining relationship are protected by the construction industry proviso to 8(e) of the National Labor Relations Act (29 USCS 158(e)). Section 8(e) prohibits "secondary" agreements between unions and employers which require an employer to cease doing business with another party, but the construction industry proviso to 8(e) exempts from this proscription agreements between a union and an employer in the construction industry over the contracting or subcontracting of work to be performed at a construction site. In one instance, a construction industry subcontractor, during collective bargaining negotiations, reached an impasse with a union over the union's demand that the contract include a union signatory subcontracting clause barring subcontracting except to firms who are signatories to agreements with particular unions. In support of their demands for a subcontracting clause, union locals picketed the subcontractor's construction site causing work stoppages, but the subcontractor filed unfair labor practice charges with the National Labor Relations Board asserting that the clause violated 8(e) of the Act. It was further argued that because the clause violated 8(e), the picketing violated 8(b)(4)(A) of the Act (29 USCS 158(b)(4)(A)), which forbids coercion "to enter into any agreement which is prohibited by" 8(e). The Board ruled that the union signatory subcontracting clause at issue was saved by the construction industry proviso, and rejected the contention that the proviso sheltered subcontracting clauses only if the clauses were limited in application to particular job sites at which both union and nonunion workers were employed. According to the Board, such clauses are lawful when sought or negotiated in the context of collective bargaining relationships, and therefore picketing to obtain the clause was permitted under 8(b)(4)(A) (239 NLRB 241). A second dispute involved unfair labor practice charges filed against a union by a member of an association of construction industry employers asserting that a contract between the association and the union containing a union signatory subcontracting clause violated 8(e). The Board held that such clauses were protected by the proviso (239 NLRB 274). The subcontractor, the industry association, and the association member sought review of the Board's orders in the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit which, after consolidating the cases, ultimately enforced the orders. The court ruled that union signatory subcontracting clauses are protected so long as they are sought or negotiated in the context of a collective bargaining relationship, and that economic pressure may be used to obtain a subcontracting agreement, but that it may not be employed to enforce a subcontracting agreement (654 F2d 1301).

The present action was instituted in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi by Negroes living in Mississippi, seeking injunctions to enforce their constitutional rights to nonsegregated service in interstate and intrastate transportation, alleging that such rights had been denied them under color of state statutes, municipal ordinances, and state custom and usage. A three-judge District Court was convened and abstained from further proceedings pending construction of the challenged laws by the state courts. (199 F Supp 595.)

A county association for retarded citizens brought an action in the United States District Court for the District of Montana, seeking a declaratory judgment that the Fair Labor Standards Act (29 USCS 201 et seq.) did not apply to employees of a mental health facility operated by the association, or, in the alternative, that an application of the Act to the facility would be unconstitutional. The District Court held that the Act was unconstitutional as applied to the association in its operation of the facility, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed.

After union members who had crossed picket lines and worked during an authorized strike were fined by their local unions and the unions brought suit in the state courts to enforce such fines, the unions were charged--in a complaint before the National Labor Relations Board--with having committed unfair labor practices by imposing and suing to collect the fines. Referring to a proviso in 8(b)(1)(A) of the amended National Labor Relations Act, which proviso was to the effect that the unfair labor practice provisions of 8(b)(1)(A) were not intended to impair the right of a labor organization to prescribe its own rules with respect to the acquisition or retention of membership therein, the Board rejected the charges against the unions and dismissed the complaint. (149 NLRB 67.) The Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed, holding that the unions' conduct violated 8(b)(1)(A), which declared it an unfair labor practice for a union to restrain or coerce employees in the exercise of their right to refrain from concerted activities. (358 F2d 656.)

A municipal ordinance prohibited the use of amplifying devices casting sound upon streets and public places, except with the permission of the chief of police, without prescribing standards for the exercise of his discretion. A majority of the court, whose opinion was written by Douglas, J., thought that it violated the constitutional right of free speech.

In a private antitrust suit brought in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, a motion was made to dismiss the suit on grounds of improper venue and lack of personal jurisdiction over the defendants; the court, agreeing that the venue was improper, transferred the action to the Southern District of New York, relying on 28 USC 1406(a), which provides that if it be in the interest of justice, a Federal District Court in which is filed a case laying venue in the wrong division or district shall transfer such case to any district or division in which it could have been brought. The defendants then made a motion in the District Court for the Southern District of New York to dismiss the suit, on the ground that the transferring court lacked personal jurisdiction over them and, lacking such jurisdiction, had no power under 28 USC 1406(a) to transfer the action. The District Court for the Southern District of New York granted this motion on the ground asserted (175 F Supp 793), and the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed on the same ground. (288 F2d 579.)

The motion for leave to proceed further in forma pauperis and the petition for a writ of certiorari are granted. The judgment of the Supreme Court of California is vacated and the case is remanded to that court for further consideration in light of Bruton v. United States, 391 U.S. 123. See Roberts v. Russell, ante, p. 293.

Petitioners, who worked in a Government-owned plant in which respondent produced munitions under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract with the War Department, sued respondent for overtime compensation under the Fair Labor Standards Act. The District Court's summary judgment for respondent was affirmed by the Circuit Court of Appeals. Among other issues involved were whether petitioners were employees of the Government or of the private contractor and whether munitions produced for shipment across state lines are produced for "commerce" and are "goods" within the meaning of the Act. Substantial claims of the petitioners would be denied or large sums added to the cost of the war by the answers to the questions raised, and many other cases would be governed by the decision. Also, certain contentions were made in this Court which were not made in the courts below; and an adequate consideration of the problem would require consideration of three different acts of Congress, two of which were not properly before this Court on the record in this case.

A manufacturer owning a dominant patent on a certain type of electric fuse cut-out, and another manufacturer owning a patent for an improvement, which patents in separate hands produced a deadlock, united in an arrangement by which each gave the other a royalty-free cross-license and one was authorized to grant sublicenses to other manufacturers upon condition of adherence to prices fixed by the licensor.

Title III of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 (18 USCS 2510 et seq.), regulating the interception of wire, oral, and electronic communications, contains a provision (18 USCS 2518(8)(a)) which requires that (1) recording during electronic surveillance shall be done in such a way as will protect the recording from alteration, (2) immediately upon expiration of a surveillance order, or extensions thereof, such recordings shall be sealed under the directions of the judge who issued the order, and (3) the presence of the seal, or a "satisfactory explanation" for its absence, is a prerequisite for the use or disclosure of any evidence derived from the recordings. During a criminal investigation, the Federal Government, under Title III, obtained a series of court orders authorizing electronic surveillance of certain suspects. The first order, which was obtained on April 27, 1984 and extended until July 23, 1984, authorized electronic surveillance of a suspect's residence and some public telephones near the residence. After the suspect moved to a new residence, the government, on July 27, 1984, obtained a second surveillance order that covered the new residence, which order was extended until September 24, 1984. On October 13, 1984, three days after the expiration of a third order authorizing surveillance of the suspect's car, all tapes created during the surveillance of the suspect were sealed by the United States District Court for the District of Connecticut. On November 1, 1984, the government obtained a fourth court order that authorized it to wiretap a residence shared by two other suspects, which order was extended until May 30, 1985. On January 18, 1985, the government obtained a fifth court order that authorized it to wiretap two public telephones near the two suspects' residence, which order expired on February 17, 1985. On March 1, 1985, when the government applied for an extension of the fifth order, the court issued a sixth order, which expired on May 30, 1985. All tapes from the wiretaps concerning the two suspects who shared a residence were judicially sealed on June 15, 1985. After all three suspects were indicted for offenses related to the robbery of a security service company's depot, the suspects moved to suppress all evidence that the government had obtained as a result of electronic surveillance. Following a suppression hearing, the District Court--determining that (1) there had been at least an 82-day delay, beginning on July 23, 1984, in sealing the tapes obtained from the first suspect's old residence under the first order, since the second order was not an extension of the first, and (2) the sealing of the tapes concerning the other two suspects had been delayed 118 days after the February 17, 1985 expiration of the fifth order, regarding the public telephones near their residence, since the sixth order was not an extension of the fifth--suppressed the first and fifth tapes on the basis of the delays alone (695 F Supp 649). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, affirming, rejected the government's explanation for the delays (875 F2d 17).

A Colorado statute made it unlawful, within 100 feet of the entrance to any health care facility, for any person to "knowingly approach" within 8 feet of another person, without that person's consent, for the purpose of passing a leaflet or handbill to, displaying a sign to, or engaging in oral protest, education, or counseling with such other person. Individuals who had previously engaged in antiabortion "sidewalk counseling" within the areas now regulated by the statute filed an action against the state in the District Court for Jefferson County, Colorado, and sought (1) a declaration that the statute was facially invalid, in part because it violated the rights of free speech and press under the Federal Constitution's First Amendment, and (2) an injunction barring the statute's enforcement. The District Court, dismissing the complaint, found that the statute permissibly imposed content-neutral "time, place, and manner" restrictions that were narrowly tailored to serve significant state interests and left open ample alternative means of communication. The Colorado Court of Appeals affirmed. After the United States Supreme Court, vacated and remanded for reconsideration in the light of an intervening decision (519 US 1145, 137 L Ed 2d 213, 117 S Ct 1077), (1) the Court of Appeals reinstated its judgment (949 P2d 1107), and (2) the Colorado Supreme Court affirmed (973 P2d 1246).

Shortly after a corporation which had acquired most of the assets of another corporation brought an action in an Illinois state court seeking recovery for breach of covenants not to compete which the acquired corporation and one of its stockholders had entered into as part of the acquisition agreement, the acquired corporation, its stockholder, and another brought an action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, alleging that the covenants against competition were unreasonable restraints of trade violative of the Sherman Act (15 USCS 1 et seq.). Ultimately, after nine years of litigation in the state courts (see 105 Ill App 2d 261, 245 NE2d 263, and 13 Ill App 3d 291, 300 NE2d 632), the Supreme Court of Illinois affirmed a judgment in favor of the acquiring company for some $ 7,000,000 (see 58 Ill 2d 289, 321 NE2d 1), and the plaintiffs in the Federal District Court antitrust action moved for a preliminary injunction against collection of the state court judgment that had been rendered against them. The District Court granted the motion, finding that the covenants against competition were overly broad and that the acquiring corporation's activities in the state litigation were not a genuine attempt to use the adjudicative process legitimately. The District Court held that injunctive relief was not barred by the Anti-Injunction Act (28 USCS 2283)--which prohibits a federal court from granting an injunction staying state court proceedings "except as expressly authorized by Act of Congress, or where necessary in aid of its jurisdiction, or to protect or effectuate its judgments"--since 16 of the Clayton Act (15 USCS 26), which authorizes private injunctive relief in federal courts against threatened loss or damage from antitrust violations, constituted an express exception by Act of Congress to the Anti-Injunction Act, and since an injunction was necessary to protect the jurisdiction of the court in view of the fact that collection of the state court judgment would, in effect, eliminate two of the three plaintiffs in the federal action (403 F Supp 527). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed, holding that 16 of the Clayton Act was an express exception by Act of Congress to the Anti-Injunction Act (545 F2d 1050).

Upon the failure of the North Dakota Legislative Assembly to reapportion itself after the 1970 census, an action was instituted in the United States District Court for the Southeastern District of North Dakota for declaratory and injunctive relief, the plaintiffs alleging that the reapportionment plan then in effect, which plan had been fashioned by a federal court in 1965 and included multimember Senate districts, no longer complied with equal protection requirements. The relief sought included a request that the court fashion a new apportionment plan using single-member districts, based on the 1970 census figures. The District Court found that the 1965 apportionment plan was unconstitutional, and after considering several plans presented by a court-appointed commission, ultimately adopted a new plan which included multimember Senate districts, and which contained a population variance of 20.14 percent between the largest and smallest Senate districts (372 F Supp 371).

Separate actions for declaratory and injunctive relief, consolidated for trial, were instituted in the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas, by certain minority political parties, their candidates and supporters, and certain independent candidates, challenging the constitutionality of Texas statutes relating to the securing of ballot positions at general elections. The statutes--attacked as violating the plaintiffs' First and Fourteenth Amendment rights to associate for the advancement of political beliefs, and as violating the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment--required that (1) to obtain a place on the general election ballot, a new political party, a party whose nominee for governor in the preceding election received less than 2 percent of the total votes cast for governor, or a party which did not nominate a candidate for governor at the last general election (a) must nominate candidates by conventions held at the same time that larger political parties qualified for the ballot by holding primary elections, (b) must be supported at the convention by qualified voters amounting to at least 1 percent of the total gubernatorial vote at the last election, and (c) if the required support was not evidenced at the convention, must file supplemental petitions, obtained in a 55-day period after the convention, containing enough signatures of qualified voters to meet the 1 percent support requirement, which voters must sign an authorized oath that they were qualified voters and had not voted at any primary election or participated in any convention of any other party; and (2) an independent candidate seeking a place on the ballot must file a petition containing notarized signatures of voters constituting a specified percentage of the vote cast for governor in the relevant electoral district in the preceding general election, with the maximum number of signatures for any district, county, or precinct office being limited to a maximum of 500, and with the signatures being restricted to those of qualified voters who had not signed a petition for another independent candidate for the same office and had not voted at a political party's primary election for the same office. The plaintiffs also challenged the state's practice of printing on absentee ballots only the names of the two major political parties and their candidates, and the constitutionality of a Texas statute providing for public financing for primary elections of the two major political parties, but not authorizing any payment of state funds to minority parties to reimburse them for the costs incurred in conducting convention or petition procedures for nominating candidates and meeting ballot qualifications. Following trial, the three-judge District Court denied all relief, holding that the challenged Texas laws served a compelling state interest and were not unconstitutional (349 F Supp 1272).

Following his layoff from employment and failure to be rehired despite several applications, an engineer filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission asserting that his discharge and failure to be rehired were due to his national origin (Polish) and his religion (Jewish) and were therefore violative of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42 USCS 2000e et seq.). The Commission referred his charges to the New York State Division of Human Rights, the state agency which enforces the New York law prohibiting job discrimination, pursuant to the requirement in Title VII that the Commission may not consider a claim until a state agency has had at least 60 days to resolve the matter (42 USCS 2000e-5(c)). After investigating the complaint, the state agency concluded that there was no probable cause to believe that the employer had engaged in the alleged discriminatory practices, and this determination was upheld in an administrative appeal and in an appeal to the Appellate Division of the New York Supreme Court. The complainant could have, but did not seek review by the New York Court of Appeals. Later, a District Director of the Commission ruled that there was no reasonable cause to believe that the charge of discrimination was true, and the Commission issued a right-to-sue notice to the complainant pursuant to 706(f) of Title VII (42 USCS 2000e-5(f)). After the complainant's request for reconsideration was refused by the Commission, the complainant brought suit under Title VII in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York claiming discrimination on the basis of national origin and religion. The District Court ultimately dismissed the complaint on grounds of res judicata (447 F Supp 587), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed (623 F2d 786) and denied a motion for rehearing en banc.

The facts admitted by an accused, in pleading guilty to kidnapping his estranged wife, supported, under some statutes of the state of Washington, a maximum prison sentence of 53 months. However, the judge, after hearing the wife's description of the kidnapping, imposed--on the basis of other state statutes allowing in some cases an "exceptional sentence" exceeding the general statutory limit--a 90-month prison sentence on the ground that the accused had acted with "deliberate cruelty," which was a statutorily enumerated ground for an enhanced sentence in a domestic-violence case.

Individuals owning interests in allotments of land, and the Quinault Indian Tribe, which also held some of the allotments, filed suit in the United States Court of Claims, seeking damages from the United States for its alleged mismanagement of timberlands on the Quinault Indian Reservation. Acting on a motion to dismiss by the United States, the Court of Claims held that the United States was subject to suit for money damages on most of the claims. The court ruled that the federal timber management statutes (25 USCS 406, 407, and 466), various federal statutes governing road building and rights of way (25 USCS 318a, 323-325), statutes governing Indian funds management and government fees (25 USCS 162a, 413), and the regulations promulgated under these statutes, imposed fiduciary duties on the United States in its management of forested allotted lands, the court concluding that the statutes and regulations implicitly required compensation for damages sustained as a result of the government's breach of its duties (664 F2d 265).

Two aliens who were Mexican nationals were arrested in Nebraska by agents of the Immigration and Naturalization Service and, after a group deportation hearing, were ordered deported. At the time of their deportation, they were informed that a return to the United States without permission following deportation would constitute a felony. Subsequently, they were again arrested in Nebraska. They were indicted on charges of violating 8 USCS 1326, which provides that any alien who has been deported and thereafter enters the United States is guilty of a felony. Holding that the aliens could collaterally attack their previous deportation orders, the United States District Court for the District of Nebraska dismissed their indictments on the grounds that at their deportation hearing, they had not made knowing and intelligent waivers of their rights to apply for suspension of deportation or of their rights to appeal. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed, holding that the deportation orders, which could be collaterally attacked, had been obtained unlawfully and thus could not stand as a material element forming the basis of the charges under 1326 (781 F2d 111).

After a Federal District Court dismissed an employment discrimination claim, the employee appealed to the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. The employer moved for dismissal of the appeal and for sanctions. The employer argued that the appeal was frivolous in light of the Court of Appeals' prior decisions holding that 101 of the Civil Rights Act of 1991 (amending 42 USCS 1981) did not apply to cases, such as the present case, that arose before 101's enactment. In an order dated September 30, 1992, the Court of Appeals granted the employer's motion, dismissed the appeal, and imposed a $ 500 sanction on the employee's attorney.

A Washington state statute (1) permitted any person to petition a state court for child visitation rights at any time, and (2) authorized the court to order visitation rights for any person when visitation might serve the best interest of the child. Pursuant to the statute, paternal grandparents filed a petition to obtain visitation rights with their deceased son's children. After the Washington Superior Court for Skagit County granted the grandparents more visitation time than the children's mother desired, the mother appealed. While the appeal was pending, the mother, who had never married the children's father, was married to a father of six, who adopted the two children. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the visitation order and dismissed the petition for visitation (87 Wash App 131, 940 P2d 698). The Washington Supreme Court, affirming the judgment of the Court of Appeals, expressed the view that the statute infringed on the fundamental right, under the Federal Constitution, of parents to rear their children (137 Wash 2d 1, 969 P2d 21).

The National Labor Relations Board issued an order directing an employer to cease and desist from its refusal to bargain collectively with the union certified by the Board as the exclusive bargaining representative of the employees in a bargaining unit. In enforcement proceedings the employer filed a motion for the taking of additional evidence before the Board, alleging that it had complied with the Board's order, and that the union no longer represented a majority of employees in the bargaining unit. The motion was granted by the Court of Appeals.

A federally licensed Indian trader who operated a general store on an Indian reservation brought suit seeking a declaratory judgment that she did not need a California license for retail sale of distilled spirits for off-premises consumption. The United States District Court for the Southern District of California dismissed the action, ruling that the trader was required to have a state license under 18 USCS 1161, which provides that liquor transactions in Indian country are not subject to prohibition under federal law if such transactions are in conformity with state laws and tribal ordinances. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that 1161 pre-empted state licensing and distribution jurisdiction over tribal liquor sales in Indian country (678 F2d 1340).

After an ex parte investigation, the Interstate Commerce Commission issued an order incorporating findings that certain commodities were not agricultural commodities within the meaning of the provision of the Federal Motor Carrier Act exempting motor vehicles used in carrying such commodities from, inter alia, the statutory requirement of a certificate of public convenience and necessity or a permit issued by the commission. A motor carrier who was not a party to the administrative proceedings sought to enjoin the order of the Commission and the District Court denied relief, holding that the Commission's order was not subject to judicial review.

The defendant, after a one-day trial and 18 minutes of jury deliberation, was convicted under 18 USC 2114 of jeopardizing the lives of custodians in a post office while he and another were robbing them, which offense carried a mandatory 25-year sentence. After the jury had returned its verdict, the defendant's counsel, upon the trial judge's refusal to allow the defendant to spend a few days with his family before commencing to serve sentence, asked for a presentence investigation, but the judge replied that such an investigation had been made and that he had read the report thereof. The defendant sought a reversal of his conviction on the ground that the record revealed that the trial judge had read the presentence report before the jury returned its verdict, in violation of Rule 32 (c)(1) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure.

After his first murder trial in the Superior Court, Craven County, North Carolina, had ended in a mistrial because of a deadlocked jury, the defendant, alleging indigency, sought a free transcript of the mistrial to prepare for his scheduled retrial. The trial court denied such motion, and on retrial one month later, before the same judge, with the same counsel, and the same court reporter, the defendant was convicted. The North Carolina Court of Appeals affirmed the conviction, and held that a sufficient need for the mistrial transcript had not been shown, the availability of the court reporter to read the testimony given at the mistrail, in the event that inconsistent testimony was offered at the second trial, constituting an adequate alternative to the transcript (8 NC App 262, 174 SE2d 69). The North Carolina Supreme Court denied certiorari.

A Rhode Island municipality assessed a tax against a resident of Rhode Island for half the value of intangibles held jointly by him and a resident of New York as trustees under the will of a resident of New York. The evidences of the intangible property were at all times in New York and the life beneficiary of the trust resided there, the future beneficiaries being undetermined. The Rhode Island resident did not actually exercise his powers as trustee in Rhode Island.

A federal statute (18 USC 1461) provides that obscene, lewd, lascivious, filthy, or indecent material is nonmailable, and that whoever knowingly deposits such material for mailing or delivery is criminally punishable.

While serving a sentence for the sale and possession of heroin, petitioner was called before a federal grand jury sitting in Chicago, Illinois, inquiring into narcotics offenses. Although given immunity from future prosecution pursuant to 201 of the Narcotic Control Act of 1956 (18 USC 1406) and ordered by the District Court to testify relative to the inquiry of the grand jury, the petitioner refused to answer all questions concerning his crime as well as other transactions in narcotics, under the claim of his privilege against self-incrimination. The District Court declared petitioner guilty of contempt of court and imposed a sentence of 18 months, to commence at the termination of the present imprisonment he was serving. The contempt judgment was affirmed by the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. (276 F2d 148.)

The present two consolidated actions were brought by the United States in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California to determine the applicability of the California minimum wholesale price regulations as respects milk sold to the United States at military installations located within California, the milk being used for (1) strictly military consumption, (2) resale at federal commissaries, and (3) consumption or resale at various military clubs and post exchanges. Milk used for the first two categories was paid for with appropriated funds, while that used for the third category was purchased with nonappropriated funds. The United States alleged that state price regulation of milk sales at these installations, which were federal enclaves, was barred by the Federal Constitution, since such enclaves were subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the United States; it also alleged that the state regulation was an unconstitutional burden on the United States in the exercise of its constitutional power to establish and maintain the Armed Forces and to acquire and manage a federal enclave. The District Court, sitting as a three-judge court, granted the motion of the United States for summary judgment. (190 F Supp 645.)

Approximately 120,000 Japanese-Americans were removed by the United States Government during World War II from their homes and placed in internment camps. An organization of Japanese-Americans and a number of former internees and their representatives brought an action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, seeking damages and declaratory relief for the tangible and intangible injuries suffered because of these internments. Jurisdiction was based on (1) the Little Tucker Act (28 USCS 1346(a)(2)), which provides for the District Court's original jurisdiction, concurrently with the Federal Court of Claims, over nontort claims against the United States not exceeding $ 10,000, and (2) the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) (28 USCS 1346(b)). The District Court concluded that all claims were barred by either sovereign immunity or the applicable statute of limitations (586 F Supp 769). Reversing the District Court's dismissal of certain claims under the Little Tucker Act, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit held (1) that it, rather than the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, had jurisdiction over the appeal, because while 28 USCS 1295(a)(2) generally grants the Federal Circuit exclusive jurisdiction of appeals in cases involving nontax claims under the Little Tucker Act, Congress did not intend the Federal Circuit to hear appeals of such cases when they also included FTCA claims, and (2) that certain claims under the Little Tucker Act were not barred by the statute of limitations (782 F2d 227). A petition for rehearing en banc was denied (793 F2d 304).

Two borrowers refinanced their house in Florida in 1986 with a loan from a bank. In 1991, the borrowers stopped making mortgage payments, and in 1992, the bank began a foreclosure proceeding. The borrowers acknowledged their default but raised affirmative defenses, alleging that the bank's failure to make disclosures required by the Truth in Lending Act (15 USCS 1601 et seq.) gave them rights under 15 USCS 1635 and 1640 to rescind the mortgage agreement and to reduce the bank's claim by the amount of their actual and statutory damages. The Circuit Court of the 15th Judicial Circuit of Florida agreed that under 1640, the borrowers were entitled to offset the amount owed to the bank in actual and statutory damages because the bank had overstated the monthly mortgage payment and finance charge. But the court, rejecting the borrowers' effort to rescind the mortgage, expressed the view that the loan at issue was immune to rescission because under 1635, the right to rescind had expired after 3 years, in 1989. The Florida Fourth District Court of Appeals affirmed (670 So 2d 986). The Supreme Court of Florida also affirmed, remarking that the plain language of 1635(f) was evidence of the unconditional congressional intent to limit the right of rescission to 3 years (692 So 2d 146).

Under Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, as amended (20 USCS 1681 et seq.), 20 USCS 1681(a) proscribes sex discrimination in "any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance." An individual (1) brought suit in the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania against a private, unincorporated, and nationwide athletic association of public and private colleges and universities; and (2) included a Title IX claim alleging that the association--through refusing to waive, on behalf of the individual during her postgraduate years, a bylaw restricting postbaccalaureate participation in intercollegiate athletics--had discriminated against her on the basis of sex by denying her permission to play intercollegiate volleyball at federally assisted institutions. However, the District Court, in granting a defense motion to dismiss, expressed the view that (1) the individual's Title IX claim had to be dismissed because of her failure to allege that the association was a recipient of federal funds; and (2) even if it were assumed that the association received dues from member schools which received federal funds, the association's connections with federal funding would be "too far attenuated" to subject it to the mandates of Title IX (978 F Supp 213, 1997 US Dist LEXIS 12220). The District Court then denied a motion by the individual for leave to amend her complaint. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, in reversing the refusal to allow an amendment of the complaint and in ordering a remand, expressed the view that an allegation in the individual's proposed amended complaint--that the association received dues from member institutions which received federal funds--would be sufficient, if proven, to bring the association within the scope of Title IX as a recipient of federal funds (139 F3d 180, 1998 US App LEXIS 4694).

The owners of several nightclubs, bars, and restaurants, which had for a number of years offered topless dancing, brought a declaratory judgment action in a New York state court, alleging that a New York statute prohibiting nude dancing in establishments licensed by the state to sell liquor for on-premises consumption, violation of which might cause an establishment to lose its liquor license, violated the First Amendment insofar as it prohibited all topless dancing on all licensed premises. The New York Supreme Court declared the statute unconstitutional, and the Court of Appeals of New York affirmed, reasoning that topless dancing was a form of protected expression under the First Amendment and that the state had not demonstrated a need for prohibiting licensees from presenting nonobscene topless dancing performances to willing customers.

One against whom a state public service commission had instituted suit in a state court to prevent him from transporting goods between points in the state without its leave, sought in a federal court a declaratory judgment that such transportation is an integral part of interstate commerce, and an injunction restraining the state public service commission from interfering with such transportation.

After the Internal Revenue Service had informed the defendant that he might be criminally prosecuted for violation of the federal income tax laws, the Service made jeopardy assessments against the defendant, his wife, and his wholly owned corporation, seized their assets, and recorded tax liens. In subsequent proceedings in the Tax Court, the defendant contested the Commissioner of Internal Revenue's proposed deficiencies, alleging errors in the Commissioner's determination. More than a year later, the defendant was indicted in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California on various income tax evasion counts involving the same years as the jeopardy assessments and Tax Court proceedings involved. The defendant's pretrial motion for dismissal of the indictment was granted on the ground that the defendant "has been compelled and will be compelled to come forward on the same matters as are concerned in this criminal case, to testify against himself." The government appealed, and the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit certified the case to the Supreme Court, determining that the District Court had sustained "a motion in bar, when the defendant has not been put in jeopardy," so that, under 28 USC 3731, a direct appeal lay to the Supreme Court. (350 F2d 267.)

FBI agents investigating a theft from an interstate shipment of whisky had information, given by the defendant's employer, of an undisclosed nature, concerning defendant's implication with interstate shipments. They observed him when he placed some cartons in his car, without, however, being able to determine the size, number, or contents of the cartons. After defendant's car was stopped by the agents, he was heard to say that "It is the G's," followed by a request to a passenger in his car to tell them that he, the passenger, had picked the defendant up. The agents searched the car and seized the cartons found therein. Later they learned that the cartons contained stolen radios, whereupon they placed defendant under formal arrest Defendant was convicted, in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, of unlawfully possessing three cartons of radios stolen from an interstate shipment. The issue was whether, under the circumstances described above, there was probable cause for the arrest, without warrant, leading to the search that produced the evidence on which the conviction rested. A timely motion to suppress the evidence was overruled by the District Court. The judgment of conviction was affirmed by the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit on a divided vote. (259 F2d 725.)

In their 1943 and 1944 income tax returns the taxpayers, engaged in the retail optical business in North Carolina and Virginia, deducted as business expenses payments made by them to physicians of one-third of the sales price of glasses sold to their patients. This was the general practice in the optical business at that time. The deductions were disallowed on the ground that the payments were contrary to public policy.

Prior to acquiring through merger various railroad lines, including the line on which the plaintiffs were employees, the defendant railroad entered into an agreement with several labor unions for the protection of the employees on the railroad lines which were to be acquired. The agreement provided that the employees of these lines would not be adversely affected in their employment as a result of the merger, and specific provisions were included for compensation of those employees, including the plaintiffs, whose postmerger earnings would be lower than their premerger earnings. In its order approving the merger, the Interstate Commerce Commission stated that the agreement respecting the rights of the employees was made pursuant to and in conformity with 5(2)(f) of the Interstate Commerce Act, which provides that as a condition to the Commission's approval of a railroad merger, the Commission shall require a fair and equitable arrangement to protect the interests of the employees affected by the merger, and that in the order of approval of the merger, the Commission shall include terms and conditions providing that the merger will not result in such employees being in a worse position with respect to their employment. After the merger went into effect, the plaintiffs were not paid the compensation promised, and when they were about to obtain arbitration, their union and the defendant entered into a new agreement which reduced substantially the compensation payable to the plaintiffs. The union refused to arbitrate the plaintiffs' claim that they were entitled to the compensation provided under the premerger agreement, and the plaintiffs then sued for damages in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio. The District Court held the postmerger agreement invalid and upheld the plaintiffs' right of action (287 F Supp 221, 309 F Supp 575). The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (436 F2d 841).

In May 1978 the National Labor Relations Board found that a local union (Local) had violated 8(b)(1)(A) and (2) of the National Labor Relations Act (29 USCS 158(b)(1)(A), (2)) by discriminating against nonmembers in its hiring hall referral practice and ordered the Local to compensate the charging parties and other similar situated employees for earnings lost because of discrimination. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit granted enforcement of the Board's order in May 1973, and the Board then began preparation of a backpay specification. In April 1982, as no backpay specification had yet issued, the Local filed a motion seeking relief from that portion of the Court of Appeals order that directed backpay for nonmember applicants similarly situated as the charging parties and the Court of Appeals denied the motion without prejudice to renew such motion after 90 days. The Local renewed the motion and the Court of Appeals ordered the Board to enter its formal backpay specification by a specific date. To meet the deadline set by the court order, the Board prepared a specification based upon projected earnings. After the Board submitted the specification on December 21, 1982, the Local filed its third motion requesting the court to require backpay only for the named parties, and contended that since the Board's backpay specification was not based upon actual earnings, it was inconsistent with the Board's rules and with the Board's original backpay order. The Court of Appeals then modified the Board's order to require that the Local tender backpay only to the charging parties and only as calculated by the backpay specification of December 21, 1982, giving as its justification for modifying the Board's order the length of time that had elapsed since the entry of the court's original judgment.

In a union's complaint before the National Labor Relations Board, an employer was charged with committing an unfair labor practice by inaugurating a premium pay plan during the term of a collective bargaining agreement, without prior consultation with the union. The agreement provided that although wages under the classified wage scale were closed for the term of the agreement, the employer reserved the right to pay a premium rate over and above the classified wage rate to reward a particular employee for some special fitness, skill, aptitude, or the like, and the agreement also provided that the employer and the union would not be obligated to bargain collectively with respect to any subject matter not specifically referred to or covered in the agreement, but the agreement contained no arbitration clause. The Board issued a cease and desist order against the employer, rejecting the claim that the employer's action--granting premium pay to all members of certain crews if the crews met specified production standards--was authorized by the agreement. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit refused to enforce the Board's order, holding that since the provisions of the agreement arguably allowed the employer to institute the premium pay plan, the question whether the agreement positively sanctioned the employer's action was a matter for adjudication by the courts, in the absence of an arbitration clause, and that the Board therefore lacked jurisdiction to entertain the unfair practice charges. (351 F2d 224.)

A British drug manufacturer held an American patent on the dosage form of griseofulvin, a fungicide, and another British drug manufacturer held an American patent on a microsize dosage form of griseofulvin. The two manufacturers made a patent pooling agreement containing certain restrictions on the sale of bulk-form griseofulvin. Similar bulk-sale restrictions were contained in sublicensing agreements made by the two manufacturers with three American drug companies. In a civil antitrust action in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, the United States Government sought to enjoin enforcement of the bulk-sale restrictions on the ground that they involved unreasonable restraints of trade, in violation of 1 of the Sherman Act. Also, the government challenged the validity of the American patents which had been obtained by the British manufacturers. The District Court held that the bulk-sales restrictions constituted per se violations of 1 of the Sherman Act, but that since the manufacturers were not relying on the patents in defense of the government's antitrust claims, the government could not challenge the validity of the patents (302 F Supp 1). Although the District Court granted the government's request for injunctive relief against future violations, the District Court denied the government's request that the manufacturers be ordered (1) to make bulk sales on reasonable and nondiscriminatory terms and prices to all bona fide applicants, and (2) to grant reasonable-royalty licenses for the manufacture of griseofulvin (328 F Supp 709).

The Department of Pensions and Security of Alabama--a state participating in the Federal Government's Aid to Families With Dependent Children Program (AFDC)--issued a so-called "substitute father" regulation which denied AFDC payments to children of a mother who "cohabits" in or outside her home with any single or married man. The present class action, instituted in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama, sought declaratory and injunctive relief against enforcement of this regulation. A three-judge District Court granted relief, finding the regulation to be inconsistent with the Social Security Act and the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. (277 F Supp 31.)

An instructor at a foreign language institute, an agency of the Federal Government, obtained a newly reopened "course developer" position through a competitive examination process.
