Another instructor, who had held that position prior to its abolition 5 years earlier and had declined to take the examination, filed a grievance alleging that he should have been assigned the position without a competitive process and that the appointment of the first instructor violated the institute's collective bargaining agreement with the union representing its professional employees. The union arbitrated on behalf of the second instructor, who was a member of its board, and successfully argued that the position should be declared vacant for refilling, whereupon the first instructor, who was not a union member but was a member of the bargaining unit represented by the union, was demoted, and the second instructor won the position through a new examination. The union refused to prosecute the first instructor's grievance against the institute because of a perceived conflict of interest with its previous advocacy of the second instructor, and the first instructor filed unfair labor practice charges with the Federal Labor Relations Authority (FLRA) in which he alleged that the union had breached its duty of fair representation under a provision of Title VII of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA) (5 USCS 7114(a)(1)). The FLRA's General Counsel upheld that charge and directed that a complaint be issued against the union, but the union entered into a settlement with the FLRA whereby the union posted a notice guaranteeing representation to all employees seeking a single position. When the General Counsel rejected the first instructor's contention that the settlement provided him with no relief, the first instructor filed an action against the union in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, which held that (1) the case was judicially cognizable, because the CSRA's grant of exclusive union representation impliedly gives federal employees a private right of action to safeguard their right to fair representation, and (2) the union had breached its duty of fair representation (613 F Supp 440). The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed the judgment of the District Court and dismissed the case, as it held that the CSRA, by creating both the duty of fair representation and a remedy in the FLRA for infringement thereof (5 USCS 7118(a)(7)), precluded implication of a private right of action in the federal courts (821 F2d 1389).

The Washington statute that the felon was convicted of violating stated that, upon conviction, a defendant could be imprisoned for not more than five years, Wash. Rev. Code _ 69.50.401(a)(1)(ii)-(iv) (1994), but another provision specified that any person convicted of a second or subsequent offense could be imprisoned for a term up to twice the term otherwise authorized, Wash. Rev. Code _ 69.50.408(a). By virtue of the recidivist provision, the felon faced a maximum penalty of imprisonment for 10 years. At issue was whether the maximum term of imprisonment prescribed by law was the five-year ceiling for first offenses or the 10-year ceiling for second or subsequent offenses. The Court held that including the recidivist enhancement was compelled by the language of ACCA. The felon's textual argument was not faithful to the statutory text. The Court also rejected an argument based on the ACCA's manifest purpose because it rested on the erroneous proposition that a defendant's prior record of convictions had no bearing on the seriousness of an offense. It also rejected the argument that offenses that were not really serious would be included because of recidivist enhancements.

The petitioner, a mother of a minor child, filed an action in Florida state court on March 8, 1979, seeking custody of her son. On March 23, 1979, the respondent-father filed an action in Georgia state court also seeking custody. The Florida court entered a judgment on April 18, 1979, granting the mother custody, while the Georgia court entered a judgment on June 21, 1979, granting the father custody. On appeal, the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the lower Georgia court (245 Ga 650, 266 SE2d 463). In a certiorari petition filed in the United States Supreme Court, the petitioner raised the question whether Article IV, 1 of the United States Constitution demanded that Georgia give full faith and credit to a Florida decree rendered immediately prior to Georgia's acceptance of unqualified jurisdiction, and the petitioner alleged that she had properly raised this federal question in the Georgia state courts.

In 1971 the Indiana Legislature enacted a statute providing that a severed mineral interest that is not used for a period of 20 years automatically lapses and reverts to the current surface owner of the property, unless the mineral owner files a statement of claim in the local county recorder's office. The statute also provided for a two-year grace period from the date of its enactment, during which owners of such mineral interests could file their statements of claim. In addition, an exception to automatic lapse was built into the statute whereby an owner of 10 or more mineral interests in the same county, under certain circumstances, was entitled to 60 days within which to file a supplemental statement of claim after having received notice of lapse or having obtained actual knowledge of the lapse. Several owners and lessees of lapsed mineral interests, all owning less than 10 such interests within one county, filed actions challenging the constitutionality of the statute, claiming that, in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment, (1) the lack of prior notice of the lapse deprived them of property without due process of law, (2) the statute effected a taking of private property without just compensation, and (3) the exception for owners of 10 or more mineral interests denied them equal protection, and that, in violation of the contract clause of the United States Constitution (Art I, 10), the statute constituted an impairment of contracts. The Circuit Court of Gibson County, Indiana, held that the statute deprived the mineral interest owners of property without due process and was a taking of property without just compensation. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Indiana reversed, rejecting all of the claims of the mineral interest owners (406 NE2d 625).

The owner of a patent for fluxes used in electric welding and the process of welding by using them, brought suits for infringement in which both the District Court and the Court of Appeals found that the composition of the fluxes involved invention in view of the fact that their use eliminated glare, open arc, splatter, and to a great extent, smoke, permitted the welding of thicker plates, increased welding speeds, and produced welds of superior quality.

A corporation that operated stores in New York City brought, against a competitor in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, an action alleging that the competitor had violated (1) _ 1962(c) by failing to charge New York state sales tax to cash-paying customers--thus allowing the competitor to reduce its prices without affecting its profit margin--and submitting fraudulent state tax returns to conceal that conduct, and (2) _ 1962(a) by using funds generated by the fraudulent tax scheme to open a store that caused the corporation to lose business and market share.

A dealership contract, negotiated by an Alabama dealer and a corporate manufacturer of copier products with headquarters in New Jersey and significant corporate operations in New York City's borough of Manhattan, contained a forum-selection clause providing that "any appropriate state or federal district court" located in Manhattan would have "exclusive jurisdiction over any case or controversy arising under" the contract. In September 1984, the dealer brought an action against the manufacturer in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Alabama, on both diversity of citizenship and federal question jurisdictional grounds, alleging breach of the dealership contract, breach of warranty, fraud, and federal antitrust violations arising out of the dealer-manufacturer contractual relationship. In response, the manufacturer moved, pursuant to the forum-selection clause, to transfer the action under 28 USCS 1404(a) to the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, which is located in Manhattan. The District Court denied the manufacturer's motion to transfer, refusing to enforce the forum-selection clause, based in part on its conclusion that state law--in this case, Alabama law, which deemed such clauses contrary to public policy--governed the clause's enforceability. On interlocutory appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, on rehearing en banc, reversed the District Court, concluding that the forum-selection clause was in all respects enforceable generally as a matter of federal law (810 F2d 1066).

The San Antonio Metropolitan Transit Authority (SAMTA), a public mass-transit authority that is the major provider of transportation in the San Antonio, Texas, metropolitan area, filed an action in the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas seeking a declaratory judgment that, contrary to the determination of the Wage and Hour Administration of the Department of Labor, its operations are constitutionally immune from the application of the minimum-wage and overtime requirements of the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) under National League of Cities v Usery (1976) 426 US 833, 49 L Ed 2d 245, 98 S Ct 2465, in which it was held that the commerce clause of the United States Constitution (Art I 8 cl 3) does not empower Congress to enforce such requirements against the states in areas of traditional governmental functions. The District Court entered judgment for SAMTA, holding that municipal ownership and operation of a mass-transit system is a traditional governmental function and thus, under National League of Cities, is exempt from the obligations imposed by the Fair Labor Standards Act (557 F Supp 445).

Pursuant to a West Virginia statute which imposed a gross receipts tax on persons, other than local manufacturers, selling tangible property at wholesale, the West Virginia Tax Department assessed a tax deficiency against a corporation for the corporation's wholesale sales of coal in West Virginia during a 5-year period. The state tax commissioner upheld the assessment. A few days before the corporation appealed to the Circuit Court of Kanawha County, West Virginia, the United States Supreme Court decided Armco, Inc. v Hardesty (1984) 467 US 638, 81 L Ed 2d 540, 104 S Ct 2620, in which the Supreme Court held that the imposition of the West Virginia tax discriminated against interstate commerce, in violation of the Federal Constitution's commerce clause (Art I, 8, cl 3). The Circuit Court then held the corporation's action in abeyance while the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals considered a similar challenge to the state tax in light of the Armco decision. After the Supreme Court of Appeals ruled in that case that the Armco decision did not apply retroactively, the Circuit Court upheld the assessment against the corporation, and the Supreme Court of Appeals denied review.

Under _ 8 (c) of the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940, the expiration of one year of reemployment of a veteran by his preservice employer does not terminate the veteran's right to the seniority to which he is entitled by virtue of the Act's treatment of him as though he had remained continuously in his civilian employment.

The writ of certiorari is dismissed as improvidently granted. The question in this case is whether or not the courts below correctly applied Rules 404(b) and 403 of the Federal Rules of Evidence in order to assure a fair trial below.

The patentee of a floor-to-ceiling "pole lamp" brought a patent infringement and unfair competition suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois against the retailer of substantially similar lamps. The District Court held the patents invalid for want of invention, but enjoined the retailer from unfairly competing by selling pole lamps identical to or confusingly similar to the patentee's lamps. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed on the ground that the likelihood of confusion as to the source of the products was sufficient to make out a case of unfair competition under Illinois law, without a showing that the retailer had palmed off its lamps as the patentee's lamps. (313 F2d 115.)

A writ of certiorari granted to review a judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit was dismissed as improvidently granted, for the reasons stated in the headnote below. A writ of certiorari granted an indigent prisoner on the assumption that a question involving the construction of 28 USC 2255 called for adjudication will be dismissed as improvidently granted, where, after argument, it becomes clear that the question of construction is not appropriately presented by the record because petitioner's claim upon the merits was fully considered and decided below, and his challenge of that action is so insubstantial as not to have warranted the grant of the writ.

An employer and a CIO union, the authorized bargaining representative of the employees, entered into a closed shop contract of indefinite duration, providing that, with certain exceptions not material to the litigation, the employer should employ no workers other than members of the union. Upon demand by the union the employer discharged employees who were expelled from the union because, shortly after the making of an agreement supplementing the closed shop contract, they engaged in activities in behalf of a rival union. The National Labor Relations Board, relying upon the doctrine of Rutland Court Owners, 44 NLRB 587, 46 NLRB 1040, found that the employer had committed an unfair labor practice in violation of 8(1) and 8(3) of the National Labor Relations Act. The Board took the view that, by virtue of the indefinite term of the contract, which had run for more than four years, the discharged employees had undertaken to oust the CIO as their bargaining representative at a period during which it was appropriate to seek a redetermination of representatives, and that for this reason the employer was not permitted to discharge them, the valid closed shop contract notwithstanding. The court of appeals enforced the Board's order.

Alaska adopted a constitutional amendment establishing a fund into which the state must deposit at least 25 percent of its mineral income each year. The Alaska legislature enacted a dividend program to distribute annually a portion of the fund's earnings directly to the state's adult residents. Under the plan, each citizen 18 years of age or older would receive one dividend unit for each year of residency subsequent to 1959, the first year of statehood. Plaintiffs, residents of Alaska since 1978, brought suit challenging the dividend distribution plan. The Superior Court for Alaska's Third Judicial District granted summary judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, holding that the plan violated the rights of interstate travel and equal protection. The Supreme Court of Alaska reversed and upheld the statute (619 P2d 448).

In a stockholder's derivative action brought in a Federal court on the ground of diversity of citizenship, the trial court denied the defendant's motion to require that the plaintiff give security, as provided in a state statute, which also made such a stockholder liable for the reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, to which he put the corporation and other defendants, if he did not make good his claim.

A California resident employed by an interstate autobus company was killed while driving a bus of his employer in Arizona. A claim for workmen's compensation was denied by the Arizona Industrial Commission on the ground that the deceased was not regularly employed in Arizona as that term is used in the Arizona compensation statute. Upon certiorari, the Supreme Court of Arizona, rejecting the Commission's construction of the statute, held that the commerce clause of the Federal Constitution precluded recovery under the Arizona statute because the employee was covered by the California statute and to require his interstate employer to insure also in Arizona would place an undue burden on interstate commerce.

The city of Indianapolis operated a checkpoint program under which the police, acting without individualized suspicion, stopped a predetermined number of vehicles at roadblocks in various locations on city roads for the primary purpose of the discovery and interdiction of illegal narcotics. Under the program, at least one officer would (1) approach each vehicle, (2) advise the driver that he or she was being stopped briefly at a drug checkpoint, (3) ask the driver to produce a driver's license and the vehicle's registration, (4) look for signs of impairment, and (5) conduct an open-view examination of the vehicle from the outside. In addition, a narcotics-detection dog would walk around the outside of each stopped vehicle. Two motorists who had been stopped at such a checkpoint filed suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana on behalf of themselves and a class of all motorists who had been stopped or were subject to being stopped in the future at the Indianapolis checkpoints. One of the claims asserted in the suit was that the checkpoint program violated the Federal Constitution's Fourth Amendment. The District Court, in denying the motorists' motion for a preliminary injunction, concluded that the program did not violate the Fourth Amendment (38 F Supp 2d 1016). The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed, on the grounds that (1) the program was meant to intercept a completely random sample of drivers, (2) there was neither probable cause nor articulable suspicion to stop any given driver, and (3) the program did not fit any of the exceptions allowed under the Fourth Amendment (183 F3d 659).

A lawyer having both a general practice and law offices in Kansas and Missouri brought an action in mandamus in a Kansas state court to compel a judge of a Kansas probate court to permit him to try cases in the probate court without the appearance or association of Kansas counsel, and to declare unconstitutional as contravening the Fourteenth Amendment of the Federal Constitution a Kansas statute and rules of court providing in substance that an attorney admitted to the Kansas bar, who has also been admitted to the bar of another state and who is regularly engaged in the practice of law in that state, must associate local counsel before he can appear in the courts or before boards or commissions of Kansas. The Kansas District Court quashed the writ and the Supreme Court of Kansas affirmed. (187 Kan 473, 357 P2d 782.)

In a suit for damages under the Federal Employers' Liability Act for the death of a railroad employee, held that there was no evidence in the record, nor any inference which reasonably could be drawn from the evidence, when viewed in a light most favorable to plaintiff, which could sustain a recovery.

The Fifth Circuit appeared have concluded that Batson supported its decision because Batson required a judge ruling on an objection to a peremptory challenge to undertake a sensitive inquiry into such circumstantial and direct evidence of intent as may be available. This general requirement, however, did not clearly establish the rule on which the Fifth Circuit's decision rested. Batson noted the need for a judge ruling on an objection to a peremptory challenge to take into account all possible explanatory factors in the particular case. Thus, where the explanation for a peremptory challenge was based on a prospective juror's demeanor, the judge should take into account, among other things, any observations of the juror that the judge was able to make during the voir dire. But Batson plainly did not go further and hold that a demeanor-based explanation must be rejected if the judge did not observe or cannot recall the juror's demeanor. Nor did was such a rule in established Snyder v. Louisiana. The Court held that no decision of the Court clearly established the categorical rule on which the Fifth Circuit appeared to have relied.

The judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded to the United States Court of [**1519]  Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit for further consideration in light of Teague v. Lane, ante, p. 288.-dissenting opinion is written. This is a second application for federal habeas corpus relief that raises both old and new grounds. On the new grounds, they allege that a change in the law permits them to present these new claims for the first time in a second or subsequent application. It's the Petitioner's position that the failure of the Respondent to include these so-called new claims in his first application was inexcusable neglect and, therefore, this application should have been dismissed as an abuse of the writ.

Petitioner joined an ongoing enterprise distributing ecstasy while in college, but he withdrew from the conspiracy after seven months and ceased all drug activity. Three and one-half years after withdrawing from the conspiracy, petitioner pled guilty to his participation. The court of appeals characterized the difference between the sentence of probation and the bottom of petitioner's advisory Guidelines range of 30 months as "extraordinary," and it held that the variance was not supported by extraordinary circumstances. Although the Court agreed that the court of appeals could take the degree of variance into account and consider the extent of a deviation from the Guidelines, the Court held that the court of appeals erred in requiring "extraordinary" circumstances. The court of appeals' rule requiring "proportional" justifications for departures was not consistent with Booker. Under the deferential abuse-of-discretion standard that applied to review of sentencing decisions, the Court found that the court of appeals failed to give due deference to the district court's reasoned and reasonable decision that the 18 U.S.C.S. _ 3553(a) factors justified the sentence of probation.

A railroad which had condemned Iowa land for railroad use, pursuant to a state statute permitting such condemnation, filed a complaint in a federal District Court, alleging diversity of citizenship, and seeking to have the assessment of damages resulting from the condemnation reduced. The railroad also filed an appeal from the assessment in a state court (the Iowa condemnation statute providing for state court review of such assessments), and then filed a petition to remove the cause to the federal District Court. The landowner moved to dismiss the railroad's original complaint, and to remand the case removed.

A provision of the Missouri Constitution authorized the creation of a "board of freeholders" to propose a reorganization plan for St. Louis County and the city of St. Louis and further provided that (1) nine members of the board were to be "electors" of the city, to be appointed by the mayor; (2) nine were to be "electors" of the county, to be appointed by the county executive; and (3) one was to be an "elector" of some other county, to be appointed by the governor. In selecting appointees, the appointing officials proceeded on the premise that board members had to be owners of real property--"freeholders"--and the mayor withdrew one of his original nominees, a priest who had served in prestigious posts at a local university, because the man did not own real property. A state legislator and others filed a class action in the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri on behalf of Missouri residents who did not own real property, which action sought a declaration that the provision, by restricting board membership to real-property owners, violated the equal protection clause of the Federal Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment both on its face and as applied. The defendants in that action, including the appointing officials and the board members, (1) filed an action in the Circuit Court of St. Louis County, Missouri seeking a declaratory judgment that the provision did not violate the Federal Constitution; (2) argued in both actions that, contrary to their earlier assumption, the provision required not that board members be real-property owners, but only that they be "electors"; and (3) urged the District Court to abstain from adjudicating the merits of the case while the state action was pending in the Circuit Court, on the basis of their contention that the meaning of the term "freeholder" was an unsettled question of state law. The District Court refused to abstain from deciding the case and ruled that the provision violated the equal protection clause by imposing a qualification which was irrelevant to the competency of potential board members (681 F Supp 1422). The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, however, reversed and held that the District Court should have abstained (855 F2d 856). The Circuit Court thereafter upheld the validity of the provision, as it ruled that (1) in public law, as opposed to property law, the term "board of freeholders" was equivalent to a "board of commissioners," and (2) even if the provision did impose the alleged requirement, it might not violate the equal protection clause. The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed that judgment, on the ground that the equal protection clause did not apply in this case because the board did not exercise any general governmental powers (757 SW2d 591).

A thirty-eight year old Mexican farmhand, who could neither speak nor write English, while being detained by the police in Texas, at the request of the United States Immigration Service, without a charge and arraignment, confessed to killing his paramour in Nebraska. A few days after he had been transported into Nebraska, he repeated his confession. Fifteen days after his arrival he was brought before a magistrate before whom he pleaded guilty. A few days afterwards counsel was appointed for him. At his trial both confessions and his plea of guilty were admitted in evidence. His conviction of manslaughter was affirmed by the Supreme Court of Nebraska. Although the defendant had testified that he had been maltreated and threatened with violence while being detained in Texas, he challenged the judgment on the sole ground that the confessions and plea were inadmissible because obtained during a period of twenty-five days illegal detention before being brought before a magistrate and before appointment of counsel.

Pursuant to the New York unemployment insurance law authorizing the payment of benefits to a claimant whose loss of employment is caused by a "strike, lockout, or other industrial controversy in the establishment in which he was employed," approximately 33,000 employees of four companies received more than $ 49 million in unemployment insurance benefits while they were out of work during a prolonged strike called against the four companies by the union to which the employees belonged. A substantial part of the cost of the $ 49 million in benefits paid by the state was ultimately imposed upon the four companies, since New York's unemployment insurance system is financed primarily by employer contributions based on the benefits paid to former employees of each employer in past years. The four companies brought an action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, claiming that the New York law authorizing the payment of unemployment compensation benefits to strikers conflicted with federal law. The District Court, concluding that the availability of unemployment compensation was a substantial factor in a worker's decision regarding a strike and had a measurable impact on the progress of a strike, held that the payment of unemployment compensation to strikers conflicted with the policy of free collective bargaining established in federal labor laws and violated the supremacy clause of the United States Constitution (Art VI, cl 2) (434 F Supp 810). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed on appeal, holding that although the New York unemployment compensation law conflicted with federal labor policy, such conflict was one which Congress had decided to tolerate in view of the legislative histories of the National Labor Relations Act (29 USCS 151 et seq.) and Title IX of the Social Security Act (26 USCS 3301 et seq., 42 USCS 501 et seq. and 1101 et seq.) (566 F2d 388).

Under the Assignment of Claims Act of 1940, payments to an assignee of any claim arising under a War or Navy Department contract were, if the contract so provided, free from reduction or setoff for an indebtedness of the assignor to the United States arising independently of such contract. A corporation engaged in work for the Navy Department, under a contract containing an anti-setoff provision, assigned the proceeds to a bank to which, subsequent to the termination of the contract, the government refused to pay the amount due to the assignor under the contract. The refusal was grounded upon the government's claim that the assignor, by his failure to pay federal taxes withheld from the wages of employees engaged in work under the contract, had incurred an indebtedness which was not one arising independently of the contract and was thus not within the scope of the Assignment of Claims Act. In a suit by the assignee in the Court of Claims, the government's contentions were sustained.

In a proceeding for the reorganization of a railroad under _ 77 of the Bankruptcy Act, the reorganization court confirmed a report of a special master finding that (1) certain proofs of claim of New Jersey for taxes were properly filed by state officers acting in pursuance of their statutory authority, (2) _ 77 confers on the reorganization court jurisdiction over the kind of claims asserted by the State in the proceeding, and such construction of the Act is not unconstitutional, and (3) the entire property of the debtor is in custodia legis, subject to the rights of lienholders, and the reorganization court is the proper court to determine the validity and amount of the tax claims, subject to certain limitations.

Workers who had been injured in a mine accident in Arizona brought, against the United States on the basis of federal mine inspectors' alleged negligence, a suit under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) (28 U.S.C.S. __ 1346, 2671 et seq.), which in 28 U.S.C.S. _ 1346(b)(1), authorized private tort actions against the United States "under circumstances where the United States, if a private person, would be liable to the claimant in accordance with the law of the place where the act or omission occurred."

A particular pesticide had been registered by the pesticide's manufacturer with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), purportedly pursuant to the latter's authority under FIFRA. Some Texas peanut farmers alleged that in the 2000 growing season, their crops had been severely damaged by the application of this pesticide. The manufacturer filed a declaratory-judgment action in a Federal District Court, asserting that the farmers' claims were expressly or impliedly pre-empted by FIFRA. The farmers brought a variety of counterclaims under state law. However, the District Court granted a motion by the manufacturer for summary judgment, as the court (1) rejected one claim on state-law grounds, and (2) dismissed the remainder as expressly pre-empted by _ 136v(b).

Motion for leave to use as part of the record the printed record heretofore filed with this Court in No. 48, October Term, 1955, _[*952]_ granted. Petition for writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit granted.

In separate complaint proceedings, the National Labor Relations Board held that locals of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers violated 29 USCS 158(b)(1)(B) by disciplining their members who were supervisors for crossing union picket lines to perform work for the employers which would otherwise have been performed by striking nonsupervisory employees (192 NLRB 85, 193 NLRB 30). The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, after consolidating the cases and considering them en banc, denied enforcement of the NLRB's orders (159 US App DC 272, 487 F2d 1143).

A motor carrier, licensed under the Federal Motor Carrier Act as a contract carrier, was ordered by the Interstate Commerce Commission to cease operations as a common carrier, the Commission taking the views (1) that the carrier had not sufficiently specialized its operations, and (2) that advertising by the carrier which did not indicate whether it was a common carrier or a contract carrier, as well as active solicitation of business, established that the carrier had held itself out as a common carrier.

A deceased serviceman's father, who was named as beneficiary in his son's policy under the National Service Life Insurance Act, died without having received any part of the policy's proceeds. His second wife, who was the insured's stepmother, and his former wife, who was the insured's natural mother, filed claims to the proceeds. During the pendency of an action for determination of the proper taker, the stepmother also died. The issue in the present case concerns the distribution of the proceeds under the act of 1940, prior to its 1946 amendment. The District Court awarded to the father's estate the instalments which had matured during his lifetime. The court found that both the stepmother and the natural mother were parents who "last bore that relationship" and thus qualified to take the remaining proceeds by devolution under 602(h) (3) (C) of the act. The instalments which had matured during the stepmother's lifetime were divided equally between her estate and the natural mother; instalments thereafter maturing were awarded to the natural mother alone. The Court of Appeals agreed.

A married couple filed against the United States and the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) a suit asserting, among other claims, that the CIA had violated the couple's due process rights by failing to provide the couple with financial assistance that the CIA had promised in return for the couple's espionage services during the Cold War. The United States District Court for the Western District of Washington (1) dismissed some of the couple's claims; (2) denied the government's motion to dismiss on the basis of Totten; and (3) ruled that the due process claims could proceed ( 99 F. Supp. 2d 1284).

Colorado permits its citizens to place propositions on the ballot through an initiative process. Under state law, (1) each initiative measure must be submitted to state officials for the preparation of an approved draft, (2) proponents of the measure must obtain the necessary signatures on an initiative petition within 6 months after the preparation of the draft, (3) it is a crime to forge a signature on a petition, to make false or misleading statements relating to a petition, or to pay someone to sign a petition, and (4) persons who circulate petitions for signatures must sign affidavits attesting to the validity of each signature. In addition, state law made it a felony to pay any person, corporation, or association to circulate an initiative petition. In 1984, proponents of an amendment to the Colorado Constitution that would have removed motor carriers from the jurisdiction of the state public utilities commission brought an action under 42 USCS 1983 against state officials. In the action, the proponents sought a declaration that the prohibition against the use of paid circulators violated the proponents' rights under the Federal Constitution's First and Fourteenth Amendments. The District Court upheld the prohibition, and a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed, but on rehearing en banc, the Court of Appeals reversed, on the grounds that (1) the prohibition impeded the proponents' opportunity to disseminate their views to the public, and (2) various justifications asserted by the state were inadequate to support the prohibition (828 F2d 1446).

A Louisiana corporation, with its principal place of business and department store outlets located within Louisiana, contracted with companies outside Louisiana to design and print merchandise catalogs over a 3-year period. Approximately 82% of the catalogs were directly mailed during the period, at the corporation's cost, from the out-of-state cities where the printing was done to residents of Louisiana. The corporation did not pay any sales tax where the catalogs were designed or printed. The Louisiana Department of Revenue and Taxation, upon auditing the corporation's tax returns for the 3 years within the period, assessed the corporation for delinquent use taxes, under two state statutes which imposed a tax on the use of tangible personal property items, at the rate of 3% of the catalogs' cost price. When the corporation refused to pay the assessed use tax on the catalogs, the state filed an action in Louisiana Civil District Court to collect the tax. The District Court, holding that the corporation was liable for the assessed use taxes, rejected the corporation's contention that the imposition of use taxes on the catalogs violated the Federal Constitution's commerce clause. The Louisiana Court of Appeal, Fourth Circuit, affirmed the judgment of the District Court (505 So 2d 102). The Supreme Court of Louisiana denied review (506 So 2d 1224).

Following a decision by the United States District Court for the Western District of Texas concerning the constitutionality of multimember election districts in Texas (378 F Supp 640), new apportionment legislation was passed in Texas providing for the replacement of the multimember districts by single-member districts.

A judgment creditor of an incompetent Air Force veteran attached two accounts in federal savings and loan associations which had been established by the veteran's committee with funds received from the Veterans' Administration as disability compensation to the veteran. The United States District Court for the District of Columbia quashed the attachments on the ground that the funds in the accounts were exempt from attachment under 38 USC 3101(a), which provides that payments of benefits due or to become due under any law administered by the Veterans' Administration shall be exempt from the claims of creditors and shall not be liable to attachment, levy, or seizure by or under any legal or equitable process whatever, either before or after receipt by the beneficiary. (185 F Supp 302.) The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia reversed. (111 App DC 267, 296 F2d 389.)

The defendant was convicted of murder upon trial in an Alabama state court, and the conviction was affirmed by the Supreme Court of Alabama, as against the defendant's contention that his rights under the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment had been violated by the use in evidence of alleged coerced written confessions, which had been obtained 5 days after the defendant had been shot upon being captured, and while the defendant was in a prison hospital. (280 Ala 283, 193 So 2d 505.)

The employees of a taxicab operator went out on strike on the day the local city council was to consider the renewal of the operator's franchise, and the council ultimately decided to reject any renewal or extension of the franchise while leaving open the possibility that the matter could be reopened if the labor dispute were settled before the franchise expired. The franchise subsequently expired by its own terms. The taxicab operator filed suit against the city in the United States District Court for the Central District of California, alleging that the city's action was pre-empted by the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), and seeking declaratory and injunctive relief and damages. After a series of decisions and appeals on other issues, the District Court granted summary judgment in favor of the city. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that the city's action was not pre-empted under the NLRA because (1) there was nothing in the record to indicate that the city's action was not concerned with transportation, a concern which does not implicate or conflict with federal labor policy, and (2) in order to avoid undue restriction of the local regulation of utilities, only actions seeking to directly alter the substantive outcome of a labor dispute, which the city had not done, should be pre-empted (754 F2d 830).

An employee of the Nevada human resources department sought leave to care for his ailing wife under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) (29 USCS _ 2601 et seq.), which (1) in 29 USCS _ 2612(a)(1)(C), entitled some private and public employees to unpaid leave of up to 12 workweeks per 12-month period to care for a family member who had a serious health condition; (2) in 29 USCS _ 2617(a)(2), enabled employees to seek damages "against any employer (including a public agency) in any Federal or State court of competent jurisdiction;" and (3) in 29 USCS _ 2611(4)(A)(iii), defined "public agency" to include state governments, their agencies, and their political subdivisions. The department granted the employee the full 12 weeks of FMLA leave, but eventually informed him that he had exhausted the 12 weeks and had to return to work. He failed to return and was terminated. The employee brought in the United States District Court for the District of Nevada, against the department and two of its officers, a suit seeking damages and injunctive and declaratory relief for, among other things, violation of _ 2612(a)(1)(C). The District Court granted the department and the officers summary judgment on the grounds that (1) the FMLA claim was barred by the state's immunity, under the Federal Constitution's Eleventh Amendment, from suit in federal court; and (2) the employee's rights under the Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment had not been violated. The employee appealed, and, after the United States intervened to defend  [***954]  the applicability of the FMLA to the states, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed (273 F3d 844).

A derivative suit against a corporation, which was a citizen of Delaware, and other citizens of Delaware and California, was instituted in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California, Central Division, by a shareholder who was a citizen of New York. The suit was based on alleged fraudulent wastage of assets of the corporation. Defendants contended that since the cause of action sought to be enforced belonged to the corporation and the corporation was not antagonistic to the stockholder, the corporation was properly to be aligned as a party plaintiff, thereby ousting diversity jurisdiction (since Delaware corporations would be on both sides of the suit). After a hearing on the question of the existence of antagonism, the District Court realigned the corporation as a party plaintiff and dismissed the suit (117 F Supp 781).

An armed robbery in Ohio left a victim dead and the victim's husband wounded. An accused admitted to participating in the robbery and to shooting the husband, but denied shooting the victim. The accused agreed to plead guilty to aggravated murder and attempted aggravated murder, and the state dropped other charges against him. With respect to the aggravated murder charge, the accused pleaded guilty to one of three capital specifications and was thus eligible for the death penalty. In an Ohio Court of Common Pleas, a contested penalty hearing was held in which the accused's principal mitigation argument was that (1) he had participated in the plot only at the urging and under the influence of an alleged accomplice, and (2) the accomplice had fired the fatal shots at the victim. Nevertheless, the court sentenced the accused to death. Subsequently, the accomplice was tried in the same court. Although the prosecutor claimed that the accomplice was the principal offender in the murder, the accomplice argued that the same prosecutor had taken a contrary position in the accused's case. A jury sentenced the accomplice to life imprisonment.

A dispute arose between a railroad and a labor union as to the railroad's obligation under their collective-bargaining agreement to give conductors extra pay for certain services. The railroad refused the demand of the union and commenced a declaratory judgment action in a state court. The union thereafter filed a petition for hearing and award before the Adjustment Board under the Railway Labor Act.

In 1964, following a trial in which the government introduced as part of its case numerous monthly wagering excise tax returns which had been filed by the accused, a jury in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana found the accused guilty of income tax evasion. In 1965, the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed his conviction (345 F2d 499) and the United States Supreme Court denied certiorari (382 US 824, 15 L Ed 2d 69, 86 S Ct 54). On January 29, 1968, the Supreme Court, overruling earlier decisions, held in Marchetti v United States, 390 US 39, 19 L Ed 2d 889, 88 S Ct 697, and Grosso v United States, 390 US 62, 19 L Ed 2d 906, 88 S Ct 709, that the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination was a valid defense to a prosecution for failure to register as a gambler and to pay wagering excise taxes. A few days later, the accused filed a motion under 28 USC 2255 to vacate his sentence and set aside his conviction on the basis of the Marchetti and Grosso decisions. The District Court, holding that the Marchetti and Grosso decisions were not retroactively applicable, denied the 2255 motion, and the Court of Appeals affirmed (411 F2d 504).

To prevent evasion of limitations upon the establishment of branch banks, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System attached to a bank's admission to the System a condition requiring it to withdraw upon notice if any interest in the bank should be acquired by a holding company without the Board's prior approval. Shares in the bank having been acquired by a holding company, but without subversion of the bank's independence. The bank advised the Board of Governors of the fact and requested that it be relieved of the condition. Upon the Board's refusal of the request, the bank, being apprehensive that the Board might invoke the condition, brought suit under the Declaratory Judgment Act to have the condition declared invalid. Thereafter the Board, having satisfied itself that the stock purchase by the holding company would not affect the bank's control declared that there was no present need in the public interest for invoking the condition.
The petition for writ of certiorari is granted. The judgment is vacated and the case is remanded for consideration in light of Goldlawr, Inc., v. Heiman, ante, p. 463.

After the United States Supreme Court's decision in Furman v Georgia (1972) 408 US 238, 33 L Ed 2d 346, 92 S Ct 2726--which held that the imposition of the death sentence under certain state statutes constituted cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments because under such statutes the juries had untrammeled discretion to impose or withhold the death penalty--the Louisiana legislature amended its statutes relating to murder and the death penalty. Under the new statutory scheme, (1) the death sentence is mandatory whenever the jury finds the defendant guilty of first-degree murder, (2) first-degree murder is defined to include the killing of a human being when the offender has a specific intent to kill or to inflict great bodily harm, and when the murder involves killing in connection with the commission of certain felonies, killing of a fireman or a peace officer in the performance of his duties, killing for remuneration, killing with the intent to inflict harm on more than one person, or killing by a person with a prior murder conviction or under a current life sentence, and (3) the jury in every first-degree murder case must be instructed on the crimes of first-degree murder, second-degree murder, and manslaughter, whether or not raised by the evidence or requested by the defendant, and must be provided with verdicts of guilty, guilty of second-degree murder, guilty of manslaughter, and not guilty. Upon a jury trial in a Louisiana state court under the new statutes, the defendant was convicted of first-degree murder for a killing which occurred during an armed robbery, and was sentenced to death. The Supreme Court of Louisiana affirmed (319 So 2d 317).

A city charter barred from employment persons who advise, advocate, or teach the violent overthrow of the government or who are members of or become affiliated with any group doing so. A city ordinance required every employee to take an oath that within a period subsequent to the enactment of the charter provision he has not been a member of or become affiliated with such a group, and also to execute an affidavit to the same effect, the affidavit, however, containing no time limitations. Some of the plaintiffs took the oath, but refused to execute the affidavit, the others refused to do both; all were discharged for such cause and sought reinstatement, raising various constitutional objections. Relief was denied in the state courts.

Appellee was indicted in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California with having violated 1 of the Elkins Act by having knowingly solicited from a freight forwarder rebates respecting interstate motor carrier shipments of the corporation of which appellee was transportation manager, but the indictment failed to allege that the rebate would have been for the benefit of the shipper. The District Court dismissed the indictment on the theory that the act applies only where some advantage or discrimination is practiced in favor of the shipper.

The defendant was indicted by the grand jury of Fulton County for violation of the anti-trespass law (Ga. L. 1960, p. 142; Code Ann. _ 26-3005) making it a misdemeanor for any person who refuses to leave the premises of another, "when requested to do so by the owner or any person in charge of said premises, as the agent or employee of such owner or person in charge," and was found guilty by a jury and duly sentenced by the trial judge. She excepts and assigns error on the overruling of the general demurrer, the denial of the plea in abatement, motion in arrest of judgment, and the motion for new trial, as amended.

Petitioner obtained a divorce from her husband in an Illinois state court with a judgment for monthly instalments of alimony until remarriage. Subsequently she married in Nevada a person who had on the same day obtained a Nevada divorce from his wife, a New York resident, who had not been served in Nevada nor appeared in the divorce proceedings. After this Nevada divorce decree had been declared void by a New York court having jurisdiction of the parties, petitioner obtained a valid New York decree against her second husband annulling her Nevada marriage and then married a third man. In the present case she invoked the diversity jurisdiction of a federal district court in Illinois in an action against her first husband for unpaid instalments of alimony for the period from her Nevada marriage to her New York marriage.

Under 28 USCS 1915, an indigent "person" is eligible to proceed in forma pauperis in federal courts without prepayment of fees. Also, the Dictionary Act (1 USCS 1) generally provides that in determining the meaning of any act of Congress, "unless the context indicates otherwise," the word "person" includes artificial entities such as corporations and associations. An association of California prison inmates filed a civil rights action in a Federal District Court against state correctional officials. The association, which claimed that it had been prohibited by the prison's warden from holding funds of its own, sought leave to proceed in forma pauperis, but the District Court--without expressly deciding whether the association was a "person" for purposes of 1915--denied the motion on the ground of an inadequate showing of indigency. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, reversing and ordering a remand, expressed the view that (1) the plain meaning of 1915, when read in conjunction with 1, indicated that associations could proceed in forma pauperis if they met the indigency requirements; and (2) the inmates' association had established its indigency such that the association ought to be permitted to proceed in forma pauperis in the case at hand (939 F2d 854).

A failure to report under 720 ILCS 5/31-6(a) was a separate crime, different from escape under section 5/31-6(a) and from failure to abide by the terms of home confinement. The behavior of failing to report seemed less likely to involve a risk of physical harm than escape. Moreover, escape and failure to report were listed separately and the behaviors were placed in two different felony classes of different degrees of seriousness. Failure to report was characterized by a failure to present oneself for detention on a specified occasion. It did not have as an element the use, attempted use, or threatened use of physical force against another for purposes of _ 924(e)(2)(B)(i) and did not involve conduct presenting a serious potential risk of physical injury to another. There was no reason to believe that an offender who failed to report was doing something that was posing a serious potential risk of physical injury under _ 924(e). Statistics showed only a small risk of physical violence for those who failed to report. The felon's crime fell outside the scope of ACCA's definition of "violent felony" in _ 924(e)(2)(B)(ii).

After leaving a Minneapolis, Minnesota apartment building which was considered by police officers to be a place of cocaine traffic, or a "crack house," the accused began walking toward a marked squad car in which two police officers were patrolling. Upon making eye contact with one of the officers, the accused abruptly halted, began walking in the opposite direction, and turned and entered an alley on the other side of the building. The officers pulled the squad car into the alley and ordered the accused to stop and submit to a patdown search. The search revealed no weapons, but the officer who conducted the search felt a small lump in the front pocket of the accused's nylon jacket. As the officer later testified, the officer examined the lump with his fingers, and "it slid and it felt to be a lump of crack cocaine in cellophane." The officer then reached into the pocket and retrieved a small plastic bag containing one fifth of one gram of crack cocaine. The accused was arrested and charged with possession of a controlled substance. Prior to trial in a Minnesota county court, the accused moved to suppress the cocaine. Denying the motion, the trial court ruled that (1) under Terry v Ohio (1968) 392 US 1, 20 L Ed 2d 889, 88 S Ct 1868, the officers were justified in (a) stopping the accused to investigate whether he might be engaged in criminal activity, and (b) frisking the accused to insure that he was not carrying a weapon; and (2) the officers' warrantless seizure of the cocaine, after the officer who searched the accused "formed the opinion" that the small lump was cocaine, was supported by "plain feel" and hence did not violate the Federal Constitution's Fourth Amendment. The accused was tried and found guilty. On appeal, the Minnesota Court of Appeals, reversing, (1) concluded that the seizure of the cocaine was unconstitutional under Terry v Ohio; and (2) declined to adopt a "plain feel" exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement (469 NW2d 462). On further appeal, the Supreme Court of Minnesota, affirming, expressed the view that (1) the "plain view" exception to the warrant requirement did not extend to the sense of touch; and (2) even if a "plain feel" exception was recognized, an examination of the record indicated that the officer who searched the accused did not immediately recognize the lump in the accused's pocket as cocaine, but rather that the officer determined that the lump was contraband only after squeezing, sliding, and otherwise manipulating the contents of the pocket, which the officer already knew contained no weapon (481 NW2d 840).

A group of unincorporated Wisconsin townships filed suit against an adjacent city in the United States District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin, alleging that the city had violated the Sherman Act (15 USCS 1 et seq.) by acquiring a monopoly over sewage treatment in the area and providing that service only to areas which were willing to be annexed by the city and to use its sewage collection services rather than those of the towns. The District Court ruled in favor of the city, pointing to a Wisconsin law which authorized cities providing sewage services to limit the unincorporated areas covered by their service unless ordered by the state to service certain areas, and holding that the city's conduct fell within the "state action" exemption from the federal antitrust laws. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed (700 F2d 376).

In a patent infringement suit by a research company in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, the defendant, a radio and television set manufacturer, counterclaimed for treble damages and injunctive relief, alleging antitrust violations consisting of both misuse of the research company's patents and a conspiracy in restraint of trade by the research company, its parent corporation, and Canadian, English, and Australian patent pools. Holding that the research company had misused its patents, the District Court awarded the manufacturer treble damages and injunctive relief against the research company; and further holding that the research company and its parent corporation had conspired in restraint of trade, the District Court, relying upon a pretrial stipulation that the research company and its parent corporation were to be considered as an entity for purposes of the litigation, awarded the manufacturer treble damages and injunctive relief against both the research company and its parent corporation (239 F Supp 51). On appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, affirming the treble damage award for patent misuse, but otherwise reversing the judgment of the District Court, (1) held that the District Court lacked jurisdiction over the research company's parent corporation, and that the stipulation relied upon by the District Court was an insufficient basis for entering judgment against the parent corporation, (2) modified in certain respects the District Court's injunction against patent misuse, (3) held that the manufacturer had failed to prove that it had sustained damage as a result of the conspiracy in restraint of trade, and (4) struck the injunction against the research company's participation in conspiracies restricting the manufacturer's trade in foreign markets (388 F2d 25).

An indictment filed in the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri charged the defendants with violating, by making sales below cost with the requisite predatory purpose, 3 of the Robinson- Patman Act (15 USC 13a) making it a crime to sell goods at "unreasonably low prices for the purpose of destroying competition or eliminating a competitor." The District Court dismissed the indictment on the ground that the statute was unconstitutionally vague.

An association of coal producers engaged in surface coal mining operations in Virginia, a number of member oil companies, and individual landowners brought a preenforcement challenge to the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (30 USCS 1201 et seq.) in the United States District Court for the Western District of Virginia, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief against various provisions of the Act. The plaintiffs alleged that provisions of the Act establishing an interim regulatory program violated the commerce clause of the United States Constitution (Art I, 8, cl 3), the equal protection and due process guarantees of the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment, the Tenth Amendment, and the just compensation clause of the Fifth Amendment. After a trial on the plaintiff's request for a permanent injunction, the District Court rejected their commerce clause, equal protection, and due process challenges to the Act, held that the Act operated to displace the state's freedom to structure integral operations in numerous areas of traditional functions and thus was in contravention of the Tenth Amendment, ruled that various provisions of the Act effected an uncompensated taking of private property in violation of the just compensation clause, and agreed with the plaintiffs' due process challenge to some of the Act's enforcement provisions (483 F Supp 425).

A Texas state teachers association, a local affiliate, and several individual members and employees of both organizations brought suit under 42 USCS 1983, in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, against a Texas school district and various district officials and alleged that the district's policy of prohibiting communications by or with teachers during the schoolday concerning employee organizations violated the plaintiffs' rights under the Federal Constitution's First and Fourteenth Amendments. On cross motions for summary judgment, however, the District Court rejected those claims in almost all respects, except that the District Court held to be unconstitutionally vague a requirement for school-principal approval of teacher meetings with union representatives after school hours--an issue the District Court said was of minor significance, since there was no evidence in the record to indicate that school officials had ever denied employee organizations the use of school premises during nonschool hours. The after-school-hours ruling was not appealed, but, on appeal as to other issues, a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, affirming in part, reversing in part, and ordering a remand, expressed the view that (1) the First Amendment did not require the school district to allow union representatives access to school facilities during school hours; but (2) it was unconstitutional for the district to prohibit (a) teacher-to-teacher speech promoting union activity during school hours, and (b) teacher use of internal mail and billboard facilities to discuss employee organizations (777 F2d 1046). The Court of Appeals denied a petition for rehearing and a suggestion for rehearing en banc (784 F2d 1113), and the United States Supreme Court summarily affirmed the Court of Appeals' judgment (479 US 801, 93 L Ed 2d 4, 107 S Ct 41). The plaintiff organizations, members, and employees then filed an application for the award of attorneys' fees pursuant to 42 USCS 1988, but the District Court ruled that the plaintiffs were not "prevailing parties" within the meaning of 1988 and were ineligible for any fee award, because, under a "central issue" test, the plaintiffs had not carried the "central issue" in the lawsuit or achieved the "primary relief sought." On appeal, the Court of Appeals affirmed, expressing the view that, under the "central issue" test, the plaintiffs were not prevailing parties eligible for a fee award under 1988, because, while the plaintiffs had succeeded on significant secondary issues, the main thrust of their lawsuit had been the desire to gain access to school campuses during school hours for outside representatives of employee organizations (837 F2d 190).

A prisoner in Montana's state prison, who had been trained by the prison as an inmate law clerk, offered to give legal advice to a fellow inmate who had been charged with assaulting a prison guard. Because the prisoner was precluded by prison regulations from visiting the fellow inmate directly, the offer was made by letter. The letter was intercepted and read by prison officials who sanctioned the prisoner, on the basis of the letter's content, for violating prison rules prohibiting insolence and interfering with due process hearings. The prisoner, alleging a violation of his rights under the First Amendment of the Federal Constitution, brought suit against prison officials, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief in the United States District Court for the District of Montana. The District Court, in granting summary judgment for the prison officials, concluded that there was a valid rational connection between the prison's inmate correspondence policy and the objectives of prison order, security, and inmate rehabilitation such as to render the regulations impinging on inmates' constitutional rights valid. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, in reversing, (1) reasoned that inmates have a First Amendment right to assist other inmates with their legal claims, and (2) concluded that the prison rules, as applied to the prisoner, impermissibly infringed his First Amendment rights (195 F3d 1121).

Agents of a union picketed a mill with the object of securing recognition as the collective bargaining representative of the employees, none of whom took part in the picketing. The pickets requested the driver of a truck of a neutral customer to turn back from an intended trip to the mill, which he sought to enter to obtain goods for his employer. The pickets also threw stones at the truck. A complaint charging the union with an unfair labor practice in violation of the secondary boycott sections of the National Labor Relations Act as amended by the Labor Management Relations Act was dismissed by the National Labor Relations Board. The Court of Appeals set aside the dismissal.

As a result of having deducted various nondeductible items on his income tax returns, the defendant, an attorney, was prosecuted in a Federal District Court under 7206(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. Section 7206(1) makes it a felony for any person to "willfully" make and subscribe, under penalties of perjury, any return, statement, or other document which he does not believe to be true and correct as to every material matter. The trial judge instructed the jury under 7206(1), but refused to grant a lesser-included-offense instruction under 7207 of the Code, which makes it a misdemeanor for any person to "willfully" deliver or disclose to the Secretary of the Treasury or his delegate any list, return, account, statement, or other document known by him to be fraudulent or to be false as to any material matter. The defendant was convicted under 7206(1), but the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that since the word "willfully" required less scienter under 7207 than under 7206(1), it was error to refuse a lesser-included-offense instruction (455 F2d 612).

After a company engaged in the business of renting automobile trailers had petitioned for a composition of creditors under Chapter XI of the Bankruptcy Act, the Securities and Exchange Commission filed a motion to dismiss the company's proceeding or, in effect, to transfer it to Chapter X of the Bankruptcy Act, involving corporate reorganization proceedings. The Commission's motion, based on the need for protecting the rights of widespread public investor-creditors of the company, was referred to a referee in bankruptcy as a special master, and the referee recommended that the motion be denied. The District Court, accepting and adopting the referee's findings, denied the motion, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed (325 F2d 47).

In a Louisiana trial court, a defendant was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death after the jury was instructed, in part, that it must acquit the defendant if it entertained a reasonable doubt as to any element necessary to constitute his guilt, but that this doubt must be such "as would give rise to a grave uncertainty" and must be "an actual substantial doubt," and that what is required is "a moral certainty." On appeal, the defendant contended that this instruction was improper; but the Supreme Court of Louisiana--while noting that the phrases "grave uncertainty" and "moral certainty," if taken out of context, might overstate the requisite degree of uncertainty and confuse the jury--determined that, taking the instructions as a whole, reasonable persons of ordinary intelligence would understand the definition of reasonable doubt (554 So 2d 39).

The Wisconsin Employment Relations Commission ordered a union to cease and desist from "authorizing, encouraging or condoning any concerted refusal to accept overtime assignments" after the termination of the previous collective bargaining agreement and during negotiations for a new agreement. The Circuit Court for Milwaukee County affirmed and entered judgment enforcing the Commission's order, and the Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed (67 Wis 2d 13, 226 NW2d 203).

After a corporation (National) had purchased 34 percent of the voting securities of another corporation (TSC), the two corporations issued to their shareholders a joint proxy statement recommending approval of a proposal for the exchange of TSC stock for National stock. A TSC corporate shareholder brought the instant action, in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, against both corporations, seeking money damages and restitution upon its claims, among others, that in violation of the SEC Rule 14a- 9 (CFR 240.14a-9)--which prohibits proxy solicitations containing any statement which is false or misleading with respect to any material fact, or which omits to state any material fact necessary in order to make the statements therein not false or misleading--the defendants omitted from their proxy statement material facts relating to the degree of National's control, at the time of the proxy solicitation, over TSC and the favorability of the terms of the proposal to TSC shareholders. The District Court denied the plaintiff's motion for partial summary judgment on the issue of the defendants' liability (361 F Supp 108), but the Court of Appeals for Seventh Circuit reversed the denial of summary judgment to the plaintiff on its 14a-9 claims (512 F2d 324).

The Victims of Crime Act of 1984, in establishing a federal source of funds for programs to compensate and assist crime victims, provided in part (1) in 42 USCS 10601(b)(2), that one of the sources from which these funds were to be derived were special assessments imposed under 18 USCS 3013 upon persons convicted of federal offenses; and (2) in 42 USCS 10601(c)(1), that if the total annual income to the fund from all sources exceeded a certain amount--initially $ 100 million--the excess would be deposited in the general fund of the United States Treasury. Section 10601(c)(1) went into effect only in 1 year, when total receipts for the fund exceeded the then-applicable cap by less than $ 9 million. A defendant who had been charged in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California with aiding the illegal entry of aliens into the United States, and had pleaded guilty to two misdemeanor counts concerning illegal immigration, was sentenced to probation by a federal magistrate and ordered to pay a special assessment of $ 25 on each count under 3013. The defendant moved to correct his sentence on the ground that the special assessments were unconstitutional because Congress had passed 3013 in violation of the Federal Constitution's origination clause (Art I, 7, cl 1), which requires that all bills for raising revenue originate in the United States House of Representatives. The magistrate denied the motion, and the District Court affirmed. On appeal, however, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit vacated the portion of the District Court's sentencing order that imposed the special assessments, as it determined that (1) the defendant's claim did not raise a nonjusticiable political question; and (2) 3013 was invalid because (a) the primary purpose of the special assessments was to raise revenue and not to finance victim assistance programs or to punish offenders, (b) 3013 was thus a bill for raising revenue within the meaning of the origination clause, and (c) 3013 had originated in the United States Senate (863 F2d 654).

After having repeatedly filed unsuccessful applications for admission to the bar of the state of New York, the petitioner filed the present application with the Appellate Division of the State Supreme Court requesting leave to file again an application for admission. The Appellate Division denied the petition without opinion. Before the New York Court of Appeals petitioner argued that he had been denied his constitutional rights in that he had been denied confrontation of his accusers and that he could not be sure of the reasons for which the committee investigating his character had refused to certify him for admission. The Court of Appeals, after oral argument, affirmed the order without opinion (11 NY2d 866, 227 NYS2d 682, 182 NE2d 288), subsequently amending its remittitur to recite that it necessarily passed upon the question whether petitioner had been denied due process of law in violation of the Federal Constitution.

In arrangement proceedings under Chapter XI of the Bankruptcy Act, the debtor was ordered by the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois to deposit into a special account for the United States Government the income and social security taxes withheld from the debtor's employees. The debtor withheld such taxes from its employees, but failed to deposit them into the special account. After the debtor was adjudicated a bankrupt, the government requested that the amount of the withheld taxes be treated as a trust fund entitled to priority over claims for the costs and expenses of administration of the bankruptcy proceedings. The referee in bankruptcy denied the government's request, the District Court upheld the referee's decision (302 F Supp 614), and the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed (419 F2d 1068).

An Illinois state trooper stopped a driver for speeding on a highway. When the trooper radioed the police dispatcher to report the stop, a second trooper overheard the transmission. Although the second trooper presumably had no information about the driver except that the driver had been stopped for speeding, the second trooper headed for the scene with a narcotics-detection dog. While the first trooper was writing a warning ticket, the second trooper walked the dog around the car, and the dog alerted at the trunk. On the basis of the alert, the troopers searched the trunk, found marijuana, and arrested the driver. The entire incident lasted less than 10 minutes.

A witness before a Kings County, New York, grand jury refused, on October 14, 1965, to answer questions put to him then, and continued his refusal notwithstanding a trial judge's finding and direction, on December 8, 1965, that the questions were proper and should be answered. The trial court found the witness guilty of "criminal contempt of court," sentenced him to 30 days, and fined him $ 250. After appellate proceedings proved fruitless, the witness offered to testify, but the offer was refused and the witness paid his fine and served his sentence. Later he was indicted for criminal contempt for failure to testify before the grand jury. The trial court dismissed the indictment on double jeopardy grounds, but the Appellate Division of the New York Supreme Court reversed, and the New York Court of Appeals sustained the reversal on the grounds that there were two acts of contempt--one before the grand jury and one before the trial judge--and that the previous commitment was for civil, and not criminal, contempt (29 NY2d 1, 323 NYS2d 161, 271 NE2d 694).
On Writ of Certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

A Belgian corporation which had entered into a joint business venture with an American corporation filed an action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York, asserting, inter alia, claims against the American corporation and two of its officers under 18 USCS 1964(c) of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) for alleged violations of 18 USCS 1962(c), based on predicate acts of mail and wire fraud. The District Court dismissed the RICO counts for failure to state a claim (574 F Supp 963). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed, holding that the complaint was defective (1) for failing to allege a "racketeering injury"--an injury "different in kind from that occurring as a result of the predicate acts themselves, or not simply caused by the predicate acts, but also caused by an activity which RICO was designed to deter," and (2) for not alleging that the defendants had already been criminally convicted of the predicate acts of mail and wire fraud, or of a RICO violation (741 F2d 482).

Individual foster parents and an organization of foster parents sued New York State and New York City officials in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, challenging the constitutionality of procedures governing the removal of foster children from foster homes. A three-judge District Court concluded that the preremoval procedures were constitutionally defective (418 F Supp 277).

Petitioners Xiulu Ruan and Shakeel Kahn are medical doctors licensed to prescribe controlled substances. Each was tried for violating 21 U. S. C. ¬ß841, which makes it a federal crime, ‚Äú[e]xcept as authorized[,] . . . for any person knowingly or intentionally . . . to manufacture, distribute, or dispense . . . a controlled substance.‚Äù A federal regulation authorizes registered doctors to dispense controlled substances via prescription, but only if the prescription is ‚Äúissued for a legitimate medical purpose by an individual practitioner acting in the usual course of his professional practice.‚Äù 21 CFR ¬ß1306.04(a). At issue in Ruan‚Äôs and Kahn‚Äôs trials was the mens rea required to convict under ¬ß841 for distributing controlled substances not ‚Äúas authorized.‚Äù Ruan and Kahn each contested the jury instructions pertaining to mens rea given at their trials, and each was ultimately convicted under ¬ß841 for prescribing in an unauthorized manner. Their convictions were separately affirmed by the Courts of Appeals.

The United States brought a civil antitrust suit in the Federal District Court for the Southern District of New York against an American sewing- machine manufacturer, alleging that the American manufacturer combined with its Swiss and Italian competitors to exclude Japanese zigzag sewing machines from the United States by cross-licensing agreements under which they did not oppose each other's patent applications and by the assignment of the Swiss manufacturer's application for a United States patent to the American manufacturer, for the purpose of the American manufacturer's suppression of infringing Japanese machines.
