The District Court dismissed, finding that the dominant and sole purpose of the cross-licensing agreement between the American and the Swiss manufacturer was to settle the conflict in priority between their patents, and that the secondary purpose of the agreement, and the only purpose disclosed to the Swiss manufacturer, was protection against Japanese machines infringing the Swiss manufacturer's patent. (205 F Supp 394.)

An Indiana state court (Lake Superior Court) entered a judgment distributing the assets in the hands of a testamentary trustee in disregard of a vesting order issued by the Attorney General of the United States pursuant to the Trading With the Enemy Act (50 USC Appx 1 et seq). The Appellate Court of Indiana affirmed, holding that the Attorney General improperly exercised his discretion in making the vesting order. (128 Ind App 628, 149 NE2d 214.)

In a decision rendered on January 19, 1959 (358 US 283, 3 L ed 2d 312, 79 S Ct 297), the United States Supreme Court ruled that the state of Ohio could not invalidate, as violative of its antitrust law, a provision of a collective bargaining contract between motor carriers and a teamsters' union, prescribing terms and conditions regulating the minimum rental and other terms of lease when a motor vehicle is leased to a carrier by an owner who drives the vehicle in the carrier's service, this being a subject of mandatory collective bargaining under the amended National Labor Relations Act, and thus within the rule that a state may not apply its antitrust law to prevent a union and an employer from carrying out portions of a collective bargaining contract between them dealing with a subject as to which the federal labor relations statutes direct them to bargain. On remand, the Court of Appeals of the State of Ohio, Ninth Judicial District, conformed to the Supreme Court's decision, in so far as the lessor of the motor vehicles, acting as a lessor-driver, was concerned; but the Ohio court barred enforcement against the lessor of provisions of the collective bargaining contract in so far as the lessor was acting as a lessor-employer (that is, leasing trucks driven by his employees). The Supreme Court of Ohio dismissed the union's appeal. (170 Ohio St 207, 163 NE2d 383.)

In a criminal trial for selling waste paper at a price above the ceiling fixed by Maximum Price Regulation 30 pursuant to _ 205 (b) of the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942, evidence that the defendant sold at a price above the ceiling by falsely describing the grade and that he accepted payment at the excessive price, held sufficient to support a conviction, although it also showed that the sales were subject to the right of customers to reject paper of lower grade than represented and that, in three out of five cases covered by a five-count information where customers objected and the Office of Price Administration had made an investigation, defendant subsequently adjusted the price to the ceiling price for the grade actually delivered. Pp. 210, 211.

he Child Online Protection Act (COPA) (47 USCS 231) prohibits any person from knowingly, in interstate or foreign commerce by means of the World Wide Web, making any communication for commercial purposes that is available to any minor and that includes any material that is harmful to minors. COPA defines "material that is harmful to minors" as any communication, picture, image, graphic image file, article, recording, writing, or other matter that is obscene or that (1) the average person, applying contemporary community standards, would find, taking the material as a whole and with respect to minors, is designed to appeal or pander to the prurient interest; (2) depicts, describes, or represents, in a manner patently offensive with respect to minors, an actual or simulated sexual act or sexual contact, an actual or simulated normal or perverted sexual act, or a lewd exhibition of the genitals or post-pubescent female breast; and (3) taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value for minors (47 USCS 231(e)(6)). One month before COPA was scheduled to go into effect, a group of organizations filed suit against the United States Attorney General in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania to challenge COPA's validity under the Federal Constitution's First Amendment. The organizations alleged a fear of prosecution under COPA on the ground that some sexually oriented material on the organizations' Web sites, although valuable for adults, could be construed as "harmful to minors" in some communities. The District Court, concluding that the organizations had established a likelihood of success on the merits, granted the organizations' motion for a preliminary injunction barring the Federal Government from enforcing COPA until the merits of the organizations' claims could be adjudicated (31 F Supp 2d 473). The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, in affirming, reasoned that COPA's use of "contemporary community standards" to identify material that was harmful to minors rendered COPA substantially overbroad (217 F3d 162).

Under California's three strikes law, a defendant who is convicted of a felony and has previously been convicted of two or more serious or violent felonies must receive an indeterminate life imprisonment term. Such a defendant becomes eligible for parole on a date calculated by reference to a minimum term, which, in this case, is 25 years. While on parole, petitioner Ewing was convicted of felony grand theft for stealing three golf clubs, worth $ 399 apiece. As required by the three strikes law, the prosecutor formally alleged, and the trial court found, that Ewing had been convicted previously of four serious or violent felonies. In sentencing him to 25 years to life, the court refused to exercise its discretion to reduce the conviction to a misdemeanor -- under a state law that permits certain offenses, known as "wobblers," to be classified as either misdemeanors or felonies -- or to dismiss the allegations of some or all of his prior relevant convictions. The State Court of Appeal affirmed. Relying on Rummel v. Estelle, 445 U.S. 263, 63 L. Ed. 2d 382, 100 S. Ct. 1133, it rejected Ewing's claim that his sentence was grossly disproportionate under the Eighth Amendment and reasoned that enhanced sentences under the three strikes law served the State's legitimate goal of deterring and incapacitating repeat offenders. The State Supreme Court denied review.

A passenger engineer employed by the National Railroad Passenger Corp. (Amtrak) was not a member of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers (BLE), which was the collective bargaining agent for Amtrak engineers, but instead belonged to the rival United Transportation Union (UTU). When an internal disciplinary hearing was convened pursuant to the BLE-Amtrak collective bargaining agreement to consider charges that the engineer had violated company work rules, the engineer requested that the UTU be allowed to represent him at the hearing. This request was denied on the ground that, under the collective bargaining agreement, only the BLE could represent engineers at such hearings. The engineer represented himself at the hearing and received a 30-day suspension. Instead of appealing this decision to the National Railroad Adjustment Board, where he would have been entitled to representation by the UTU, the engineer filed suit against Amtrak and the BLE in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts. In this action the engineer sought declaratory and injunctive relief on the claim that the denial of his request for UTU representation had violated his rights under 2, Eleventh (a) and (c) of the Railway Labor Act (RLA) (45 USCS 152, Eleventh), which (1) allows a railroad and a union representing its employees to enter into a union-shop agreement, but (2) requires that certain employees, including engineers, be allowed to satisfy the requirement of union membership by holding or acquiring membership in another union. The District Court dismissed the engineer's complaint following a bench trial; and the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit affirmed, holding that nothing in the language or legislative history of the RLA supported the contention that railroad operating employees have a statutory right to be represented by the union of their choice at company-level grievance or disciplinary proceedings (814 F2d 41).

A construction company, which had purchased concrete from a company which manufactured and sold ready-mixed concrete, filed a civil action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana against the cement manufacturer, alleging that the manufacturer and certain unnamed concrete firms had conspired to raise prices in violation of 1 of the Sherman Act (15 USCS 1) and seeking treble damages, plus attorney's fees, under 4 of the Clayton Act (15 USCS 15). Through discovery, the defendant manufacturer learned that certain other companies were the concrete producers that had participated in the alleged price-fixing scheme and filed a third-party complaint against the other manufacturers seeking contribution from them should it be held liable in the action filed by the construction company. The District Court dismissed the third-party complaint for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted, holding that federal law did not allow an antitrust defendant to recover in contribution from co-conspirators. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed, concluding that no common law rule of contribution should be fashioned by the courts (604 F2d 897).

Agreements between two customers and a brokerage firm which was registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission provided for arbitration of any controversy relating to the accounts the customers maintained with the firm. The customers filed a complaint with the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleging that the brokerage firm and its representative violated the antifraud provisions of 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 USCS 78j(b)) and SEC Rule 10b-5. The complaint also alleged a claim under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (18 USCS 1962(c)) (RICO). The brokerage firm moved to compel arbitration of the claims pursuant to 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act (9 USCS 3). The District Court granted the motion in part, holding that the Securities Exchange Act claims were arbitrable but that the RICO claim was not (618 F Supp 384). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed as to the RICO claim but reversed on the Securities Exchange Act claims (788 F2d 94).

Respondent was convicted of rape and related crimes. A few years before his scheduled release, prison officials ordered respondent to participate in a Sexual Abuse Treatment Program (SATP). As part of the program, participating inmates are required to complete and sign an "Admission of Responsibility" form, in which they accept responsibility for the crimes for which they have been sentenced, and complete a sexual history form detailing all prior sexual activities, regardless of whether the activities constitute uncharged criminal offenses. The information obtained from SATP participants is not privileged, and might be used against them in future criminal proceedings. There is no evidence, however, that incriminating information has ever been disclosed under the SATP. Officials informed respondent that if he refused to participate in the SATP, his prison privileges would be reduced, resulting in the automatic curtailment of his visitation rights, earnings, work opportunities, ability to send money to family, canteen expenditures, access to a personal television, and other privileges. He also would be transferred to a potentially more dangerous maximum-security unit. Respondent refused to participate in the SATP on the ground that the required disclosures of his criminal history would violate his Fifth Amendment privilege against compelled self-incrimination. He brought this action for injunctive relief under 42 U.S.C. _ 1983. The District Court granted him summary judgment. Affirming, the Tenth Circuit held that the compelled self-incrimination prohibited by the Fifth Amendment can be established by penalties that do not constitute deprivations of protected liberty interests under the Due Process Clause; ruled that the automatic reduction in respondent's prison privileges and housing accommodations was such a penalty because of its substantial impact on him; declared that respondent's information would be sufficiently incriminating because an admission of culpability regarding his crime of conviction would create a risk of a perjury prosecution; and concluded that, although the SATP served Kansas' important interests in rehabilitating sex offenders and promoting public safety, those interests could be served without violating the Constitution by treating inmate admissions as privileged or by granting inmates use immunity.

Certain individuals who were originally indicted in the Eastern District of Kentucky on two counts for violations of 18 USCS 371 and 545 obtained a change of venue to the Central District of California. In the latter district the government secured a superseding indictment charging four new substantive counts of making false statements to Customs officers in violation of 18 USCS 542, in addition to the two original counts. The government then obtained a voluntary dismissal of the original conspiracy count and two of the false statement counts. The defendants moved to dismiss the remaining counts on the ground that the superseding indictment manifested prosecutorial vindictiveness. The United States District Court for the Central District of California denied the defendants' motion, but stayed the commencement of the trial to permit an appeal. The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, ruling that the denial of a motion to dismiss based on the ground of vindictive prosecution is immediately appealable as a final decision under 28 USCS 1291, held that the defendants established a case of prosecutorial vindictiveness requiring dismissal of the superseding indictment (646 F2d 384).

In a prosecution in a state court for a state crime, the Fourteenth Amendment of the Federal Constitution does not forbid the admission of relevant evidence even though obtained by an unreasonable search and seizure. Pp. 25-33. (a) Arbitrary intrusion into privacy by the police is prohibited by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. (b) While the doctrine of Weeks v. United States, 232 U.S. 383, making evidence secured in violation of the Fourth Amendment inadmissible in federal courts is adhered to, it is not imposed on the States by the Fourteenth Amendment.

The investors alleged that the underwriters, during initial public offerings, unlawfully agreed with one another that they would not sell shares of a popular new issue to an investor unless that investor committed (1) to buy additional shares of that security later at escalating prices ("laddering"), (2) to pay unusually high commissions on subsequent security purchases from the underwriters, or (3) to purchase from the underwriters other less desirable securities ("tying"). The Court determined that the securities laws implicitly precluded the application of the antitrust laws to the conduct alleged because the securities laws were "clearly incompatible" with the application of the antitrust laws in this context since (1) the conduct was squarely within the heartland of securities regulations, (2) the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) had a clear and adequate authority to regulate the conduct, (3) the SEC actively enforced the rules and regulations regarding the conduct, and (4) there was a serious conflict between the antitrust and regulatory regimes. An antitrust action in this context would be accompanied by a substantial risk of injury to the securities markets.

In an action brought in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri by Missouri-licensed physicians to challenge the federal constitutionality of a Missouri statute excluding abortions that are not medically indicated from the purposes for which needy persons may obtain Medicaid benefits, the District Court granted the defendant state official's pre-trial motion to dismiss, holding that the physicians lacked standing (380 F Supp 1137). On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, holding that the physicians had standing and that the challenged statute was unconstitutional, reversed (508 F2d 1211).

A person claiming disability benefits under the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program established by Title XVI of the Social Security Act (42 USCS 1381 et seq.) was found by an administrative law judge (ALJ) not to be disabled within the meaning of the Act. After the Appeals Council denied review of the ALJ's decision, the claimant sought judicial review in the United States District Court for the Central District of California, pursuant to 42 USCS 1383(c)(3), which incorporates the review provisions of 42 USCS 405(g). Also, shortly before seeking such judicial review, the claimant filed a second application for SSI disability benefits, accompanied by new evidence of disability, which application was approved as of the date it was filed. Then, while cross motions for summary judgment were pending in the action for judicial review with regard to the first application, the Secretary of Health and Human Services moved for remand of the case to the Appeals Council so that the claimant's first application could be reconsidered in the light of the new evidence. The claimant eventually moved the court to either issue its decision or remand the case, and the court granted the Secretary's remand motion. On remand, the Appeals Council vacated the ALJ's prior decision and found the claimant disabled as of the date of his first SSI application, thus granting the claimant all the relief he had initially requested. More than a year later, the claimant applied to the District Court for an award of attorney's fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA) (28 USCS 2412), which provides that a party prevailing against the United States in a civil action is entitled in certain circumstances to an award of attorneys' fees, court costs, and other expenses. The court denied the fee application on the ground that the Secretary's decision to deny the claimant's first application for SSI benefits had been substantially justified at the time, because the original record had not established that the claimant had been disabled. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit vacated the judgment, stating that (1) the EAJA requires an application for fees to be filed within 30 days of the "final judgment in the action"; (2) the decision of the Appeals Council, on remand from the District Court, to award benefits was, in effect, a "final judgment" under the EAJA which commenced the 30-day period for filing the fee application; and (3) because the claimant had waited more than a year after the Appeals Council's decision, his application was untimely (895 F2d 556).

A dealer brought suit in a Puerto Rican court for damages for breach of his distributorship contract with a manufacturer, relying on the Dealer's Contract Law enacted by the Legislature of Puerto Rico, which statute imposes liability on a manufacturer for unilaterally terminating a contract with a local dealer, regardless of the terms of the contract itself, for other than "just cause" as defined by the statute. The suit was removed on the basis of diversity of citizenship to the United States District Court for the District of Puerto Rico, which denied a motion to dismiss based on a claim that the statute was unconstitutional. Allowing an interlocutory appeal, the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit held that the statute placed substantial liability on a manufacturer as to contracts which could have been terminated without liability prior to enactment of the statute, and that such retrospective impact of the statute violated the due process clause of the Federal Constitution (423 F2d 563).

Under a reapportionment plan for the Connecticut state legislature, population variations among the state's 36 Senate districts and 151 House of Representatives districts were such that (1) the population of the smallest Senate district (83,441) was approximately 1.81% smaller than that of the largest Senate district (84,973), and (2) the population of the smallest House of Representatives district (19,297) was approximately 7.83% smaller than that of the largest House district (20,870). The plan was based on a "political fairness" principle which was designed to reflect the relative strength of the major political parties by creating a certain number of "safe" districts for each party and a certain number of "swing" districts. The plan was challenged in the United States District Court for the District of Connecticut. A three-judge District Court was convened and held (1) that the population variations among the districts were not justified by any sufficient state interest and violated the equal protection clause, and (2) that the policy of partisan political structuring was not a legitimate reason for violating the requirement of numerical equality in districting (341 F Supp 139).

Defendants, who were non-Indians, operated a bar on privately owned land located within the boundaries of an Indian reservation, on the outskirts of an unincorporated village, without having obtained a tribal liquor license as required under a tribal ordinance adopted pursuant to the authority conferred on Indian tribes by Congress under 18 USCS 1161. Upon a non-jury trial in the United States District Court for the District of Wyoming, the defendants were convicted of unauthorized introduction of alcoholic beverages into "Indian country" in violation of 18 USCS 1154, which defines "Indian country" as not to include fee-patented lands "in non-Indian communities" (18 USCS 1154(c))--the District Court having concluded that the evidence of the largely Indian composition of the area surrounding the defendants' bar established that the bar was located in "Indian country." The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed, holding that (1) it had not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the bar was not excluded from "Indian country" by the 1154(c) exception for fee-patented lands in "non-Indian communities," (2) because of the indefiniteness of the term "non-Indian communities" 1154 was unconstitutionally vague, and (3) 18 USCS 1161, insofar as it authorized Indian tribes to control the introduction by non-Indians of alcoholic beverages onto non-Indian land, was an invalid delegation of congressional authority (487 F2d 14).

After a patient at a Veterans' Administration hospital in Wisconsin suffered irreversible brain damage and was left permanently comatose as a result of negligence by hospital employees, the patient's guardian ad litem filed an action on the patient's behalf in a Federal District Court, which action sought to recover damages from the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) (28 USCS 2671-2680). The United States admitted liability, and the case proceeded to a bench trial on the issue of damages. The District Court (1) ordered the hospital to continue its free medical services for the patient at the existing level of care, (2) awarded damages of $ 75,750 for supplemental care not provided by the hospital--physical and respiratory therapy and doctor visits, (3) refused to award damages for medical care that would duplicate the free medical services being provided by the hospital, and (4) declined to award damages for the patient's loss of enjoyment of life. The patient died after the District Court's final judgment was entered, and his widow was substituted as plaintiff in her capacity as personal representative of his estate. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed the District Court's judgment, as the Court of Appeals--noting that the FTCA barred awards of punitive damages (28 USCS 2674), and defining punitive damages as any damages in excess of those necessary to compensate victims or their survivors for the pecuniary loss suffered by reason of the tort--held that (1) since the government had provided free medical care to the patient and the widow appeared satisfied with that care, any additional award for future medical expenses would be punitive in effect and therefore was barred under 2674, and (2) even assuming that a comatose patient can recover damages for loss of enjoyment of life under Wisconsin law, such damages could not redress the patient's loss and therefore were also barred as punitive (911 F2d 18).

The Indian Major Crimes Act, 18 USCS 1153, provides that Indians who commit specified felonies within Indian country are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the United States. The Kansas Act, 18 USCS 3243, provides (1) in 3243's first sentence, that Kansas has jurisdiction over offenses committed by or against Indians on Indian reservations in Kansas, to the same extent as Kansas courts have jurisdiction, in accordance with state law, over offenses committed elsewhere in the state, and (2) in 3243's second sentence, that nothing in 3243 shall deprive federal courts of jurisdiction over federal offenses committed by or against Indians on reservations. After a jury in a Kansas county court found an Indian guilty of the state-law offense of aggravated battery for shooting another Indian on an Indian reservation in Kansas, the county court set aside the conviction, on the ground that, under 1153, the Federal Government had exclusive jurisdiction to prosecute the accused for the shooting. The Kansas Supreme Court, reinstating the conviction (239 Kan 127, 716 P2d 585), held that 3243 conferred jurisdiction on the county court, and on remand, the county court sentenced the accused to a term of imprisonment. The accused filed a petition for a federal writ of habeas corpus, on the ground that Kansas lacked jurisdiction to prosecute him for aggravated battery. After the United States District Court for the District of Kansas dismissed the petition (696 F Supp 561), the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit (1) held that Kansas had jurisdiction to prosecute the accused for aggravated battery, and (2) affirmed the District Court judgment (933 F2d 818).

A Federal Employees Health Benefits Act of 1959 (FEHBA) provision (5 U.S.C.S. _ 8902(a)) authorized the United States Office of Personnel Management (OPM) to negotiate and regulate health-benefits plans for federal employees. Also, FEHBA (5 U.S.C.S. __ 8901 et seq.) contained a pre-emption clause (5 U.S.C.S. _ 8902(m)(1)) that displaced state law on issues relating to "coverage or benefits" afforded by health-care plans. A private insurer that contracted with OPM to provide health insurance to many federal employees provided a plan that obligated the insurer to make "a reasonable effort" to recoup amounts paid for medical care. Moreover, the statement of benefits that the insurer distributed alerted enrollees that all medical-expense recoveries received from parties other than the insurer were required to be used to reimburse the plan for benefits paid. The administrator of the estate of a deceased former plan enrollee who had been injured in an accident brought, in a New York state court against third parties who allegedly had caused the injuries, a tort suit that eventually was settled for $3,175,000. The insurer, invoking 28 U.S.C.S _ 1331--which authorized federal-court jurisdiction over civil actions "arising under" the laws of the United States--filed, against the administrator in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, a suit seeking to recover from the  [**132]  settlement the $157,309 that the insurer had paid for the decedent's medical care. The District Court granted the administrator's motion to dismiss for want of subject-matter jurisdiction ( 2003 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 16276). The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit (1) concluded that the insurer's claim arose under state law, and (2) affirmed the District Court's judgment ( 396 F. 3d 136).

After defendant's motion to suppress as evidence clearinghouse slips allegedly obtained by an unlawful search of his person following his arrest without warrant had been overruled, he was convicted in the Municipal Court of Cleveland, Ohio, of possession of these slips in violation of an Ohio statute. His conviction was affirmed by an Ohio Court of Appeals, and ultimately by the Supreme Court of Ohio, with two judges dissenting. (175 Ohio St 73, 23 Ohio Ops 2d 377, 191 NE2d 825.)

Section 19 (a) of the Immigration Act of 1917, as amended, which provides that an alien who is "sentenced more than once" to imprisonment for a term of one year or more because of conviction of a crime involving moral turpitude committed after entry shall be deported, does not apply to an alien who, in a single trial, has been convicted on two different counts of a single indictment for murdering two different persons and sentenced to life imprisonment.

California and Nevada entered into a compact, later consented to by Congress (83 Stat 360), to create the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency and to authorize the agency to adopt and to enforce a regional plan for land use, transportation, conservation, recreation, and public services in the Lake Tahoe Basin resort area. Several Basin property owners, alleging that the agency, the individual members of its governing board, and its executive officer had adopted a land use plan, and had engaged in other conduct, that destroyed the economic value of the property owners land, thereby taking their property without due process of law and without just compensation in violation of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, filed a complaint in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of California. The District Court dismissed the complaint, holding, among other things, that the individual defendants were immune from liability for the exercise of the discretionary functions alleged in the complaint. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the planning agency, but reinstated the complaint against the individuals, finding, among other things, that the Eleventh Amendment immunized the agency from suit in a federal court, and that, with respect to the individuals, absolute immunity should be afforded for conduct of a legislative character and qualified immunity afforded for executive action (566 F2d 1353).

Notwithstanding uncontroverted evidence as to petitioner's "good moral character," the Illinois Committee on Character and Fitness refused to certify petitioner upon his application for admission to the bar; the refusal was based on the ground that his refusal to answer questions relating to Communist Party membership prevented full inquiry into his qualifications. Upon review, the Illinois Supreme Court, over three dissents, confirmed the committee's report and refusal to certify petitioner. (18 Ill 2d 182, 163 NE2d 429, 928.)

Taxpayers engaged in gambling enterprises, alleged to be illegal under applicable state law, sought to deduct as "ordinary and necessary" business expenses, within the meaning of 23(a)(1)(A) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939, amounts expended to lease premises and hire employees. The Tax Court denied the deductions on the ground that they were for expenditures made in connection with illegal acts (15 CCH TC Mem Dec 23, 25 TC 513). The Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed (241 F2d 46, 242 F2d 558).

Upon petition of a labor union for a representation election to determine whether the union would be certified as the bargaining representative of 25 buyers in the purchasing and procurement department at the employer's plant, the National Labor Relations Board held that the buyers constituted an appropriate unit and directed an election (190 NLRB 431), which resulted in the Board's certification of the union as the exclusive bargaining representative for the buyers. The employer's motion for reconsideration of the Board's earlier order was denied by the Board on the ground that the employer had not shown that union organization of its buyers would create a conflict of interest in labor relations (196 NLRB 827). However, the employer refused to bargain with the union and the Board found that the employer was guilty of an unfair labor practice in violation of 8(a)(5) and (1) of the amended National Labor Relations Act (29 USCS 158(a)(5 and 1)) and the Board issued an order compelling the company to bargain with the union (197 NLRB No. 30). The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit denied the Board's cross petition for enforcement of this order on the grounds that (1) it was not certain that the Board's decision rested on a factual determination that the buyers were not true "managerial employees" rather than on its new, and in the court's view, erroneous holding, that the Board was free to regard all managerial employees as covered by the Act unless their duties met the conflict of interest touchstone and (2) the Board was required to proceed by rulemaking rather than by adjudication in determining the status of the buyers as "managerial employees" (475 F2d 485).

Defendants were charged in a single-count indictment with conspiracy and an attempt to obstruct interstate commerce by means of extortion, in violation of the Hobbs Act (18 USCS 1951). Prior to, and during trial before the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, the defendants challenged the indictment on grounds of duplicity of offenses, claiming that its single count improperly charged both a conspiracy and an attempt to violate the Hobbs Act. The District Court did not dismiss the indictment, but required the Government to establish both offenses and instructed the jury that it would have to find that the Government had established all of the elements of both crimes before it could return a verdict of guilty against the defendants. The defendants were convicted after a general guilty verdict was returned by the jury. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed the convictions and ordered a new trial on evidentiary grounds, also directing the Government to elect between the conspiracy and attempt charges on remand (see 515 F2d 112). On remand, the Government elected to proceed on the conspiracy charge, and the defendants made a pretrial motion to dismiss the indictment, arguing that retrial would expose them to double jeopardy and that the indictment, as modified, failed to charge an offense. The District Court denied the motion, and, on interlocutory appeal, the Court of Appeals affirmed, failing to address the government's argument challenging the Court of Appeals' jurisdiction to hear the appeal (530 F2d 963).

Under its broad authority to regulate broadcast media in the public interest, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has long maintained several ownership rules that limit the number of radio stations, television stations, and newspapers that a single entity may own in a given market. Section 202(h) of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 directs the FCC to review its media ownership rules every four years and to repeal or modify any rules that no longer serve the public interest. In 2017, the FCC concluded that three of its ownership rules were no longer necessary to promote competition, localism, or viewpoint diversity. The Commission further concluded that the record evidence did not suggest that repealing or modifying those three rules was likely to harm minority and female ownership. Based on that analysis, the agency decided to repeal two of those three ownership rules and modify the third. Prometheus Radio Project and several other public interest and consumer advocacy groups (collectively, Prometheus) petitioned for review, arguing that the FCC‚Äôs decision to repeal or modify the three rules was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The Third Circuit vacated the FCC‚Äôs reconsideration order, holding that the record did not support the agency‚Äôs conclusion that the rule changes would have minimal effect on minority and female ownership.

Under 29 USCS 623(f)(2), age-based employment decisions taken pursuant to the terms of any bona fide employee benefit plan, such as a retirement, pension, or insurance plan, which is not a subterfuge to evade the purposes of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) (29 USCS 621 et seq.) are exempt from the prohibitions of the ADEA, which forbids arbitrary discrimination by public and private employers against employees on account of age. Before the ADEA was made applicable to the states in 1974, the state of Ohio established for state and local government employees a retirement plan under which retirees receive either age-and-service benefits or disability benefits, employees are required to be under 60 years of age upon retirement to qualify for disability benefits, and once an individual retires on either age-and-service or disability benefits, he or she continues to receive that type of benefit throughout retirement, regardless of age. In 1976, the plan was amended to provide that disability payments would in no event constitute less than 30 percent of a disability retiree's final average salary, but no such floor was applied to age-and-service payments. An employee who was covered by the plan and who, because she was no longer able to perform adequately in any employment capacity, retired in 1985 at the age of 61 was denied disability retirement benefits because of her age and was instead granted age-and-service retirement benefits amounting to $ 158.50 per month. The employee, who would have received some $ 355 per month had she been permitted to receive disability benefits subject to the 30-percent floor, filed an age discrimination charge against the plan with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) and filed suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio, claiming that the refusal to grant her application for disability benefits violated the ADEA. The District Court granted summary judgment in favor of the employee, holding that, because the retirement plan's reduction in available benefits at age 60 was not shown to be justified by considerations of increased cost, the plan was not entitled to claim the protection of the 623(f)(2) exemption. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, holding that the 623(f)(2) exemption is available only to those retirement plans that can provide age-related cost justifications or a substantial business purpose for any age-based reduction in benefits, affirmed the District Court's judgment (848 F2d 692).

The motion for leave to proceed in forma pauperis and the petition for writ of certiorari are granted. The judgment is vacated and the case is remanded for further consideration in light of Peterson v. City of Greenville, 373 U.S. 244: The petitioners, 10 Negroes, remained seated at the lunch counter of a store even though the manager, in the presence of the police, announced "that the lunch counter was being closed and would everyone leave" the area. The manager asked petitioners to leave because integrated service was not only contrary to local customs but also in violation of a city ordinance requiring separation of the races in restaurants. The petitioners were convicted in the Recorder's Court of the City of Greenville, South Carolina, for violating the state trespass statute. An appeal to the Greenville County Court was dismissed, and the Supreme Court of South Carolina affirmed. (239 SC 298, 122 SE2d 826.)

A state-court jury in Tennessee convicted an accused of a woman's murder on the basis of factors including (1) evidence seeming to show semen consistent with the accused's on the victim's clothing, and (2) evidence showing small bloodstains consistent with the victim's blood but not the accused's on the accused's jeans. At the trial's sentencing phase, the jury found, among other things, the aggravating factor that the accused committed the murder while he was committing, attempting to commit, or fleeing from the commission of rape or kidnapping. The Tennessee Supreme Court (1) affirmed the accused's conviction and sentence (743 S.W.2d 141); and (2) eventually, held that the accused's state-court claims for postconviction relief were procedurally barred by state law (911 S.W.2d 705). Subsequently, the accused sought federal habeas corpus relief. The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee (1) held, after an evidentiary hearing, that the accused had failed to make a showing sufficient for application of the actual-innocence exception to state-law procedural default recognized as to substantive offenses in Schlup v. Delo (1995) 513 U.S. 298, 115 S. Ct. 851, 130 L. Ed. 2d 808, and as to death sentences in Sawyer v. Whitley (1992) 505 U.S. 333, 112 S. Ct. 2514, 120 L. Ed. 2d 269; and (2) denied habeas corpus relief. Ultimately, the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed the District Court's judgment (386 F. 3d 668).

The Municipal Court for the District of Columbia found that the District of Columbia Emergency Rent Act was not applicable to the United States and ordered possession of premises owned by it in a defense-housing project in the District of Columbia given to the United States. The Municipal Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia affirmed. 75 Wash. Law Rep. 982, 54 A. 2d 747. The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed. 83 U. S. App. D. C. 377, 171 F.2d 8. This Court granted certiorari. 336 U.S. 931.

A group of English Language-Learner (ELL) students and their parents (plaintiffs) filed a class action, alleging that Arizona, its State Board of Education, and the Superintendent of Public Instruction (defen- dants) were providing inadequate ELL instruction in the Nogales Unified School District (Nogales), in violation of the Equal Educa- tional Opportunities Act of 1974 (EEOA), which requires States to take “appropriate action to overcome language barriers” in schools, 20 U. S. C. §1703(f). In 2000, the Federal District Court entered a declaratory judgment, finding an EEOA violation in Nogales because the amount of funding the State allocated for the special needs of ELL students (ELL incremental funding) was arbitrary and not re- lated to the actual costs of ELL instruction in Nogales. The District Court subsequently extended relief statewide and, in the years fol- lowing, entered a series of additional orders and injunctions. The de- fendants did not appeal any of the District Court’s orders. In 2006, the state legislature passed HB 2064, which, among other things, in- creased ELL incremental funding. The incremental funding increase required District Court approval, and the Governor asked the state attorney general to move for accelerated consideration of the bill. The State Board of Education, which joined the Governor in opposing HB 2064, the State, and the plaintiffs are respondents here. The Speaker of the State House of Representatives and the President of the State Senate (Legislators) intervened and, with the superinten- dent (collectively, petitioners), moved to purge the contempt order in light of HB 2064. In the alternative, they sought relief under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(5). The District Court denied their mo- tion to purge the contempt order and declined to address the Rule 60(b)(5) claim. The Court of Appeals vacated and remanded for an evidentiary hearing on whether changed circumstances warranted Rule 60(b)(5). On remand, the District Court denied the Rule 60(b)(5) motion, holding that HB 2064 had not created an adequate funding system. Affirming, the Court of Appeals concluded that Nogales had not made sufficient progress in its ELL programming to warrant re- lief.

Until its amendment in 1985, a Georgia statute imposed an excise tax on imported alcohol and distilled spirits at a rate double that imposed on alcohol and distilled spirits manufactured from Georgia-grown products. The United States Supreme Court, in Bacchus Imports, Ltd. v Dias (1984) 468 US 263, 82 L Ed 2d 200, 104 S Ct 3049, held that a Hawaii statute that similarly distinguished between imported and local alcoholic products violated the Federal Constitution's commerce clause (Art I, 8, cl 3). In the wake of the Supreme Court's Bacchus decision, a Kentucky bourbon manufacturer, claiming that the Georgia statute violated the commerce clause, brought an action against the state of Georgia in a Georgia trial court. The manufacturer sought a refund of excise taxes which the manufacturer had paid under the statute for the years 1982-1984. The trial court, denying the manufacturer's refund request, determined that (1) the tax imposed against the manufacturer for the years in question was unconstitutional under the commerce clause, but (2) such ruling would be applied prospectively only. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed in both respects (259 Ga 363, 382 SE2d 95).

A New York town had about 200,000 residents, 95 percent of whom were white and less than 4 percent black. Almost 75 percent of the black population was clustered in 6 tracts in two areas, and, of the town's remaining 42 tracts, 30 were at least 99 percent white. The town had a zoning classification permitting multifamily housing projects, but a provision of the town code restricted the private construction of such housing to the town's urban renewal area, a section which (1) lay in and around one such minority-cluster area, and (2) contained 52 percent minority residents. Although the restriction permitted the town's housing authority to build multifamily housing townwide, the only such existing public housing-authority project was within the urban renewal area. A private developer, who was assertedly interested in fostering residential integration and who had acquired an option on a site in a 98 percent white section of town zoned for single-family residences, requested the town board to amend the town code to permit multifamily rental construction by a private developer. After the board refused the request, the developer, a branch of a civil rights organization, and two black, low-income residents of the town filed a complaint in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York against various defendants, including the town and members of the town board. The complaint included allegations that Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (42 USCS 3601 et seq.) had been violated by refusing (1) to amend the zoning code to allow for private construction of multifamily housing outside the urban renewal area, and (2) to rezone the proposed site to the town's classification that would permit multifamily housing. The District Court eventually rejected the Title VIII claims (668 F Supp 762). On appeal, even though the town and the town board members argued that the restriction of multifamily housing projects to the town's urban renewal area would encourage developers to invest in a deteriorated and needy section of town, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, reversing as to both Title VIII claims, (1) directed the town to strike from its town code the restriction of private multifamily housing projects to the urban renewal area, and (2) ordered the town to rezone the project site to the classification which permitted private multifamily housing projects. The Court of Appeals expressed the view that (1) in order to establish a prima facie case, a Title VIII plaintiff needed only to demonstrate that the action or rule challenged had a disparate impact; (2) in order to rebut such a prima facie case, Title VIII defendants had to (a) put forth bona fide and legitimate reasons for their action, and (b) demonstrate that no less discriminatory alternative could serve those ends; and (3) in the case at hand, such a prima facie case had been established, while the rebuttal was inadequate (844 F2d 926).

Petitioner, a railroad employee, suffered injuries through the negligence of employees of an independent corporation engaged in switching, within a terminal area, the railroad car on which petitioner was working. The independent corporation, although free from detailed supervision by the railroad, conducted all switching operations for the railroad within the terminal area. Petitioner successfully sought recovery for his injuries in a suit against the railroad, under the Federal Employers' Liability Act instituted in the District Court of Harris County, Texas, but the Court of Civil Appeals for the Ninth Judicial District of Texas reversed on the ground that under the federal statute the railroad was not liable to an employee injured through the fault of employees of the independent company (295 SW2d 508). The Supreme Court of Texas denied the petitioner's application for writ of error.

The United States brought an original action in the United States Supreme Court against the state of Alaska to resolve a dispute between the United States and Alaska over the ownership of submerged lands along Alaska's Arctic Coast. In 1979, the Supreme Court granted the United States leave to file the complaint (442 US 937, 61 L Ed 2d 307, 99 S Ct 2876). The complaint set out a dispute over the right to offer lands in the Beaufort Sea for mineral leasing. Alaska counterclaimed, seeking a decree quieting its title to coastal submerged lands within two federal reservations, the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska and the Arctic National Wildlife Range (since renamed the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge). The court appointed a Special Master (444 US 1065, 62 L Ed 2d 747, 100 S Ct 1005), and the Special Master filed a report with some findings and recommendations concerning ownership of the disputed submerged lands.

The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976 (RCRA) (42 USCS 6901-6987), which deals with solid waste management, contains a provision ( 6972) authorizing citizen suits against alleged violators of regulations established under the RCRA. A portion of the citizen suit provision ( 6972(b)(1)) states that except under certain circumstances, no action may be commenced against an alleged violator prior to 60 days after the plaintiff has given notice of the alleged violation to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the state in which the alleged violation occurred, and the alleged violator. The owners of an Oregon farm that was located next to a county landfill believed that the landfill operation violated standards established under the RCRA. In April 1981, the farmowners sent the county written notice of their intention to file a citizen suit under the RCRA, and they commenced the action a year later in the Federal District Court for the District of Oregon. On March 1, 1983, the county moved for summary judgment on the ground that the farmowners had failed to notify the EPA and Oregon's Department of Environmental Quality of the alleged violation, as required by 6972(b)(1). The District Court, denying the county's motion, said that the farmowners had cured any defect in notice by formally notifying the state and federal agencies on March 2, 1983, and that the agencies would then have 60 days to take appropriate steps to cure any violation at the landfill. The action subsequently went to trial, and the District Court held that the county had violated the RCRA. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, remanding the case to the District Court with instructions to dismiss the action, held that the farmowners' failure to comply with the notice and 60-day-delay requirements deprived the District Court of subject matter jurisdiction (844 F2d 598).

At his trial in a Florida state court on sexual battery charges, the accused moved to suppress evidence seized in a second search of his automobile, after it had been impounded in a locked, secure area. The motion was denied and the accused was convicted. The Florida District Court of Appeal for the Fourth District reversed, holding that even though the accused conceded that the initial search of the automobile was valid, the second search violated the Fourth Amendment. The court also ruled that the accused's cross-examination of the victim had been unduly restricted by the trial court. The Florida Supreme Court denied the state's petition for discretionary review.

These two, consolidated cases presented the question whether the written order clause of the definition of "displaced person" in 101(6) of the Uniform Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition Policies Act (42 USCS 4601(6))--which provides that a displaced person is "any person ... who moves ... as a result of the acquisition of ... real property ... or as a result of the written order of the acquiring agency to vacate real property, for a program or project undertaken by a Federal agency"--encompasses tenants required to vacate housing projects that the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) acquired under the National Housing Act (12 USCS 1701 et seq.) after the projects' sponsors defaulted on federally insured loans, even though HUD's orders to vacate were not motivated by a governmental acquisition of property to further a public program or project. In the first case (No. 77-874), the United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana rejected a claim that tenants of a project that HUD had managed after purchasing at a foreclosure sale were "displaced persons" because the tenants had moved upon receiving written orders to vacate property acquired by a government agency, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed (555 F2d 166). In the second case (No. 77-1463), the United States District Court for the District of Columbia granted summary judgment to project tenants seeking full relocation benefits from HUD after being ordered to vacate a project in connection with HUD's plan to demolish the project buildings and sell the land to private developers, and the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia affirmed, agreeing that the tenants were "displaced persons" under the written order clause of 101(6) (571 F2d 590).

n a civil suit in a federal district court, the jury rendered a verdict for plaintiff; but the court dismissed the complaint for lack of jurisdiction. The circuit court of appeals reversed and directed that judgment be entered on the verdict for plaintiff; but its mandate made no provision for interest.

A tax lien of the United States is prior in right over a garnishment lien obtained by a creditor of the taxpayer in an action on an open account, where the tax lien arose and was filed prior to the date the garnishor obtained judgment against the taxpayer, though subsequent to the date of the garnishment lien.

In 1964, six years after the first of two patent applications had been filed with respect to oil shale claims located on public lands in Colorado prior to the 1920 enactment of the Mineral Leasing Act (30 USCS 181 et seq.)--a statute which altered the program of the general mining law of 1872 (30 USCS 22 et seq.) (the general mining law provides that citizens may enter and explore the public domain in search for minerals, and, upon discovering "valuable mineral deposits," obtain title to the land on which such deposits are located through the patent process) by withdrawing oil shale and certain other minerals from the general mining law and requiring that such minerals can be disposed of only through leases, while preserving, in a savings clause (30 USCS 193), "valid claims existent at date of the passage of [the] Act and thereafter maintained in compliance with the laws under which initiated, which claims may be perfected under such laws, including discovery"--the Department of the Interior issued administrative complaints asserting that oil shale was not a "valuable mineral" prior to enactment of the Mineral Leasing Act, and that the oil shale claims for which patent applications had been filed were invalid. A hearing examiner upheld the claims as valid and patentable, his decision being based on the view that a 1927 decision of the Department holding that "present marketability" is not a prerequisite to the patentability of oil shale deposits as "valuable mineral deposits" compelled the conclusion that oil shale is a valuable mineral subject to appropriation under the mining laws. Thereafter, the Board of Land Appeals revesed, concluding that oil shale claims located prior to 1920 failed the test of value because at the time of location there did not appear "as a present fact" that a reasonable prospect of success in developing oil shale would yield a reasonable profit. Recognizing that its conclusion was at odds with the 1927 decision of the Department relied upon by the hearing examiner, the Board nonetheless rejected such decision as being inconsistent with general mining law. Applying the newly enunciated interpretation to the oil shale claims with respect to which the Department had filed complaints, the Board ruled that the claims were invalid. Subsequently, on appeal, the United States District Court for the District of Colorado reversed the Board's ruling and upheld the claims as valid, the District Court finding that the 1927 Department decision had liberalized the traditional valuable mineral test by not requiring proof of "present marketability," that Congress, in later years, had considered the patentability of oil shale and implicitly ratified the liberalized rule, and that the Department was estopped from departing from the standard under the 1927 decision because of investors' reliance upon it (426 F Supp 894). The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed (591 F2d 597).

In 1964, a minor was sentenced to life imprisonment upon pleading guilty in a North Carolina prosecution for first degree burglary--an offense punishable by death under state statutes applicable at the time unless the jury recommended life imprisonment, whereas a guilty plea, if accepted, resulted in a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment under North Carolina statutes. The defendant, who had given a confession before consulting with an attorney, entered the guilty plea more than one month later, after discussion with retained counsel and the defendant's mother, and the plea was accepted after the trial court questioned the defendant and was told that the plea was tendered freely without any fear or compulsion. In 1967, the defendant sought relief from his conviction under the North Carolina Post- Conviction Hearing Act, urging that his guilty plea was the product of a coerced confession, and that the indictment to which he had pleaded was invalid because members of his race had been systematically excluded from the grand jury. After a hearing, the Superior Court of Halifax County, North Carolina, found that there had been no deliberate exclusion of Negroes from the grand jury, and that the guilty plea had been voluntarily made, without threat, coercion, or duress. The Court of Appeals of North Carolina affirmed, refusing to consider the grand jury claim, since under North Carolina law an objection to the composition of the grand jury was required to be raised by motion to quash the indictment prior to the entry of the guilty plea, which the defendant had failed to do, and also rejecting the additional assertion that the defendant's guilty plea was involuntary because North Carolina statutes at that time allowed the defendant to escape the possibility of a death penalty by pleading guilty (2 NC App 27, 162 SE2d 526).

A large independent distributor of gasoline and oil, who was both a wholesaler, operating storage plants and trucking equipment, and a retailer through his own service stations, brought a civil antitrust action in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon against the Standard Oil Company of California, seeking treble damages under 2 of the Clayton Act, as amended by the Robinson-Patman Act, for injuries allegedly resulting from Standard's price discriminations in the sale of gasoline and oil during a 2-year period, such discriminations consisting of Standard's charging the plaintiff a higher price for its gasoline and oil than Standard charged to its own Branded Dealers (independent operators of Standard's Signal and Chevron stations), who competed with the plaintiff, and to a wholesaler who sold the gasoline to a subsidiary who in turn sold it to its subsidiary, an operator of service stations and a major competitor of the plaintiff. The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff and assessed damages against Standard of $ 333,404.57, which, after trebling by the District Court and after addition of attorneys' fees, resulted in a total judgment of $ 1,298,213.71. On review, the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed the judgment and ordered a new trial, holding that any harm suffered by the plaintiff from impaired competition with those service stations operated by the subsidiary who was supplied with Standard's gas by the subsidiary of the wholesaler to whom Standard sold the gas was beyond the scope of the Robinson-Patman Act, as being "fourth level," because the operator of such service stations was too far removed from Standard and the chain of distribution, and that since a substantial part of the damages the jury assessed might have been based upon a finding that the plaintiff suffered competitive harm from the price advantage held by these stations, and since the amount reflected in the verdict by the conduct of the operator of these stations could not be ascertained, the whole verdict was tainted (396 F2d 809).

The University of Michigan's college of literature, science, and the arts used an undergraduate admissions policy under which, beginning in 1998, an applicant could be awarded a maximum of 150 points and generally was automatically admitted if awarded at least 100 points. Each applicant could receive points based on high school grades, standardized test scores, high school quality, strength of high school curriculum, in-state residency, alumni relationships, a personal essay, and personal achievement or leadership, and membership in an "underrepresented" racial or ethnic minority group. The university, which considered African Americans, Hispanics, and Native Americans as underrepresented minorities, (1) beginning in 1998, automatically distributed 20 points to every applicant who was a member of such a group; (2) beginning in 1999, established a committee to provide an additional level of review for some applications; and (3) admitted virtually every qualified applicant from these groups. A qualified Caucasian applicant who had been denied admission to the college for the fall of 1995, and a qualified Caucasian applicant who had been denied admission for the fall of 1997, filed, in October 1997 in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, a purported class action against the university, the college, and each of the two people who had been president of the university when one of the Caucasians had applied for admission. The suit (1) alleged that the university's use of racial preference violated (a) the equal protection clause of the Federal Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment, and (b) federal statutes including a provision of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (42  [***258]  USCS _ 2000d) and 42 USCS _ 1981; and (2) sought remedies including compensatory and punitive damages, declaratory and injunctive relief, and an order requiring the college to admit the later applicant as a transfer student. The District Court (1) granted the applicants class certification, (2) designated the later applicant as the class representative, and (3) bifurcated the proceedings into a liability phase and a damages phase.

An individual convicted at a state criminal trial for robbery subsequently brought an action under 42 USCS 1983 in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Iowa alleging that a public defender who was a full-time employee of the county had failed to represent him adequately in an appeal to the state's highest court. The individual asserted that the public defender--who had moved for permission to withdraw as counsel on the ground that the claims asserted on appeal were frivolous--had deprived him of his right to counsel, subjected to him to cruel and unusual punishment, and had denied him due process of law. To establish that the public defender had acted "under color of state law," a jurisdictional requisite for a 1983 action, the individual relied on the public defender's employment by the county. In addition to the public offender, the individual also sued the county, its board of supervisors, and its offender advocate. The District Court dismissed the claims against all the defendants, holding that the relevant actions of the public defender had not occurred under color of state law (483 F Supp 347). However, the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed (628 F2d 1104).

The Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) (18 USCS 1961 et seq.) (1) makes it unlawful to engage in certain activities through a pattern of racketeering (18 USCS 1962(a)-(c)); (2) makes it unlawful for a person to conspire to violate any of the provisions of 1962(a)-(c) (18 USCS 1962(d)); (3) states that a cause of action is available to anyone injured by reason of a violation of 1962 (18 USCS 1964(c)); and (4) contains an exhaustive list of acts of "racketeering" (18 USCS 1961(1)). An individual who had been the president and chief executive officer, as well as a director and shareholder, of a corporation brought an action in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida under 1964(c) against certain officers and directors of the corporation, which action alleged that (1) the officers and directors had engaged in a pattern of racketeering in violation of 1962(a), (b), and (c); (2) the officers and directors had conspired to commit the aforementioned acts, in violation of 1962(d); (3) the individual had discovered the officers' and directors' unlawful conduct and had contacted regulators; and (4) the officers and directors had then orchestrated a scheme to remove the individual from the company. The officers and directors filed a motion for summary judgment, whereupon the District Court dismissed the individual's RICO conspiracy claim. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit (1) affirmed the judgment of the District Court, and (2) expressed the view that (a) a cause of action under 1964(c) for a violation of 1962(d) was not available to a person injured by an overt act in furtherance of a RICO conspiracy unless the overt act was an act of racketeering, and (b) the overt act that allegedly caused the individual's injury in the present case was not an act of racketeering under 1961(1) (162 F3d 1090).

A dispute arose between a railroad employee and his union on the one side and the employer on the other as to whether an order of the National Railroad Adjustment Board sustaining the employee's claim for reinstatement "with pay for time lost as the rule is construed on the property" entitled the employee to full pay for lost time without deduction for outside income. After the railroad had submitted that dispute to the Board, the union set a definite strike deadline. The employer then brought the present lawsuit in the United States District Court for the Western District of Kentucky, requesting injunctive relief against the threatened strike. After the Board refused to clarify its award, the District Court issued an injunction, holding that under the Railway Labor Act the union could not legally strike for the purpose of enforcing its interpretation of the Board's money order, but must instead utilize the judicial enforcement procedure provided by 3 First (p) of the Railway Labor Act and institute an action in the appropriate District Court. (190 F Supp 829.) The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed. (297 F2d 608.)

An indictment against the defendants was filed on August 12, 1966, for crimes relating to allegedly false income tax returns. The returns in question were filed on August 12 and 15, 1960, pursuant to an extension of time obtained by the defendants from the original due date of May 15, 1960. The United States District Court for the Southern District of Indiana dismissed two counts charging an attempt to evade taxes by filing a false return and aiding in the preparation and presentation of a false return, on the ground that the 6-year statute of limitations (26 USC 6531) barred prosecution under such counts. (270 F Supp 929.)

A joint loan of $ 20,000 was given to a small business by a private bank and the Small Business Administration under the Small Business Act of 1953; $ 5,000 of the loan came from the funds of the bank and $ 15,000 from the Government Treasury. Nine months later, an involuntary petition in bankruptcy was filed against the borrower by other creditors. The Administration claimed priority for its 75 per cent interest in the unpaid balance of the loan. The referee in bankruptcy denied priority on the ground that the Administration was a legal entity and therefore not entitled to the "privileges and immunities of the United States." The United States District Court for the District of Kansas, on review, held that the debt was not entitled to priority since the bankrupt's note evidencing the loan was not assigned by the bank to the Administration until after the commencement of bankruptcy proceedings. (168 F Supp 483.) The Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed on the ground that the Administration, having contracted to pay the participating private bank one-fourth of any distribution received, could not assert its priority and thus permit a private party to benefit from the governmental priority. (272 F2d 143.)

In the United States District Court for the Northern District of Maine, a railroad brought suit to recover damages from its former owners for mismanagement which allegedly violated the federal antitrust and securities laws, state statutes, and the common law. The present owner of over 99 percent of the railroad's stock was a corporation which had purchased 98.3 percent of the railroad's stock from the former owners after the alleged mismanagement had occurred. Dismissing the action, the District Court held that although the action purported to be brought in the name of the railroad, the present owner was the real party in interest and the actual beneficiary of any recovery, and that under the contemporaneous ownership requirement which was applicable under both federal and state law, and which could not be evaded through the use of the corporate fiction, the fact that the present owner had not yet purchased the railroad's stock at the time of the alleged mismanagement precluded the action from being maintainable (353 F Supp 724). Reversing the District Court's judgment, the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit held that the public's interest in the financial health of the railroad provided a separate interest, quite apart from the present owner's, which was served by the corporate cause of action, and that the action was not barred either by the failure of the present owner to own its stock at the time of the alleged wrongs or by the present owner's purchase of the stock from the alleged wrongdoers (482 F2d 865).

Regulation Z‚Äîpromulgated by the Federal Reserve Board (Board) pursuant to its authority under the Truth in Lending Act‚Äîrequires credit card issuers to disclose certain information to cardholders. The version of the regulation in effect at the time this dispute arose obliges issuers to provide to cardholders an ‚Äú[i]nitial disclosure statement,‚Äù 12 CFR ¬ß226.6, specifying ‚Äúeach periodic rate that may be used to compute the finance charge,‚Äù ¬ß226.6(a)(2). It also imposes ‚Äú[s]ubsequent disclosure requirements,‚Äù ¬ß226.9, including notice to cardholders ‚Äú[w]henever any term required to be disclosed under ¬ß226.6 is changed,‚Äù ¬ß226.9(c)(1). When ‚Äúa periodic rate or other finance charge is increased because of the consumer‚Äôs delinquency or default,‚Äù notice must be given ‚Äúbefore the effective date of the change.‚Äù Ibid. At the time respondent McCoy filed suit, he was the holder of a credit card issued by petitioner Chase Bank. The cardholder agreement provided, in relevant part, that McCoy was eligible for ‚ÄúPreferred rates‚Äù as long as he met certain conditions. If any of those conditions were not met, Chase reserved the right to raise the rate, up to a pre-set maximum, and to apply the change to both existing and new balances. McCoy alleges that Chase increased his interest rate due to his delinquency or default and applied that increase retroactively, and that this action violated Regulation Z because Chase did not notify him of the increase until after it had taken effect. The District Court dismissed his complaint, holding that because the increase did not constitute a ‚Äúchange in terms‚Äù under ¬ß226.9(c), Chase was not required to notify him of the increase before implementing it. The Ninth Circuit reversed in relevant part, holding that Regulation Z requires issuers to provide notice of an interest-rate increase prior to its effective date.

After the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, in habeas corpus proceedings, had set aside, on account of the systematic exclusion of Negroes from both the grand and petit juries, defendants' murder convictions in a Georgia state court, defendants were reindicted. The trial court denied their claim of discrimination as to the grand jury which reindicted them, and, upon their interlocutory appeal, this denial was affirmed by the Georgia Court of Appeals. (112 Ga App 328, 145 SE2d 83.) The defendants were again convicted and their convictions were affirmed by the Supreme Court of Georgia. ( Whitus v State, 222 Ga 103, 149 SE2d 130; Davis v State, 222 Ga 114, 149 SE2d 130.)

After a trial in the Circuit Court, Cook County, Illinois, the accused was convicted of murder, with the death penalty imposed by the jury. At a postconviction hearing, he claimed that he was denied a fair trial because the state suppressed (1) a state witness' misidentification of him as a man known as "Slick," statements by two other persons that he was not "Slick," a police lieutenant's unsuccessful attempts to find "Slick," and the witness' statement on the day of the trial that "Slick" looked different from the accused, and (2) a policeman's diagram of the seating arrangement at the bar- restaurant murder scene, showing that the door through which the accused allegedly entered was behind a state eyewitness' chair. He also argued that a 16-gauge shotgun in his possession at the time of his arrest was improperly received in evidence because the state ballistics technician's opinion was that the victim was killed by a 12-gauge shotgun shell. The trial court denied the petition for postconviction relief, and the Supreme Court of Illinois affirmed both the conviction and the denial of postconviction relief (42 Ill 2d 73, 246 NE2d 299).

In 1952 the United States brought the present suit under 338 (a) of the Nationality Act of 1940 in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan to set aside a naturalization decree obtained by the defendant in 1938. The government filed with its complaint an affidavit showing good cause, as required by 338 (a), and alleged that the defendant had obtained his citizenship both fraudulently and illegally. As to fraudulent procurement, the government alleged that the defendant falsely answered in the negative a question in the preliminary naturalization form as to whether he was a believer in anarchy and belonged to or was associated with any organization which teaches or advocates anarchy or the overthrow of existing government in this country. The answer was alleged to be false because the defendant, during five years preceding his naturalization, was an active member and functionary of the Communist Party. As to illegal procurement, the government alleged that for the same reason he was not attached to the principles of the Constitution. After a trial the District Court granted the relief requested by the United States on the grounds alleged by the government (133 F Supp 191). The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed (238 F2d 282).

A restaurant owner was convicted in a Federal District Court of violating 7 USCS 2024(b), which provides that "whoever knowingly uses, transfers, acquires, alters, or possesses coupons or other authorization cards in any manner not authorized by [the statute] or the regulations" is subject to a fine and imprisonment, for having purchased food stamps from an undercover Department of Agriculture agent for substantially less than their face value. The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed, rejecting the defendant's contention that the District Court erred in refusing to instruct the jury that "specific intent" is required in a prosecution under 7 USCS 2024(b) (735 F2d 1044).

Post-conviction proceedings were instituted in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California by a federal prisoner who, after pleading guilty to a charge of entering a bank with intent to commit a felony, was denied rehabilitative treatment as a narcotic addict under Title II of the Narcotic Addict Rehabilitation Act of 1966 (18 USCS 4251- 4255), the sentencing judge having concluded that the prisoner, who had three prior non-narcotics felony convictions, was not eligible for rehabilitative treatment in lieu of penal incarceration because of the Act's exclusion of addicts with two or more prior felony convictions (18 USCS 4251(f)(4)). Denying the prisoner's motion to vacate his sentence of 10 years' imprisonment, the District Court in the post-conviction proceedings held that the two prior felony conviction exclusion of the Narcotic Addict Rehabilitation Act did not violate equal protection as embodied in the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment, and the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed (470 F2d 34).

Following a determination by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) that incumbent local exchange carriers (LECs) need not provide competitive LECs with cost-based unbundled access to entrance facilities under ¬¨√ü 251(c)(3), the incumbent provider announced that it would charge higher rates for access to entrance facilities for interconnection. The FCC, as amicus, interpreted its regulations, including 47 C.F.R. ¬¨√ü 51.321, as requiring the incumbent provider to provide access at cost-based rates to its existing entrance facilities for the purpose of interconnection. The Supreme Court found that the FCC's interpretation of its regulations was neither plainly erroneous nor inconsistent with the regulatory text.
