On review of the NLRB's order, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that the companies had committed an unfair labor practice by refusing to extend the terms of the union's agreement with the one company to the employees of the other company and by refusing to recognize the union as the bargaining representative of the employees, such holding being based upon the Court of Appeals' finding that the two companies constituted a single employer rather than separate employers as the NLRB had found, and its further finding that the employees of the two companies constituted the appropriate unit for purposes of collective bargaining (518 F2d 1040).

After having executed a release for a consideration of $ 105, a railroad employee, without offering to return the consideration, instituted, in a Georgia state court, an action under the Federal Employers' Liability Act for injuries sustained. The trial court's judgment overruling the railroad's demurrer to the petition was reversed by the Court of Appeals of Georgia on the ground that restitution by the claimant was a prerequisite of setting aside the release of a claim under the Act. (116 Ga App 194, 156 SE2d 412.)

A suit brought by the United States to enjoin one holding directorships in several competing corporations, and the corporations themselves, from violating the provisions of the Clayton Act prohibiting interlocking corporate directorates, was summarily dismissed on the ground that the specific interlocks charged had been voluntarily terminated and any intention to resume them had been disclaimed.

On May 19, 1970, a three-judge United States District Court for the District of Arizona ordered that the 1970 Arizona legislative elections be conducted under the Legislature's apportionment plan which the court found to be invalid, on the stated assumption that the Arizona Legislature would enact a valid apportionment plan by November 1, 1971, failing which any party to the action might apply to the court for appropriate relief. (313 F Supp 148.)

Under the Utah Enabling Act of 1894 (28 Stat 109), Congress granted Utah, upon admission to the Union, four numbered sections in each township for the support of public schools, and if the designated sections had been otherwise disposed of, allowed the state to select, with the approval of the Secretary of the Interior, substitute grants, denominated "indemnity lands." Since much of the state was not surveyed until long after admission to the Union, it was not until 1965 that Utah filed the first of 194 selection lists for indemnity lands with the Department of Interior. The selections included over 150,000 acres of land that were located within federal grazing districts created pursuant to the Taylor Grazing Act (43 USCS 315 et seq.). In 1974, the Secretary of the Interior advised Utah that he would not approve any indemnity applications that involved "grossly disparate values," citing Department of the Interior policy that, in the exercise of its discretion under 7 of the Act (43 USCS 315f), the Department would refuse to convey applied-for land to a state where the value of those lands greatly exceeded the value of the lost school lands for which the state sought indemnity. The state then brought an action in the United States District Court for the District of Utah, claiming the right to select extremely valuable oil shale lands located within federal grazing districts in lieu of, and as indemnification for, original school land grants of significantly lesser value that were frustrated by federal preemption or private entry prior to survey. The District Court entered summary judgment in favor of the state, holding that if Utah's selections satisfied all of the statutory criteria governing indemnity selections when filed, the Secretary of the Interior had no discretion to refuse them pursuant to a "grossly disparate value" policy. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed, holding that 7 of the Act gave the Secretary no authority to classify land as eligible for selection and that the state had a right to select indemnity land of equal acreage without regard to the relative values of the original grants and the indemnity selections (586 F2d 756).

At the close of an Indian's trial under the Major Crimes Act for assault with intent to commit serious bodily injury, the United States District Court for the District of South Dakota refused his request for a jury instruction that the jury might convict him of simple assault. The Indian was convicted of the offense with which he was charged, and was sentenced to 5 years' imprisonment. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Cicuit affirmed (459 F2d 757).

Student editors and former student editors of the New York University Law Review, after being denied access to case summaries of Air Force Academy hearings as to cadets' violations of the Academy's Honor and Ethics Codes, with personal references or other identifying information deleted, instituted an action against the Department of the Air Force and certain of its officers in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York to compel disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act (5 USCS 552). Without first requiring production of the case summaries for inspection, the District Court granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment, holding that although the summaries were not exempt from disclosure under the Act's sixth exemption (5 USCS 552(b)(6))--which exempts from disclosure personnel and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy--nevertheless the summaries were exempt under the Act's second exemption ( 552(b)(2)), which exempts from disclosure matters related solely to the internal personnel rules and practices of an agency. The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed, holding that 552(b)(2) was not applicable, and that the summaries should be produced for the District Court's in camera inspection and redaction of identifying material to safeguard the privacy of affected persons under 552(b)(6) (495 F2d 261).

A street railway company in the District of Columbia installed in its passenger vehicles receivers and loud speakers for the transmission of radio programs consisting mainly of music interspersed with commercials. The Public Utilities Commission of the District, after notice, investigation, and public hearings, concluded that this practice did not interfere with public convenience, comfort, and safety, but tended to improve the public service.

In the instant case the United States Supreme Court, in a per curiam opinion, dismissed an appeal from the judgment of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri setting aside an order of the Interstate Commerce Commission. The dismissal was rested on the ground that the appellant, in violation of Supreme Court Rule 13(1), did not docket the case nor file the record until 22 days after the expiration of the 60-day period provided by the Rule, and that the appellant made no application for an enlargement of time nor did any explanation accompany the untimely docketing. (252 F Supp 162.)

Three union members brought suit in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York to enjoin the union from preparing for or conducting any election until it revised its constitution and bylaws insofar as they deprived a union member of the right to nominate anyone for office but himself and provided that no member could be eligible for election to union office unless he had been a union member for five years and had served 180 days or more of sea time in each of two of the preceding three years on vessels covered by the union's collective bargaining agreements. The District Court dismissed the complaint for want of jurisdiction, reasoning that it did not allege a denial of the equal rights of union members to nominate candidates, guaranteed by 101(a)(1) of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959, and therefore was beyond the court's jurisdiction under 102 of that statute. (221 F Supp 545.) The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed on the ground that the complaint alleged a violation of 101(a)(1). (324 F2d 486.)

The petitioner, a state prisoner who had repeatedly assisted other prisoners to prepare petitions for postconviction relief, was placed in disciplinary confinement and deprived of certain privileges for violating a prison regulation prohibiting inmates from helping other inmates to prepare writs or other legal papers. The United States District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, ordering that the petitioner be restored to his status as an ordinary prisoner, held the prison regulation invalid on the ground that it was in conflict with an illiterate prisoner's federal right to habeas corpus (252 F Supp 783). The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed, holding that the state's interest in preserving prison discipline and limiting the practice of law to licensed attorneys justified whatever burden the regulation might place on access to federal habeas corpus (382 F2d 353).

A union agent picketed a dwelling under construction because a subcontractor for electrical work therein employed nonunion men. Thereupon another subcontractor for carpentry work and his men stopped work. Both the latter subcontractor and the agent informed the general contractor that he would not receive any skilled trades if he did not replace the subcontractor. The National Labor Relations Board found the union and its agent guilty of an unfair labor practice within the secondary boycott sections of the National Labor Relations Act as amended by the Labor Management Relations Act.

The plaintiff, a member of the crew of a fishing trawler operated by the defendant, came on deck to go ashore and was injured when his foot slipped off the ship's rail onto which he had stepped in order to reach a ladder attached to the pier. The ship's rail, where the plaintiff had lost his footing, was covered with slime and fish gurry, apparently remaining there from the earlier unloading operations. To recover for his injuries the plaintiff brought the present action in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts, the complaint containing a count alleging unseaworthiness. With respect to that count the district judge instructed the jury that in order to allow recovery, they must find that the slime and gurry had been on the ship's rail for a period of time long enough for the defendant to have learned about it and to have removed it. (167 F Supp 434.) Plaintiff's request to instruct the jury that notice was not a necessary element in proving liability based upon unseaworthiness of the vessel was denied. The jury found for the defendant shipowner on the unseaworthiness count. Upon plaintiff's appeal, taken upon the sole ground that the district judge had been in error in instructing the jury as stated above, the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit affirmed, holding that at least with respect to an unseaworthy condition which arises only during the progress of the voyage, the shipowner's obligation is merely to see that reasonable care is used under the circumstances incident to the correction of the newly arisen defect. (265 F2d 426.)

In  Stanford v Kentucky (1989) 492 U.S. 361, 106 L. Ed. 2d 306, 109 S. Ct. 2969, reh den  492 U.S. 937, 106 L. Ed. 2d 635, 110 S. Ct. 23, the United States Supreme Court held that imposition of the death penalty on offenders for murders committed at 16 and 17 years of age did not constitute cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Federal Constitution's Eighth Amendment. After an accused had reached the age of 18 years, he was convicted in a Missouri state court of murder, and was sentenced to death, for a homicide committed when he was aged 17. The Missouri Supreme Court affirmed ( 944 S.W.2d 165, cert den 522 U.S. 953, 139 L. Ed. 2d 293, 118 S. Ct. 376), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit denied the accused's petition for a writ of habeas corpus ( 235 F.3d 1124, cert den 534 U.S. 924, 151 L. Ed. 2d 206, 122 S. Ct. 280).

A minor procedural defect which petitioners tried to correct does not constitute an adequate independent state ground for decision barring review by this Court. The petition for writ of certiorari is granted and the judgment is reversed. Robinson v. Florida, 378 U.S. 153.

Two privately retained lawyers represented three criminal defendants charged with first degree murder throughout the state proceedings which followed their indictment in Pennsylvania. All the defendants were tried separately. The first defendant to come to trial was found guilty in the Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas wholly on the basis of circumstantial evidence after his defense rested without presenting any evidence. At no time did such defendant or his lawyers object to the multiple representation. The other two codefendants were subsequently acquitted. The first defendant eventually petitioned for collateral relief under state law, alleging, among other claims, that he had been denied the effective assistance of counsel because his defense lawyers represented conflicting interests. After hearing testimony from both lawyers--one of whom testified that concern for the other two codefendants had influenced his judgment not to present a defense--the Court of Common Pleas denied relief. The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania affirmed both the first defendant's original conviction and the denial of collateral relief (472 Pa 129, 371 A2d 468). The court ruled that there was no dual representation "in the true sense of the term," and that resting the defense was a reasonable tactic which did not amount to a denial of the effective assistance of counsel. The defendant then sought habeas corpus relief in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, which accepted the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania's conclusion that there had been no multiple representation. The District Court also decided that, even assuming multiple representation, the evidence adduced in the state post-conviction proceeding revealed no conflict of interest. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed, holding that the two lawyers' participation in the trial of the defendants established multiple representation as a matter of law, and further ruling that a sufficient possibility of conflict of interest had been raised to prove a violation of the defendant's Sixth Amendment right to the effective assistance of counsel, since a defendant was entitled to reversal of a conviction whenever some showing of a possible conflict of interest or prejudice, however remote, was made (593 F2d 512).

The Government conceded that it violated the plea agreement when it objected to a reduction for acceptance of responsibility after petitioner assisted in another crime while awaiting sentencing. The Court of Appeals found that petitioner forfeited the breach of plea agreement claim by failing to raise it in the district court. In applying Rule 52(b)'s plain error standard, the Court of Appeals held that petitioner did not satisfy the third prong of plain-error analysis because he did not show that his ultimate sentence was affected. The Court held that Rule 52(b)'s plain-error test applied to petitioner's forfeited claim that the Government failed to meet its obligations under the plea agreement and that it applied in the usual fashion. Noting that the question was actually whether a conceivable reason existed for disregarding the evident application of Rule 52(b), the Court found that neither petitioner's doctrinal arguments nor the practical considerations that he raised counseled against applying plain-error review in the present context. Contrary to petitioner's claim, the Government's breach did not retroactively cause his guilty plea to have been unknowing or involuntary.

In 1994, the Missouri legislature enacted a statute to restrict the permissible amounts of monetary contributions to candidates for state office. The statute took effect in 1995, after a ballot initiative with even stricter contribution limits--although approved by 74 percent of Missouri voters--had been invalidated as violative of the Federal Constitution's First Amendment by the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, which had nevertheless noted alleged improprieties with respect to contributions to Missouri political figures (72 F3d 633, cert den 518 US 1033, 135 L Ed 2d 1094, 116 S Ct 2579). The statute provided, among other matters, that (1) with respect to elections for statewide offices, including state auditor, the amount of contributions made by or accepted from any person other than the candidate was not to exceed 1,000; (2) contributions to candidates for some other state offices were to be limited to as little as 250; and (3) the statutory dollar amounts were to be adjusted each even-numbered year by taking into account the consumer price index. Thus, as of 1998, the limit was adjusted to 1,075 for contributions to candidates for statewide office, while the limit on contributions to candidates for some other state offices was adjusted to 275. A political action committee (PAC) gave a candidate for state auditor 1,025 in 1997 and another 50 in 1998. The PAC, alleging that it would have contributed more to the candidate's campaign but for the limitation--and the candidate, alleging that he could campaign effectively only with more generous contributions than those allowed by the statute--brought suit in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri against various Missouri officials to enjoin enforcement of the statute as assertedly violating the Federal Constitution's First and Fourteenth Amendments. The District Court, in granting summary judgment in favor of the officials, (1) cited evidence including (a) an affidavit from a Missouri state senator--the co-chair of the legislature's campaign finance reform committee at the time that the contribution limits were enacted--who said that large contributions had the real potential to buy votes, and (b) newspaper reports supporting inferences of impropriety with respect to contributions to Missouri political figures; (2) found adequate support for the statute in the proposition that large contributions raised suspicions of influence peddling that tended to undermine citizens' confidence in the integrity of government; and (3) concluded that the case was controlled by Buckley v Valeo (1976) 424 US 1, 46 L Ed 2d 659, 96 S Ct 612, in which the United States Supreme Court had upheld the constitutionality of a federal statute establishing a 1,000 limitation on contributions to any single candidate for federal office (5 F Supp 2d 734). However, the Court of Appeals (1) enjoined enforcement of the law pending appeal (151 F3d 763); and (2) ultimately reversed and ordered a remand, as the Court of Appeals reasoned in part that Missouri's claim of a compelling interest in avoiding the corruption or the perception of corruption with respect to large campaign contributions was insufficient by itself to satisfy the requisite strict scrutiny (161 F3d 519, reh, en banc, den 1999 US App LEXIS 5241).

After the guilt phase of a trial in the Superior Court of Orange County, California, a defendant was convicted of murder and other crimes. During the trial's penalty phase, several witnesses testified that in the 1 year and 9 months that the defendant had spent in prison since his arrest, he had (1) undergone a religious conversion, (2) participated in prison Bible study classes and a prison ministry, and (3) had a calming effect on other prisoners. The trial judge gave the jury a catchall "factor (k)" instruction--as set forth in a California statute then in force--directing the jurors to consider "[a]ny other circumstance which extenuates the gravity of the crime even though it is not a legal excuse for the crime." The prosecutor's closing argument included statements that (1) factor (k) did not allow the jury to consider anything that had happened after the crime; and (2) the circumstances of the case outweighed the mitigating effect of the defendant's religious conversion. When the defense objected to this argument, the trial judge (1) admonished the jury that the prosecutor's comments were merely argument, but (2) did not explicitly instruct that the prosecutor's interpretation of factor (k) was incorrect. The jury returned a verdict recommending a death sentence, and the judge sentenced the defendant to death.

In the 1970 Ohio primary election, appellant voted as a Republican and was a candidate for the Republican nomination to the House of Representatives from the 22d Congressional District of Ohio. Political allegiances change and, in the upcoming election, appellant seeks the nomination to Congress of the American Independent Party. He is prevented from pursuing this nomination, however, by an intricate statutory scheme. Central to this scheme is a statute which provides, with various exceptions not relevant here, e. g., Ohio Rev. Code Ann. _ 3517.013 et seq. (Supp. 1970), that "no person shall be a candidate for nomination or election at a party primary if he voted as a member of a different political party at any primary election within the next preceding four calendar years." Ohio Rev. Code Ann. _ 3513.191 (1960). Other provisions also being attacked require those working for primary candidates or signing their nominating petitions to be members of the party in which nomination is sought, id., _ 3513.05 (Supp. 1970).

After a bench trial on a federal criminal charge, a United States District Court in the Tenth Federal Judicial Circuit found the defendant guilty, the court having previously denied the defendant's motion to suppress evidence that had been discovered during a search by Border Patrol agents after they had stopped the defendant's car. Following the trial, but before sentencing, the District Court dismissed the indictment, relying on the United States Supreme Court's decision in Almeida-Sanchez v United States (1973) 413 US 266, 37 L Ed 2d 596, 93 S Ct 2535, which held that a warrantless roving patrol search of a vehicle for aliens, conducted without probable cause at a point removed from the border or its functional equivalent, violated the Fourth Amendment. The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit held that the government's appeal in the instant case was barred by double jeopardy.

With respect to the quadrennial election of the United States President by means of Presidential electors, (1) Art II, 1, cl 2 of the Federal Constitution provides that each state shall appoint, "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct," a specified number of electors; and (2) 3 USCS 5 in effect provides, insofar as congressional consideration of a state's electoral votes is concerned, that if the state's legislature has provided for final determination of contests or controversies by a law made prior to election day, then that determination shall be conclusive if made at least 6 days prior to the time of meeting of the electors. On November 8, 2000, the day following a Presidential election, the Florida division of elections reported that the Republican candidate for President had received 2,909,135 votes and the Democratic candidate had received 2,907,351 votes, a margin of 1,784 votes. Pursuant to a Florida statute, an automatic machine recount occurred and resulted in a smaller margin of victory for the Republican candidate. The Democratic candidate then exercised his state statutory right to submit written requests for manual recounts in four counties. On November 14, in an action brought by one such county--and joined by a second such county's canvassing board, the Democratic candidate, and the Florida Democratic party--the state's Circuit Court of the Second Judicial Circuit ruled that (1) a 7-day deadline set by a state statutory provision for filing election returns was mandatory, (2) a county's board could amend its returns at a later date, and (3) Florida's secretary of state could exercise her discretion in deciding whether to include the late amended returns in the secretary's statewide certification of the election results. After the secretary determined that none of the submissions by four counties justified an extension of the deadline, the Circuit Court, on November 17, ruled that the secretary had not acted arbitrarily and had exercised her discretion in a reasonable manner. On appeal, Florida's First District Court of Appeal certified the matter to the Florida Supreme Court, which enjoined the secretary and a Florida commission from finally certifying the election results and declaring a winner until further order of that court. On November 21, the Florida Supreme Court issued a decision which effectively extended the 7-day statutory deadline--assuming that it would have applied--by 12 days and directed the secretary to accept manual recounts submitted prior to the extended deadline, as the Florida Supreme Court (1) determined that under the plain text of the Florida statutes, a discrepancy between a sample manual recount and machine returns, due to the way in which a ballot was punched or marked, constituted an error in vote tabulation that was sufficient to trigger the state statutory provisions for a full manual recount; (2) ruled that with respect to ignoring late returns, the "may"-ignore language of one statutory provision controlled over the "shall"-ignore language of another provision; (3) relied in part upon a right-to-vote provision in the Florida constitution in concluding that late manual recounts could be rejected only under limited circumstances; and (4) invoked the equitable powers of the court to fashion a remedy, in view of what the court said was a reluctance to rewrite Florida's election code (772 So. 2d 1220, 2000 Fla LEXIS 2311). On November 24, the United States Supreme Court granted a certiorari petition by the Republican candidate and set an expedited schedule for review (531 US ‚àö¬∂‚àö¬∂‚àö¬∂, 148 L Ed 2d 478, 121 S Ct ‚àö¬∂‚àö¬∂‚àö¬∂).

A petition for certiorari was filed on December 14, 1978, some 17 months out of time as a conventional petition for certiorari under Rule 22(2) of the Rules of the United States Supreme Court, by a pro se petitioner whose convictions in a Federal District Court on criminal charges had been affirmed on June 9, 1977, by the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. The petitioner, whose petition presented a single question--"What remedy is available for petitioner when court-appointed attorney failed and refused to file timely petition for writ of certiorari in defiance of the petitioner's written request that same be done?"--alleged that he had asked the court-appointed lawyer representing him at the time to file a timely petition for certiorari after the Court of Appeals' decision, that in September of 1977 he had received an assurance from the lawyer that such request had been honored, that in July of 1978, he had learned from the Clerk of the United States Supreme Court that no petition had been filed, and that subsequent letters to the attorney were never answered.

The liability insurer for the driver of a truck which had collided with a bus brought an action in the nature of interpleader in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon. The action was brought under the federal interpleader statute, 28 USC 1335, and the insurer paid into court the amount of the truckdriver's insurance policy and interpleaded the owner and driver of the truck, the owner and driver of the bus, and the bus passengers who were injured in the collision. The District Court granted an injunction restraining the injured passengers from further prosecuting any proceedings against the insurer, the truckdriver, the bus owner, and the busdriver. On interlocutory appeal, the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed, and ordered the injunction dissolved and the action dismissed, holding that since the insurance policy and state law precluded the injured passengers from being able to sue the insurer until judgments were obtained against the insured, the passengers were not "claimants" against whom the insurer could bring an action in the nature of interpleader under 1335. (363 F2d 7.)

In 1984, a Cuban immigrant with little education and almost no knowledge of English was charged with murder. After the accused was provided with a defense attorney and an interpreter, an Oregon judge held a plea hearing, and accepted the accused's plea of nolo contendere to first-degree manslaughter. Two years later, the accused brought a collateral attack on the plea in a postconviction proceeding in the Circuit Court for Marion County, Oregon. In his petition, the accused alleged that his plea had not been knowing and intelligent, and therefore was invalid, because the interpreter had not translated accurately and completely for him the mens rea element of manslaughter. The Oregon Circuit Court, dismissing the petition after a hearing, found that the accused had been properly served by his interpreter and that the interpreter had correctly, fully, and accurately translated the communications between the accused and his attorney. The Oregon Court of Appeals affirmed, and the Oregon Supreme Court denied review. Thereafter, the accused filed a habeas corpus petition in the United States District Court for the District of Oregon. The accused, seeking a federal evidentiary hearing on whether his plea of nolo contendere was unconstitutional, alleged that the material facts concerning the interpreter's translation were not adequately developed at the state postconviction hearing. The District Court, however, ruled that no evidentiary hearing was required, since the accused's failure to develop the material facts relevant to his federal claim was attributable to inexcusable neglect. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, reversing in pertinent part, expressed the view that (1) the material facts had not been adequately developed in the accused's state postconviction proceedings due to the negligent failure of the accused's counsel; and (2) since the accused had not deliberately bypassed the orderly procedure of the state courts, the accused was entitled to a federal evidentiary hearing on the question whether the mens rea element of manslaughter had been properly explained to him (926 F2d 1492).

Among the matters prohibited by 18 USCS 2314 is the knowing transportation in interstate commerce of "falsely made, forged, altered, or counterfeited securities." Another statute defines "securities," for purposes of 2314, to include valid motor vehicle titles. During the period from December 1984 through July 1985, several individuals participated in a "title washing" scheme involving motor vehicle titles. Pursuant to such scheme, (1) used cars were purchased in Pennsylvania; (2) the cars' odometers were "rolled back" to indicate lower mileage figures; (3) the titles to the cars were altered to reflect such figures; (4) the altered titles were submitted to Virginia officials, who issued Virginia titles incorporating the false mileage figures; and (5) the "washed" titles were sent back to Pennsylvania, where they were used in connection with car sales to unsuspecting buyers. The scheme participant who received the "washed" titles when they were returned was indicted and convicted, in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania, for violating 2314. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, affirming the conviction, ruled that the purpose of the term "falsely made" in 2314 was to prohibit the fraudulent introduction into commerce of falsely made documents regardless of the precise method by which the documents' introducer, or the introducer's confederates, effected the documents' lack of authenticity (888 F2d 283).

An accused was convicted of theft in an Illinois state court after the court, at an earlier trial for the same offense, declared a mistrial on the state's motion, and over the accused's objection, because the indictment was fatally deficient under Illinois law. On the accused's petition for habeas corpus, the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois dismissed the petition, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed (447 F2d 733).

The ultimate issue in the present cases was whether under 5(11) of the Interstate Commerce Act--providing that voluntary consolidations of railroads must have the assent of a majority vote of all shares, "unless a different vote is required under applicable State law, in which case the number so required shall assent, of the votes of the holders of the shares entitled to vote"--the holders of the class B stock of a Missouri railroad company were entitled to vote separately, as a class, on the proposed plan of consolidation of the Missouri company with another railroad company controlled by it into a newly formed corporation. The Missouri corporation, by its plan of consolidation, proposed to change its class A stock from voting shares preferentially entitled to noncumulative dividends of not to exceed $ 5 per share annually to shares that participated equally in all of the earnings of the company, and to relegate to ordinary shares the class B stock, now enjoying all of the earnings and the equity in excess of the present class A preferences. The board of directors of the Missouri corporation announced that its class B shareholders were not entitled to vote on the plan separately and apart from its class A shareholders, and that it intended to submit the plan only to the collective vote of the class A and class B shareholders. In three separate declaratory judgment actions filed by different class B shareholders seeking a declaration that the plan required the separate approval of the holders of the class B shares by majority vote, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri held that Missouri law, as adopted in 5(11) of the Act, required the separate approval of each class of shareholders. (233 F Supp 747.) The Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed on the ground that despite Missouri law, the plenary character of 5(11) compelled a contrary result. (359 F2d 106.)

The operator of a fleet of oil tankers transporting petroleum products between Texas and Atlantic Coast ports sued a union in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas, seeking a judgment declaring invalid an agency shop agreement executed by the union on behalf of unlicensed seamen on the tankers. The District Court held the agreement invalid under the Texas right-to-work laws. A three-member panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed (483 F2d 603), but on rehearing en banc, the Court of Appeals affirmed (504 F2d 272).

The Federal Kidnapping Act (28 USC 1201) provides for the death penalty if the kidnapped person has not been liberated unharmed. The main issue in the present case was whether a charge of kidnapping omitting a statement that the victim has not been liberated unharmed is the charge of a capital offense, which can be made only by way of indictment, and not by way of information. In an information filed in the United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama defendant was charged with transporting a kidnapping victim across state lines, in violation of the act. He waived indictment, counsel, and venue, and upon his plea of guilty he was convicted and sentenced. Prior to his waivers and plea the trial judge, at the instance of an Assistant United States Attorney, had an interview with a special agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in the judge's chambers, dealing with defendant's background and his connection with the kidnapping, neither the defendant nor anyone representing him being present at the interview. Defendant sought relief in the District Court under 28 USC 2255 from his conviction and sentence, alleging the invalidity. After protracted litigation the District Court resentenced petitioner, but refused him permission to withdraw his waivers and plea of guilty. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed, one of the judges dissenting. (250 F2d 842.)

Neither declaratory nor injunctive relief should be granted to an air carrier in an action seeking to prevent, on the ground that the Civil Aeronautics Board has exclusive jurisdiction, a state public utilities commission from exercising its claimed jurisdiction over rates charged by the carrier for transportation between points on the mainland and an island, both parts of the same state, but separated by the high seas.

A federal mine inspector attempted to inspect the premises of a stone quarry operator under authority granted by 103(a) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 (30 USCS 813(a)), which provides that federal mine inspectors are to inspect all mines at set intervals to insure compliance with health and safety standards, and to make follow-up inspections to determine whether previously discovered violations have been corrected, and which also authorizes mine inspectors to inspect any coal or other mine without having first obtained a warrant. Although the inspection was a follow-up to one which uncovered numerous safety and health violations, the quarry operator refused to allow the inspection to be completed because the inspector did not have a search warrant. In response to an action filed by the Secretary of Labor to enjoin the quarry operator from refusing to permit the warrantless search, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin granted summary judgment in favor of the quarry operator on the ground that the Fourth Amendment prohibited the warrantless search of stone quarries authorized by the Act (493 F Supp 963).

While representing the inmate in his habeas proceedings, counsel developed evidence relating to the inmate's culpability and the appropriateness of his sentence that led to the clemency request. The Tennessee courts refused to appoint counsel for the inmate in the clemency proceedings. The Supreme Court held that the inmate was not required to obtain a certificate of appealability (COA) in order to appeal the district court's denial of his _ 3599 request. A COA was not required under 28 U.S.C.S. _ 2253(c)(1)(A) because the denial of the inmate's motion to enlarge counsel's authority was not an order that disposed of the merits of a habeas proceeding. The motion was erroneously denied because _ 3599 authorized appointed counsel to represent the inmate in his state clemency proceedings. Section 3599(e) provided that counsel appointed to represent a state death-sentenced prisoner in 28 U.S.C.S. _ 2254 proceedings would also provide representation in subsequent proceedings for executive or other clemency that might be available. As federal clemency was exclusively executive, "other" clemency encompassed state clemency. Applicability of _ 3599(e) was not limited to federal litigants.

Upon trial in the United States District Court for the Western District of Kentucky, the defendant was convicted under an indictment which included, inter alia, counts for violations of 18 USCS 1341, which prohibits use or causing the use of the mails for the purpose of executing a scheme or artifice to defraud. The record showed that the defendant had unlawfully used another person's bank credit card at out-of-state motels, resulting in the mailing of sales invoices by the motels to the bank and by the bank to the credit card owner. The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed the convictions under the mail fraud statute (468 F2d 529).

The present case involves federal reclamation projects, the Central Valley Project (Nos. 122, 123, 124) and the Santa Barbara County Project (No. 125). In the course of carrying out these projects, the United States entered into contracts with two California irrigation districts and the Santa Barbara County Water Agency. In accordance with the pertinent federal statutes (43 USC 423e; 485h), these contracts contained provisions that project water should not be furnished to lands in excess of 160 acres in a single ownership; that the United States would, after construction of the water supply facilities and the lateral distribution system for the irrigation districts, furnish water to the districts and the agency for a period of 40 years; and that, as to the distribution systems, liquidation of the maximum stated expenditure of the United States would be spread by instalments over 40 years, without interest. The validity of these contracts was attacked in the present proceedings on various grounds. In Nos. 122 and 123 the irrigation districts instituted proceedings in California state courts for confirmation of the contracts. In each case the court denied confirmation and the Supreme Court of California affirmed (47 Cal2d 597, 306 P2d 824; 47 Cal2d 681, 306 P2d 886). In No. 124 two property owners instituted a proceeding for a writ of mandate to compel one of these districts to vacate its resolution denying the exclusion from the district of the petitioners' lands in excess of 320 acres. Exclusion was sought on the ground that, in view of the excess acreage provisions of the contracts, such excess lands would not be benefited by the operations of the district. In so far as the trial court denied relief, the Supreme Court of California affirmed (47 Cal2d 695, 306 P2d 894). In No. 125 the water agency sued for a confirmation of the validity of the contract. The trial court held the contract valid, but the Supreme Court of California reversed the judgment below (47 Cal2d 699, 306 P2d 875).

After members of the Ohio National Guard had killed or injured several students at Kent State University, the plaintiffs, who were students at the University, brought suit in a Federal District Court in Ohio. The plaintiffs sought (1) an injunction restraining the Governor of Ohio from prematurely ordering the National Guard to duty in the future, (2) an injunction restraining leaders of the National Guard from violating the plaintiffs' constitutional rights in the future, and (3) a declaratory judgment to the effect that an Ohio statute granting immunity to riot-suppression personnel was unconstitutional. The District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed with respect to the request for injunctive relief against the Governor's use of the National Guard and with respect to the request for declaratory relief against the immunity statute, but the Court of Appeals reversed and remanded the case with directions that the District Court resolve the question whether there was and is a pattern of training, weaponry, and orders in the Ohio National Guard which singly or together require or make inevitable the use of fatal force in suppressing civilian disorders when the total circumstances at the critical time are such that nonlethal force would suffice to restore order and the use of lethal force is not reasonably necessary (456 F2d 608). After granting certiorari, the United States Supreme Court was informed that none of the named plaintiffs was still enrolled in the University, that the officials originally named as party defendants no longer held offices in which they could exercise any authority over the state's National Guard, that the National Guard had adopted new "use-of-force" rules differing substantially from those in effect when the complaint was filed, and that the initial training of National Guard recruits relating to civil disorder control had been revised.

The petition for rehearing is granted and the order denying the petition for writ of certiorari, 389 U.S. 835, is set aside. The petition for a writ of certiorari is granted. The judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit is vacated and the case is remanded to that court for further consideration in light of Bruton v. United States, 391 U.S. 123. See Roberts v. Russell, ante, p. 293.

On remand from the decision in Deen v Gulf, Colorado & Santa Fe R. Co. 253 US 925, 1 L ed 2d 721, 77 S Ct 715, the Court of Civil Appeals of Texas, Eleventh Supreme Judicial District, whose judgment (reversing a judgment for plaintiff, a railroad employee suing under the Federal Employers' Liability Act) the United States Supreme Court had reversed on the ground that the proofs justified the jury's conclusion that employer negligence played a part in causing plaintiff's injury, affirmed the judgment for plaintiff, viewing the question of employer negligence as foreclosed by the United States Supreme Court's ruling. On review, the Texas Supreme Court remanded the case to the Court of Civil Appeals, directing it to make an independent determination whether the jury finding was so against the weight of the evidence as to require a new trial, and then to affirm the judgment of the trial court or order a new trial. Plaintiff thereupon sought leave from the United States Supreme Court to petition for mandamus to require the Texas Supreme Court to conform its decision to the United States Supreme Court's earlier ruling.

The United States District Court for the District of Kansas entered judgment for petitioner upon a jury verdict in a products liability suit brought by the respondents against the petitioner and denied the respondents' motion for new trial. The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed the District Court's judgment and ordered a new trial, holding that the failure of a juror to respond affirmatively to a question on voir dire seeking to elicit information about previous injuries to members of the juror's immediate family had prejudiced the respondents' right of peremptory challenge and that a new trial was necessary to cure this error (687 F2d 338).

In 1970 and 1971, a wholly owned foreign subsidiary of a domestic corporation paid income taxes to the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland and distributed dividends to the domestic corporation. After reporting these dividends on its federal income tax return, the domestic corporation sought an indirect tax credit in the amount specified in 26 USCS 902 (later amended)--under which a domestic parent's tax credit was calculated by multiplying the foreign tax paid by the portion of its foreign subsidiary's after-tax accumulated profits that was issued to the domestic parent in the form of a taxable dividend--for a portion of the foreign taxes paid by the subsidiary. In 1973, after the subsidiary carried back a net loss on its British tax return to offset portions of its 1970 and 1971 income, British taxing authorities refunded a substantial portion of the subsidiary's 1970 and 1971 foreign tax payments. Because the deductions that created, for British tax purposes, the subsidiary's 1973 loss would not have been allowable under domestic income tax principles, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, in recalculating the domestic corporation's indirect tax credit for 1970 and 1971, lowered the foreign taxes paid to reflect the subsidiary's refund, but refused to lower the subsidiary's accumulated profits for those years. The Commissioner thus assessed substantial tax deficiencies against the domestic corporation for 1970 and 1971. After paying the deficiencies and having the Internal Revenue Service deny its administrative refund claim, the domestic corporation, averring that foreign tax law principles governed the calculation of accumulated profits in 902, sought a refund in the United States Claims Court. The Claims Court, however, finding that the purposes underlying 902 favored calculation of "accumulated profits" under domestic tax concepts, rejected the domestic corporation's refund claim (14 Cl Ct 23). The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, reversing, expressed the view that the plain meaning of 902 required accumulated profits to be determined under foreign law (856 F2d 170).

In an action in the United States District Court for the District of Hawaii, the State of Hawaii asserted various antitrust claims against the defendants in connection with the defendants' sale, marketing, and distribution of refined petroleum products. One of the counts of the complaint alleged that the state brought the action as parens patriae and was entitled to recover treble damages under 4 of the Clayton Act for injury to the state's economy and prosperity. Such injury allegedly included the wrongful extraction from the state of its citizens' revenues; increased taxes to offset such losses of revenues; curtailment of manufacturing, shipping, and commerce; and competitive disadvantages to Hawaiian goods in the national market. The District Court denied the defendants' motion to dismiss this count (301 F Supp 982), but the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed and directed the count to be dismissed on the ground that injury to the state's general economy was not an injury to "business or property" and thus did not fall within 4 of the Clayton Act, which authorized the recovery of treble damages for injuries to a person's "business or property" by reason of violations of the federal antitrust laws (431 F2d 1282).

An action for wrongful death was brought in a federal court in Pennsylvania more than one year, but within two years, after the death had occurred in Alabama. The action was brought under an Alabama statute, which, in conferring the right of action, required that the action be brought within two years from the death. In view of a one-year limitation in the analogous Pennsylvania statute, summary judgment was entered for defendant, the court proceeding on the theory that it was bound by the Pennsylvania conflict of laws rule calling for the application of its own law rather than that of the place of the accident.

Defendant, Sanchez, was charged in a one count indictment with knowingly and unlawfully transporting aliens within the United States in violation of 8 U.S.C. _ 1324(a)(2). After an evidentiary hearing the district court granted Sanchez's motion to suppress evidence unlawfully seized by police. The government has appealed. We affirm.

The Death on the High Seas Act (DOHSA) (46 USCS Appx 761 et seq.) provides that (1) where a wrongful death has occurred on the high seas, the personal representative of the decedent may maintain a suit for damages in Federal District Court for the exclusive benefit of the decedent's wife, husband, parent, child or dependent relative (46 USCS Appx 761); and (2) the recovery in such suit is to be a fair and just compensation for the pecuniary loss sustained by the persons for whose benefit the action is brought (46 USCS Appx 762). In 1983, an air carrier's passenger flight en route from Anchorage, Alaska, to Seoul, South Korea, strayed into air space of the then Soviet Union and was shot down over the Sea of Japan. All passengers on board the flight were killed. Personal representatives of three of the passengers brought actions in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia against the carrier. The District Court jury, after a trial, found that the carrier had committed willful misconduct and awarded punitive damages. However, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit vacated the punitive damages award on the ground that the Warsaw Convention did not permit the recovery of punitive damages. The United States Supreme Court denied certiorari. Following remand to the District Court, while the representatives' cases were awaiting trial, the Supreme Court held in Zicherman v Korean Air Lines Co. (1996) 516 US 217, 133 L Ed 2d 596, 116 S Ct 629, that DOHSA supplied the substantive law where an airplane crash occurred on the high seas. Thereafter, the carrier moved to dismiss the representatives' claims for nonpecuniary damages, and the District Court granted the motion (935 F Supp 10, 1996 US Dist LEXIS 7957). On appeal, the Court of Appeals, affirming, expressed the view that assuming that there was a survival cause of action under general maritime law which allowed a decedent's estate to recover for injuries sustained by the decedent--including predeath pain and suffering--such an action was unavailable when the death was on the high seas (117 F3d 1477, 1997 US App LEXIS 17372).

The present action was brought by the plaintiff in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York to recover from the government taxes illegally collected. The plaintiff's motion for summary judgment was granted by the District Court in an opinion (130 F Supp 322) which, after finding that plaintiff had paid taxes to the government in a specified amount, made no finding of the date or dates of payment or as to the amount of interest to be included in the judgment. Thereupon the clerk made a notation in the civil docket to the effect that the motion for a summary judgment had been granted. Thereafter counsel for the plaintiff presented to the judge, and the latter signed and filed, a formal document captioned "Judgment," ordering the defendant to pay to the plaintiff specified amounts, one for the principal and one for interest thereon. The clerk then made a notation in the civil docket to the effect that judgment was filed and docketed against defendant in the specified sums. The government appealed from the judgment and this appeal was timely if the date from which the time for appeal ran was fixed by the formal judgment and its entry, but was not timely if the time for appeal was fixed by the clerk's first entry of judgment based on the court's opinion. Taking the latter view, the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, six judges sitting en banc, unanimously dismissed the appeal (236 F2d 889).

The motion for leave to proceed in forma pauperis and the petition for writ of certiorari are granted. The judgment is vacated and the case is remanded for consideration in light of Elkins v. United States, ante, p. 206, decided this day. Search and Seizure

The appeal is dismissed for want of a substantial federal question. MR. JUSTICE FRANKFURTER would note probable jurisdiction and hear the case, the more so inasmuch as the transactions which New York has taxed concerned foreign commerce

Petitioners brought suit against respondent after a catheter ruptured in the patient's coronary artery during surgery. The catheter was a Class III device that received premarket approval from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The Court agreed with the lower courts' determination that 21 U.S.C.S. _ 360k(a) preempted the common-law claims challenging the safety and effectiveness of the catheter. The Court found that the federal government had established "requirements applicable to" respondent's catheter within the meaning of _ 360k(a)(1). Premarket approval imposed "requirements" under MDA because the FDA required devices that received premarket approval to be made with almost no deviations from the specifications in the approval application. Further, New York's tort duties constituted "requirements" under the MDA. Thus, petitioners' negligence and strict liability claims that related to safety and effectiveness were based on New York "requirements" with respect to the catheter that were "different from, or in addition to" the federal requirements. The Court rejected the contention that the general common-law duties were not requirements maintained "with respect to devices."

The plaintiffs, who were a minor political party and others, brought an action in the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington to challenge the validity of a Washington statute which (1) required minor-party candidates for office to appear on the primary election ballot, and (2) prohibited any candidate's name from being placed on the general election ballot for an office unless he or she received at least 1% of all votes cast for that office in the primary. The District Court entered summary judgment against the plaintiffs, but the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed and directed the District Court to enter summary judgment for the plaintiffs. As applied to statewide election contests, the Court of Appeals held, this statute was invalid because (1) it infringed the First and Fourteenth Amendment rights of individuals to associate for the advancement of political beliefs, and of qualified voters to cast their ballots effectively, by substantially barring minor-party candidates from the statewide general election ballot, and (2) the state's purported goal of preventing overcrowded ballots and voter confusion (a) was not supported by any evidence of such confusion and (b) could have been served by measures less restrictive of individual liberties (765 F2d 1417).

The City of Miami filed suit against Bank of America and Wells Fargo (Banks), alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act (FHA or Act). The FHA prohibits, among other things, racial discrimination in connection with real-estate transactions, 42 U. S. C. ¬ß¬ß3604(b), 3605(a), and permits any ‚Äúaggrieved person‚Äù to file a civil damages action for a violation of the Act, ¬ß¬ß3613(a)(1)(A), (c)(1). The City‚Äôs complaints charge that the Banks intentionally targeted predatory practices at African-American and Latino neighborhoods and residents, lending to minority borrowers on worse terms than equally creditworthy nonminority borrowers and inducing defaults by failing to extend refinancing and loan modifications to minority borrowers on fair terms. The City alleges that the Banks‚Äô discriminatory conduct led to a disproportionate number of foreclosures and vacancies in majorityminority neighborhoods, which impaired the City‚Äôs effort to assure racial integration, diminished the City‚Äôs property-tax revenue, and increased demand for police, fire, and other municipal services. The District Court dismissed the complaints on the grounds that (1) the harms alleged fell outside the zone of interests the FHA protects and (2) the complaints failed to show a sufficient causal connection between the City‚Äôs injuries and the Banks‚Äô discriminatory conduct. The Eleventh Circuit reversed.

During its 1983 through 1988 taxable fiscal years, an employer maintained several tax-qualified defined benefit pension plans that were subject to the minimum funding requirements prescribed by 302 of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (29 USCS 1082). The employer contributed, to the trust fund that supported the plans, five unencumbered truck terminals in 1983 and certain other unencumbered real property in 1984. The employer credited the fair market value of the truck terminals against the employer's minimum funding obligation to the plans for the employer's 1982 and 1983 fiscal years and credited the fair market value of the other real property against the minimum funding obligation for the employer's 1984 fiscal year. Under 4975 of the Internal Revenue Code (26 USCS 4975), a two-tier excise tax is imposed on specified "prohibited transactions," which are defined under 4975(c)(1)(A) to include any direct or indirect sale or exchange of property between a plan and a disqualified person, and 4975(e)(2)(C) provides that the employer of the employees covered by a plan is a disqualified person. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue, ruling that the employer's transfers to the trust fund of the truck terminals and the other real property were sales or exchanges prohibited under 4975(c)(1)(A), determined that the employer owed a first-tier excise tax for each of the employer's 1983 through 1988 fiscal years and a second-tier excise tax for the employer's 1988 fiscal year. On the employer's petition for redetermination, the United States Tax Court, holding that the transfers were not sales or exchanges under 4975, entered a summary judgment for the employer (60 TCM 1423). The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court judgment (951 F 2d 76).

The operator of a California ski resort, upon encountering financial difficulties, became a debtor in bankruptcy by filing a petition for relief under Chapter 11 of the Bankruptcy Code in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the Eastern District of California. The debtor's appointed receiver, upon approval of the Bankruptcy Court, sold the debtor's assets, which included the debtor's inventory of skis, to a corporation that also was interested in operating a ski resort. When the California State Board of Equalization assessed a sales tax on the transaction, the receiver brought an adversary proceeding in Bankruptcy Court against the board and asked that the court enjoin collection of the assessment. In 1983, the Bankruptcy Court ruled that the transaction was exempt from taxation by the board, pursuant to the holdings of the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in (1) California State Board of Equalization v Goggin (1957, CA9 Cal) 245 F2d 44, cert den 353 US 961, 1 L Ed 2d 910, 77 S Ct 863 (Goggin II), where the court--while construing 28 USCS 960, which generally subjects those conducting business under authority of United States courts to the same taxation applicable to individuals or corporations, to be inapplicable to "essential sales in liquidation"--held that the collection of use taxes imposed on the use of goods from a bankruptcy liquidation sale on which no sales taxes had been paid was unlawful because such taxes burdened the essential processes of a Bankruptcy Court, and (2) an earlier case involving the same parties (Goggin I). The Bankruptcy Court granted the injunctive relief that the receiver had requested, in the form of an order prohibiting the board from assessing "a sales or other tax" against the receiver "or other parties" by reason of the receiver's sale of the debtor's assets to the corporation. The corporation began its ski resort operations, including the rental of ski equipment previously purchased from the debtor. In 1985, the board audited the corporation, determined that the corporation owed use taxes on its income from rentals of the skis, and assessed liability for such taxes. The corporation, seeking to prevent the board's imposition of use taxes on its ski rentals, petitioned the Bankruptcy Court for such relief pursuant to its 1983 order. The Bankruptcy Court denied the requested relief, holding on the merits that its 1983 order did not bar the use tax that the board sought to impose. On appeal by the corporation, the United States Bankruptcy Appellate Panel of the Ninth Circuit reversed, ruling that, in light of the injunction previously entered by the Bankruptcy Court and the holdings in the Goggin decisions, the board's assessment of a use tax upon the rentals of skis that had been acquired at a bankruptcy liquidation sale was improper (76 BR 757). On appeal by the board, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that the board's attempt to tax the ski rentals was prohibited by Goggin II and the Bankruptcy Court's injunction, and rejecting the board's argument that Goggin II had been wrongly decided (847 F2d 570).

Petitioner, who had been convicted in a Florida state court of "assault to murder in the second degree," filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus in the Supreme Court of Florida which alleged that he was an indigent, ignorant, and mentally ill Negro, that his request for counsel was denied, and that he was thus deprived of due process of law as guaranteed by the United States Constitution. The Florida Supreme Court, without any hearing upon petitioner's allegations, discharged the writ and remanded petitioner to custody. (113 So 2d 381.)

In 2015, ISIS terrorists unleashed a set of coordinated attacks across Paris, France, killing 130 victims, including Nohemi Gonzalez, a 23-year-old U. S. citizen.1 Gonzalez‚Äôs parents and brothers then sued Google, LLC, under 18 U. S. C. ¬ß¬ß2333(a) and (d)(2), alleging that Google was both directly and secondarily liable for the terrorist attack that killed Gonzalez.2 For their secondary-liability claims, plaintiffs alleged that Google aided and abetted and conspired with ISIS. All of their claims broadly center on the use of YouTube, which Google owns and operates, by ISIS and ISIS supporters. The District Court dismissed plaintiffs‚Äô complaint for failure to state a claim, though it offered plaintiffs leave to amend their complaint. Instead, plaintiffs stood on their complaint and appealed, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed in a consolidated opinion that also addressed Twitter, Inc. v. Taamneh, ___ U. S. ___ (2023). 2 F. 4th 871 (2021). With respect to this case, the Ninth Circuit held that most of the plaintiffs‚Äô claims were barred by ¬ß230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996, 110 Stat. 137, 47 U. S. C. ¬ß230(c)(1). The sole exceptions were plaintiffs‚Äô directand secondary-liability claims based on allegations that Google approved ISIS videos for advertisements and then shared proceeds with ISIS through YouTube‚Äôs revenuesharing system. The Ninth Circuit held that these potential claims were not barred by ¬ß230, but that plaintiffs‚Äô allegations failed to state a viable claim in any event. We granted certiorari to review the Ninth Circuit‚Äôs application of ¬ß230. See 598 U. S. ___ (2022). Plaintiffs did not seek review of the Ninth Circuit‚Äôs holdings regarding their revenue-sharing claims. In light of those unchallenged holdings and our disposition of Twitter, on which we also granted certiorari and in which we today reverse the Ninth Circuit‚Äôs judgment, it has become clear that plaintiffs‚Äô complaint‚Äîindependent of ¬ß230‚Äîstates little if any claim for relief. As plaintiffs concede, the allegations underlying their secondary-liability claims are materially identical to those at issue in Twitter. See Tr. of Oral Arg. 58. Since we hold that the complaint in that case fails to state a claim for aiding and abetting under ¬ß2333(d)(2), it appears to follow that the complaint here likewise fails to state such a claim. And, in discussing plaintiffs‚Äô revenue-sharing claims, the Ninth Circuit held that plaintiffs plausibly alleged neither that ‚ÄúGoogle reached an agreement with ISIS,‚Äù as required for conspiracy liability, nor that Google‚Äôs acts were ‚Äúintended to intimidate or coerce a civilian population, or to influence or affect a government,‚Äù as required for a directliability claim under ¬ß2333(a). 2 F. 4th, at 901, 907. Perhaps for that reason, at oral argument, plaintiffs only suggested that they should receive leave to amend their complaint if we were to reverse and remand in Twitter. Tr. of Oral Arg. 58, 163. We need not resolve either the viability of plaintiffs‚Äô claims as a whole or whether plaintiffs should receive further leave to amend. Rather, we think it sufficient to acknowledge that much (if not all) of plaintiffs‚Äô complaint seems to fail under either our decision in Twitter or the Ninth Circuit‚Äôs unchallenged holdings below. We therefore decline to address the application of ¬ß230 to a complaint that appears to state little, if any, plausible claim for relief. Instead, we vacate the judgment below and remand the case for the Ninth Circuit to consider plaintiffs‚Äô complaint in light of our decision in Twitter.

Part of the Trade Act of 1974 (19 USCS 2271-2321) allows extra unemployment benefits for workers who lose their jobs because of competition from imports, provided they have had at least 26 weeks of qualifying employment in the previous 52 weeks, and allows the Secretary of Labor to delegate eligibility determinations to certain state agencies. The Secretary issued guidelines, later prospectively superseded by statute, which advised those agencies not to count sick leave, vacation, military leave, or the like toward the 26-week requirement. A union, together with some of its members who had been denied benefits under those guidelines or who faced appeals from awards made in spite of them, filed an action for declaratory and injunctive relief in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, in which they contended that the guidelines violated the provisions of the Trade Act and, insofar as they affected military leave, violated other federal laws. The District Court (1) rejected the Secretary's contention that 19 USCS 2311(d), which makes entitlement determinations reviewable only in the same manner and to the same extent as determinations under the applicable state law, precluded federal jurisdiction over this action; and (2) rendered summary judgment in favor of the union, (a) declaring that sick leave and the like should be counted toward the 26-week requirement, for purposes of determining eligibility for benefits prior to the effective date of the superseding statute, and (b) ordering the Secretary to direct state agencies to review all denials of benefits in that period (568 F Supp 1047). The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed without reaching the merits of the case, holding (1) that the union lacked standing to bring the action either on behalf of nonmembers affected by the guidelines, for whom it was not an appropriate representative, or on behalf of its members, since it had not alleged any injury to itself or to the members' associational interest; and (2) that the individual members could not maintain the action because the state agencies which had processed their claims, and which were necessary parties to the action under state judicial review rules made applicable by 2311(d), had not been joined as defendants (241 US App DC 106, 746 F2d 839).

For some time, federal law had provided that an order for removing an alien unlawfully present in the United States could be reinstated if the alien left and unlawfully entered again. An Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) provision added a new _ 241(a)(5) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C.S. _ 1231(a)(5)). This new version of the reinstatement provision (1) enlarged the class of illegal re-entrants whose removal orders could be reinstated, and (2) limited the possible relief available from a removal order. Another IIRIRA provision (_ 309(a), at a note following 8 U.S.C.S. _ 1101) generally set an effective date of April 1, 1997, for the new _ 241(a)(5). However, Congress did not complement the new _ 241(a)(5) with any clause expressly dealing with individuals who had illegally re-entered the United States before IIRIRA's effective date. The case at hand involved an alien who had last illegally re-entered the United States in 1982. The alien, who apparently remained undetected for many years, started a business and married a United States citizen. However, in 2003, the Federal Government began proceedings under _ 241(a)(5) that eventually resulted in the reinstatement of a 1981 deportation order without the possibility of adjusting the alien's status to lawful residence.

In consolidated actions in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, the major creditors and sole stockholder of a railroad in reorganization challenged the constitutionality of the Regional Rail Reorganization Act of 1973 (45 USCS 701 et seq.), which, in an effort to solve a rail transportation crisis precipitated when eight major railroads in the northeast and midwest regions of the country entered reorganization proceedings under 77 of the Bankruptcy Act (11 USCS 205), was enacted to supplement 77. The Regional Rail Reorganization Act provides generally for (1) reorganization of the regions' railroads pursuant to a final system plan to be established by a government corporation, whereby rail properties are to be transferred to a private state-incorporated corporation (Conrail) in return for securities of Conrail, plus a limited amount of federally guaranteed obligations of the government corporation and other benefits accruing to the railroads under the transfer (45 USCS 716(d)); (2) the submission of the final plan to Congress, with the plan to become effective unless disapproved by either House (45 USCS 718); (3) a Special Court which has exclusive jurisdiction of proceedings regarding the final plan, and which after directing the conveyance of rail properties to Conrail, shall determine whether such conveyances are fair and equitable, directing any necessary reallocation or issuance of Conrail or government securities to assure the fairness of the consideration exchanged for the rail properties (45 USCS 743); and (4) continuation of rail service until the final system plan becomes effective, unless discontinuance is authorized by the government corporation and not reasonably opposed by any state or local transportation authority (45 USCS 744(f)). The plaintiffs' primary contention was that the Act's provisions as to conveyance of the railroad properties to Conrail and the mandatory continuation of rail service pending implementation of the final reorganization plan effected a taking of rail properties without payment of just compensation in violation of the Fifth Amendment. The plaintiffs also asserted that the Act violated the uniformity requirement of the bankruptcy clause (Article I, 8, cl 4), which authorizes Congress to establish "uniform laws" on the subject of bankruptcies throughout the United States. The three-judge District Court found for the plaintiffs, holding, inter alia, that (1) the Act's provisions as to continuation of rail services violated the Fifth Amendment, since the Act precluded an action against the government under the provisions of the Tucker Act (28 USCS 1491) conferring jurisdiction on the Court of Claims of any claim against the United States founded upon the Constitution, and (2) certain provisions of the Regional Rail Reorganization Act violated the uniformity requirement of the bankruptcy clause (383 F Supp 510).

Timothy Smith was indicted in the Northern District of Florida for theft of trade secrets from a website owned by StrikeLines. Before trial, Smith moved to dismiss the indictment for lack of venue, citing the Constitution‚Äôs Venue Clause, Art. III, ¬ß2, cl. 3, and its Vicinage Clause, Amdt. 6. Smith argued that trial in the Northern District of Florida was improper because he had accessed StrikeLines‚Äô website from his home in Mobile (in the Southern District of Alabama) and the servers storing StrikeLines‚Äô data were located in Orlando (in the Middle District of Florida). The District Court concluded that factual disputes related to venue should be resolved by the jury and denied Smith‚Äôs motion to dismiss without prejudice. The jury found Smith guilty, and Smith moved for a judgment of acquittal based on improper venue. See Fed. Rule Crim. Proc. 29. The District Court denied the motion, reasoning that the effects of Smith‚Äôs crime were felt at StrikeLines‚Äô headquarters, located in the Northern District of Florida. On appeal, the Eleventh Circuit determined that venue was improper, but disagreed with Smith that a trial in an improper venue barred reprosecution. The Eleventh Circuit therefore vacated Smith‚Äôs conviction for theft of trade secrets.
